Linked Discourses 51.25
3. The Iron Ball
Fruits (1st)
“Mendicants, there are these four bases of psychic power.
What four?
It’s when a mendicant develops the basis of psychic power that has immersion due to enthusiasm …
energy …
mental development …
inquiry, and active effort.
These are the four bases of psychic power.
Because of developing and cultivating these four bases of psychic power, one of two results can be expected:
enlightenment in this very life, or if there’s residue left behind, non-return.”
Linked Discourses 51.26
3. The Iron Ball
Fruits (2nd)
“Mendicants, there are these four bases of psychic power.
What four?
It’s when a mendicant develops the basis of psychic power that has immersion due to enthusiasm …
energy …
mental development …
inquiry, and active effort.
These are the four bases of psychic power.
Because of developing and cultivating these four bases of psychic power, seven fruits and benefits can be expected.
What seven?
They attain enlightenment early on in this very life.
If not, they attain enlightenment at the time of death.
If not, with the ending of the five lower fetters, they’re extinguished between one life and the next … they’re extinguished upon landing … they’re extinguished without extra effort … they’re extinguished with extra effort … they head upstream, going to the Akaniṭṭha realm.
Because of developing and cultivating these four bases of psychic power, these seven fruits and benefits can be expected.”
Linked Discourses 51.27
3. The Iron Ball
With Ānanda (1st)
At Sāvatthī.
Then Venerable Ānanda went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him:
[context] “Sir, what is psychic power? What is the basis of psychic power? What is the development of the bases of psychic power? And what is the practice that leads to the development of the bases of psychic power?”
[context] “Ānanda, take a mendicant who wields the many kinds of psychic power: multiplying themselves and becoming one again … controlling the body as far as the realm of divinity.

2. Monks, there are these four bases of power <term>iddhipādā</term> <gloss>pathways to spiritual success or potency</gloss>. These are the four bases of power.

Monks, because these four bases of power have been developed and cultivated <note>original: "bhāvitattā bahulikatattā"</note>, one of two fruits <note>original: "phalānam"</note> may be expected: final knowledge <term>aññā</term> <gloss>highest realization or arahantship</gloss> in this very life, or, if there is a residue of clinging remaining, the state of a non-returner <term>anāgāmitā</term> <gloss>one who will not be reborn in the human realm</gloss>.

If not at the time of death, then with the total destruction of the five lower fetters <term>orambhāgiyānam samyojanānam</term> <gloss>the bonds that tie a being to the sensual world</gloss>, one becomes:
an attainer of final liberation in the interval <term>antarāparinibbāyī</term> <gloss>attaining Nirvana in the intermediate state after death</gloss>;
an attainer of final liberation upon landing <term>upahaccaparinibbāyī</term> <gloss>attaining Nirvana shortly after rebirth in a higher realm</gloss>;
an attainer of final liberation without exertion <term>asaṅkhāraparinibbāyī</term>;
an attainer of final liberation with exertion <term>sasaṅkhāraparinibbāyī</term>;
or one who is bound upstream, heading toward the Highest Realm <term>uddhamsoto akaniṭṭhagāmī</term> <gloss>the Akanistha heaven, the highest of the Pure Abodes</gloss>.

5. Monks, because these four bases of power have been developed and cultivated, these seven fruits and seven benefits may be expected.

4. Ālassam³ anuṭṭhānam bhogānam paripantho. Amaṇḍanā⁴ avibhūsanā vaṇṇassa paripantho⁵. Asappāyakiriyā ārogyassa paripantho. Pāpamittatā sīlānam paripantho. Indriyāsamvaro⁶ brahmacariyassa paripantho. Visamvādanā mittānam paripantho. Asajjhāyakiriyā bāhusaccassa paripantho. Asussusā⁷ aparipucchā paññāya paripantho. Ananuyogo apaccavekkhaṇā⁸ dhammānam paripantho. Micchāpaṭipatti saggānam paripantho.

Imesam kho bhikkhave dasannam dhammānam iṭṭhānam kantānam manāpānam dullabhānam lokasmim ime dasa dhammā paripanthā.

5. Imesam kho bhikkhave dasannam dhammānam iṭṭhānam kantānam manāpānam dullabhānam lokasmim dasa dhammā āhārā: —

6. Anālassam⁹ uṭṭhānam¹⁰ bhogānam āhāro. Maṇḍanā vibhūsanā vaṇṇassa āhāro. Sappāyakiriyā ārogyassa āhāro. Kalyāṇamittatā sīlānam āhāro. Indriyasamvaro brahmacariyassa āhāro. Avisamvādanā mittānam āhāro. Sajjhāyakiriyā bāhusaccassa āhāro. Sussusā paripucchā paññāya āhāro. Anuyogo paccavekkhaṇā¹¹ dhammānam āhāro. Sammāpaṭipatti saggānam āhāro.

Imesam kho bhikkhave dasannam dhammānam iṭṭhānam kantānam manāpānam dullabhānam lokasmim ime dasa dhammā āhārā ti.

[context] wisdom,
[context] good qualities,
[context] and heaven are likable, desirable, and agreeable things that are rare in the world.
Ten things are roadblocks for these ten likable, desirable, and agreeable things that are rare in the world.
Sloth and lack of initiative are a roadblock for wealth. Lack of adornment and decoration are a roadblock for beauty. Unsuitable activity is a roadblock for health. Bad friendship is a roadblock for ethical conduct. Lack of sense restraint is a roadblock for the spiritual life. Dishonesty is a roadblock for friends. Not rehearsing is a roadblock for learning. Not wanting to listen and ask questions are roadblocks for wisdom. Lack of commitment and reviewing are roadblocks for good qualities. Wrong practice hinders heaven.
These ten things are roadblocks for these ten likable, desirable, and agreeable things that are rare in the world.
Ten things nourish these ten likable, desirable, and agreeable things that are rare in the world.
Application and initiative nourish wealth. Adornment and decoration nourish beauty. Suitable activity nourishes health. Good friendship nourishes ethical conduct. Sense restraint nourishes the spiritual life. Honesty nourishes friends. Rehearsing nourishes learning. Eagerness to listen and ask questions nourishes wisdom. Commitment and reviewing nourish good qualities. Right practice nourishes heaven.
These ten things nourish these ten likable, desirable, and agreeable things that are rare in the world.”

Pañca kho ime, māṇava, nīvaraṇā. Katame pañca? — Kāmacchandanīvaraṇaṃ vyāpādanīvaraṇaṃ thinamiddhanīvaraṇaṃ¹ uddhaccakukkuccanīvaraṇaṃ vicikicchānīvaraṇaṃ. Ime kho, māṇava, pañca nīvaraṇā. Imehi kho, māṇava, pañcahi² nīvaraṇehi brāhmaṇo Pokkharasāti Opamañño Subhagavaniko āvaṭo³ nivuṭo ophiṭo⁴ pariyonaddho. So vata uttarimanussadhammā alamariyañāṇadassanavisesaṃ ñassati vā dakkhiti vā sacchi vā karissatīti, — n’ etaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati. Pañca kho ime, māṇava, kāmaguṇā. Katame pañca? — Cakkhuviññeyyā rūpā iṭṭhā kantā manāpā piyarūpā kāmūpasaṃhitā rajanīyā⁵ sotaviññeyyā saddā, —pe— ghānaviññeyyā gandhā, jivhāviññeyyā rasā, kāyaviññeyyā phoṭṭhabbā⁶ iṭṭhā kantā manāpā piyarūpā kāmūpasaṃhitā rajanīyā. Ime kho, māṇava, pañca kāmaguṇā. Imehi kho⁷, māṇava, pañcahi⁸ kāmaguṇehi brāhmaṇo Pokkharasāti Opamañño Subhagavaniko gathito⁹ mucchito ajjhopanno anādinavadassāvī anissaraṇapañño paribhuñjati. So vata uttarimanussadhammā alamariyañāṇadassanavisesaṃ ñassati vā dakkhiti vā sacchi vā karissatīti, — n’ etaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati. Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, māṇava? Yaṃ vā tiṇakaṭṭhupādānaṃ paṭicca aggiṃ jāleyya¹⁰, yaṃ vā nissaṭṭhatiṇakaṭṭhupādānaṃ aggiṃ¹¹ jāleyya, — katamo nu khvassa aggi accimā ca¹² vaṇṇimā ca pabhassaro cāti?

Sace taṃ, bho Gotama, ṭhānaṃ¹³ nissaṭṭhatiṇakaṭṭhupādānaṃ aggiṃ jālitum¹⁴, svāssa aggi accimā ca vaṇṇimā ca pabhassaro cāti.

Aṭṭhānaṃ kho etaṃ, māṇava, anavakāso, yaṃ nissaṭṭhatiṇakaṭṭhupādānaṃ aggiṃ jāleyya¹⁵ aññatra iddhimatā. Seyyathāpi, māṇava, tiṇakaṭṭhupādānaṃ¹⁶ paṭicca aggi¹⁷ jalati, tathūpamāhaṃ, māṇava, imaṃ pītiṃ vadāmi, yāyaṃ pīti

“Student, there are these five hindrances.
What five?
The hindrances of sensual desire, ill will, dullness and drowsiness, restlessness and remorse, and doubt.
These are the five hindrances.
Pokkharasāti is obstructed, hindered, engulfed, and enveloped by these five hindrances.
It is quite impossible for him to know or see or realize a superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones.
There are these five kinds of sensual stimulation.
What five?
There are sights known by the eye, which are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing.
There are sounds known by the ear …
smells known by the nose …
tastes known by the tongue …
touches known by the body, which are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing.
These are the five kinds of sensual stimulation.
Pokkharasāti enjoys these five kinds of sensual stimulation, tied, infatuated, attached, blind to the drawbacks, and not understanding the escape.
It is quite impossible for him to know or see or realize a superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones.
What do you think, student?
Which would have better flames, color, and radiance: a fire that depends on grass and logs as fuel, or one that does not?”
“If it were possible for a fire to burn without depending on grass and logs as fuel, that would have better flames, color, and radiance.”
“But it isn’t possible, except by psychic power.
Rapture that depends on the five kinds of sensual stimulation is like a fire that depends on grass and logs as fuel.
Rapture that’s apart from sensual pleasures and unskillful qualities is like a fire that doesn’t depend on grass and logs as fuel.
[context] And what is rapture that’s apart from sensual pleasures and unskillful qualities?
[context] It’s when a mendicant, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, enters and remains in the first absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of seclusion, while placing the mind and keeping it connected.
[context] This is rapture that’s apart from sensual pleasures and unskillful qualities.

### 9. Discourse to Subha (99)

Young man, there are these five <term>nīvaraṇā</term> <gloss>hindrances</gloss>. Which five? The hindrance of sensual desire, the hindrance of ill-will, the hindrance of sloth and torpor, the hindrance of restlessness and remorse, and the hindrance of doubt. These, young man, are the five hindrances. By these five hindrances, the Brahmin <note>a member of the priestly caste</note> Pokkharasāti Opamañño of Subhaga Grove is obstructed, secluded, blocked, and enveloped. That he should know or see or realize any superhuman state, any distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones—this is impossible.

Young man, there are these five <term>kāmaguṇā</term> <gloss>strands of sensual pleasure</gloss>. Which five? Forms cognizable by the eye that are wished for, desired, agreeable, likeable, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust. Sounds cognizable by the ear... odors cognizable by the nose... flavors cognizable by the tongue... touches cognizable by the body that are wished for, desired, agreeable, likeable, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust. These, young man, are the five strands of sensual pleasure. With these five strands of sensual pleasure, the Brahmin Pokkharasāti Opamañño of Subhaga Grove is tied, infatuated, and obsessed; he enjoys them without seeing the danger or knowing the escape. That he should know or see or realize any superhuman state, any distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones—this is impossible.

What do you think, young man? Suppose someone were to kindle a fire depending on grass and wood as fuel, and another person were to kindle a fire without any grass or wood as fuel. Which of these two fires would have flame, color, and radiance?

If it were possible, Master Gotama, to kindle a fire without any grass or wood as fuel, that fire would have flame, color, and radiance.

Young man, it is impossible, there is no way, that a fire could be kindled without grass or wood as fuel, except by one with psychic power. Just as a fire burns depending on grass and wood as fuel, even so, young man, do I describe this rapture—that <term>pīti</term> <gloss>rapture</gloss> which...

<summary>The Buddha explains to the young man Subha how the five hindrances and five strands of sensual pleasure prevent spiritual realization. He uses an analogy of a fire requiring fuel to illustrate the nature of worldly rapture compared to spiritual attainment.</summary>

5. 9. SUBHASUTTAM (99).

These five, young man, are the hindrances. Which five? The hindrance of sensual desire, the hindrance of ill-will, the hindrance of sloth and torpor, the hindrance of restlessness and worry, and the hindrance of doubt. These, young man, are the five hindrances. By these five hindrances, the brahmin Pokkharasāti of the Opamañña clan, a resident of Subhaga, is obstructed, hindered, covered, and enveloped. That he should know, see, or realize a state of super-human knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones—such a thing cannot happen.

These five, young man, are the strands of sensual pleasure. Which five? Forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, pleasant, agreeable, attractive, associated with sensual desire, and stimulating; sounds cognizable by the ear; <note>etc.</note> odors cognizable by the nose; flavors cognizable by the tongue; and tangibles cognizable by the body that are desirable, pleasant, agreeable, attractive, associated with sensual desire, and stimulating. These, young man, are the five strands of sensual pleasure. By these five strands of sensual pleasure, the brahmin Pokkharasāti of the Opamañña clan, a resident of Subhaga, is bound, infatuated, attached, not seeing the danger, and lacking the wisdom of escape, as he enjoys them. That he should know, see, or realize a state of super-human knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones—such a thing cannot happen.

What do you think, young man? Whether one were to kindle a fire dependent on grass and wood, or kindle a fire without depending on grass and wood—which of these would be a fire that is radiant, colorful, and brilliant?

If, Master Gotama, one were able to kindle a fire without depending on grass and wood, that would be the fire that is radiant, colorful, and brilliant.

That is an impossible state, young man, a situation that cannot occur, that one could kindle a fire without depending on grass and wood, unless one were a person of psychic power. Just as a fire burns dependent on grass and wood, young man, so do I describe this joy, which is the joy <unclear>that</unclear>

5. 9. SUBHASUTTAM. (99).

There are, young man, these five hindrances. What are the five? The hindrance of sensual desire, the hindrance of ill-will, the hindrance of sloth and torpor, the hindrance of restlessness and worry, and the hindrance of doubt. [context] “Someone with ten qualities is placed in hell as if delivered there.
[context] What ten?
[context] It’s when someone kills living creatures. They’re violent, bloody-handed, a hardened killer, merciless to all living beings.
They steal. With the intention to commit theft, they take the wealth or belongings of others from village or wilderness.
They commit sexual misconduct. They have relations with women who have their mother, father, both mother and father, brother, sister, relatives, or clan as guardian. They have relations with a woman who is protected on principle, or who has a husband, or whose violation is punishable by law, or even one who has been garlanded as a token of betrothal.
They lie. They’re summoned to a council, an assembly, a family meeting, a guild, or to the royal court, and asked to bear witness: ‘Please, my man, say what you know.’ Not knowing, they say ‘I know.’ Knowing, they say ‘I don’t know.’ Not seeing, they say ‘I see.’ And seeing, they say ‘I don’t see.’ So they deliberately lie for the sake of themselves or another, or for some trivial worldly reason.
They backbite. They repeat in one place what they heard in another so as to divide people against each other. And so they divide those who are harmonious, supporting division, delighting in division, loving division, speaking words that promote division.
They speak harshly. They use the kinds of words that are cruel, nasty, hurtful, offensive, bordering on anger, not leading to immersion.
They talk nonsense. Their speech is untimely, and is neither factual nor beneficial. It has nothing to do with the teaching or the training. Their words have no value, and are untimely, unreasonable, rambling, and pointless.
They’re covetous. They covet the wealth and belongings of others: ‘Oh, if only their belongings were mine!’
They have ill will and malicious intentions: ‘May these sentient beings be killed, slaughtered, slain, destroyed, or annihilated!’
They have wrong view. Their perspective is distorted:
‘There’s no meaning in giving, sacrifice, or offerings. There’s no fruit or result of good and bad deeds. There’s no afterlife. There’s no such thing as mother and father, or beings that are reborn spontaneously. And there’s no ascetic or brahmin who is rightly comported and rightly practiced, and who describes the afterlife after realizing it with their own insight.’
Someone with these ten qualities is placed in hell as if delivered there.
Someone with ten qualities is placed in heaven as if delivered there.
What ten?
It’s when someone gives up killing living creatures, renouncing the rod and the sword. They’re scrupulous and kind, living full of sympathy for all living beings.
They give up stealing. They don’t, with the intention to commit theft, take the wealth or belongings of others from village or wilderness.
They give up sexual misconduct. They don’t have relations with women who have their mother, father, both mother and father, brother, sister, relatives, or clan as guardian. They don’t have relations with a woman who is protected on principle, or who has a husband, or whose violation is punishable by law, or even one who has been garlanded as a token of betrothal.
They give up lying. They’re summoned to a council, an assembly, a family meeting, a guild, or to the royal court, and asked to bear witness: ‘Please, my man, say what you know.’ Not knowing, they say ‘I don’t know.’ Knowing, they say ‘I know.’ Not seeing, they say ‘I don’t see.’ And seeing, they say ‘I see.’ So they don’t deliberately lie for the sake of themselves or another, or for some trivial worldly reason.
They give up backbiting. They don’t repeat in one place what they heard in another so as to divide people against each other. Instead, they reconcile those who are divided and support those who are united, delighting in harmony, loving harmony, speaking words that promote harmony.
They give up harsh speech. They speak in a way that’s mellow, pleasing to the ear, endearing, going to the heart, polite, and likable and agreeable to the people.
They give up talking nonsense. Their words are timely, true, and meaningful, in line with the teaching and training. They say things at the right time which are valuable, reasonable, succinct, and beneficial.
They’re content. They don’t covet the wealth and belongings of others: ‘Oh, if only their belongings were mine!’
They have a kind heart and loving intentions: ‘May these sentient beings live free of enmity and ill will, untroubled and happy!’
They have right view, an undistorted perspective:
‘There is meaning in giving, sacrifice, and offerings. There are fruits and results of good and bad deeds. There is an afterlife. There are such things as mother and father, and beings that are reborn spontaneously. And there are ascetics and brahmins who are rightly comported and rightly practiced, and who describe the afterlife after realizing it with their own insight.’
[context] Someone with these ten qualities is placed in heaven as if delivered there.”

Monks, one possessed of these ten qualities is cast into hell as if led there by his own actions.

3. Monks, one possessed of ten qualities is placed in heaven as if led there by his own actions. What are the ten?

4. In this case, monks, someone gives up killing living beings and abstains from it. Having laid aside the rod and the sword, such a person is conscientious, merciful, and dwells with compassion for the welfare of all living beings. Giving up taking what is not given, they abstain from theft. They do not take with intent to steal the wealth and property of others, whether in the village or the forest. Giving up sexual misconduct, they abstain from it. They do not have sexual relations with those protected by their mother, father, brother, sister, or relatives, nor those protected by the Law <note>original: "dhamma"</note>, nor those who have a husband, nor those subject to punishment, nor even those adorned with a garland of flowers <note>referring to those betrothed or engaged</note>. Giving up false speech, they abstain from lying. When called to a council, a public gathering, a meeting of relatives, a guild, or a royal court, and asked to testify: "Come, good man, tell us what you know," if they do not know, they say, "I do not know," and if they know, they say, "I know." If they did not see, they say, "I did not see," and if they saw, they say, "I saw." They do not deliberately tell a lie for their own sake, for the sake of another, or for the sake of some worldly gain.

Thus, he does not speak falsehood for his own sake, for the sake of another, or for the sake of some trivial gain.

He is covetous; he looks upon the wealth and assets of another with the thought: "Oh, that what belongs to another might be mine." He has a mind of ill-will, with malicious intentions, thinking: "May these beings be slaughtered, or bound, or annihilated, or destroyed, or may they not exist at all." He holds wrong view, possessing a distorted perspective: "There is no benefit in giving, no benefit in sacrifice, no benefit in offerings; there is no fruit or result of good or evil actions; there is no this world and no other world; there is no mother and no father; there are no beings who are spontaneously reborn; there are no ascetics and brahmins in the world who are rightly practicing, who have realized this world and the other world through their own direct knowledge and proclaim it."

Endowed with these ten qualities, monks, a person is placed in hell as if brought and set down there.

3. Endowed with ten qualities, monks, a person is placed in heaven as if brought and set down there. With which ten?

4. Here, monks, a certain person, having abandoned the taking of life, abstains from taking life, having laid down the rod and the weapon, conscientious, compassionate, and living with kindness for the welfare of all living beings. Having abandoned taking what is not given, he abstains from taking what is not given; he does not take as theft the wealth and assets of another, whether in the village or the forest. Having abandoned sexual misconduct, he abstains from sexual misconduct; he does not have relations with those protected by mother, protected by father, protected by brother, protected by sister, protected by kin, protected by Dhamma, those who have husbands, those who have protection, or even those garlanded as a sign of betrothal. Having abandoned false speech, he abstains from false speech; when summoned to a council, an assembly, a gathering of kin, a guild, or a royal court, and asked as a witness to tell what he knows, he says "I know" when he knows, or "I do not know" when he does not know, or "I see" when he sees, or "I do not see" when he does not see; thus, he does not speak deliberate lies for his own benefit, for the benefit of another, or for some trifling worldly gain.

He is covetous. He covets that which belongs to another, the wealth and property of others, thinking: 'Oh, that what belongs to another were mine!' He is malevolent in mind, possessed of corrupt intentions, thinking: 'May these beings be killed, or slaughtered, or destroyed, or perished, or may they cease to exist.' He has wrong view and a distorted perspective: 'There is no gift, there is no offering, there is no sacrifice. There is no fruit or result of good and bad deeds. There is no this world, no other world. There is no mother, no father. There is no spontaneously born being. There are no contemplatives and brahmins in the world who have reached the right path and are practicing rightly, who, having directly known and realized for themselves this world and the other world, make them known.'

Monks, one endowed with these ten qualities is cast into hell according to his deeds.

3. Monks, one endowed with ten qualities is cast into heaven according to his deeds. With which ten?

4. Here, monks, a certain person, having abandoned the taking of life, abstains from taking life. With the rod laid aside and the sword laid aside, he is conscientious, kind, and dwells compassionate for the welfare of all living beings. Having abandoned taking what is not given, he abstains from taking what is not given. Whatever is the wealth and property of another, whether in the village or the forest, he does not take it by way of theft. Having abandoned sexual misconduct, he abstains from sexual misconduct. He does not have sexual relations with those protected by their mother, protected by their father, protected by their brother, protected by their sister, protected by their relatives, protected by their lineage <note>original: "dhammarakkhitā"; likely refers to legal or traditional protection</note>, those who have a husband, those under the threat of punishment, or even those garlanded with flowers <note>referring to those betrothed or engaged</note>. Having abandoned false speech, he abstains from false speech. When he goes to an assembly, a gathering, among his relatives, among a guild, or into the royal court, and is called as a witness and asked: 'Now, good man, tell what you know,' if he does not know, he says: 'I do not know'; if he knows, he says: 'I know'; if he has not seen, he says: 'I have not seen'; if he has seen, he says: 'I have seen.' Thus, neither for his own sake, nor for the sake of another, nor for the sake of some small material gain, does he speak a deliberate lie.

Looking among various views and not grasping them, I saw and searched for inner peace <note>original: "ajjhattasanti"</note>."

838. <note>Māgandiya speaks:</note> "O Sage <gloss>muni</gloss>," said Māgandiya, "you speak of not grasping those conclusions that have been constructed. This matter called 'inner peace,' how is that explained by the wise?"

839. <note>The Blessed One speaks:</note> "Māgandiya," said the Blessed One, "one does not speak of purity <gloss>suddhim</gloss> through views, nor through learning, nor through knowledge, nor even through habitual moral vows. Nor is purity achieved through lack of views, lack of learning, lack of knowledge, or lack of vows. Having abandoned these without grasping, being peaceful and independent, one would not long for becoming <note>original: "bhavaṃ," referring to future existence or rebirth</note>."

840. <note>Māgandiya speaks:</note> "If, as you say, one does not speak of purity through views, nor through learning, nor through knowledge, nor even through habitual moral vows..."

838. "Those determinations that have been fabricated," said Māgandiya, "you speak of those indeed as without support, O Sage. How is this meaning of 'internal peace' explained by the wise?"

Relinquishing these and not grasping, being at peace, one does not long for existence."

836. "If you do not desire such a jewel, a woman desired by many great men, then tell me, what do you say regarding views, virtuous conduct, and rebirth?"

837. "There is no 'this is what I maintain' for him," said the Blessed One, "O Māgandiya, among things grasped by determination. Seeing no support in views, he seeks internal peace, having seen through <note>the nature of</note> it."

838. "Those determinations that have been fabricated," said Māgandiya, "you speak of those indeed as without support, O Sage. How is this meaning of 'internal peace' explained by the wise?"

839. "Not by view, not by tradition, not by knowledge," said the Blessed One, "O Māgandiya, nor by virtuous conduct and rites does one say purity is attained. Neither by lack of view, lack of tradition, nor lack of knowledge, nor by lack of virtuous conduct, nor by lack of rites, is it attained. Relinquishing these and not grasping, being at peace, one does not long for existence."

[context] Then Māra’s daughter Lust addressed the Buddha in verse:
“He lives with his community after cutting off craving,
and many of the faithful will cross over for sure.
Alas, this homeless one will snatch many men away,
and lead them past the King of Death!”
“The great heroes they lead
by means of the true teaching.
When the Realized Ones are leading by the teaching,
how could anyone who knows be jealous?”
Then Māra’s daughters Craving, Malignancy, and Lust went up to Māra the Wicked.
Māra the Wicked saw them coming off in the distance,
and addressed them in verse:
“Fools! You drill into a mountain
with lotus stalks!
You dig up a hill with your nails!
You chew iron with your teeth!
You seek a footing in the abyss, as it were,
while lifting a rock with your head!
After attacking a stump with your breast, as it were,
you leave Gotama disappointed.”
They came dazzling—
Craving, Malignancy, and Lust.
But the Teacher brushed them off right there,
like the gale, a fallen tuft.

19. Then Ragā, the daughter of Māra, spoke this verse in the presence of the Blessed One:
"Having cut off craving, the leader of a company and community <note>original: "gaṇa-saṅgha-vârî"; usually read gaṇasaṅghacārī, "one who moves at the head of a group and an order"</note>,
surely many beings too will follow his course¹ <note>the manuscripts marked SS. read "will cross over"</note>.
Alas, this homeless one <note>original: "anoko", "one without a house", that is, the Buddha</note> will snatch away
many people and lead them to the far shore, beyond the King of Death."
20. "The great heroes, the <term>Tathāgatas</term> <gloss>Thus-gone Ones, a title of the Buddhas</gloss>, lead indeed by the true Dhamma.
When those who understand are led by the Dhamma, what room is there for envy?"
21. Then Taṇhā, Arati and Ragā, the daughters of Māra, went to where Māra the Evil One was.
22. Māra the Evil One saw Taṇhā, Arati and Ragā, his daughters, coming from afar. Seeing them, he addressed them in verses:
"Fools! You tried to crush a mountain with lotus stalks,
to dig up a hill with your fingernails, to chew iron with your teeth.
As though you had lifted a rock upon your heads, you sought a footing in the bottomless abyss;
as though you had struck your breast against a stump, you come away from Gotama disheartened."
23. Glittering they had come, Taṇhā, Arati and Ragā;
the Teacher swept them away right there, as the wind sweeps off a fallen tuft of cotton.
<note>Taṇhā, Arati and Ragā are personifications: "Craving", "Discontent" and "Lust". Their failed attempt to seduce the Buddha closes the collection of discourses on Māra.</note>

->The Third Chapter.<-
->Its summary verse:<-
The Many, and Samiddhi, Godhika, the Seven Years,
the Daughters: this pentad on Māra was taught by the Buddha, the Teacher. The Connected Discourses on Māra are complete.
<note>The summary verse <term>uddāna</term> <gloss>mnemonic list of the discourses in a chapter</gloss> names the five suttas of this chapter by key words.</note>

Seyyathā pi bhante rajoharaṇaṃ sucim pi puñchati¹ asucim pi puñchati gūthagataṃ pi puñchati² mutta-gataṃ pi puñchati³ kheḷagataṃ pi puñchati⁴ pubbagataṃ⁵ pi puñchati⁶ lohitagataṃ pi puñchati, na ca tena rajoharaṇaṃ aṭṭiyati vā jigucchati vā: evam eva kho ahaṃ bhante rajoharaṇasamena cetasā viharāmi vipulena mahaggatena appamāṇena⁷ averena avyāpajjhena. Yassa nūna bhante kāye kāyagatā sati anupaṭṭhitā assa, so idha aññataraṃ sabrahmacāriṃ āsajja appaṭinissajja cārikaṃ pakkameyya.

Seyyathā pi bhante caṇḍālakumārako⁸ vā caṇḍālakumārikā⁹ vā kaḷopihattho¹⁰ nantikavāsī¹¹ gāmaṃ vā nigamaṃ vā pavisanto nicacittaṃ yeva upaṭṭhapetvā pavisati: evam eva kho ahaṃ bhante caṇḍālakumārakasamena¹² cetasā viharāmi vipulena mahaggatena appamāṇena⁷ averena avyāpajjhena. Yassa nūna bhante kāye kāyagatā sati anupaṭṭhitā assa, so idha aññataraṃ sabrahmacāriṃ āsajja appaṭinissajja cārikaṃ pakkameyya.

Seyyathā pi bhante usabho chinnavisāṇo sorato¹³ sudanto suvinīto¹⁴ rathiyāya¹⁵ rathiyaṃ siṅghāṭakena siṅghāṭakaṃ anvāhiṇḍanto na kiñci himsati. pādena vā visāṇena vā: evam eva kho ahaṃ bhante usabhachinnavisāṇasamena cetasā viharāmi vipulena mahaggatena⁷ appamāṇena averena avyāpajjhena. Yassa nūna bhante kāye kāyagatā sati anupaṭṭhitā assa, so idha aññataraṃ sabrahmacāriṃ āsajja appaṭinissajja cārikaṃ pakkameyya.

Seyyathā pi bhante itthi vā puriso vā daharo vā¹⁶ yuvā vā³ maṇḍanakajātiko¹⁷ sīsaṃ³ nahāto¹⁸ ahikuṇapena vā

[context] Now Venerable Sāriputta will roar his lion’s roar in the presence of the Buddha!”
[context] Then Venerable Sāriputta went up to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. The Buddha said to him:
[context] “Sāriputta, one of your spiritual companions has made this complaint:
‘Venerable Sāriputta attacked me and left without saying sorry.’”
“Sir, someone who had not established mindfulness of the body might well attack one of their spiritual companions and leave without saying sorry.
Suppose they were to toss both clean and unclean things on the earth, like feces, urine, spit, pus, and blood. The earth isn’t horrified, repelled, and disgusted because of this.
In the same way, I live with a heart like the earth, abundant, expansive, limitless, free of enmity and ill will.
Someone who had not established mindfulness of the body might well attack one of their spiritual companions and leave without saying sorry.
Suppose they were to wash both clean and unclean things in water, like feces, urine, spit, pus, and blood. The water isn’t horrified, repelled, and disgusted because of this.
In the same way, I live with a heart like water, abundant, expansive, limitless, free of enmity and ill will.
Someone who had not established mindfulness of the body might well attack one of their spiritual companions and leave without saying sorry.
Suppose a fire were to burn both clean and unclean things, like feces, urine, spit, pus, and blood. The fire isn’t horrified, repelled, and disgusted because of this.
In the same way, I live with a heart like fire, abundant, expansive, limitless, free of enmity and ill will.
Someone who had not established mindfulness of the body might well attack one of their spiritual companions and leave without saying sorry.
Suppose the wind was to blow on both clean and unclean things, like feces, urine, spit, pus, and blood. The wind isn’t horrified, repelled, and disgusted because of this.
In the same way, I live with a heart like the wind, abundant, expansive, limitless, free of enmity and ill will.
Someone who had not established mindfulness of the body might well attack one of their spiritual companions and leave without saying sorry.
Suppose a rag was to wipe up both clean and unclean things, like feces, urine, spit, pus, and blood. The rag isn’t horrified, repelled, and disgusted because of this.
In the same way, I live with a heart like a rag, abundant, expansive, limitless, free of enmity and ill will.
Someone who had not established mindfulness of the body might well attack one of their spiritual companions and leave without saying sorry.
Suppose a boy or girl of a corpse-worker tribe, holding a pot and clad in rags, were to enter a town or village. They’d enter with a humble mind.
In the same way, I live with a heart like a boy or girl of a corpse-worker tribe, abundant, expansive, limitless, free of enmity and ill will.
Someone who had not established mindfulness of the body might well attack one of their spiritual companions and leave without saying sorry.
Suppose there was a bull with his horns cut, gentle, well tamed and well trained. He’d wander from street to street and square to square without hurting anyone with his feet or horns.
In the same way, I live with a heart like a bull with horns cut, abundant, expansive, limitless, free of enmity and ill will.
Someone who had not established mindfulness of the body might well attack one of their spiritual companions and leave without saying sorry.
Suppose there was a woman or man who was young, youthful, and fond of adornments, and had bathed their head. If the carcass of a snake or a dog or a human were hung around their neck, they’d be horrified, repelled, and disgusted.
In the same way, I’m horrified, repelled, and disgusted by this rotting body.
Someone who had not established mindfulness of the body might well attack one of their spiritual companions and leave without saying sorry.
Suppose someone was to carry around a bowl of fat that was leaking and oozing from holes and cracks.
In the same way, I carry around this body that’s leaking and oozing from holes and cracks.
Someone who had not established mindfulness of the body might well attack one of their spiritual companions and leave without saying sorry.”
[context] Then that monk rose from his seat, placed his robe over one shoulder, bowed with his head to the Buddha’s feet, and said,
[context] “I made a mistake, sir. It was foolish, stupid, and unskillful of me to speak ill of Venerable Sāriputta with an incorrect, hollow, false, untruthful claim.
[context] Please, sir, accept my mistake for what it is, so I will restrain myself in future.”

<meta>This page continues the confession of the Venerable Sariputta, who is responding to a false accusation of offending a fellow monk. He uses a series of similes to demonstrate his humble and disciplined state of mind.</meta>

### The Numerical Discourses of the Buddha: The Elevens

Just as, venerable sir, a dusting-cloth <note>original: "rajoharaṇaṃ"</note> wipes up what is clean and wipes up what is unclean, wipes up excrement, wipes up urine, wipes up saliva, wipes up pus, and wipes up blood, yet the dusting-cloth is not troubled, ashamed, or disgusted by it: even so, venerable sir, I dwell with a mind like a dusting-cloth, vast, exalted, measureless, without enmity, and without ill-will. Only one who has not established mindfulness of the body <note>original: "kāyagatā sati"</note> would, after offending a fellow monk here, set out on a journey without making amends.

Just as, venerable sir, a youth of the outcaste class <note>original: "caṇḍālakumārako"</note> or a maiden of the outcaste class, carrying a begging-basket and dressed in rags, enters a village or a town with a lowly heart: even so, venerable sir, I dwell with a mind like an outcaste youth, vast, exalted, measureless, without enmity, and without ill-will. Only one who has not established mindfulness of the body would, after offending a fellow monk here, set out on a journey without making amends.

Just as, venerable sir, a bull with its horns cut off, gentle, well-tamed, and well-trained, wanders from street to street and crossroad to crossroad without harming anyone with its feet or its horns: even so, venerable sir, I dwell with a mind like a bull with its horns cut off, vast, exalted, measureless, without enmity, and without ill-will. Only one who has not established mindfulness of the body would, after offending a fellow monk here, set out on a journey without making amends.

<meta>continues from previous page: Sāriputta's "lion's roar", in which he answers a charge of having offended a fellow monk by describing the state of his own mind through a series of similes</meta>
<header>Aṅguttara-Nikāya. XI.</header>

Just as, venerable sir, a duster¹ wipes up what is clean and wipes up what is unclean, wipes up excrement², wipes up urine³, wipes up spittle⁴, wipes up pus⁵ ⁶, wipes up blood, and yet that duster is not troubled, ashamed or disgusted by it: in just the same way, venerable sir, I dwell with a mind like a duster, vast, exalted, measureless⁷, free of enmity, free of ill will. Surely, venerable sir, it is one in whom mindfulness directed to the body has not been established who might offend some fellow monk here and then set out on his wanderings without asking his pardon.

Just as, venerable sir, an outcaste boy⁸ or an outcaste girl⁹, bowl in hand¹⁰ and dressed in rags¹¹, enters a village or a town with a humble mind already set up: in just the same way, venerable sir, I dwell with a mind like an outcaste boy¹², vast, exalted, measureless⁷, free of enmity, free of ill will. Surely, venerable sir, it is one in whom mindfulness directed to the body has not been established who might offend some fellow monk here and then set out on his wanderings without asking his pardon.
<note>The <term>caṇḍāla</term> <gloss>outcaste</gloss> was the lowest group in Indian society, expected to show deference on entering a settlement.</note>

Just as, venerable sir, a bull with its horns cut off, gentle¹³, well tamed and well trained¹⁴, wandering from street to street¹⁵ and from crossroads to crossroads, harms no one at all, whether with foot or with horn: in just the same way, venerable sir, I dwell with a mind like a bull with its horns cut off, vast, exalted⁷, measureless, free of enmity, free of ill will. Surely, venerable sir, it is one in whom mindfulness directed to the body has not been established who might offend some fellow monk here and then set out on his wanderings without asking his pardon.

Tyâham evam vadâmi :—Tena h' âyasmanto pânâtipâtino bhavissanti pubbe katahetu, adinnâdâyino bhavissanti pubbe katahetu, abrahmacârino bhavissanti pubbe katahetu, musâvâdino bhavissanti pubbe katahetu, pisuṇâvâcâ¹ bhavissanti pubbe katahetu, pharusâvâcâ¹ bhavissanti pubbe katahetu, samphappalâpino bhavissanti pubbe katahetu, abhijhâluno bhavissanti pubbe katahetu, vyâpannacittâ bhavissanti pubbe katahetu, micchâdiṭṭhikâ bhavissanti pubbe katahetu. Pubbe katam kho pana bhikkhave sârato paccâgacchatam² na hoti chando vâ vâyâmo vâ idam vâ karaṇîyam idam vâ akaraṇîyan ti. Iti karaṇîyâkaraṇîye kho pana saccato thetato aupapabhbiyamâne muṭṭhasatinam anârakkhânam viharatam na hoti paccattam sahadhammiko samaṇavâdo.

Ayam kho me bhikkhave tesu samaṇabrâhmaṇesu evamvâdisu evamdiṭṭhisu paṭhamo sahadhammiko niggaho hoti.

3. Tatra bhikkhave ye te samaṇabrâhmaṇâ evamvâdino evamdiṭṭhino—yam kiñcâyam purisapuggalo paṭisamvedeti sukham vâ dukkham vâ adukkhamasukham vâ sabbam tam issaranimmânahetu ti tyâham upasaṅkamitvâ evam vadâmi :—Saccam kira tumhe âyasmanto evamvâdino evamdiṭṭhino—yam kiñcâyam purisapuggalo paṭisamvedeti sukham vâ dukkham vâ adukkhamasukham vâ sabbam tam issaranimmânahetu ti?

Te ce me evam puṭṭhâ âmâ³ ti paṭijânanti.

Tyâham evam vadâmi :—Tena h' âyasmanto pânâtipâtino bhavissanti issaranimmânahetu . . . pe . . . micchâdiṭṭhino bhavissanti issaranimmânahetu. Issaranimmânânam kho pana bhikkhave sârato paccâgacchatam na hoti chando vâ vâyâmo vâ idam vâ karaṇîyam idam vâ akaraṇîyan ti. Iti karaṇîyâkaraṇîye kho pana saccato thetato anupalabbhiyamâne muṭṭhasatinam anârakkhânam viharatam na hoti paccattam sahadhammiko samaṇavâdo.

Ayam kho me bhikkhave tesu samaṇabrâhmaṇesu evamvâdisu evamdiṭṭhisu dutiyo sahadhammiko niggaho hoti.

[context] There are some ascetics and brahmins who have this doctrine and view:
[context] ‘Everything this individual person experiences—pleasurable, painful, or neutral—has no cause or reason.’
[context] Regarding this, I went up to the ascetics and brahmins whose view is that
everything an individual person experiences is because of past deeds, and I said to them:
‘Is it really true that this is the venerables’ view?’
And they answered, ‘Yes’.
I said to them:
‘In that case, you might kill living creatures, steal, be unchaste; use speech that’s false, backbiting, harsh, or nonsensical; be covetous, malicious, or have wrong view, all because of past deeds.’
Those who believe that past deeds are the most important thing have no enthusiasm or effort, no idea that there are things that should and should not be done.
Not finding as a genuine fact that there are things that should and should not be done, they’re unmindful and careless, and can’t rightly be called ascetics.
This is my first legitimate refutation of the ascetics and brahmins who have this doctrine and view.
Regarding this, I went up to the ascetics and brahmins whose view is that
everything that an individual person experiences is because of God Almighty’s creation, and I said to them:
‘Is it really true that this is the venerables’ view?’
And they answered, ‘Yes’.
I said to them:
‘In that case, you might kill living creatures, steal, be unchaste; use speech that’s false, backbiting, harsh, or nonsensical; be covetous, malicious, or have wrong view, all because of God Almighty’s creation.’
Those who believe that God Almighty’s creative power is the most important thing have no enthusiasm, no effort, no idea that there are things that should and should not be done.
Not finding as a genuine fact that there are things that should and should not be done, they’re unmindful and careless, and can’t rightly be called ascetics.
This is my second legitimate refutation of the ascetics and brahmins who have this doctrine and view.
Regarding this, I went up to the ascetics and brahmins whose view is that
everything that an individual person experiences has no cause or reason, and I said to them:
‘Is it really true that this is the venerables’ view?’
And they answered, ‘Yes’.
I said to them:
‘In that case, you might kill living creatures, steal, be unchaste; use speech that’s false, backbiting, harsh, or nonsensical; be covetous, malicious, or have wrong view, all without cause or reason.’
Those who believe that the absence of cause or reason is the most important thing have no enthusiasm, no effort, no idea that there are things that should and should not be done.
Not finding as a genuine fact that there are things that should and should not be done, they’re unmindful and careless, and can’t rightly be called ascetics.
[context] This is my third legitimate refutation of the ascetics and brahmins who have this doctrine and view.
[context] These are the three sectarian tenets—as pursued, pressed, and grilled by the astute—which, when taken to their conclusion, end with inaction.
[context] But the Dhamma that I’ve taught is irrefutable, uncorrupted, beyond reproach, and not scorned by sensible ascetics and brahmins.

# The Great Section <note>original: Mahâ-vagga</note>

To them, I say this: "Then, venerable sirs, you would be those who take life <note>original: pânâtipâtino</note> because of past actions; you would be those who take what is not given <note>original: adinnâdâyino</note> because of past actions; you would be those who are unchaste <note>original: abrahmacârino</note> because of past actions; you would be those who speak lies <note>original: musâvâdino</note> because of past actions; you would be those who speak malicious words <note>original: pisuṇâvâcâ</note> because of past actions; you would be those who speak harsh words <note>original: pharusâvâcâ</note> because of past actions; you would be those who engage in idle chatter <note>original: samphappalâpino</note> because of past actions; you would be those who are covetous <note>original: abhijhâluno</note> because of past actions; you would be those who have ill-will in their hearts <note>original: vyâpannacittâ</note> because of past actions; and you would be those who hold wrong views <note>original: micchâdiṭṭhikâ</note> because of past actions."

Monks, for those who fall back on past actions as the essential truth <note>original: sârato paccâgacchatam</note>, there is neither desire to act, nor effort, nor the thought: "This should be done," or "This should not be done." Thus, when what should be done and what should not be done are not truly and firmly established, those who live with muddled mindfulness and without self-protection lack any justified, righteous claim to being true ascetics <note>original: samaṇavâdo</note>.

Monks, this is my first righteous refutation <note>original: sahadhammiko niggaho</note> of those ascetics and brahmins who hold such views and such opinions.

3. Regarding this, monks, there are those ascetics and brahmins who hold such views and such opinions as this: "Whatever pleasure, pain, or neutral feeling a person experiences, all of it is caused by the creation of a Supreme Lord <note>original: issaranimmânahetu</note>." I approach them and say: "Is it true, venerable sirs, that you hold such a view and such an opinion: that whatever pleasure, pain, or neutral feeling a person experiences, all of it is caused by the creation of a Supreme Lord?"

If, when asked this by me, they admit it is so.

Then I say to them: "Then, venerable sirs, you would be those who take life because of the creation of a Supreme Lord... <note>The text indicates a repetition of the previous list of ten unwholesome actions</note> ...you would be those who hold wrong views because of the creation of a Supreme Lord. Monks, for those who fall back on the creation of a Supreme Lord as the essential truth, there is neither desire to act, nor effort, nor the thought: 'This should be done,' or 'This should not be done.' Thus, when what should be done and what should not be done are not truly and firmly established, those who live with muddled mindfulness and without self-protection lack any justified, righteous claim to being true ascetics."

Monks, this is my second righteous refutation of those ascetics and brahmins who hold such views and such opinions.

<margin>2. The manuscripts here and below vary between <term>gacchantam</term> and <term>gacchatam</term>.</margin>
<margin>3. Manuscripts D. and T. read <term>âmo</term>.</margin>

<summary>The Buddha refutes the views that human behavior and experiences are solely determined by past actions or by the will of a Supreme Lord. He argues that such fatalistic beliefs remove personal responsibility and the motivation for moral effort.</summary>
<keywords>determinism, fatalism, Supreme Lord, moral responsibility, refutation, ten unwholesome actions, past kamma</keywords>

MAHĀ-VAGGA. [III. 61. 2.]

I say to them: If that is so, then venerable ones, you will be killers of living beings because of prior deeds, you will be takers of what is not given because of prior deeds, you will be unchaste because of prior deeds, you will be speakers of falsehood because of prior deeds, you will be speakers of malicious words because of prior deeds, you will be speakers of harsh words because of prior deeds, you will be speakers of frivolous gossip because of prior deeds, you will be covetous because of prior deeds, you will be malevolent because of prior deeds, and you will hold wrong views because of prior deeds. But for those who fall back on prior deeds as the essential truth, there is no desire or effort, nor the thought that this is to be done or this is not to be done. Because the distinction between what is to be done and what is not to be done cannot be truly and reliably found, those who dwell with confused mindfulness and lack of self-guarding do not have a firm foundation for a doctrine of righteous living.

This, monks, is my first refutation of those ascetics and brahmins who hold such views and opinions.

3. Regarding this, monks, to those ascetics and brahmins who hold the view and opinion that whatever a person experiences—whether pleasure, pain, or neutral feeling—is all due to the creation of a supreme deity <term>issaranimmânahetu</term> <gloss>due to the creation of a god</gloss>, I approach them and say: Is it true, venerable ones, that you hold this view and opinion?

If, when asked, they answer yes.

I say to them: If that is so, then venerable ones, you will be killers of living beings because of the creation of a god . . . [and so on] . . . you will be holders of wrong views because of the creation of a god. But for those who fall back on the creation of a god as the essential truth, there is no desire or effort, nor the thought that this is to be done or this is not to be done. Because the distinction between what is to be done and what is not to be done cannot be truly and reliably found, those who dwell with confused mindfulness and lack of self-guarding do not have a firm foundation for a doctrine of righteous living.

This, monks, is my second refutation of those ascetics and brahmins who hold such views and opinions.

<note>³ D. and T. have "āmo" <gloss>yes</gloss>.</note>

MAHÂ-VAGGA. [III. 61. 2.

I say this to them: If, venerable ones, it is because of past actions that people will be killers of living creatures, takers of what is not given, unchaste, speakers of falsehood, speakers of malicious words, speakers of harsh words, gossipers, covetous, malevolent, and holders of wrong views, then for those who fall back on past deeds as the essential reason, there is no desire or effort to say "this should be done" or "this should not be done." Thus, for those who do not establish as a truth or reality what should and should not be done, and who live with confused mindfulness and unguarded faculties, there is no firm basis for a rightful doctrine <note>or "a valid argument in the Dhamma"</note>.

This, monks, is my first rightful refutation of those ascetics and brahmins who hold such views and opinions.

3. Regarding this, monks, to those ascetics and brahmins who hold such views and opinions—that whatever pleasure, pain, or neutral feeling a person experiences is all caused by the creation of a supreme deity <term>issaranimmânahetu</term> <gloss>caused by a supreme deity's creation</gloss>—I approach them and say: Is it true, venerable ones, that you hold this view?

If they, being asked by me, answer "Yes," I say to them: If so, venerable ones, you will be killers of living creatures because of a supreme deity's creation... <note>The text uses an ellipsis to indicate the repetition of the previously mentioned unwholesome actions</note> ...you will be holders of wrong views because of a supreme deity's creation. For those who fall back on a supreme deity's creation as the essential reason, there is no desire or effort to say "this should be done" or "this should not be done." Thus, for those who do not establish as a truth or reality what should and should not be done, and who live with confused mindfulness and unguarded faculties, there is no firm basis for a rightful doctrine.

This, monks, is my second rightful refutation of those ascetics and brahmins who hold such views and opinions.

<summary>The Buddha refutes two deterministic views: the belief that all human experience is caused by past actions (kamma) or by the will of a supreme deity, arguing that both views remove the necessity for moral effort and free will.</summary>
<keywords>kamma, determinism, supreme deity, moral responsibility, right view, asceticism, refutation</keywords>

<header>MAHÂ-VAGGA. [III. 61. 2.</header>

I say to them: "Then, venerable sirs, you will be destroyers of life because of past actions, takers of what is not given because of past actions, unchaste because of past actions, speakers of falsehood because of past actions, speakers of divisive speech because of past actions, speakers of harsh speech because of past actions, chatterers because of past actions, covetous because of past actions, malevolent because of past actions, and holders of wrong views because of past actions." For those who fall back on past actions as the essential reason, there is no desire, nor effort, nor the necessity to do this or avoid that. Thus, for those who do not find a solid and truthful basis for what should and should not be done, and who live with confused mindfulness and without guard, there is no valid foundational doctrine for being a contemplative.

This, bhikkhus, is my first valid refutation of those ascetics and Brahmins who hold such views and theories.

3. In this matter, bhikkhus, to those ascetics and Brahmins who hold the view and theory that whatever a person experiences—whether pleasure, pain, or neutral feeling—is all due to creation by a supreme deity, I approach them and ask: "Is it true, venerable sirs, that you hold this view and theory—that whatever a person experiences, whether pleasure, pain, or neutral feeling, is all due to creation by a supreme deity?"

If, when asked by me, they reply "Yes,"

I say to them: "Then, venerable sirs, you will be destroyers of life because of creation by a supreme deity... <note>the text indicates the repetition of the previous list of negative actions</note>... and you will be holders of wrong views because of creation by a supreme deity." For those who fall back on creation by a supreme deity as the essential reason, there is no desire, nor effort, nor the necessity to do this or avoid that. Thus, for those who do not find a solid and truthful basis for what should and should not be done, and who live with confused mindfulness and without guard, there is no valid foundational doctrine for being a contemplative.

This, bhikkhus, is my second valid refutation of those ascetics and Brahmins who hold such views and theories.

<note>² The manuscripts here and below vary between <term>gacchantam</term> <gloss>going</gloss> and <term>gacchatam</term> <gloss>coming/falling back on</gloss>.</note>
<note>³ D. and T. versions read <term>âmo</term> <gloss>yes</gloss>.</note>

<summary>The Buddha refutes two deterministic views, asserting that attributing all human experience to either past karma or divine creation negates the possibility of moral responsibility and conscious effort.</summary>
<keywords>determinism, karma, divine creation, moral agency, refutation, ascetics, Brahmins</keywords>

# The Great Chapter <note>original: Mahâ-vagga</note>

To them I say this: "If that is so, venerable sirs, then people will be killers of living beings <term>pânâtipâtino</term> <gloss>those who destroy life</gloss> because of what was done in the past. They will be takers of what is not given <term>adinnâdâyino</term> <gloss>thieves</gloss> because of what was done in the past. They will be unchaste <term>abrahmacârino</term> <gloss>not living a holy life</gloss> because of what was done in the past. They will be speakers of lies <term>musâvâdino</term> because of what was done in the past. They will be speakers of slander <term>pisuṇâvâcâ</term> <margin>All manuscripts read pisuṇâvâcâ and pharusâvâcâ. Compare below XVI. 8.</margin> because of what was done in the past. They will be speakers of harsh words <term>pharusâvâcâ</term> because of what was done in the past. They will be idle chatterers <term>samphappalâpino</term> because of what was done in the past. They will be covetous <term>abhijhâluno</term> because of what was done in the past. They will be ill-willed in mind <term>vyâpannacittâ</term> because of what was done in the past. They will be holders of wrong views <term>micchâdiṭṭhikâ</term> because of what was done in the past."

Monks, for those who fall back on what was done in the past as the essential truth <margin>The manuscripts here and below vary between gacchantam and gacchatam.</margin>, there is no desire to act, nor effort, nor the thought: "This must be done," or "This must not be done." Thus, when what should be done and what should not be done are not truly and firmly found, those who live with muddled mindfulness and without protection have no legitimate ground to call themselves ascetics <note>original: sahadhammiko samaṇavâdo</note>.

This, monks, is my first legitimate rebuke <term>sahadhammiko niggaho</term> <gloss>a righteous refutation based on the teaching</gloss> of those ascetics and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and such a view.

3. In that regard, monks, there are some ascetics and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and view as this: "Whatever a person experiences, whether pleasure, pain, or neutral feeling, all that is caused by the creation of a Supreme Lord <term>issaranimmânahetu</term> <gloss>the cause being the creation by God/Ishvara</gloss>." I approach them and say: "Is it true, venerable sirs, that you hold such a doctrine and view: that whatever a person experiences... all that is caused by the creation of a Supreme Lord?"

If, when asked, they acknowledge it by saying, "Yes," <margin>Manuscripts D. and T. read âmo.</margin> then I say this to them:

"If that is so, venerable sirs, then people will be killers of living beings because of the creation of a Supreme Lord... <note>The text uses the ellipsis marker "pe" to indicate the repetition of the list of ten unwholesome actions found in the previous paragraph.</note> they will be holders of wrong views because of the creation of a Supreme Lord. For those who fall back on the creation of a Supreme Lord as the essential truth, monks, there is no desire to act, nor effort, nor the thought: 'This must be done,' or 'This must not be done.' Thus, when what should be done and what should not be done are not truly and firmly found, those who live with muddled mindfulness and without protection have no legitimate ground to call themselves ascetics."

This, monks, is my second legitimate rebuke of those ascetics and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and such a view.

<summary>The Buddha refutes two fatalistic views: that all current experiences are caused solely by past actions, and that all experiences are caused by a Supreme Creator. He argues these views lead to moral inaction and a lack of personal responsibility.</summary>
<keywords>determinism, fatalism, karma, creationism, moral responsibility, ten unwholesome actions, asceticism, refutation</keywords>

I speak to them thus: "In that case, venerable sirs, you will be those who destroy life due to past actions, those who take what is not given due to past actions, those who engage in sexual misconduct due to past actions, those who speak falsehood due to past actions, those who speak maliciously due to past actions, those who speak harshly due to past actions, those who indulge in idle chatter due to past actions, those who are covetous due to past actions, those who have a mind of ill will due to past actions, and those who hold wrong views due to past actions. For those who rely on past actions as the essential reason, there is no desire, no effort, no idea that 'this must be done' or 'this must not be done.' Since in this way, what should be done and what should not be done cannot be established as a true and reliable reality for those who dwell heedless and unprotected, there is no valid basis for the title of 'ascetic' <term>samaṇavâdo</term> <gloss>the doctrine of the ascetics</gloss>."

This, bhikkhus, is my first valid refutation of those ascetics and Brahmins who hold such views and such doctrines.

3. "In this matter, bhikkhus, those ascetics and Brahmins who hold the view that whatever a person experiences—be it pleasure, pain, or neutral—is all due to creation by a supreme deity <term>issaranimmânahetu</term> <gloss>the cause of being created by a supreme lord/God</gloss>, I approach them and ask: 'Is it true, venerable sirs, that you hold such views and such doctrines—that whatever a person experiences, be it pleasure, pain, or neutral, is all due to creation by a supreme deity?'

"If, being asked by me, they reply 'Yes.'

"I speak to them thus: 'In that case, venerable sirs, you will be those who destroy life due to creation by a supreme deity... <note>The text indicates an abbreviated repetition of the list above.</note> ...you will be those who hold wrong views due to creation by a supreme deity. For those who rely on creation by a supreme deity as the essential reason, there is no desire, no effort, no idea that "this must be done" or "this must not be done." Since in this way, what should be done and what should not be done cannot be established as a true and reliable reality for those who dwell heedless and unprotected, there is no valid basis for the title of "ascetic".'

"This, bhikkhus, is my second valid refutation of those ascetics and Brahmins who hold such views and such doctrines."

I say to them: If that is so, then venerable ones, you will be killers of living beings because of prior deeds, you will be takers of what is not given because of prior deeds, you will be unchaste because of prior deeds, you will be speakers of falsehood because of prior deeds, you will be speakers of malicious words because of prior deeds, you will be speakers of harsh words because of prior deeds, you will be speakers of frivolous gossip because of prior deeds, you will be covetous because of prior deeds, you will be malevolent because of prior deeds, and you will hold wrong views because of prior deeds. 3. This, monks, is my second refutation of those ascetics and brahmins who hold such views and opinions.

[context] What four?
[context] One thunders but doesn’t rain,
[context] one rains but doesn’t thunder,
one neither thunders nor rains, and
one both rains and thunders.
These are the four kinds of clouds.
In the same way, these four individuals similar to clouds are found in the world.
What four?
One thunders but doesn’t rain,
one rains but doesn’t thunder,
one neither thunders nor rains, and
one both rains and thunders.
And how does an individual thunder but not rain?
It’s when an individual memorizes the teaching—
statements, mixed prose & verse, discussions, verses, inspired exclamations, legends, stories of past lives, amazing stories, and elaborations.
But they don’t truly understand: ‘This is suffering’ … ‘This is the origin of suffering’ … ‘This is the cessation of suffering’ … ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering’.
That’s how an individual thunders but doesn’t rain.
That individual is like a cloud that thunders but doesn’t rain, I say.
And how does an individual rain but not thunder?
It’s when an individual doesn’t memorize the teaching …
But they truly understand: ‘This is suffering’ …
And how does an individual neither thunder nor rain?
It’s when an individual doesn’t memorize the teaching …
Nor do they truly understand: ‘This is suffering’ …
And how does an individual both thunder and rain?
It’s when an individual memorizes the teaching …
And they truly understand: ‘This is suffering’ …
[context] These four individuals similar to clouds are found in the world.”

# THE CLOUD CHAPTER <note>original: Valāhakavagga</note>

102.

1. Monks <note>original: bhikkhave</note>, there are these four types of clouds. Which four?
The one that thunders but does not rain <note>original: gajjitā no vassitā</note>... <note>the text elides the intermediate types here</note> ...and the one that both thunders and rains.
These, monks, are the four types of clouds.

2. In the same way, monks, these four people who resemble clouds are found existing in the world. Which four?
The one who thunders but does not rain... and the one who both thunders and rains.

3. And how, monks, is a person one who thunders but does not rain?
In this case, monks, a certain person masters the Teaching <note>original: dhammam</note>, namely: the discourses <note>original: suttam</note>, the mixed prose and verse <note>original: geyyam</note>, the explanations <note>original: veyyākaraṇam</note>, the verses <note>original: gātham</note>, the inspired utterances <note>original: udānam</note>, the "as it was said" quotations <note>original: itivuttakam</note>, the birth stories <note>original: jātakam</note>, the marvelous qualities <note>original: abbhutadhammam</note>, and the interpretations <note>original: vedallam</note>. Yet he does not understand as it really is: "This is suffering" <note>original: dukkhan</note>... <note>the text elides the second and third truths</note> ...he does not understand as it really is: "This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering" <note>original: dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā</note>.
Thus, monks, a person is one who thunders but does not rain. I say this person is like that cloud which thunders but does not rain.

4. And how, monks, is a person one who rains but does not thunder?
In this case, monks, a certain person does not master the Teaching, namely: the discourses... the interpretations. Yet he understands as it really is: "This is suffering"... he understands as it really is: "This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering." Thus, monks, a person is one who rains but does not thunder. I say this person is like that [cloud]...

5. And how, monks, is a person one who neither thunders nor rains?
In this case, monks, a certain person does not master the Teaching, namely: the discourses... the interpretations. He does not understand as it really is: "This is suffering"... he does not understand as it really is: "This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering." Thus, monks, a person is one who neither thunders nor rains. I say this person is like that [cloud]...

6. And how, monks, is a person one who both thunders and rains?
In this case, monks, a certain person masters the Teaching, namely: the discourses... the interpretations. He understands as it really is: "This is suffering"... he understands as it really is: "This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering." Thus, monks, a person is one who both thunders and rains. Just as that cloud, monks, both thunders and rains, I say this person is like that.

<summary>The Buddha uses a metaphor of four types of clouds to categorize individuals based on their theoretical knowledge of the scriptures versus their actual realization of the Four Noble Truths.</summary>
<keywords>Four Noble Truths, clouds, metaphor, scripture, realization, Anguttara Nikaya, Buddhist psychology, suffering</keywords>

VALĀHAKAVAGGA. 103

1. These four, monks, are clouds. Which four? 
Those that thunder but do not rain... (and so on)... and those that both thunder and rain. 
These, monks, are the four types of clouds.

2. Just so, monks, these four individuals like unto clouds are found in the world. Which four? 
Those that thunder but do not rain... (and so on)... and those that both thunder and rain.

3. And how, monks, is an individual like a cloud that thunders but does not rain? 
Here, monks, a certain individual learns the <term>Dhamma</term> <gloss>teaching</gloss>: discourses, songs, expositions, verses, inspired utterances, legendary tales, birth stories, marvelous events, and analytical descriptions. Yet, he does not understand as it really is: "This is suffering"... (and so on)... he does not understand as it really is: "This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering." In this way, monks, an individual is one who thunders but does not rain. Just as that cloud, monks, thunders but does not rain, so do I compare this individual to it.

4. And how, monks, is an individual like a cloud that rains but does not thunder? 
Here, monks, a certain individual does not learn the <term>Dhamma</term>: discourses... (and so on)... analytical descriptions. Yet, he understands as it really is: "This is suffering"... (and so on)... he understands as it really is: "This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering." In this way, monks, an individual is one who rains but does not thunder. Just as that cloud, monks... I compare him to it.

5. And how, monks, is an individual like a cloud that neither thunders nor rains? 
Here, monks, a certain individual does not learn the <term>Dhamma</term>: discourses... analytical descriptions. Furthermore, he does not understand as it really is: "This is suffering"... he does not understand as it really is: "This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering." In this way, monks, an individual is one who neither thunders nor rains. Just as that cloud, monks... I compare him to it.

6. And how, monks, is an individual like a cloud that both thunders and rains? 
Here, monks, a certain individual learns the <term>Dhamma</term>: discourses... analytical descriptions. Furthermore, he understands as it really is: "This is suffering"... he understands as it really is: "This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering." In this way, monks, an individual is one who both thunders and rains. Just as that cloud, monks, both thunders and rains, so do I compare this individual to it.

VALĀHAKAVAGGA. 103

102.

1. Monks, there are these four kinds of clouds. What are the four?
Those that thunder but do not rain... (and so on)... and those that both thunder and rain.
These, monks, are the four kinds of clouds.

2. In the same way, monks, there are these four kinds of individuals, resembling clouds, found in the world. What are the four?
Those who thunder but do not rain... (and so on)... and those who both thunder and rain.

3. And how, monks, is an individual like one who thunders but does not rain?

However, they do not understand as it really is: "This is suffering,"... (and so on)... "This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering."
In this way, monks, an individual is like one who thunders but does not rain. Just as that cloud thunders but does not rain, so do I describe this individual.

4. And how, monks, is an individual like one who rains but does not thunder?
Here, monks, a certain individual does not learn the <term>Dhamma</term>... (and so on)... including the analytical discussions. However, they understand as it really is: "This is suffering,"... (and so on)... "This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering."
In this way, monks, an individual is like one who rains but does not thunder. Just as that cloud... (and so on)... so do I describe this individual.

Here, monks, a certain individual does not learn the <term>Dhamma</term>... (and so on)... including the analytical discussions. And they do not understand as it really is: "This is suffering,"... (and so on)... "This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering."
In this way, monks, an individual is like one who neither thunders nor rains. Just as that cloud... (and so on)... so do I describe this individual.

6. And how, monks, is an individual like one who both thunders and rains?
Here, monks, a certain individual learns the <term>Dhamma</term>... (and so on)... including the analytical discussions. And they understand as it really is: "This is suffering,"... (and so on)... "This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering."
In this way, monks, an individual is like one who both thunders and rains. Just as that cloud, monks, both thunders and rains, so do I describe this individual.

102.

1. There are these four types of clouds, monks. Which four?

2. In the same way, there are these four types of persons like clouds, monks, found existing in the world. Which four?

<summary>This passage categorizes four types of individuals by comparing them to clouds based on their ability to study the teachings and their depth of insight into the Four Noble Truths.</summary>

VALĀHAKAVAGGA. 103

1. These four, monks, are clouds. Which four? 
Those that thunder but do not rain... (and so on)... and those that both thunder and rain. 
These, monks, are the four types of clouds.

2. Just so, monks, these four individuals like unto clouds are found in the world. Which four? 
Those that thunder but do not rain... (and so on)... and those that both thunder and rain.

3. And how, monks, is an individual like a cloud that thunders but does not rain? 
Here, monks, a certain individual learns the <term>Dhamma</term> <gloss>teaching</gloss>: discourses, songs, expositions, verses, inspired utterances, sayings, birth stories, marvelous events, and analytical descriptions. Yet, he does not understand as it really is: "This is suffering"... (and so on)... he does not understand as it really is: "This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering." In this way, monks, an individual is one who thunders but does not rain. Just as that cloud, monks, thunders but does not rain, so do I compare this individual to it.

4. And how, monks, is an individual like a cloud that rains but does not thunder? 
Here, monks, a certain individual does not learn the <term>Dhamma</term>: discourses... (and so on)... analytical descriptions. Yet, he understands as it really is: "This is suffering"... (and so on)... he understands as it really is: "This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering." In this way, monks, an individual is one who rains but does not thunder. Just as that cloud, monks... I compare him to it.

5. And how, monks, is an individual like a cloud that neither thunders nor rains? 
Here, monks, a certain individual does not learn the <term>Dhamma</term>: discourses... analytical descriptions. Furthermore, he does not understand as it really is: "This is suffering"... he does not understand as it really is: "This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering." In this way, monks, an individual is one who neither thunders nor rains. Just as that cloud, monks... I compare him to it.

6. And how, monks, is an individual like a cloud that both thunders and rains? 
Here, monks, a certain individual learns the <term>Dhamma</term>: discourses... analytical descriptions. Furthermore, he understands as it really is: "This is suffering"... he understands as it really is: "This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering." In this way, monks, an individual is one who both thunders and rains. Just as that cloud, monks, both thunders and rains, so do I compare this individual to it.

<summary>This page presents an analogy between four types of rain clouds and four types of people based on their knowledge of Buddhist doctrine and their realization of the Four Noble Truths.</summary>
<keywords>Clouds, Individuals, Dhamma, Four Noble Truths, Analogy, Wisdom, Knowledge</keywords>
