102.

1. "There are, monks, these four kinds of rain-cloud <note>original: "valāhakā"</note>. Which four?
The one that thunders but does not rain . . . and so on . . . the one that both thunders and rains. <note>The Pali "pe" is an abbreviation mark, standing for repeated material the editor has left out; here the full list was given in the preceding discourse.</note>
These, monks, are the four kinds of rain-cloud.

2. "In just the same way, monks, there are these four kinds of persons like rain-clouds
to be found existing in the world. Which four?
The one who thunders but does not rain . . . and so on . . . the one who both thunders and rains.

3. "And how, monks, is a person one who thunders but does not rain?
Here, monks, a certain person masters the teaching <note>original: "dhammam pariyāpuṇāti", literally "learns the Dhamma thoroughly", that is, by heart</note>:
the discourses, the mixed prose and verse, the expositions, the verses, the inspired utterances, the sayings "thus it was said",
the birth stories, the marvels, and the question-and-answer catechisms. <note>These are the nine traditional "limbs" of the Buddha's teaching: <term>sutta</term>, <term>geyya</term>, <term>veyyākaraṇa</term>, <term>gāthā</term>, <term>udāna</term>, <term>itivuttaka</term>, <term>jātaka</term>, <term>abbhutadhamma</term> and <term>vedalla</term>.</note> Yet he does not understand as it really is: "This is suffering"
. . . and so on . . . he does not understand as it really is: "This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering." <note>The abbreviation stands for the full formula of the Four Noble Truths: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path to its cessation.</note>
In this way, monks, a person is one who thunders but does not rain. Just as,
monks, that rain-cloud thunders but does not rain, of such a kind,
monks, do I declare this person to be.

4. "And how, monks, is a person one who rains but does not thunder?
Here, monks, a certain person does not master the teaching:
the discourses . . . and so on . . . the question-and-answer catechisms. Yet he understands as it really is: "This is
suffering" . . . and so on . . . he understands as it really is: "This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering." In this way,
monks, a person is one who rains but does not thunder. Just as
that, monks, . . . do I declare.

5. "And how, monks, is a person one who neither thunders nor
rains?
Here, monks, a certain person does not master the teaching:
the discourses . . . the question-and-answer catechisms. Nor does he understand as it really
is: "This is suffering" . . . he does not understand as it really is: "This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering." In this way, monks,
a person is one who neither thunders nor rains. Just as that,
monks, . . . do I declare.

6. "And how, monks, is a person one who both thunders and rains?
Here, monks, a certain person masters the teaching:
the discourses . . . the question-and-answer catechisms. And he understands as it really is: "This is suffering"
. . . he understands as it really is: "This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering." In this way, monks, a person both thunders
and rains. Just as, monks, that rain-cloud
both thunders and rains, of such a kind, monks, do I declare this

[context] “Mendicants, there are these five elements of escape.
[context] What five?
[context] Take a case where a mendicant focuses on sensual pleasures, but on that their mind does not leap forth, gain confidence, settle down, and become decided.
But when they focus on renunciation, on that their mind leaps forth, gains confidence, settles down, and becomes decided.
Their mind is in a good state, well developed, well risen, well freed, and well detached from sensual pleasures.
They’re freed from the distressing and feverish defilements that arise because of sensual pleasures, so they don’t experience that kind of feeling.
This is how the escape from sensual pleasures is explained.
Take another case where a mendicant focuses on ill will, but their mind does not leap forth …
But when they focus on good will, their mind leaps forth …
Their mind is in a good state … well detached from ill will.
They’re freed from the distressing and feverish defilements that arise because of ill will, so they don’t experience that kind of feeling.
This is how the escape from ill will is explained.
Take another case where a mendicant focuses on harming, but their mind does not leap forth …
But when they focus on compassion, their mind leaps forth …
Their mind is in a good state … well detached from harming.
They’re freed from the distressing and feverish defilements that arise because of harming, so they don’t experience that kind of feeling.
This is how the escape from harming is explained.
Take another case where a mendicant focuses on form, but their mind does not leap forth …
But when they focus on the formless, their mind leaps forth …
Their mind is in a good state … well detached from forms.
They’re freed from the distressing and feverish defilements that arise because of form, so they don’t experience that kind of feeling.
This is how the escape from forms is explained.
Take a case where a mendicant focuses on substantial reality, but their mind does not leap forth, gain confidence, settle down, and become decided.
But when they focus on the cessation of substantial reality, their mind leaps forth, gains confidence, settles down, and becomes decided.
Their mind is in a good state, well developed, well risen, well freed, and well detached from substantial reality.
They’re freed from the distressing and feverish defilements that arise because of substantial reality, so they don’t experience that kind of feeling.
This is how the escape from substantial reality is explained.
Delight in sensual pleasures, ill will, harming, form, and substantial reality don’t linger within them.
That’s why they’re called a mendicant who is without underlying tendencies, who has cut off craving, cast off the fetters, and by rightly comprehending conceit has made an end of suffering.
[context] These are the five elements of escape.”

However, when he directs his mind toward the cessation of self-identity <note>original: <term>sakkāyanirodhaṃ</term></note>, his mind leaps forward, finds confidence, settles, and releases into the cessation of self-identity. His mind is well-directed, well-developed, well-uplifted, well-released, and well-detached from self-identity. Those taints, distresses, and fevers that arise conditioned by self-identity—he is freed from them; he does not feel that sensation. This is declared to be the escape from self-identity.

In such a monk, delight in sensual pleasure <note>original: <term>kāmanandi</term></note> no longer underlies his tendency; delight in ill-will <note>original: <term>vyāpādanandi</term></note> no longer underlies it; delight in cruelty <note>original: <term>vihesānandi</term></note> no longer underlies it; delight in form <note>original: <term>rūpanandi</term></note> no longer underlies it; and delight in self-identity <note>original: <term>sakkāyanandi</term></note> no longer underlies it. Because he has no underlying tendency toward delight in sensual pleasure, ill-will, cruelty, form, or self-identity, he is called, monks, a monk without underlying tendencies <note>original: <term>niranusayo</term></note>. He has cut off craving, struck off the fetters <note>original: <term>samyojanaṃ</term></note>, and by the full understanding of conceit, he has made an end of suffering <note>original: <term>dukkhassa</term></note>.

These, monks, are the five elements of escape <note>original: <term>nissaraṇiyā dhātuyo</term></note>.

->The Chapter on Brahmins <note>original: <term>Brāhmaṇavaggo</term></note>, the twentieth section.<-

<summary>This text concludes the teaching on the five elements of escape, describing how a monk achieves liberation by directing the mind away from form and self-identity toward their cessation. By removing underlying delights in these concepts, the practitioner cuts off craving and ends suffering.</summary>
<keywords>escape, formless, self-identity, cessation of suffering, underlying tendencies, liberation, Buddhist psychology</keywords>

5. "Furthermore, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu directs his mind toward <term>rūpa</term> <gloss>form</gloss>, his mind does not leap out toward form, does not become clear, does not stand firm, and is not liberated. But when he directs his mind toward the <term>arūpa</term> <gloss>formless</gloss>, his mind leaps out toward the formless, becomes clear, stands firm, and is liberated. His mind is well-made, well-developed, well-risen, and well-liberated and detached from forms. He is freed from the <term>āsavā</term> <gloss>mental effluents</gloss> and the distress and burning that arise due to forms. He does not experience that feeling. This is called the deliverance from forms.

6. "Furthermore, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu directs his mind toward <term>sakkāya</term> <gloss>identity/personality</gloss>, his mind does not leap out toward identity, does not become clear, does not stand firm, and is not liberated. But when he directs his mind toward the cessation of identity, his mind leaps out toward the cessation of identity, becomes clear, stands firm, and is liberated. His mind is well-made, well-developed, well-risen, and well-liberated and detached from identity. He is freed from the <term>āsavā</term> <gloss>mental effluents</gloss> and the distress and burning that arise due to identity. He does not experience that feeling. This is called the deliverance from identity."

He does not harbor delight in sensual desire, he does not harbor delight in ill-will, he does not harbor delight in cruelty, he does not harbor delight in form, and he does not harbor delight in identity. Because he has no underlying tendency toward delight in sensual desire, delight in ill-will, delight in cruelty, delight in form, or delight in identity, this bhikkhu is called, bhikkhus, one without underlying tendencies. He has cut off <term>taṇhā</term> <gloss>craving</gloss>, he has turned back the <term>samyojana</term> <gloss>fetters</gloss>, and through the right attainment of conceit <note>original: "mānābhisamayā"</note>, he has made an end to <term>dukkha</term> <gloss>suffering</gloss>.

These, bhikkhus, are the five elements of deliverance.

->The Chapter on Brahmins.<-

<summary>This page concludes a discourse on the five elements of deliverance, detailing the mental liberation from form and identity, and describes the state of a monk who has abandoned all underlying tendencies and fetters.</summary>

Anguttara-Nikāya. CC.5—6

5. Furthermore, monks, when a monk reflects on form <note>original: "rūpa"</note>, his mind does not leap forward, does not grow clear, does not stand firm, and is not liberated regarding form. But when he reflects on the formless <note>original: "arūpa"</note>, his mind leaps forward, grows clear, stands firm, and is liberated regarding the formless. His mind is well-made, well-developed, well-risen, well-liberated, and well-detached from forms. Those <term>āsavā</term> <gloss>influences/corruptions</gloss> and the distress and burning heat that arise based on form, he is freed from them, and he does not experience that feeling. This is called the escape from forms.

6. Furthermore, monks, when a monk reflects on personality <note>original: "sakkāya"</note>, his mind does not leap forward, does not grow clear, does not stand firm, and is not liberated regarding personality. But when he reflects on the cessation of personality, his mind leaps forward, grows clear, stands firm, and is liberated regarding the cessation of personality. His mind is well-made, well-developed, well-risen, well-liberated, and well-detached from personality. Those <term>āsavā</term> <gloss>influences/corruptions</gloss> and the distress and burning heat that arise based on personality, he is freed from them, and he does not experience that feeling. This is called the escape from personality.

The delight in sensual pleasure does not lie latent in him; the delight in ill-will does not lie latent in him; the delight in harming does not lie latent in him; the delight in form does not lie latent in him; the delight in personality does not lie latent in him. Because the delight in sensual pleasure is not latent in him, and the delight in ill-will, harming, form, and personality are not latent in him, this monk, monks, is called one without latent tendencies. He has cut off <term>taṇhā</term> <gloss>craving</gloss>, untwisted the <term>samyojana</term> <gloss>fetters</gloss>, and by the correct realization of pride, he has made an end of suffering.

These, monks, are the five elements of escape.

[context] “Mendicants, you should know bad principles and good principles.
And you should know bad results and good results.
Knowing these things, your practice should follow the good principles with good results.”
That is what the Buddha said.
When he had spoken, the Holy One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling.
Soon after the Buddha left, those mendicants considered,
“The Buddha gave this brief summary recital, then entered his dwelling without explaining the meaning in detail.
‘You should know bad principles and good principles.
And you should know bad results and good results.
Knowing these things, your practice should follow the good principles with good results.’
Who can explain in detail the meaning of this brief summary recital given by the Buddha?”
Then those mendicants thought,
“This Venerable Mahākaccāna is praised by the Buddha and esteemed by his sensible spiritual companions.
He is capable of explaining in detail the meaning of this brief summary recital given by the Buddha.
Let’s go to him, and ask him about this matter.
As he answers, so we’ll remember it.”
Then those mendicants went to Mahākaccāna, and exchanged greetings with him.
When the greetings and polite conversation were over, they sat down to one side. They told him what had happened, and said,
“May Venerable Mahākaccāna please explain this.”
“Reverends, suppose there was a person in need of heartwood. And while wandering in search of heartwood he’d come across a large tree standing with heartwood. But he’d pass over the roots and trunk, imagining that the heartwood should be sought in the branches and leaves.
Such is the consequence for the venerables. Though you were face to face with the Buddha, you bypassed him, imagining that you should ask me about this matter.
For he is the Buddha, the one who knows and sees. He is vision, he is knowledge, he is the manifestation of principle, he is the manifestation of divinity. He is the preacher, the proclaimer, the elucidator of meaning, the bestower of freedom from death, the lord of truth, the Realized One.
That was the time to approach the Buddha and ask about this matter.
You should have remembered it in line with the Buddha’s answer.”
“Certainly he is the Buddha, the one who knows and sees. He is vision, he is knowledge, he is the manifestation of principle, he is the manifestation of divinity. He is the preacher, the proclaimer, the elucidator of meaning, the bestower of freedom from death, the lord of truth, the Realized One.
That was the time to approach the Buddha and ask about this matter.
We should have remembered it in line with the Buddha’s answer.
Still, Venerable Mahākaccāna is praised by the Buddha and esteemed by his sensible spiritual companions.
He is capable of explaining in detail the meaning of this brief summary recital given by the Buddha.
Please explain this, if it’s no trouble.”
“Well then, reverends, listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.”
“Yes, reverend,” they replied.
Mahākaccāna said this:

CLXXII.

1. Monks, one should understand what is unrighteous and what is righteous, what is unprofitable and what is profitable. [context] If you get upset over that,
[context] over others’ food and drink,
[context] you’ll not, by day or by night,
become immersed in samādhi.
Those who have cut that out,
dug it up at the root, eradicated it,
they will, by day or by night,
become immersed in samādhi.
There is no fire like greed,
no crime like hate,
no net like delusion,
no river like craving.
It’s easy to see the faults of others,
hard to see one’s own.
For the faults of others
are tossed high like hay,
while one’s own are hidden,
as a cheat hides a bad hand.
When you look for the flaws of others,
always finding fault,
your defilements only grow,
you’re far from ending defilements.
In the atmosphere there is no track,
there’s no true ascetic outside here.
People enjoy proliferation,
the Realized Ones are free of proliferation.
In the atmosphere there is no track,
there’s no true ascetic outside here.
No conditions last forever,
the Awakened Ones are not shaken.
[context] Minor Collection
[context] Sayings of the Dhamma 256–272

# Chapter on Impurities

250 But for one in whom this <note>referring to the faults mentioned in previous verses</note> is entirely cut off, uprooted at the foundation, and destroyed, he indeed, whether by day or by night, attains meditative absorption <term>samadhi</term> <gloss>a state of deep concentration and mental stillness</gloss>.
<margin>8 The Story of the Young Tissa, Volume III, page 357</margin>

251 There is no fire like lust; there is no grip like hatred. There is no net like delusion; there is no river like craving.
<margin>9 The Story of the Five Lay-Devotees, Volume III, page 360</margin>

252 The faults of others are easy to see, but one’s own are difficult to perceive. One winnows the faults of others like chaff, but hides one’s own faults as a dishonest gambler hides an unlucky throw of the dice.
<margin>10 The Story of the Merchant Mendaka, Volume III, page 363</margin>

253 For one who sees only the faults of others and is constantly irritable, their mental fermentations <term>asava</term> <gloss>deep-seated mental taints or pollutions</gloss> increase. Such a person is far from the destruction of these taints.
<margin>11 The Story of the Elder Ujjhanasannin, Volume III, page 376</margin>

254 There is no track in the sky. There is no true ascetic <term>samana</term> <gloss>one who has calmed the mind</gloss> outside the path. Mankind delights in worldliness and conceptual proliferation <term>papanca</term> <gloss>the tendency of the mind to expand on and complicate sensory input</gloss>, but the Awakened Ones <term>Tathagata</term> <gloss>those who have thus gone or thus come</gloss> are free from such proliferation.

255 There is no track in the sky. There is no true ascetic outside the path. No conditioned things are eternal. There is no instability in the Buddhas.
<margin>12 The Story of the Wanderer Subhadda, Volume III, page 377</margin>

[context] The first rains residence: observance day outside monastery
[context] “It may happen that a monk agrees to spend the first rains residence in a particular monastery.
[context] While on his way to that monastery, he does the observance-day ceremony outside. On the following day, he enters and prepares the dwelling, sets out water for drinking and water for washing, and sweeps the yard.
He then leaves on that very day, despite not having any business.
The first rains residence doesn’t count for that monk. And there’s an offense of wrong conduct for agreeing.
It may happen that a monk agrees to spend the first rains residence in a particular monastery.
While on his way to that monastery, he does the observance-day ceremony outside. On the following day, he enters and prepares the dwelling, sets out water for drinking and water for washing, and sweeps the yard.
He then leaves on that very day because of business.
The first rains residence doesn’t count for that monk. And there’s an offense of wrong conduct for agreeing.
It may happen that a monk agrees to spend the first rains residence in a particular monastery.
While on his way to that monastery, he does the observance-day ceremony outside. On the following day, he enters and prepares the dwelling, sets out water for drinking and water for washing, and sweeps the yard.
After staying there for two or three days, he leaves, despite not having any business.
The first rains residence doesn’t count for that monk. And there’s an offense of wrong conduct for agreeing.

The first rains residence doesn’t count for that monk. And there’s an offense of wrong conduct for agreeing.

While on his way to that monastery, he does the observance-day ceremony outside. On the following day, he enters and prepares the dwelling, sets out water for drinking and water for washing, and sweeps the yard.

The Third Chapter, the <term>Vassūpanāyikakkhandhaka</term> <gloss>Chapter on Entering the Rainy Season Retreat</gloss>, is concluded.

Its summary:
Entering, and when, how many, during the rains,
and if they do not wish, intentionally, to postpone, a lay follower.

<summary>This page concludes the regulations regarding the two periods for the rainy season retreat, detailing the conditions under which a monk's undertaking of the retreat is considered valid or invalid when he departs for business. It also provides a mnemonic summary for the entire chapter.</summary>
<keywords>Vassa, rainy season retreat, monastic discipline, Pavarana, Uposatha, dukkata, offense, Mahavagga, Vinaya Pitaka</keywords>

III. 14. 6-11.] MAHÂVAGGA. 155

He spends that seven-day period within the residential boundary. For that monk, the first-period rains retreat is accounted for, and there is no offense for the promise. ||6|| But in this case... he departs having a seven-day obligation before the <term>pavâraṇâ</term> <gloss>invitation/conclusion of the rains retreat</gloss>. Whether that monk returns to that residence or not, for that monk, the first-period rains retreat is accounted for, and there is no offense for the promise. ||7|| But in this case, monks, a monk has promised a rains retreat for the first period. He goes to that residence and performs the <term>uposatha</term> <gloss>observance day</gloss>. On the following day, he approaches the monastery, prepares the sleeping quarters, sets out drinking and utility water, and cleans the grounds. He departs that same day having nothing to do. For that monk, the first-period rains retreat is not accounted for, and there is an offense of wrong-doing for the promise. ||8|| But in this case... [= § 8] ...he departs that same day having something to do—etc.—he stays for two or three days and departs having nothing to do—etc.—he stays for two or three days and departs having something to do—etc.—he stays for two or three days and departs with a seven-day obligation. He spends that seven-day period outside. For that monk, the first-period rains retreat is not accounted for, and there is an offense of wrong-doing for the promise. ||9|| He stays for two or three days and departs with a seven-day obligation. He spends that seven-day period within the residential boundary. For that monk, the first-period rains retreat is accounted for, and there is no offense for the promise. He... [= § 7] ...no offense. ||10|| But in this case, monks, a monk has promised a rains retreat for the latter period. While going to that residence, he performs the <term>uposatha</term> <gloss>observance day</gloss> outside. On the following day, he approaches the monastery, prepares the sleeping quarters, sets out drinking and utility water, and cleans the grounds. He departs that same day having nothing to do. For that monk, the latter-period rains retreat is not accounted for, and there is an offense of wrong-doing for the promise. But in this case... [the whole passage is identical with § 5-10; read instead of first-period and first-period promise: latter-period and latter-period promise, instead of before the invitation: before the <term>komudiyâ câtumâsiniyâ</term> <gloss>the full moon festival of the fourth month</gloss>] ...and there is no offense for the promise. ||11||14||

The Third Chapter on the Entering of the Rains.

Its summary:
To enter, when also, how many, and between the rains,
Those who do not wish, intentionally, to postpone, a lay follower.

<summary>This page details the specific legalities and disciplinary consequences for monks failing to fulfill their promised obligations during either the first or latter segments of the annual rains retreat.</summary>
<keywords>Vassa, Rains Retreat, Vinaya, Bhikkhu, Uposatha, Pavâraṇâ, Wrong-doing, Duty</keywords>

III. 14. 6-11.] MAHÂVAGGA. 155

. . . he stays within the <term>sannivaṭṭa</term> <gloss>residence or enclosure</gloss> for that seven-day period. For that monk, O monks, the early retreat <note>the *purimikâ*, the first three months of the rainy season retreat</note> is recognized, and there is no offense in the arrival <note>the *paṭissava*</note>. ||6|| But here, if he departs for a duty <note>the *sakaraṇîya*</note> before the <term>pavâraṇâ</term> <gloss>ceremony marking the end of the retreat</gloss> has arrived. Whether that monk returns to that residence or does not return, O monks, for that monk the early retreat is recognized, and there is no offense in the arrival. ||7|| But here, O monks, a retreat has been promised by a monk for the early period. He goes to that residence, performs the <term>uposatha</term> <gloss>observance day</gloss>, approaches the monastery on the day after the Uposatha, arranges the bedding, prepares drinking and usable water, and sweeps the courtyard. He then departs the same day without a duty. For that monk, O monks, the early retreat is not recognized, and there is an offense of wrong-doing <note>the *dukkaṭa*</note> in the arrival. ||8|| But here . . . (= § 8) . . . he departs the same day for a duty — and so on — he stays for two or three days and departs without a duty — and so on — he stays for two or three days and departs for a duty — and so on — he stays for two or three days and departs for a seven-day duty. He spends that seven-day period outside. For that monk, O monks, the early retreat is not recognized, and there is an offense of wrong-doing in the arrival. ||9|| He stays for two or three days and departs for a seven-day duty. He stays within the residence for that seven-day period. For that monk, O monks, the early retreat is recognized, and there is no offense in the arrival. He [stays] for the seven-day period . . . (= § 7) . . . no offense. ||10|| But here, O monks, a retreat has been promised by a monk for the late period <note>the *pacchimikâ*, the second three months of the rainy season retreat</note>. While going to that residence, he performs the <term>uposatha</term> outside, approaches the monastery on the day after the Uposatha, arranges the bedding, prepares drinking and usable water, and sweeps the courtyard. He then departs the same day without a duty. For that monk, O monks, the late retreat is not recognized, and there is an offense of wrong-doing in the arrival. But here . . . (the whole passage is identical with § 5-10; read instead of *purimikâ* and *purimikâya*: *pacchimikâ* and *pacchimikâya*, instead of *anâgatâya pavâraṇâya*: *anâgatâya komudiyâ câtumâsiniyâ* <gloss>before the Komudî full-moon of the four-month season</gloss>) . . . and no offense in the arrival. ||11||14||

vassupanâyikakkhandhako tatiyo.

tassa uddânam:
upagantum, kadâ c’ eva, kati, antarâ vassa ca,
na icchanti ca, sañcicca, ukkaḍḍhitum, upâsako.|

<header>III. 14. 6-11. MAHĀVAGGA. 155</header>

He comes back within that week. For that monk, O monks, the earlier rains-residence is recognized, and there is no offence in respect of his promise. ||6|| Here again . . . he leaves, having business to attend to, when the Pavāraṇā is seven days away. Whether that monk comes back to that residence or does not come back, O monks, for that monk the earlier rains-residence is recognized, and there is no offence in respect of his promise. ||7|| Here again, O monks, a monk has promised to spend the rains for the earlier period. He goes to that residence and holds the Uposatha; on the first day of the fortnight he comes to the dwelling, makes ready his lodging, sets out drinking water and water for washing, and sweeps the cell. On that very day he leaves, having no business to attend to. For that monk, O monks, the earlier rains-residence is not recognized, and in respect of his promise there is an offence of wrong-doing. ||8|| Here again . . . (= § 8) . . . he leaves on that very day, having business to attend to . . . and so on . . . having stayed two or three days, he leaves, having no business to attend to . . . and so on . . . having stayed two or three days, he leaves, having business to attend to . . . and so on . . . having stayed two or three days, he leaves on business that takes up to seven days. He spends that week outside. For that monk, O monks, the earlier rains-residence is not recognized, and in respect of his promise there is an offence of wrong-doing. ||9|| Having stayed two or three days, he leaves on business that takes up to seven days. He comes back within that week. For that monk, O monks, the earlier rains-residence is recognized, and there is no offence in respect of his promise. When seven days . . . (= § 7) . . . no offence. ||10|| Here again, O monks, a monk has promised to spend the rains for the later period. While going to that residence he holds the Uposatha outside; on the first day of the fortnight he comes to the dwelling, makes ready his lodging, sets out drinking water and water for washing, and sweeps the cell. On that very day he leaves, having no business to attend to. For that monk, O monks, the later rains-residence is not recognized, and in respect of his promise there is an offence of wrong-doing. Here again . . . (the whole passage is identical with § 5-10; read "the later" and "for the later period" instead of "the earlier" and "for the earlier period", and instead of "when the Pavāraṇā is seven days away": "when the Komudī full moon of the fourth month is seven days away") . . . there is no offence in respect of his promise. ||11||14||
<note>The <term>vassa</term> <gloss>rains retreat</gloss> could be entered for an earlier period <term>purimikā</term> or a later one <term>pacchimikā</term>, beginning a month apart. <term>Uposatha</term> is the fortnightly observance day; <term>Pavāraṇā</term> is the "invitation" ceremony that closes the earlier rains. <term>Dukkaṭa</term> <gloss>wrong-doing</gloss> is the lightest class of offence in the monastic code. The <term>Komudī</term> is the full moon of the month Kattika, closing the fourth month of the rainy season.</note>

End of the third section, on entering upon the rains.
<note>original: "vassupanâyikakkhandhako tatiyo"</note>

Its summary:
Entering, and when, and how many, and in the midst of the rains,
and they do not wish, and deliberately, to postpone, a lay follower.|

[context] Long Discourses 22
[context] The Longer Discourse on Mindfulness Meditation
[context] So I have heard.
At one time the Buddha was staying in the land of the Kurus, near the Kuru town named Kammāsadamma.
There the Buddha addressed the mendicants,
“Mendicants!”
“Venerable sir,” they replied.
The Buddha said this:
“Mendicants, the four kinds of mindfulness meditation are the path to convergence. They are in order to purify sentient beings, to get past sorrow and crying, to make an end of pain and sadness, to discover the system, and to realize extinguishment.
What four?
It’s when a mendicant meditates by observing an aspect of the body—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.
They meditate observing an aspect of feelings—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.
They meditate observing an aspect of the mind—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.
They meditate observing an aspect of principles—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.
1. Observing the Body
1.1. Mindfulness of Breathing
And how does a mendicant meditate observing an aspect of the body?
It’s when a mendicant—gone to a wilderness, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut—sits down cross-legged, sets their body straight, and brings mindfulness to the present.
Just mindful, they breathe in. Mindful, they breathe out.
Breathing in heavily they know: ‘I’m breathing in heavily.’ Breathing out heavily they know: ‘I’m breathing out heavily.’
Breathing in lightly they know: ‘I’m breathing in lightly.’ Breathing out lightly they know: ‘I’m breathing out lightly.’
They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in experiencing the whole body.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out experiencing the whole body.’
They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe in stilling the physical process.’ They practice like this: ‘I’ll breathe out stilling the physical process.’
It’s like a deft lathe-turner or lathe-turner’s apprentice. When drawing a long pull they know: ‘I’m drawing a long pull,’ and when drawing a short pull they know: ‘I’m drawing a short pull.’
And so they meditate observing an aspect of the body internally, externally, and both internally and externally.
With respect to the body, they meditate observing the liability to originate, to vanish, and to originate and vanish.
Or mindfulness is established that the body exists, to the extent necessary for knowledge and mindfulness. They meditate independent, not grasping at anything in the world.
That’s how a mendicant meditates by observing an aspect of the body.
1.2. The Postures
Furthermore, when a mendicant is walking they know: ‘I am walking.’ When standing they know: ‘I am standing.’ When sitting they know: ‘I am sitting.’ And when lying down they know: ‘I am lying down.’
Whatever posture their body is in, they know it.
And so they meditate observing an aspect of the body internally, externally, and both internally and externally.
[context] They meditate observing, with respect to the body, the liability to originate, to vanish, and to originate and vanish.
[context] Or mindfulness is established that the body exists, to the extent necessary for knowledge and mindfulness. They meditate independent, not grasping at anything in the world.
[context] That too is how a mendicant meditates by observing an aspect of the body.

<margin>1</margin>
Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was staying among the Kurus. There is a market town of the Kuru people named Kammasadhamma. There, the Blessed One addressed the monks, saying, "Monks!" "Venerable Sir!" those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:

"Monks, this is the direct path <note>original: ekāyano maggo; often translated as the only path or the one-way path</note> for the purification of beings, for the overcoming of sorrow and lamentation, for the disappearance of pain and distress, for the attainment of the true method, and for the realization of <term>Nibbana</term> <gloss>the liberation from suffering and rebirth</gloss>, namely, the four foundations of mindfulness.

What are the four? Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. He dwells contemplating the mind in the mind, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. He dwells contemplating mental qualities in mental qualities, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.

And how, monks, does a monk dwell contemplating the body in the body? Here, monks, a monk who has gone to the forest, or to the foot of a tree, or to an empty places, sits down. Having folded his legs crosswise, set his body erect, and established mindfulness before him, mindful he breathes in, mindful he breathes out.

Breathing in long, he knows, 'I breathe in long.' Breathing out long, he knows, 'I breathe out long.' Breathing in short, he knows, 'I breathe in short.' Breathing out short, he knows, 'I breathe out short.' He trains himself, 'I will breathe in experiencing the whole body.' He trains himself, 'I will breathe out experiencing the whole body.' He trains himself, 'I will breathe in calming the bodily formation.' He trains himself, 'I will breathe out calming the bodily formation.'"

<summary>This page introduces the Great Discourse on the Foundations of Mindfulness, establishing the four types of contemplation and detailing the initial practice of mindfulness of breathing.</summary>
<keywords>Satipaṭṭhāna, mindfulness, meditation, breathing, Nibbana, Kuru, Kammasadhamma, Buddhism</keywords>

<meta>The source is a manuscript written in Sinhala script containing the opening section of the Great Discourse on the Foundations of Mindfulness.</meta>
<margin>4</margin>
Thus have I heard. At one time, the Blessed One was dwelling among the Kurus, in a market town of the Kuru people named Kammāsadhamma. There, the Blessed One addressed the monks, saying, "Monks!" and they replied, "Venerable Sir!" The Blessed One said this: "This is the direct path, monks, for the purification of beings, for the overcoming of sorrow and lamentation, for the ending of suffering and distress, for the attainment of the noble path, and for the realization of <term>Nibbāna</term> <gloss>extinguishment/liberation</gloss>, which is the four foundations of mindfulness. What are the four? Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having put away covetousness and distress concerning the world. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having put away covetousness and distress concerning the world. He dwells contemplating the mind in the mind, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having put away covetousness and distress concerning the world. He dwells contemplating mental objects in mental objects, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having put away covetousness and distress concerning the world.

And how, monks, does a monk dwell contemplating the body in the body? Here, monks, a monk, having gone to the forest, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, sits down, crosses his legs, sets his body erect, and establishes mindfulness in front of him. Always mindful, he breathes in, and mindful, he breathes out. Breathing in long, he understands, "I am breathing in long." Breathing out long, he understands, "I am breathing out long." Breathing in short, he understands, "I am breathing in short." Breathing out short, he understands, "I am breathing out short." He trains, "I shall breathe in, experiencing the whole body." He trains, "I shall breathe out, experiencing the whole body." He trains, "I shall breathe in, calming the bodily formation." He trains, "I shall breathe out, calming the bodily formation."

<summary>This page introduces the Great Discourse on the Foundations of Mindfulness, defining the four foundations as the direct path to liberation and detailing the initial stages of mindfulness of breathing.</summary>
<keywords>Mindfulness, foundations of mindfulness, meditation, breathing, liberation, Kammāsadhamma, Kuru</keywords>

<note>original: "Evaṃ me sutaṃ"</note> Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was staying among the Kurus, at a market town of the Kurus named Kammāsadhamma. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks!" "Venerable Sir," those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: "Monks, this is the direct path <note>original: "ekāyano maggo"</note> for the purification of beings, for the overcoming of sorrow and lamentation, for the disappearance of pain and distress, for the attainment of the true method, and for the realization of <term>Nibbāna</term> <gloss>liberation from suffering</gloss>, namely, the four foundations of mindfulness <note>original: "cattāro satipaṭṭhāna"</note>. 

What are the four? Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. He dwells contemplating mind in mind, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. He dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena <note>original: "dhammesu dhammānupassī"</note>, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.

And how, monks, does a monk dwell contemplating the body in the body? Here, monks, a monk, having gone to the forest, or to the foot of a tree, or to an empty place, sits down. Having folded his legs cross-legged, set his body erect, and established mindfulness in front of him, mindful he breathes in, mindful he breathes out. Breathing in long, he knows, "I breathe in long"; or breathing out long, he knows, "I breathe out long." Breathing in short, he knows, "I breathe in short"; or breathing out short, he knows, "I breathe out short." 

"I shall breathe in experiencing the whole body," he trains himself. "I shall breathe out experiencing the whole body," he trains himself. "I shall breathe in calming the bodily formation," he trains himself. "I shall breathe out calming the bodily formation," he trains himself.

<summary>This page contains the opening of the Great Discourse on the Foundations of Mindfulness, establishing the purpose of the practice and describing the initial steps of mindfulness of breathing.</summary>
<keywords>Mahāsatipaṭṭhānasutta, mindfulness, meditation, breathing, Nibbāna, four foundations of mindfulness, Kammāsadhamma</keywords>

Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was staying among the Kurus, in a market town of the Kuru people named Kammāsadhamma. There the Blessed One addressed the monks, saying, "Monks." "Venerable sir," those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: "This is the direct path <note>original: "ekāyano maggo"</note>, monks, for the purification of beings, for the surmounting of sorrow and lamentation, for the passing away of pain and distress, for the attainment of the method, and for the realization of <term>Nibbāna</term> <gloss>extinguishment/liberation</gloss>: namely, the four foundations of mindfulness. What are the four? Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and distress regarding the world. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and distress regarding the world. He dwells contemplating the mind in the mind, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and distress regarding the world. He dwells contemplating mental objects in mental objects, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and distress regarding the world.

And how, monks, does a monk dwell contemplating the body in the body? Here, monks, a monk having gone to the forest, to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, sits down cross-legged, sets his body erect, and establishes mindfulness before him. Mindful, he breathes in; mindful, he breathes out. Breathing in long, he knows, 'I am breathing in long'; or breathing out long, he knows, 'I am breathing out long.' Breathing in short, he knows, 'I am breathing in short'; or breathing out short, he knows, 'I am breathing out short.' He trains, 'I shall breathe in experiencing the whole body'; he trains, 'I shall breathe out experiencing the whole body.' He trains, 'I shall breathe in tranquilizing the bodily formation'; he trains, 'I shall breathe out tranquilizing the bodily formation.'

<summary>This text introduces the Mahāsatipaṭṭhānasutta, detailing the direct path to liberation through the four foundations of mindfulness, beginning with the practice of mindful breathing.</summary>
<keywords>Mahāsatipaṭṭhānasutta, mindfulness, four foundations, breath meditation, liberation</keywords>

132 දීඝනිකායේ සීලක්ඛන්ධවග්ගො සාමඤ්ඤඵලසුත්තං

එවමෙව ඛො මහාරාජ භික්ඛු ඉමමෙව කායං තිපතිතකෙන සුඛෙන අභිසන්දෙති පරිසන්දෙති පරිපූරෙති පරිප්ඵරති. නාස්ස කිඤ්චි සබ්බාවතො කායස්ස තිපතිතකෙන සුඛෙන අප්ඵුටං හොති.

ඉදම්පි ඛො මහාරාජ සන්දිට්ඨිකං සාමඤ්ඤඵලං පුරිමෙහි සන්දිට්ඨිකෙහි සාමඤ්ඤඵලෙහි අභික්කන්තතරඤ්ච පණීතතරඤ්ච.

68. පුන ච පරං මහාරාජ භික්ඛු සුඛස්ස ච පහානා දුක්ඛස්ස ච පහානා පුබ්බෙව සොමනස්සදොමනස්සානං අත්ථඞ්ගමා අදුක්ඛමසුඛං උපෙක්ඛාසතිපාරිසුද්ධිං චතුත්ථං ඣානං උපසම්පජ්ජ විහරති. සො ඉමමෙව කායං පරිසුද්ධෙන චෙතසා පරියොදාතෙන ඵරිත්වා නිසින්නො හොති. නාස්ස කිඤ්චි සබ්බාවතො කායස්ස පරිසුද්ධෙන චෙතසා පරියොදාතෙන අප්ඵුටං හොති.

සෙය්‍යථාපි මහාරාජ පුරිසො ඔදතෙන වත්ථෙන සබ්බං පාරුපිතවා නිසින්නො අස්ස, නාස්ස කිඤ්චි සබ්බාවතො කායස්ස ඔදතෙන වත්ථෙන අප්ඵුටං අස්ස, එවමෙව ඛො මහාරාජ භික්ඛු ඉමමෙව කායං පරිසුද්ධෙන චෙතසා පරියොදාතෙන ඵරිත්වා නිසින්නො හොති. නාස්ස කිඤ්චි සබ්බාවතො කායස්ස පරිසුද්ධෙන චෙතසා පරියොදාතෙන අප්ඵුටං හොති.

ඉදම්පි ඛො මහාරාජ සන්දිට්ඨිකං සාමඤ්ඤඵලං පුරිමෙහි සන්දිට්ඨිකෙහි සාමඤ්ඤඵලෙහි අභික්කන්තතරඤ්ච පණීතතරඤ්ච.

69. පුන ච පරං මහාරාජ සො භික්ඛු එවං සමාහිතෙ චිත්තෙ පරිසුද්ධෙ පරියොදාතෙ අනඞ්ගණෙ විගතූපක්කිලෙසෙ මුදුභූතෙ කම්මනීයෙ ඨිතෙ ආනෙඞ්ජප්පත්තාය චිත්තං අභිනය්‍යති අභිහරිති. සො එවං පජානාති: “අයං ඛො මෙ කායො රූපී චාතුම්මහාභූතිකො මාතාපෙත්තිකසම්භවො ඔදනකුම්මාසුපචයො අනිච්චුච්ඡාදනපරිමද්දන-භෙදනවිද්ධංසනධම්මො. ඉදඤ්ච පන මෙ විඤ්ඤාණං එත්ථ සිතං එත්ථ පටිබද්ධ”න්ති.

70. සෙය්‍යථාපි මහාරාජ මණි වෙළුරියො සුභො ජාතිමා අට්ඨංසො සුපරිකම්මකතො අච්ඡො විප්පසන්නො අනාවිලො සබ්බාකාරසම්පන්නො, තත්ථායං සුත්තං ආවුතං නීලං වා පೀತං වා ලොහිතං වා ඔදාතං වා පණ්ඩුසුත්තං වා. තමෙනං චක්ඛුමා පුරිසො හත්ථෙ කරිත්වා පච්චවෙක්ඛෙය්‍ය “අයං ඛො මණි වෙළුරියො සුභො ජාතිමා අට්ඨංසො සුපරිකම්මකතො, අච්ඡො විප්පසන්නො අනාවිලො සබ්බාකාරසම්පන්නො. තත්ථායං සුත්තං ආවුතං නීලං වා පೀತං වා ලොහිතං වා ඔදාතං වා පණ්ඩුසුත්තං වා”ති.

[context] Quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, they enter and remain in the first absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of seclusion, while placing the mind and keeping it connected.
[context] They drench, steep, fill, and spread themselves with rapture and bliss born of seclusion. There’s no part of the body that’s not spread with rapture and bliss born of seclusion.
[context] It’s like when a deft bathroom attendant or their apprentice pours bath powder into a bronze dish, sprinkling it little by little with water. They knead it until the ball of bath powder is soaked and saturated with moisture, spread through inside and out; yet no moisture oozes out.
In the same way, a mendicant drenches, steeps, fills, and spreads themselves with rapture and bliss born of seclusion. There’s no part of the body that’s not spread with rapture and bliss born of seclusion.
This, Great King, is a fruit of the ascetic life that’s apparent in the present life which is better and finer than the former ones.
4.3.2.6. Second Absorption
Furthermore, as the placing of the mind and keeping it connected are stilled, a mendicant enters and remains in the second absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of immersion, with internal clarity and mind at one, without placing the mind and keeping it connected.
They drench, steep, fill, and spread themselves with rapture and bliss born of immersion. There’s no part of the body that’s not spread with rapture and bliss born of immersion.
It’s like a deep lake fed by spring water. There’s no inlet to the east, west, north, or south, and the heavens would not properly bestow showers from time to time.
But the stream of cool water welling up in the lake drenches, steeps, fills, and spreads throughout the lake. There’s no part of the lake that’s not spread through with cool water.
In the same way, a mendicant drenches, steeps, fills, and spreads themselves with rapture and bliss born of immersion. There’s no part of the body that’s not spread with rapture and bliss born of immersion.
This too, Great King, is a fruit of the ascetic life that’s apparent in the present life which is better and finer than the former ones.
4.3.2.7. Third Absorption
Furthermore, with the fading away of rapture, a mendicant enters and remains in the third absorption, where they meditate with equanimity, mindful and aware, experiencing for themselves the bliss of which the noble ones declare, ‘Equanimous and mindful, one meditates in bliss.’
They drench, steep, fill, and spread themselves with bliss free of rapture. There’s no part of the body that’s not spread with bliss free of rapture.
It’s like a pool with blue water lilies, or pink or white lotuses. Some of them sprout and grow in the water without rising above it, thriving underwater. From the tip to the root they’re drenched, steeped, filled, and soaked with cool water. There’s no part of them that’s not soaked with cool water.
In the same way, a mendicant drenches, steeps, fills, and spreads themselves with bliss free of rapture. There’s no part of the body that’s not spread with bliss free of rapture.
This too, Great King, is a fruit of the ascetic life that’s apparent in the present life which is better and finer than the former ones.
4.3.2.8. Fourth Absorption
Furthermore, with the giving up of pleasure and pain and the disappearance of former happiness and sadness, a mendicant enters and remains in the fourth absorption, without pleasure or pain, with pure equanimity and mindfulness.
They sit spreading their body through with pure bright mind. There’s no part of the body that’s not spread with pure bright mind.
It’s like someone sitting wrapped from head to foot with white cloth. There’s no part of the body that’s not spread over with white cloth.
In the same way, they sit spreading their body through with pure bright mind. There’s no part of the body that’s not spread with pure bright mind.
This too, Great King, is a fruit of the ascetic life that’s apparent in the present life which is better and finer than the former ones.
4.3.3. The Eight Knowledges
4.3.3.1. Knowledge and Vision
When their mind has become immersed in samādhi like this—purified, bright, flawless, rid of corruptions, pliable, workable, steady, and imperturbable—they project it and extend it toward knowledge and vision.
They understand:
‘This body of mine is formed. It’s made up of the four principal states, produced by mother and father, built up from rice and porridge, liable to impermanence, to wearing away and erosion, to breaking up and destruction.
And this consciousness of mine is attached to it, tied to it.’
Suppose there was a beryl gem that was naturally lustrous, eight-faceted, well-worked, transparent, clear, and unclouded, endowed with all good qualities.
And it was strung with a thread of blue, yellow, red, white, or golden brown.
And a person with clear eyes were to take it in their hand and examine it:
‘This beryl gem is naturally lustrous, eight-faceted, well-worked, transparent, clear, and unclouded, endowed with all good qualities.
And it’s strung with a thread of blue, yellow, red, white, or golden brown.’
In the same way, when their mind has become immersed in samādhi like this—purified, bright, flawless, rid of corruptions, pliable, workable, steady, and imperturbable—they project it and extend it toward knowledge and vision.
This too, Great King, is a fruit of the ascetic life that’s apparent in the present life which is better and finer than the former ones.
4.3.3.2. Mind-Made Body
When their mind has become immersed in samādhi like this—purified, bright, flawless, rid of corruptions, pliable, workable, steady, and imperturbable—they project it and extend it toward the creation of a mind-made body.
From this body they create another body—formed, mind-made, whole in its major and minor limbs, not deficient in any faculty.
Suppose a person was to draw a reed out from its sheath.
They’d think:
‘This is the reed, this is the sheath. The reed and the sheath are different things. The reed has been drawn out from the sheath.’
Or suppose a person was to draw a sword out from its scabbard.
They’d think:
‘This is the sword, this is the scabbard. The sword and the scabbard are different things. The sword has been drawn out from the scabbard.’
Or suppose a person was to draw a snake out from its slough.
They’d think:
‘This is the snake, this is the slough. The snake and the slough are different things. The snake has been drawn out from the slough.’
In the same way, when their mind has become immersed in samādhi like this—purified, bright, flawless, rid of corruptions, pliable, workable, steady, and imperturbable—they project it and extend it toward the creation of a mind-made body.
From this body they create another body—formed, mind-made, whole in its major and minor limbs, not deficient in any faculty.
This too, Great King, is a fruit of the ascetic life that’s apparent in the present life which is better and finer than the former ones.
4.3.3.3. Psychic Powers
When their mind has become immersed in samādhi like this—purified, bright, flawless, rid of corruptions, pliable, workable, steady, and imperturbable—they project it and extend it toward psychic power.
They wield the many kinds of psychic power: multiplying themselves and becoming one again; materializing and dematerializing; going unobstructed through a wall, a rampart, or a mountain as if through space; diving in and out of the earth as if it were water; walking on water as if it were earth; flying cross-legged through the sky like a bird; touching and stroking with the hand the sun and moon, so mighty and powerful; controlling the body as far as the realm of divinity.
Suppose a deft potter or their apprentice had some well-prepared clay. They could produce any kind of pot that they like.
Or suppose a deft ivory-carver or their apprentice had some well-prepared ivory. They could produce any kind of ivory item that they like.
Or suppose a deft goldsmith or their apprentice had some well-prepared gold. They could produce any kind of gold item that they like.
In the same way, when their mind has become immersed in samādhi like this—purified, bright, flawless, rid of corruptions, pliable, workable, steady, and imperturbable—they project it and extend it toward psychic power.
This too, Great King, is a fruit of the ascetic life that’s apparent in the present life which is better and finer than the former ones.
4.3.3.4. Clairaudience
When their mind has become immersed in samādhi like this—purified, bright, flawless, rid of corruptions, pliable, workable, steady, and imperturbable—they project it and extend it toward clairaudience.
With clairaudience that is purified and superhuman, they hear both kinds of sounds, human and heavenly, whether near or far.
Suppose there was a person traveling along the road. They’d hear the sound of drums, clay drums, horns, kettledrums, and tom-toms. They’d think: ‘That’s the sound of drums,’ and ‘that’s the sound of clay drums,’ and ‘that’s the sound of horns, kettledrums, and tom-toms.’
In the same way, when their mind has become immersed in samādhi like this—purified, bright, flawless, rid of corruptions, pliable, workable, steady, and imperturbable—they project it and extend it toward clairaudience.
[context] With clairaudience that is purified and superhuman, they hear both kinds of sounds, human and heavenly, whether near or far.
[context] This too, Great King, is a fruit of the ascetic life that’s apparent in the present life which is better and finer than the former ones.
[context] 4.3.3.5. Encompassing the Minds of Others

132 Long Discourses: Division on Morality — The Fruits of Reclusive Life Discourse <note>original: "Dīghanikāye Sīlakkhandhavagga Sāmaññaphalasuttaṃ"</note>

In the same way, Great King, a monk drenches, permeates, fills, and suffuses this very body with a happiness <note>referring to the third meditative state</note> that is free from rapture. There is no part of his entire body untouched by this happiness that is free from rapture.

This, Great King, is a fruit of reclusive life <note>term: sāmaññaphala</note> <gloss>the result of living as a monk</gloss> visible in this very life, more excellent and refined than the previous visible fruits of reclusive life.

68. Furthermore, Great King, with the giving up of pleasure and the giving up of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, a monk enters and remains in the fourth <term>jhāna</term> <gloss>meditative absorption</gloss>, which is neither painful nor pleasant and has purity of mindfulness due to equanimity. He sits suffusing this very body with a pure, bright mind. There is no part of his entire body untouched by that pure, bright mind.

Just as if, Great King, a man were to sit wrapped from head to foot in a white cloth, so that there would be no part of his entire body not covered by the white cloth; in the same way, Great King, a monk sits suffusing this very body with a pure, bright mind. There is no part of his entire body untouched by that pure, bright mind.

This, Great King, is a fruit of reclusive life visible in this very life, more excellent and refined than the previous visible fruits of reclusive life.

69. Furthermore, Great King, when the mind is thus concentrated, pure, bright, unblemished, rid of defilements, pliant, workable, steady, and attained to imperturbability, the monk directs and inclines it toward knowledge and vision. He understands thus: "This body of mine has form, it is composed of the four great elements, born of a mother and father, nourished by rice and gruel, subject to impermanence, to being worn away, broken up, and dissolved. And this consciousness <note>term: viññāṇa</note> of mine is supported here and bound up here."

70. Just as if, Great King, there were a beautiful beryl gem <note>term: veḷuriya</note> <gloss>lapis lazuli or similar precious stone</gloss> of the purest water, eight-faceted, well-cut, clear, bright, flawless, and endowed with every good quality. And through it was strung a thread—blue, yellow, red, white, or light brown. A man with good sight, taking it in his hand, would reflect: "This is a beautiful beryl gem of the purest water, eight-faceted, well-cut, clear, bright, flawless, and endowed with every good quality. Through it is strung this thread—blue, yellow, red, white, or light brown."

<summary>This page describes the fourth state of meditative absorption and the subsequent development of insight into the relationship between the physical body and consciousness. The Buddha uses the simile of a white cloth for meditation and a threaded gem to illustrate the clarity of self-knowledge.</summary>
<keywords>Fourth Jhana, meditation, mindfulness, consciousness, body and mind, beryl gem simile, Fruits of Reclusive Life, Samannaphala Sutta</keywords>

In this same way, Great King, the monk saturates, drenches, fills, and suffuses this very body with this pleasure born of seclusion <note>referring to the rapture and physical ease attained in the preceding meditative states</note>. There is no part of his entire body that is not suffused with this pleasure born of seclusion.

This, too, Great King, is a visible fruit of recluseship, more excellent and sublime than the previous visible fruits of recluseship.

68. Furthermore, Great King, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous passing away of joy and sorrow, the monk enters and remains in the fourth jhāna <note>meditative absorption</note>, which is neither painful nor pleasant and is purified by equanimity. He sits having suffused this very body with a pure, bright mind. There is no part of his entire body that is not suffused with this pure, bright mind.

Just as if, Great King, a man were sitting having covered himself from head to foot with a white cloth, such that there would be no part of his entire body not covered by the white cloth, in the same way, Great King, the monk sits having suffused this very body with a pure, bright mind. There is no part of his entire body that is not suffused with this pure, bright mind.

This, too, Great King, is a visible fruit of recluseship, more excellent and sublime than the previous visible fruits of recluseship.

69. Furthermore, Great King, when his mind is thus composed, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of impurities, pliant, workable, established, and attained to imperturbability, the monk directs and inclines his mind toward knowledge and vision. He understands thus: "This body of mine is material, composed of the four great elements, born of mother and father, nourished by boiled rice and porridge, subject to impermanence, to being rubbed and pressed, to breaking up and destruction. And this consciousness of mine is bound to it, dependent on it."

70. And through it is strung a thread—blue, yellow, red, white, or brown."

...so too, Great King, the monk permeates, drenches, fills, and suffuses this body with that happiness. There is no part of his entire body that is not suffused with that happiness. This is a visible fruit of asceticism, more excellent and refined than the previous ones.

Great King, just as if a person were sitting covered from head to foot with a white cloth, so that there was no part of his body not covered by the white cloth, so too, the monk sits having suffused his body with a pure, bright mind. This is a visible fruit of asceticism, more excellent and refined than the previous ones.

69. Again, Great King, with a mind thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of defilements, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, the monk directs his mind toward knowledge and vision. He discerns: "This is my body, formed of the four great elements, born of mother and father, nourished by rice and porridge, subject to impermanence, to being rubbed, massaged, broken, and destroyed. And this is my consciousness, situated in it, bound to it."

70. Great King, just as if there were a beautiful beryl gem of excellent quality, eight-faceted, well-polished, clear, limpid, and perfect in all aspects, and through it were strung a thread—blue, yellow, red, white, or brown—a person with good eyesight, taking it in his hand, would reflect: "This is a beautiful beryl gem, well-polished and clear, and through it is strung a thread of such and such a color."

In this way, Great King, the monk drenching, soaking, filling, and pervading this very body with a happiness that is free from physical rapture <note>the original term "tipatitakena sukhena" refers to the refined pleasure of the Third Jhana</note>. There is no part of his entire body that is not pervaded by this happiness.

This, Great King, is a fruit of the contemplative life, visible here and now, more excellent and sublime than the previous fruits of the contemplative life.

68. Furthermore, Great King, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, a monk enters and remains in the fourth <term>jhana</term> <gloss>state of deep meditative absorption</gloss>, which is beyond pleasure and pain and purified by equanimity and mindfulness. He sits pervading this very body with a pure, bright mind. There is no part of his entire body that is not pervaded by this pure, bright mind.

Great King, it is just as if a man were sitting wrapped from head to foot in a white cloth, so that there would be no part of his entire body not covered by that white cloth. In the same way, Great King, the monk sits pervading this very body with a pure, bright mind. There is no part of his entire body that is not pervaded by this pure, bright mind.

This, Great King, is a fruit of the contemplative life, visible here and now, more excellent and sublime than the previous fruits of the contemplative life.

69. He understands this: "This is my body, possessed of form, composed of the four great elements <note>earth, water, fire, and air</note>, born of mother and father, nourished by rice and gruel, subject to impermanence, rubbing, pressing, breaking, and dissolution. And this is my <term>viññāṇa</term> <gloss>consciousness</gloss>, which is fixed here and bound up with it."

70. Great King, it is just as if there were a beautiful beryl gem <note>original: "maṇi veḷuriyo"</note>, naturally pure, eight-faceted, well-cut, clear, bright, flawless, and endowed with every good quality. And through it was strung a thread—blue, yellow, red, white, or light brown. And through it is strung this thread—blue, yellow, red, white, or light brown."

132 Long Discourses <note>original: "Dīghanikāya"</note>, The Division on Morality <note>original: "Sīlakkhandhavagga"</note>, The Discourse on the Fruits of the Recluse's Life <note>original: "Sāmaññaphalasutta"</note>

In just the same way, great king, a monk drenches, steeps, fills and pervades this very body with a happiness free of rapture, so that there is no part of his whole body that is not suffused with that happiness free of rapture. <note>The printed form reads "tipatitakena", which appears to be a misreading of "nippītikena", "free of rapture", the standard phrase for the third absorption.</note>

This too, great king, is a fruit of the recluse's life visible here and now, more excellent and more sublime than the visible fruits of the recluse's life described before.

68. And further, great king, with the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the earlier disappearance of joy and sorrow, a monk enters and dwells in the fourth <term>jhāna</term> <gloss>meditative absorption</gloss>, which is neither painful nor pleasant and has a purity of mindfulness born of equanimity. He sits pervading this very body with a pure, bright mind, so that there is no part of his whole body that is not suffused with that pure, bright mind.

Just as, great king, a man might sit wrapped from head to foot in a white cloth, so that there would be no part of his whole body not covered by the white cloth; in just the same way, great king, a monk sits pervading this very body with a pure, bright mind, so that there is no part of his whole body that is not suffused with that pure, bright mind.

This too, great king, is a fruit of the recluse's life visible here and now, more excellent and more sublime than the visible fruits of the recluse's life described before.

69. And further, great king, when his mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of defilements, supple, workable, steady and attained to imperturbability, that monk directs and inclines his mind. <note>In the standard text the mind is directed "to knowledge and vision" (ñāṇadassanāya); that phrase does not appear in the printed text on this page.</note> He understands thus: "This body of mine has form; it is made of the four great elements, born of mother and father, built up out of rice and porridge, and is subject to impermanence, to rubbing and pressing, to breaking up and dispersal. And this consciousness <note>original: "viññāṇa"</note> of mine is supported here and bound up here."

70. Just as, great king, there might be a beautiful beryl gem <note>original: "maṇi veḷuriyo"</note> of the finest water, eight-faceted, well cut, clear, translucent, flawless, perfect in every respect, and through it a thread is strung, blue or yellow or red or white or brown. A man with good eyes, taking it in his hand, would examine it: "This is a beautiful beryl gem of the finest water, eight-faceted, well cut, clear, translucent, flawless, perfect in every respect; and through it a thread is strung, blue or yellow or red or white or brown."

<summary>King Ajātasattu is told of the further fruits of the recluse's life: the happiness of the third absorption and the pure, bright awareness of the fourth, each illustrated by a simile. The monk then turns his concentrated mind to insight, seeing the body as impermanent and consciousness as bound to it, illustrated by the simile of a thread seen through a clear beryl gem.</summary>
<keywords>Samaññaphala Sutta, Fruits of the Recluse's Life, Dīgha Nikāya, Ajātasattu, jhāna, fourth absorption, equanimity, mindfulness, white cloth simile, beryl gem simile, consciousness, viññāṇa, four great elements, impermanence, knowledge and vision, Pali Canon</keywords>

17. අථ වා පන උක්කණ්ඨිතො අනභිරතො සාමණෙරු ච විත්තුකාමො සික්ඛාපදං අක්ඛායමානො හරයමානො ජිගුච්ඡමානො ගිහිභාවං පත්ථයමානො --පෙ-- අසක්කසප්පතිභායමානො පත්ථයමානො ‘මාතා මෙ අත්ථි සා මං පොසෙස්සතී’ති වදති වික්ඛිපෙති, -- ‘පිතා මෙ අත්ථි සො මං පොසෙස්සතී’ති වදති වික්ඛිපෙති, -- ‘භාතා මෙ අත්ථි සො මං පොසෙස්සතී’ති වදති වික්ඛිපෙති, -- ‘භගිනී මෙ අත්ථි සා මං පොසෙස්සතී’ති වදති වික්ඛිපෙති, -- ‘පුත්තො මෙ අත්ථි සො මං පොසෙස්සතී’ති වදති වික්ඛිපෙති, -- ‘ධීතා මෙ අත්ථි සා මං පොසෙස්සතී’ති වදති වික්ඛිපෙති, --- ‘පජාපතී මෙ අත්ථි සා මං පොසෙස්සතී’ති වදති වික්ඛිපෙති, ---‘ඤාතකා මෙ අත්ථි තෙ මං පොසෙස්සන්තී’ති වදති වික්ඛිපෙති, -- ‘මිත්තා මෙ අත්ථි තෙ මං පොසෙස්සන්තී’ති වදති වික්ඛිපෙති,-- ‘ගාමො මෙ අත්ථි තෙතාහං ජීවිස්සාමී’ති වදති වික්ඛිපෙති, -- ‘නිගමො මෙ අත්ථි තෙතාහං ජීවිස්සාමී’ති වදති වික්ඛිපෙති, -- ‘ඛෙත්තං මෙ අත්ථි තෙතාහං ජීවිස්සාමී’ති වදති වික්ඛිපෙති, -- ‘වත්ථු මෙ අත්ථි තෙතාහං ජීවිස්සාමී’ති වදති වික්ඛිපෙති, -- ‘හිරඤ්ඤං මෙ අත්ථි තෙතාහං ජීවිස්සාමී’ති වදති වික්ඛිපෙති, ---‘සුවණ්ණං මෙ අත්ථි තෙතාහං ජීවිස්සාමී’ති වදති වික්ඛිපෙති, -පෙ- ‘සිප්පං මෙ අත්ථි තෙතාහං ජීවිස්සාමී’ති වදති වික්ඛිපෙති, එවම්පි සික්ඛාවෙ දුබ්බල්‍යාවිකම්මක්ඛෙව හොති සික්ඛා ච අපවචක්ඛාතා.

18. අථ වා පන උක්කණ්ඨිතො අනභිරතො සාමණෙරු ච විත්තුකාමො සික්ඛාපදං අක්ඛායමානො හරයමානො ජිගුච්ඡමානො ගිහිභාවං පත්ථයමානො --පෙ-- අසක්කසප්පතිභායමානො පත්ථයමානො ‘දුක්කර’න්ති වදති වික්ඛිපෙති -- ‘කසුකර’න්ති වදති වික්ඛිපෙති, ‘දුබ්බර’න්ති වදති වික්ඛිපෙති, -- ‘න සුවර’න්ති වදති වික්ඛිපෙති, -- ‘න උස්සාහමී’ති වදති වික්ඛිපෙති, -- ‘න විස්සාමී’ති වදති වික්ඛිපෙති, --- ‘න රමාමී’ති වදති වික්ඛිපෙති, -පෙ- ‘න අභිරමාමී’ති වදති වික්ඛිපෙති, එවම්පි බො භික්ඛවෙ දුබ්බල්‍යාවිකම්මක්ඛෙව හොති සික්ඛා ච අපවචක්ඛාතා.

19. කථඤ්ච භික්ඛවෙ දුබ්බල්‍යාවිකම්මක්ඛෙව හොති සික්ඛා ච පවචක්ඛාතා? ඉධ භික්ඛවෙ භික්ඛු උක්කණ්ඨිතො අනභිරතො සාමණෙරු ච විත්තුකාමො සික්ඛාපදං අක්ඛායමානො හරයමානො ජිගුච්ඡමානො ගිහිභාවං පත්ථයමානො -පෙ- අසක්කසප්පතිභායමානො පත්ථයමානො ‘බුද්ධං පවචක්ඛාමී’ති වදති වික්ඛිපෙති, එවම්පි භික්ඛවෙ දුබ්බල්‍යාවිකම්මක්ඛෙව හොති සික්ඛා ච පවචක්ඛාතා.

[context] troubled, ashamed, and disgusted with the monkhood;
[context] longing to be a householder …
[context] longing to be a non-monastic,
he says and declares: ‘What if I renounced the Buddha?’ …
he says and declares: ‘What if I were a non-monastic?’ …
he says and declares: ‘Perhaps I should renounce the Buddha?’ …
he says and declares: ‘Perhaps I should be a non-monastic?’ …
he says and declares: ‘Well then, I should renounce the Buddha.’ …
he says and declares: ‘Well then, I should be a non-monastic.’ …
he says and declares: ‘I think I should renounce the Buddha.’ …
he says and declares: ‘I think I should be a non-monastic.’
In this way too, monks, there’s a revealing of weakness without the training being renounced.
Or again, dissatisfied, discontent, desiring to give up the monastic life;
troubled, ashamed, and disgusted with the monkhood;
longing to be a householder …
longing to be a non-monastic,
he says and declares: ‘I remember my mother.’ …

In this way too, monks, there’s a revealing of weakness without the training being renounced.

# Pārājika Pāḷi - First Pārājika

17. Or furthermore, if a monk is dissatisfied, bored, wanting to leave, and while speaking of the <term>sikkhāpada</term> <gloss>training rules</gloss> feels ashamed, loathes them, and desires the state of a householder <note>meaning he wishes to return to lay life</note>... through various ways of expressing inability, he says and declares: "I have a mother, she will support me," and thus he gives up the training. Or he says and declares: "I have a father, he will support me." He says and declares: "I have a brother, he will support me." He says and declares: "I have a sister, she will support me." He says and declares: "I have a son, he will support me." He says and declares: "I have a daughter, he will support me." He says and declares: "I have a wife, she will support me." He says and declares: "I have relatives, they will support me." He says and declares: "I have friends, they will support me." He says and declares: "I have a village, I will live by means of that." He says and declares: "I have a town, I will live by means of that." He says and declares: "I have a field, I will live by means of that." He says and declares: "I have property, I will live by means of that." He says and declares: "I have gold, I will live by means of that." He says and declares: "I have bullion <note>original: hiraññaṃ; specifically uncoined gold or wealth</note>, I will live by means of that." ... He says and declares: "I have a craft <note>original: sippaṃ; a trade or skill</note>, I will live by means of that." In this way, monks, there is an opening of weakness and the training is renounced.

18. Or furthermore, if a monk is dissatisfied, bored, wanting to leave, and while speaking of the training rule feels ashamed, loathes it, and desires the state of a householder ... through various ways of expressing inability, he says and declares: "It is difficult to do." He says and declares: "It is hard to perform." He says and declares: "It is difficult to maintain." He says and declares: "It is not easy to maintain." He says and declares: "I am not able." He says and declares: "I do not wish to." He says and declares: "I do not find delight." ... He says and declares: "I am not satisfied." In this way too, monks, there is an opening of weakness and the training is renounced.

19. And how, monks, is there an opening of weakness and the training is renounced? Here, monks, a monk is dissatisfied, bored, wanting to leave, and while speaking of the training rule feels ashamed, loathes it, and desires the state of a householder ... through various ways of expressing inability, he says and declares: "I renounce the Buddha." In this way too, monks, there is an opening of weakness and the training is renounced.

<summary>This page details the specific verbal declarations a monk might make to renounce his training, including citing family support, material wealth, or personal inability to endure the monastic life. It establishes the legalistic framework for how a monk formally leaves the order by expressing a preference for lay life or a rejection of the Triple Gem.</summary>

<keywords>renunciation of training, monastic rules, Vinaya, lay life, family support, personal inability, Buddha, Parajika</keywords>

Pārājikapāḷi—The First Defeat

17. Or, if a <term>sāmaṇeru</term> <gloss>novice monk</gloss>, being restless, dissatisfied, wanting to give up, finding the training rules shameful, loathsome, or desiring the lay life—[ellipses]—finding them difficult to practice, says, "I have a mother, she will provide for me," and causes distraction; or, "I have a father, he will provide for me," and causes distraction; or, "I have a brother, he will provide for me," and causes distraction; or, "I have a sister, she will provide for me," and causes distraction; or, "I have a son, he will provide for me," and causes distraction; or, "I have a daughter, she will provide for me," and causes distraction; or, "I have a wife, she will provide for me," and causes distraction; or, "I have relatives, they will provide for me," and causes distraction; or, "I have friends, they will provide for me," and causes distraction; or, "I have a village, I will live from that," and causes distraction; or, "I have a town, I will live from that," and causes distraction; or, "I have fields, I will live from that," and causes distraction; or, "I have property, I will live from that," and causes distraction; or, "I have silver, I will live from that," and causes distraction; or, "I have gold, I will live from that," and causes distraction; [ellipses] or, "I have a craft, I will live from that," and causes distraction. In this way, monks, there is an expression of weakness, and the training is cast aside.

18. Or, if a <term>sāmaṇeru</term> <gloss>novice monk</gloss>, being restless, dissatisfied, wanting to give up, finding the training rules shameful, loathsome, or desiring the lay life—[ellipses]—finding them difficult to practice, says, "It is difficult," and causes distraction; or, "It is tiresome," and causes distraction; "It is unbearable," and causes distraction; or, "It is not easy," and causes distraction; or, "I am unable," and causes distraction; or, "I do not wish to," and causes distraction; or, "I do not find joy," and causes distraction; [ellipses] or, "I do not find pleasure," and causes distraction. In this way, monks, there is an expression of weakness, and the training is cast aside.

19. And how, monks, is there an expression of weakness and the training is officially renounced? Here, monks, a monk <note>referring to the novice context</note> who is restless, dissatisfied, wanting to give up, finding the training rules shameful, loathsome, or desiring the lay life—[ellipses]—finding them difficult to practice, says, "I renounce the Buddha," and causes distraction. In this way, monks, there is an expression of weakness, and the training is officially renounced.

<summary>This page details specific verbal expressions of restlessness and dissatisfaction made by a novice monk that lead to the abandonment of monastic training. It contrasts statements of intent to rely on lay support with the formal renunciation of the Buddha, which constitutes a complete rejection of the monastic path.</summary>
