# But by meditating on the Supreme, that which is hidden is revealed, for from Him come the soul’s bondage and liberation. (3.2.5)

(3.2.5)

Now, it might be argued: the <term>jīva</term> <gloss>individual soul</gloss> is a part of the Supreme Self, just as a spark is a part of a fire. Since this is the case, just as the fire and the spark share the same powers of burning and lighting, so too the individual soul and the Lord should share the powers of knowledge and sovereignty. Consequently, the soul, through its power of knowledge and sovereignty, should be able to create chariots and such in dreams merely by its will.

To this we reply: even though the individual soul and the Lord stand in the relation of part to whole, it is a matter of direct perception that the soul’s nature is opposite to that of the Lord.

But does this mean the soul does not possess the same nature as the Lord at all? No, that is not the case. Though it exists, that nature is hidden <note>original: "tirohita"</note> by the intervention of ignorance and other factors. This hidden nature is revealed only to someone who, through meditating on the Supreme Lord and putting forth effort, has wiped away their darkness—just as the power of sight, obscured by a cataract, is restored by the potency of medicine. This happens by the grace of the Lord to someone who has achieved perfection, not naturally to all living beings. Why? Because from Him, the Lord, come both the bondage and the liberation of this soul. Bondage arises from the lack of knowledge regarding the Lord's true nature, while liberation arises from the knowledge of that nature. Thus says the scripture: "By knowing the Divine, all fetters fall away; with the exhaustion of sufferings, birth and death cease. By meditating on Him, a third state is reached when the body is discarded—universal sovereignty—where one is absolute and has all desires fulfilled" <note>Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 1.11</note>, and so forth.

# Or, that hiding of nature also results from the connection with the body. (3.2.6)

(3.2.6)

But why does the soul, being a part of the Supreme Self, have its knowledge and sovereignty hidden? It would seem more logical for these powers not to be hidden, just as the burning and lighting powers of a spark are not hidden.

We reply: it is true; however, that hiding of the soul's knowledge and sovereignty results from its connection with the body—that is, its connection with the body, the senses, the mind, the intellect, and the experience of objects. There is an analogy for this: just as the burning and lighting powers of a fire, though inherent, become hidden when the fire is latent in wood <note>original: "araṇi"</note> or covered by ash. In the same way, due to the connection with the limiting adjunct of the body—which is produced by Name and Form established through ignorance—the soul's knowledge and sovereignty are hidden by the delusion of failing to discriminate between the soul and the body.

The word "or" <note>original: "vā"</note> in the aphorism is intended to dispel the doubt that the soul is something other than the Lord. One might argue: let the soul be entirely different from the Lord because its knowledge and sovereignty are hidden; why invent the idea of a connection to a body? We say no, for the soul's difference from the Lord is not tenable. Starting with the passage "That divinity thought," the scripture refers to the soul with the word "Self" in "entering by means of this living soul <note>jīva</note> which is my Self." Furthermore, the scripture teaches the soul its identity with the Lord in the statement: "That is the Truth, That is the Self, That Thou Art, O Shvetaketu." Therefore, the soul is non-different from the Lord, but its knowledge and sovereignty are hidden by its connection to the body.

Because of this, it is not possible for the soul to create chariots and so forth in dreams merely by its will. If dream creation were subject to the soul's will, no one would ever see an unpleasant dream, for no one wills what is unpleasant for themselves. As for the argument that the scripture describes the dream state as being like the waking state to show its reality: that comparison is not intended to suggest reality, as that would contradict the soul's nature as "self-luminous" and the scriptural declaration that there are no actual chariots in dreams. Rather, since dreams are caused by the impressions <note>vāsana</note> arising from the waking state, the comparison merely indicates that the dream appears similar to it. Therefore, it is established that the dream is <term>māyā-mātra</term> <gloss>mere illusion</gloss>.

# The absence of that dream occurs in the channels and in the Self, according to scripture. (3.2.7)

**Section on the Absence of Dreams (Deep Sleep)** (3.2.7)

The state of dreaming has been examined; the state of deep sleep <term>suṣupti</term> is now examined. Regarding that, there are these scriptural passages concerning deep sleep. In one place it is said: "Now when he is thus asleep, composed, serene, and knows no dream, then he has entered these <term>nāḍī</term> <gloss>subtle channels</gloss>" <note>Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.6.3</note>. Elsewhere, referring to the same channels, it says: "Having moved through them, he rests in the <term>purītat</term> <gloss>pericardium or membrane surrounding the heart</gloss>" <note>Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.1.19</note>. Similarly, elsewhere after mentioning the channels: "In them he then remains when, being asleep, he sees no dream; then he becomes one with this <term>prāṇa</term> <gloss>vital breath/life-force</gloss> alone." In another place: "He sleeps in the space within the heart." In another: "Then, my dear, he is united with the Existent, he has gone to his own Self." And: "Embraced by the Intelligent Self, he knows nothing without and nothing within."

On this point, a doubt arises: are these locations—the channels and so forth—distinct and independent places for deep sleep, or are they mutually related parts of a single location for deep sleep? What is the initial view? That they are distinct. Why? Because they serve the same purpose—and things that serve the same purpose are never mutually dependent...

<summary>Shankara explains that the soul's divine powers are hidden by its association with the body and ignorance, meaning dreams are illusory and not creations of the soul's will. The text then transitions to discussing the location of the soul during deep sleep (susupti) based on various Upanishadic passages.</summary>

# Because of meditating on the Supreme, its powers are obscured; from that, indeed, come the soul's bondage and liberation. || 3.2.5 ||

|| 3.2.5 ||

It might be argued: the individual soul <term>jiva</term> is merely a part of the Supreme Self <term>para-atman</term>, like a spark from a fire. In that case, just as a fire and its sparks possess the same power of burning and illumination, the individual soul and the Lord <term>Ishvara</term> should both possess the powers of knowledge and sovereignty. Consequently, the soul would be capable of creating chariots and other objects in a dream through the mere power of its will <term>sankalpiki</term>. To this, we reply: while it is true that the individual soul and the Lord have a part-and-whole relationship, the fact that the soul possesses qualities contrary to those of the Lord is a matter of direct perception. Does the soul then lack the qualities of the Lord entirely? No, it is not that they are entirely absent; they exist, but are obscured by the obstruction of ignorance <term>avidya</term> and the like. This obscured power only manifests in a creature who, while meditating on the Supreme Lord and exerting the mind, has cleansed away the darkness—much like the power of vision, obscured by cataracts, is restored by the potency of medicine—and this happens only to those who have become perfected through the grace of the Lord, not to all creatures by nature. Why is this? Because from that, from the Lord as the cause, depend the bondage and liberation of this soul; bondage arises from the lack of knowledge of the Lord’s nature, and liberation arises from the knowledge of that nature. The scripture also says: "By knowing the Divine, all fetters fall away; with the fading of afflictions, birth and death cease. Through meditation on Him, in the third state at the dissolution of the body, one attains universal sovereignty and becomes fulfilled" <note>This refers to the Shvetashvatara Upanishad 1.11</note>, and so on.

# Or because of the connection to the body, that too. || 3.2.6 ||

|| 3.2.6 ||

Why then does the individual soul, while being a part of the Supreme Self, have its knowledge and sovereignty obscured? It is logical that knowledge and sovereignty should remain un-obscured, just as burning and illumination are in a spark of fire. We answer: this is true; however, that obscuration of the soul's knowledge and sovereignty occurs because of the connection to the body—the connection to the body, senses, mind, intellect, and the experience of objects. There is an analogy for this: just as the power of burning and illumination in a fire, though inherent, is obscured when it is contained within a piece of wood, or when it is covered by ashes, in the same way, the obscuration of the soul's knowledge and sovereignty arises from the connection to the limiting adjuncts <term>upadhi</term>—the body, name, and form—which are set up by ignorance, and from the confusion caused by distinguishing the soul from these. The word "or" <term>va</term> is used to ward off the doubt that the soul is distinct from the Lord. But, one might ask, could the soul be something other than the Lord, precisely because its knowledge and sovereignty are obscured; why posit a connection to the body? We reply: no, it is not reasonable for the soul to be other than the Lord. The scripture begins with "That Deity thought" <note>Referring to Chandogya Upanishad 6.3.2</note> and continues with "having entered by this individual soul as the self," referring to the soul with the word "Self" <term>atman</term>. Furthermore, it instructs the soul in its lordship, saying, "That is the Truth, that is the Self, That Thou Art, O Shvetaketu." Therefore, the soul is non-different from the Lord, and it is only because of the connection to the body that its knowledge and sovereignty are obscured. Consequently, the creation of chariots and such in a dream by the soul's will does not hold. If the creation of chariots in a dream were truly a matter of will, no one would ever experience an unpleasant dream, for no one wills an unpleasant thing. Regarding the argument that the scriptural mention of the waking state proves the reality of the dream state, such a comparison does not imply equal reality, as that would contradict the soul's nature as self-luminous, and the scripture itself shows the absence of actual chariots in a dream. Such a comparison is intended to show that the dream is like the waking state because it is caused by latent impressions <term>vasana</term> from the waking state. Therefore, it is established that the dream is mere illusion <term>maya-matram</term>.

# Its absence is in the channels, according to scripture, and in the Self. || 3.2.7 ||

The Section on Its Absence || 3.2.7 ||

The dream state has been examined; now the deep sleep state <term>sushupti</term> is being examined. There are these scriptural passages concerning deep sleep: in one place, it is heard, "When a person is thus asleep, fully integrated and serene, not knowing any dream, then he is asleep in the channels <term>nadi</term>." In another place, specifically mentioning the channels, it is heard, "Having glided through them, he rests in the pericardium <term>puritat</term>." Similarly, in another place, after mentioning the channels, it says, "He remains in them when he is asleep and does not see any dream, and then he becomes unified in the Vital Breath <term>prana</term> alone." Likewise, in another place, "He rests in that space which is within the heart." In another, "O Saumya, at that time he becomes united with the Being; he has attained his own Self." And also, "Embraced by the Prajna-Self, he knows nothing external or internal."

A doubt arises here: are these—the channels and the others—separate places of deep sleep independent of each other, or are they a single place of deep sleep, depending on one another? What is the conclusion? They are separate, because, since they have the same purpose, there is no interdependence between them.

<summary>Shankara explains that the soul's limited knowledge is an effect of its identification with the body, which obscures its inherent divine nature. He then transitions to the analysis of deep sleep, questioning whether various scriptural locations for this state—the channels, the heart, the pericardium, or the Supreme Being—are independent or unified.</summary>
<keywords>Jiva, Ishvara, Avidya, Upadhi, Obscuration, Deep Sleep, Sushupti, Nadi, Puritat, Prana</keywords>

# But from meditating on the Supreme, that which is obscured; from that, the bondage and liberation of this one occur. 3.2.5.

It might be argued: The individual soul (<term>jiva</term> <gloss>individual consciousness</gloss>) is merely a part of the Supreme Self, like a spark from a fire. If this is so, just as the spark shares the same power of burning and illuminating as the fire, the individual soul and the Lord (<term>ishvara</term> <gloss>the Supreme Ruler</gloss>) must share the powers of knowledge and sovereignty. Consequently, through the power of its knowledge and sovereignty, the individual soul would be able to create chariots and other objects in a dream through mere will. 

To this, we reply: While the relationship between the individual soul and the Lord is that of part and whole, the individual soul's possession of qualities opposite to those of the Lord is a matter of direct experience. Does this mean the individual soul lacks the qualities of the Lord entirely? No, it does not lack them. Though they exist, they are obscured by the veil of ignorance (<term>avidya</term> <gloss>primordial ignorance</gloss>) and similar factors. 

This obscured power manifests only in a being who strives, who meditates on the Supreme Lord, and whose darkness has been dispelled—just as the power of sight, obscured by a cataract, becomes clear through the strength of medicine. It manifests through the grace of the Lord, not by nature for all beings. Why? Because it is from that cause, the Lord, that the bondage and liberation of this soul occur; bondage arises from not knowing the nature of the Lord, and liberation arises from knowing that nature. Thus, the scripture says: "By knowing the Divine, all fetters fall away; with the fading of afflictions, birth and death cease. Through meditation on Him, the third state <note>referring to the state beyond waking and dreaming</note> is attained at the dissolution of the body, where one becomes the master of all and reaches all desires."

# Or it is so because of connection with a body. 3.2.6.

Why is the individual soul, being a part of the Supreme Self, one whose knowledge and sovereignty are obscured? It is logical that these powers should remain unobscured, as the power of a spark to burn and illuminate remains. We respond: This is true. However, the obscuration of the soul's knowledge and sovereignty occurs because of its connection with a body—the connection with the body, senses, mind, intellect, and the experience of objects. 

There is an analogy here: just as the burning and illuminating powers of fire, even though present, become obscured when the fire is contained within a piece of wood, or covered by ashes, so too does the obscuration of the soul's knowledge and sovereignty occur due to its connection with the body, which is composed of names and forms created by ignorance, and the resulting confusion of identity. The word "or" <term>va</term> is used to address the doubt regarding the soul being distinct from the Lord. 

If one suggests that the soul is indeed distinct from the Lord because its knowledge and sovereignty are obscured, and that we need not postulate a connection to a body, we say: No. The distinctness of the soul from the Lord is not tenable. The text begins with "That Deity perceived" and continues, "I shall enter these beings with this individual soul" <note>original: "Anena jivenatmana anupravishya"</note>, referring to the soul as the Self. Furthermore, it instructs the soul in its divinity: "That is the Truth, that is the Self, you are That, O Shvetaketu." Therefore, the soul is non-different from the Lord, but it becomes one whose knowledge and sovereignty are obscured due to its connection with a body. 

Because of this, the creation of chariots and other objects in a dream by the soul's will is not possible. If the creation in a dream were merely by will, no one would see an unpleasant dream, for no one wills what is undesirable. As for the argument that the experience of the waking world proves the reality of the dream world, that comparison is not intended to suggest reality, as it would contradict the soul's nature as self-luminous, and the scripture itself shows the absence of chariots and such in a dream. That comparison simply means the dream is similar to the waking state because it is caused by impressions (<term>vasana</term> <gloss>subconscious tendencies</gloss>) resulting from waking experiences. Therefore, the conclusion that the dream is mere illusion (<term>maya-matra</term> <gloss>only an appearance</gloss>) is well-founded.

# Its absence is in the channels, the heart-membrane, and the Self, according to scripture. 3.2.7.

The Section on its Absence.

The state of dreaming has been examined. Now, the state of deep sleep (<term>sushupti</term> <gloss>dreamless sleep</gloss>) is examined. There are various scriptural passages regarding deep sleep. In one place, it is heard: "When this person is asleep, having become completely serene, and knows no dream, he has entered these channels (<term>nadi</term> <gloss>subtle energy channels</gloss>)." In another place, having mentioned the channels, it is heard: "Having moved through them, he rests in the heart-membrane (<term>puritat</term> <gloss>the pericardium</gloss>)." Elsewhere, after mentioning the channels: "He abides in them when he is asleep and sees no dreams; then in this very vital force (<term>prana</term> <gloss>life breath</gloss>) he becomes one." Elsewhere: "He rests in that space which is within the heart." Elsewhere: "O gentle one, then he becomes united with the Pure Being, he attains his own nature." And also: "Embraced by the intelligent Self, he knows nothing external or internal." 

Here is the doubt: Are these—the channels and the rest—separate places for deep sleep, independent of one another, or is there one place for deep sleep, with them being mutually dependent? What is the initial position? They are separate, because they serve the same purpose, and things serving the same purpose are never found to be mutually dependent anywhere...

## ततो मनोजवित्वं विकरण-
## भावः प्रधानजयश्च ॥ ४८ ॥

कायस्यानुत्तमो गतिलाभो मनोजवित्वम् । विदेहाना-
मिन्द्रियाणामभिप्रेतदेशकालविषयापेक्षो वृत्तिलाभो विकरण-
भावः । सर्वप्रकृतिविकारवशित्वं प्रधानजय इत्येतास्तिस्रः
सिद्धयो मधुप्रतीका उच्यन्ते । एताश्च करणपञ्चरूपजयाद-
धिगम्यन्ते ॥ ४८ ॥

## सत्त्वपुरुषान्यताख्यातिमा-
## त्रस्य सर्वभावाधिष्ठातृत्वं
## सर्वज्ञातृत्वं च ॥ ४९ ॥

निर्धूतरजस्तमोमलस्य बुद्धिसत्त्वस्य परे वैशारद्ये परस्यां
वशीकारसंज्ञायां वर्तमानस्य सत्त्वपुरुषान्यताख्यातिमात्ररूपप्र-
तिष्ठस्य सर्वभावाधिष्ठातृत्वम् । सर्वात्मानो गुणा व्यवसायव्य-

---

पञ्चरूपेन्द्रियजयात्सिद्धीराह—**ततो मनोजवित्वं विकरणभावः प्रधानज-
यश्च ।** विदेहानामिन्द्रियाणां करणभावो विकरणभावः । देशः काश्मीरादिः ।
कालोऽतीतादिः । विषयः सूक्ष्मादिः । सोन्वयेन्द्रियजयात्सर्वप्रकृतिविकारवशित्वं
प्रधानजयः । ता एताः सिद्धयो मधुप्रतीका इत्युच्यन्ते योगशास्त्रनिष्णातैः ।
स्यादेतदिन्द्रियजयादिन्द्रियाणि सविषयाणि वश्यानि भवन्तु, प्रधानादीनां तत्कार-
णानां किमायातमित्यत आह—**एताश्चेति ।** करणानामिन्द्रियाणां पञ्च रूपाणि ग्रह-
णादीनि तेषां जयात् । एतदुक्तं भवति—नेन्द्रियमात्रजयस्यैताः सिद्धयोऽपि तु पञ्च-
रूपस्य तदन्तर्गतं च प्रधानादीति ॥ ४८ ॥

त एते ज्ञानक्रियारूपैश्वर्यहेतवः संयमाः साक्षात्पारम्पर्येण च स्वसिद्धयुपसंहार-
संपादितश्रद्धाद्वारेण यदर्थास्तस्याः सत्त्वपुरुषान्यताख्यातेरवान्तरविभूतीर्दर्शयति—
**सत्त्वपुरुषान्यताख्यातिमात्रस्य सर्वभावाधिष्ठातृत्वं सर्वज्ञातृत्वं च ।** निर्धूतर-
जस्तमोमलतया वैशारद्यं ततः परा वशीकारसंज्ञा रजस्तमोभ्यामुपप्लुतं हि चित्तसत्त्वम-
वश्यमासीत्तदुपशमे तु तद्वश्यं योगिनो वशिनस्तस्मिन्वश्ये योगिनः सत्त्वपुरुषान्यता-
ख्यातिमात्ररूपप्रतिष्ठस्य सर्वभावाधिष्ठातृत्वम् । एतदेव विवृणोति—**सर्वात्मान इति ।**

48. As a result of this [there follows] speed [great as that] of the central-organ, action of the instruments of [knowledge] disjunct [from the body], and the subjugation of the primary-cause.

Speed of the mind means that the body acquires motion comparable [to that] of the mind. Action of the instruments of knowledge disjunct [from the body] is the acquisition by the discarnate organs of the fluctuation required for the place and time and object desired. Subjugation of the primary cause is the mastery over all evolving causes and evolved effects. These three perfections are called Honey-Faced (rnadhupratika). And they are acquired as the result of the subjugation in five forms of instruments [of perception].

He describes the perfections which result from the subjugation, in five kinds, of the organs. 48. As a result of this .... and the subjugation. The fact that the organs are instruments [of perception] even for the discarnate is described as being the action of the instruments [of perception] disjunct [from the body].

The place is Kashmir or some other [place]. The time is the past or some other [time]. The object is subtile or other. As a result of the subjugation of the organ and of the inherence, [there follows] mastery of all evolving-causes and evolved-effects, a subjugation of the primary cause. These perfections are called Honey- Faced by those persons who are expert in the yoga system. An objector says 'This may be true. By subjugation of the organs, the organs together with their objects may be mastered. But what is gained [by subjugation] of the primary cause and the other causes of these [organs] ? ' In reply to this he says «And they.» The instruments [of perception] are the organs. The five forms are [the five] processes-of-knowing [iii. 47]. [The result follows] from the subjugation of these. What he means to say is this : These perfections are not- a result of a subjugation of organs in general but of the five forms [of the processes-of-knowing]. And included in these [five] is the primary-cause and the rest.

49. He who has only the full discernment into the difference between the sattva and the Self is one who has authority over all states-of-existence and is one who knows all.

He who is grounded in only the full discernment into the difference between the sattva and the Self, and who is in the higher consciousness of being master in the higher clearness, and who has the sattva of his thinking-substance cleansed from the defilement of rajas and tamas is one who has authority over all states-of-existence. The aspects (guna) which are the essence of all things, which have both the determinations and the objects-of-determinations as their essence, present themselves as being the essence of the object-for-sight in its totality to their Owner, the Soul (ksetrajna). This is the meaning. — Being <one who knows alb refers to the [intuitive] knowledge, produced by discrimination and rising instantaneously [into consciousness], of the aspects (guna) which are the essence of all, whether they be [iii. 14] quiescent or uprisen or indeterminable. This is the meaning. It is this perfection that is termed [i. 36] the ' undistressed,' by attaining to which the yogin who knows all, whose hindrances and bondages have dwindled, takes his recreation as having mastery.

These same constraints, Which whether mediately or immediately lead to powers in the form of knowledge and of activity, are for the sake of the discernment into the difference between the sattva and the Self by way of the confidence produced by grasping the perfections in turn and binding them together. The supernormal powers subsidiary to this [discernment] are shown [in the sutra]. 49. Sattva . . . and. There is clearness in so far as the defilement by rajas and tamas has been washed away. As a result of this there is the higher consciousness of being master. It was inevitable that the sattva of the mind-stuff should be overwhelmed by the rajas and tamas. But when the latter subside, it is this [sattva] that is to be mastered by the yogin its master. When it is mastered, the yogin who is grounded in only the full discernment of the difference between the sattva and the Self, is one who has authority over all states-of-existence. This same he explains by the words «essence of all things.»

The attainment of unsurpassed speed of movement for the body is <term>manojavitvam</term> <gloss>speed of mind</gloss>. Mastery over all transformations of nature <note>original: prakṛti-vikāra</note> is <term>pradhānajayaḥ</term> <gloss>mastery over primary matter</gloss>. These three accomplishments are called <term>madhupratīkā</term> <gloss>honey-like reflections</gloss>. These are attained from the mastery over the five forms of the instruments of perception. (48)

At this stage, they gain sovereignty over all states of existence. All qualities <note>term: guṇas</note>, which constitute the essence of all things, become...

<column-break/>

He explains the accomplishments resulting from the mastery of the five forms of the senses: **From that comes speed of mind, perception without bodily organs, and mastery over primary matter.** <term>Vikaraṇabhāvaḥ</term> is the state of the senses acting without the body. Place refers to regions such as Kashmir; time refers to the past and other periods; objects refer to subtle things and the like. Through the mastery of the senses in their generic form <note>original: anvaya</note>, one gains mastery over primary matter, which is control over all transformations of nature. These accomplishments are called the honey-like reflections by those expert in the science of Yoga. One might ask: if through the mastery of the senses, the senses and their objects become controlled, how does this relate to primary matter <note>term: pradhāna</note> and other causes? The meaning is this: these accomplishments do not come from mastery of the senses alone, but from mastery of the five forms which include primary matter and its constituents. (48)

These meditations <note>term: saṃyamas</note> are the causes of power in the form of knowledge and action. Having established faith by producing their respective accomplishments, he now shows the intermediate glories of that very discernment of the difference between pure intelligence and the Self for which the meditations are performed: **To one who is established in the discernment of the difference between the pure intelligence and the Self, belongs sovereignty over all states of existence and omniscience.** Lucidity <note>term: vaiśāradya</note> arises from the removal of the stains of passion and darkness. Then comes the supreme consciousness of mastery. Indeed, when the mind-stuff is overwhelmed by passion and darkness, it is not under control; but when these are subsided, it comes under the control of the yogi who is a master. In that state of control, for the yogi established in the discernment of the difference between intelligence and the Self, sovereignty over all states occurs. ## From that comes speed of mind, the state of having disembodied senses, and mastery over the primal matter ॥ 48 ॥

Speed of mind is the attainment of incomparable motion for the body. The state of having disembodied senses is the attainment of the function of the senses in accordance with the desired place, time, and object. Mastery over the primal matter is the state of having control over all modifications of nature. These three accomplishments are called <term>madhupratīkā</term> <gloss>honey-like or sweet-symbolized</gloss>. These are attained through the conquest of the five forms of the senses ॥ 48 ॥

## For one established solely in the discriminative discernment between the pure conscious principle and the sattva-aspect of mind, there is sovereignty over all states of existence and omniscience ॥ 49 ॥

For one who remains in the state where the pure conscious principle is distinguished from the <term>sattva</term> <gloss>the luminous or purity-aspect of mind</gloss>—which has been cleansed of the impurities of <term>rajas</term> <gloss>activity/passion</gloss> and <term>tamas</term> <gloss>inertia/darkness</gloss>—having attained the supreme clarity and the final stage of detachment, there is sovereignty over all states of being. All modifications of nature <column-break/>
The author speaks of the accomplishments arising from the conquest of the five forms of the senses: **From that comes speed of mind, the state of having disembodied senses, and mastery over the primal matter.** The state of the senses being disembodied refers to their capacity to function without the physical body. Place refers to regions like Kashmir and others. Time refers to the past and other periods. Object refers to subtle objects and so forth. These accomplishments are termed <term>madhupratīkā</term> by those expert in the science of yoga. One might ask: if the senses are conquered and become subservient along with their objects, what does this have to do with the primal matter and its causes? Speed of mind is the attainment of incomparable motion for the body. Independence from the body is the attainment of the function of the sense organs—regardless of location, time, or object—as desired. Mastery over nature is the power over all modifications of primordial nature. These three accomplishments are called the *madhu-pratīkā* <gloss>honey-like or sweet-symbolic</gloss>. These are attained through the mastery of the five forms of the senses || 48 ||

## Only for the one who possesses the discernment of the distinction between the purity of consciousness and the self, there is supremacy over all states of existence and omniscience || 49 ||

For one whose intellect-consciousness is cleansed of the impurities of passion and inertia, who resides in the highest clarity and the supreme state of mastery, and whose firm foundation is solely the discernment of the distinction between the purity of consciousness <term>sattva</term> <gloss>the luminous aspect of nature</gloss> and the Self <term>puruṣa</term> <gloss>the conscious observer</gloss>, there is supremacy over all states. All selves are qualities, and the activity...

<column-break/>

The author presents the accomplishments arising from the mastery of the five forms of the senses: **From that, speed of mind, independence from the body, and mastery over nature.** Independence from the body is the state of the sense organs being independent of the physical form. Location refers to places like Kashmir; time refers to the past and future; objects refer to subtle entities and so forth. Mastery over nature is power over all modifications of primordial nature, achieved through the mastery of the senses. Those who are expert in the science of Yoga call these accomplishments the *madhu-pratīkā* <gloss>honey-like</gloss>. One might ask: let the senses and their objects be mastered through the mastery of the senses, but what has this to do with primordial nature and its causes? The author replies: **These are [attained through the mastery of the five forms].** This refers to the mastery of the five forms of the sense organs, such as grasping. The meaning is this: these accomplishments do not arise merely from the mastery of the senses, but from the mastery of their five forms, which include the primary causes like primordial nature || 48 ||

These are the means of achieving power in the form of knowledge and action. Through self-control, whether direct or through the succession of faith established by the attainment of these results, the author shows the intermediate manifestations of that discernment of the distinction between the purity of consciousness and the Self: **Only for the one who possesses the discernment of the distinction between the purity of consciousness and the self, there is supremacy over all states of existence and omniscience.** Clarity arises from the removal of the impurities of passion and inertia. From that comes the supreme state of mastery. The conscious mind was previously subject to passion and inertia, but upon their cessation, it becomes subject to the yogi who has attained self-control. For the yogi established in this state, who has no other foundation but the discernment of the distinction between the purity of consciousness and the Self, there is supremacy over all states of existence. The author explains this: **All selves are qualities...**

Independence of the senses is the attainment of the activity of the senses, whether they are separated from the body <note>original: "videha"</note> or not, dependent upon the desired place, time, and object. Mastery over the primal source is the control over all the modifications of the primary matter <term>prakṛti</term> <gloss>the fundamental creative force</gloss>. These three accomplishments are called "honey-like" <note>original: "madhu-pratīkā"</note>. They are attained through the mastery of the five forms of the sense-organs. ॥ 48 ॥

All beings are qualities <term>guṇas</term>, which are essentially business and...

He speaks of the accomplishments arising from the mastery of the five forms of the senses: **"From that comes speed of mind, independence of the senses, and mastery over the primal source."** The sense-organ's condition when separated from the body is the "independence of the senses." "Place" means places like Kashmir. "Time" means past time and the rest. "Object" means subtle objects and the rest. Following that, mastery over the primal source is control over all modifications of the primary matter. These accomplishments are called "honey-like" by those learned in the science of yoga.

This means: these accomplishments are not merely from mastery of the sense-organ itself, but of its five forms, and included within that is the primary source and its derivatives. ॥ 48 ॥

He shows the secondary powers <term>vibhūti</term> of that discernment between the pure intellect and the Self—which is the goal of those <term>saṃyamas</term> that are the causes of power in the form of knowledge and action—by showing it to be the fruit of the faith accomplished by one's own mastery: **"For one established only in the discernment between the pure intellect and the Self, there arises lordship over all states and omniscience."** "Clarity" comes from the removal of the impurities of activity and inertia. From that comes the "highest state of mastery." For the mind-stuff <term>citta-sattva</term> was certainly subservient when clouded by activity and inertia. But upon their cessation, when it is subservient to the yogi who has mastery, there arises in that yogi, who is established solely in the discernment between the pure intellect and the Self, lordship over all states. He clarifies this: **"All beings are..."**

## Thence comes speed of mind, the state of bodilessness, and mastery over the primal cause. ॥ 48 ॥

The state of bodilessness is the attainment of the functions of the sense organs—independent of the body—in relation to desired locations, times, and objects. Mastery over the primal cause is the control over all modifications of nature. These three accomplishments are called "honey-like" <note>This term, <term>madhupratīkā</term>, refers to a stage of yogic attainment where the fruits of practice become sweet or pleasant.</note>. For one whose intelligence has been cleansed of the impurities of <term>rajas</term> <gloss>activity/passion</gloss> and <term>tamas</term> <gloss>inertia/darkness</gloss>, who is established in supreme clarity, who remains in the state of total self-mastery, and who is fixed solely in the discriminative discernment between the intelligence <note>The <term>buddhi-sattva</term>, the purest form of cognitive faculty.</note> and the pure self <note>The <term>puruṣa</term> or conscious witness.</note>, there arises sovereignty over all states of existence. Location is <note>places like</note> Kashmir and so on. Time is the past and so on. Object is the subtle <note>elements</note> and so on. Through the mastery of the senses in their connection <note>to these objects</note>, there arises control over all modifications of nature; this is mastery over the primal cause. These accomplishments are called "honey-like" by those learned in the science of Yoga.

One might ask: "If there is mastery over the senses, the senses with their objects may be under control, but what follows for their causes, like the primal cause?" He replies: **"These are..."** This refers to the mastery of the five forms of the instruments, that is, the senses, such as the act of grasping. The meaning is this: these accomplishments are not merely from the mastery of the sense organs alone, but from the mastery of <note>their</note> five forms, which include their causes, beginning with the primal cause. ॥ 48 ॥

He now indicates the secondary manifestations of that discriminative discernment between the intelligence and the pure self—the object for which those forms of <term>saṃyama</term> <gloss>concentrated meditation</gloss>, which are the causes of knowledge, action, and lordship, are performed, either directly or indirectly through the faith produced by the realization of one's own accomplishments: **"For one established solely in the discriminative discernment between the intelligence and the pure self, there arises sovereignty over all states of existence and omniscience."** Through the removal of the impurities of <term>rajas</term> and <term>tamas</term>, clarity arises. From that, <note>there arises</note> the supreme state of self-mastery. The mind, <note>which is</note> intelligence, was previously overwhelmed by <term>rajas</term> and <term>tamas</term> and was therefore not under control. Upon the pacification of those <note>impurities</note>, it becomes subject to the control of the yogi who has attained mastery. In that state of mastery, for the yogi who is fixed solely in the discernment between the intelligence and the pure self, there arises sovereignty over all states of existence. He explains this: **"The constituents of nature, which comprise all..."**

<vocab>Manojavitva (speed of mind), Vikaraṇabhāva (state of bodilessness), Pradhānajaya (mastery over the primal cause), Sattvapuruṣānyatākhyāti (discriminative discernment between intelligence and pure self), Sarvabhāvādhiṣṭhātṛtva (sovereignty over all states of existence), Sarvajñātṛtva (omniscience), Madhupratīkā (honey-like/sweet attainments), Vaiśāradya (clarity/purity of mind).</vocab>

<summary>This page explains the yogic accomplishments—speed of mind, bodilessness, and mastery over nature—attained by mastering the five forms of the senses, followed by the omniscience and sovereignty gained through total discernment between the intelligence and the self.</summary>
<keywords>Yoga Sutras, Patañjali, Vibhuti Pada, sense mastery, discriminative discernment, omniscience, siddhis</keywords>

Patañjali’s Yoga Sūtras

## From that comes speed of mind, the state of having disembodied senses, and mastery over the primal matter ॥ 48 ॥

Speed of mind is the attainment of incomparable motion for the body. The state of having disembodied senses is the attainment of the function of the disembodied senses in accordance with the desired place, time, and object. Mastery over the primal matter is the state of having control over all modifications of nature. These three accomplishments are called <term>madhupratīkā</term> <gloss>honey-like or sweet-symbolized</gloss>. These are attained through the conquest of the five forms of the senses ॥ 48 ॥

## For one established solely in the discriminative discernment between the pure conscious principle and the sattva-aspect of mind, there is sovereignty over all states of existence and omniscience ॥ 49 ॥

For one who remains in the state where the pure conscious principle is distinguished from the <term>sattva</term> <gloss>the luminous or purity-aspect of mind</gloss>—which has been cleansed of the impurities of <term>rajas</term> <gloss>activity/passion</gloss> and <term>tamas</term> <gloss>inertia/darkness</gloss>—having attained the supreme clarity and the final stage of detachment, there is sovereignty over all states of being. The qualities, in the form of <column-break/>
The author speaks of the accomplishments arising from the conquest of the five forms of the senses: **From that comes speed of mind, the state of having disembodied senses, and mastery over the primal matter.** The state of the senses being disembodied refers to their capacity to function without the physical body. Place refers to regions like Kashmir and others. Time refers to the past and other periods. Object refers to subtle objects and so forth. Conquest of the primal matter is the state of having control over all modifications of nature through the conquest of the senses connected with them. These accomplishments are termed <term>madhupratīkā</term> by those expert in the science of yoga. One might ask: if the senses are conquered and become subservient along with their objects, what does this have to do with the primal matter and its causes? To this, he replies: **These are attained through the conquest of the five forms.** This refers to the five forms of the senses, such as grasping and others. The meaning is this: these accomplishments do not arise from the conquest of the senses alone, but from the conquest of the five forms, which include the primal matter and its derivatives within them ॥ 48 ॥

These are the <term>samyamas</term> <gloss>concentrated practices</gloss> that are the causes of power in the form of knowledge and action. By directly or indirectly establishing faith, they lead to the intermediate manifestations of that discriminative discernment between the pure conscious principle and the <term>sattva</term>-aspect of mind, which is the ultimate goal. He explains: **For one established solely in the discriminative discernment between the pure conscious principle and the sattva-aspect of mind, there is sovereignty over all states of existence and omniscience.** Clarity arises from the removal of the impurities of <term>rajas</term> and <term>tamas</term>. Following this comes the supreme state of detachment. The mind-stuff was previously overwhelmed by <term>rajas</term> and <term>tamas</term> and was not under control. When these are stilled, the yogi who has attained mastery establishes the mind solely in the discernment between the pure conscious principle and the <term>sattva</term>-aspect of mind, leading to sovereignty over all states of existence. He clarifies this: **All modifications of nature...**

PEACEFUL LIFE.

Mazgusri, the prince royal, said to the Lord: It is difficult, Lord, most difficult, what these Bodhisattvas Mahasattvas will attempt out of reverence for the Lord. How are these Bodhisattvas MahAsattvas to promulgate this Dharmaparydya at the end of time, at the last period? Whereupon the Lord answered Mazgusri, the prince royal: A Bodhisattva Mahasattva, Mazgusri, he who is to promulgate this Dharmaparydya at the end of time, at the last period, must be firm in four things. In which things? The Bodhisattva Mahasattva, Ma#gusri, must be firm in his conduct and proper sphere if he wishes to teach this Dharmaparyaya. And how, Maggusri, is a Bodhisattva Mahasattva firm in his conduct and proper sphere? When the Bodhisattva Mahdsattva, Ma#gusri, is patient, meek, has reached the stage of meekness ; when he is not rash, nor envious; when, moreover, Mazigusri, he clings to no law whatever and sees the real character of the laws (or things) ; when he is refraining from investigating and discussing these laws, Mazigusri; that is called the conduct of a Bodhisattva Mahasattva. And what is the proper sphere of a Bodhisattva Mahdsattva, Mazgusri ? When the Bodhisattva Mahasattva, Ma#gusri, does not serve, not court, not wait upon kings; does not serve, not court, not wait upon princes; when he does not approach them; when he does not serve, not court, not wait upon persons of another sect, Aarakas, Parivragakas, Agivakas, Nirgranthas, nor persons passionately fond of fine literature; when he does not serve, not court, not wait upon adepts at worldly spells, and votaries of a worldly philosophy, nor keep any intercourse with them ; when he does not go to see KAndalas, jugglers, vendors of pork, poulterers, deer-hunters, butchers, actors and dancers, wrestlers, nor resort to places whither others flock for amusement and sport; when he keeps no intercourse with them unless from time to time to preach the law to them when they come to him, and that freely; when he does not serve, not court, not wait upon monks, nuns, lay devotees, male and female, who are adherents of the vehicle of disciples, nor keep intercourse with them ; when he does not come in contact with them at the place of promenade or in the monastery, unless from time to time to preach the law to them when they come to him, and even that freely. This, Mazgusri, is the proper sphere of a Bodhisattva Mahdasattva.

Again, Maagusri, the Bodhisattva Mahdasattva does not take hold of some favourable opportunity or another to preach the law to females every now and anon, nor is he desirous of repeatedly seeing females ; nor does he think it proper to visit families and then too often address a girl, virgin, or young wife, nor does he greet them too fondly in return. He does not preach the law to a hermaphrodite, keeps no intercourse with such a person, nor greets too friendly in return. He does not enter a house alone in order to receive alms, unless having the Tathagata in his thoughts. And when he happens to preach the law to females, he does not do so by passionate attachment to the law, far less by passionate attachment to a woman. When he is preaching, he does not display his row of teeth, let alone a quick emotion on his physiognomy. He addresses no novice, male or female, no nun, no monk, no young boy, no young girl, nor enters upon a conversation with them; he shows no great readiness in answering their address, nor cares to give too frequent answers. This, Ma#gusri, is called the first proper sphere of a Bodhisattva Mahasattva.

->13. The Chapter on the Peaceful Practices<-

<margin>K 275</margin>
N 180
W 235
Then <term>Manjushri</term> <gloss>the Bodhisattva of Wisdom</gloss>, who is ever youthful, addressed the Blessed One: "It is difficult, Blessed One, extremely difficult, what these <term>Bodhisattvas</term> <gloss>beings dedicated to enlightenment</gloss> and <term>Mahasattvas</term> <gloss>great beings</gloss> have undertaken out of reverence for the Blessed One. How, Blessed One, should this <term>Dharmaparyaya</term> <gloss>religious discourse or exposition of the Law</gloss> be proclaimed by these Bodhisattvas and Mahasattvas in the later times, in the final age?"

When this was said, the Blessed One spoke to Manjushri, the youthful: "Manjushri, a Bodhisattva and Mahasattva who is established in four qualities should proclaim this religious discourse in the later times and in the final age. Which four? In this regard, Manjushri, a Bodhisattva and Mahasattva who is established in proper conduct and a proper sphere of activity should proclaim this religious discourse in the later times and in the final age. And how, Manjushri, does a Bodhisattva and Mahasattva become established in proper conduct and a proper sphere of activity?

When, Manjushri, a Bodhisattva and Mahasattva is patient, self-controlled, and has reached the stage of self-mastery; when his mind is free from fear, terror, or anxiety; and when he is not envious. Furthermore, when a Bodhisattva and Mahasattva does not dwell upon any phenomenon <note>original: "dharma"</note> as it is, but observes the true nature of all phenomena according to their own characteristics. That which is non-clinging and non-conceptualizing regarding these phenomena is called, Manjushri, the proper conduct <note>original: "acara"</note> of a Bodhisattva and Mahasattva.

And what, Manjushri, is the sphere of activity <note>original: "gocara"</note> of a Bodhisattva and Mahasattva?
<margin>K 276</margin>
W 236
When a Bodhisattva and Mahasattva does not associate with kings, nor does he associate with, attend to, serve, or approach princes, chief ministers, or royal officials. He does not associate with, attend to, or serve those of other sects, such as wandering mendicants <note>original: "caraka-parivrajaka"</note>, the <term>Ajivikas</term> <gloss>a deterministic sect</gloss>, or the <term>Nirgranthas</term> <gloss>Jains</gloss>. He does not associate with people devoted to secular poetry and literature, nor does he associate with, attend to, or serve those who hold to worldly materialist spells or the materialists themselves <note>original: "Lokayatikas"</note>; he does not form friendships with them.

He does not associate with <term>Chandalas</term> <gloss>outcastes</gloss>, nor with boxers, pig-breeders, poultry-farmers,
<margin>N 181</margin>
deer-hunters, meat-sellers, actors, dancers, or wrestlers. He does not frequent other places of amusement or gambling belonging to others, nor does he form friendships with such people. Unless they approach him, in which case he teaches them the Law at the appropriate time, doing so without any ulterior motive.

He does not associate with, attend to, or serve those of the <term>Shravakayana</term> <gloss>the Vehicle of the Hearers/Disciples</gloss>, whether they be monks, nuns, laymen, or laywomen; nor does he form friendships with them. He does not share a common sphere of activity with them, whether in the walking-path or in the monastery. Unless they approach him, in which case he teaches them the Law at the appropriate time, doing so without any ulterior motive. This, Manjushri, is the sphere of activity of a Bodhisattva and Mahasattva.

<margin>K 277</margin>
Furthermore, Manjushri, a Bodhisattva and Mahasattva does not repeatedly teach the Law to women by dwelling on the signs of attraction for one or another of them, nor does he constantly desire to see women. He does not frequent the houses of families, nor does he consider it appropriate to converse frequently with young girls, maidens, or daughters-in-law, nor does he exchange greetings with them.

He does not teach the Law to a <term>pandaka</term> <gloss>eunuch or person of indeterminate gender</gloss>, nor does he form a friendship or exchange greetings with one. He does not enter a house alone for alms, except when he is practicing the mindfulness of the <term>Tathagata</term> <gloss>the Thus-Gone One/Buddha</gloss>. If he should teach the Law to women, he should not do so even out of a passion for the Law, <note>text breaks off</note>

<summary>The Buddha instructs Manjushri on the four qualities a Bodhisattva needs to preach the Lotus Sutra in the future, focusing on proper conduct and avoiding distracting or worldly social circles.</summary>
<keywords>Manjushri, Bodhisattva, peaceful practices, proper conduct, sphere of activity, ethics, social boundaries, later age</keywords>

13. Chapter on Happy Conduct

<margin>K 275</margin>
N 180
W 235
Then, the young prince Mañjuśrī spoke to the Blessed One: "It is difficult, Blessed One, extremely difficult, what these bodhisattvas and mahāsattvas have endured out of respect for the Blessed One. How, Blessed One, should these bodhisattvas and mahāsattvas preach this discourse on the Dharma in the final age, in the final period?"

When this was said, the Blessed One replied to the young prince Mañjuśrī: "Mañjuśrī, a bodhisattva and mahāsattva should preach this discourse on the Dharma in the final age, in the final period, having established himself in four dharmas. In which four?

Here, Mañjuśrī, a bodhisattva and mahāsattva should preach this discourse on the Dharma in the final age, in the final period, having established himself in proper conduct and proper spheres of association <note>original: "ācāragocara" — conduct and range/sphere of activity</note>. And how, Mañjuśrī, is a bodhisattva and mahāsattva established in proper conduct?

When, Mañjuśrī, the bodhisattva and mahāsattva is patient, disciplined, having attained the stage of discipline, with a mind that is fearless and unagitated, and free from jealousy; when the bodhisattva and mahāsattva does not practice <note>or "dwell upon"</note> any dharma, and observes the true nature of all phenomena <note>original: "svalakṣaṇa" — own-mark/individual characteristic</note>. That which is without grasping and without conceptualization in these dharmas, this is called the conduct of the bodhisattva and mahāsattva, Mañjuśrī.

<margin>K 276</margin>
W 236
And what is the sphere of association for the bodhisattva and mahāsattva, Mañjuśrī? # 13. Chapter on Peaceful Practices

Then Manjushri, the crown prince of the Dharma, said to the Blessed One: "It is difficult, Blessed One, extremely difficult, what these Bodhisattvas, these great beings, have endured out of respect for the Blessed One. How, Blessed One, should these Bodhisattvas, these great beings, teach this <term>dharmaparyaya</term> <gloss>discourse on the Dharma</gloss> in the final age, in the final time?"

When he had said this, the Blessed One replied to Manjushri, the crown prince of the Dharma: "Manjushri, a Bodhisattva, a great being, should teach this discourse on the Dharma in the final age, in the final time, by establishing himself in four matters. In which four? Here, Manjushri, a Bodhisattva, a great being, should teach this discourse on the Dharma when established in proper conduct and proper spheres of association. 

And how, Manjushri, is a Bodhisattva, a great being, established in proper conduct? It is when, Manjushri, a Bodhisattva, a great being, is patient, disciplined, has attained the state of the disciplined, has a mind that is not fearful or terrified, and is free from envy. It is when a Bodhisattva, a great being, does not dwell on any phenomenon, and perceives the true nature of things as it really is. This lack of attachment and lack of conceptualization regarding these phenomena is called the conduct of a Bodhisattva, a great being, Manjushri. 

And what, Manjushri, is the sphere of association for a Bodhisattva, a great being? A Bodhisattva, a great being, does not cultivate, associate with, wait upon, or approach kings, princes, high-ranking royal ministers, or royal officials. He does not cultivate, associate with, or wait upon other sectarians, wandering ascetics, mendicants, or Jains; nor does he associate with people devoted to poetic or secular treatises. He does not cultivate, associate with, or wait upon those who hold the mantras of the <term>Lokayata</term> <gloss>materialist philosophical school</gloss>, nor does he enter into friendly discourse with them. He does not associate with outcasts, fowlers, butchers, swineherds, poultry farmers, hunters, meat-sellers, actors, dancers, wrestlers, or boxers. He does not approach the places of their entertainment. He does not enter into friendly discourse with them. If they should come to him, he may occasionally teach them the Dharma, but he does so without relying on them. 

He does not cultivate, associate with, or wait upon monks, nuns, laymen, or laywomen who follow the vehicle of the Disciples <note>the <term>Shravakayana</term>, or path of those seeking individual liberation</note>, nor does he enter into friendly discourse with them. He does not share the same sphere of activity with them, whether in walking meditation or in dwelling. If they should come to him, he may occasionally teach them the Dharma, but he does so without relying on them. This, Manjushri, is the sphere of association for a Bodhisattva, a great being.

Furthermore, a Bodhisattva, a great being, Manjushri, does not preach the Dharma to women by lingering on their attractive features, nor does he desire to see them frequently. He does not enter the homes of families, nor does he think it appropriate to converse frequently with young girls, unmarried maidens, or young brides, nor does he exchange greetings with them. He does not preach the Dharma to a eunuch, does not enter into friendly discourse with him, and does not exchange greetings with him. He does not enter a house alone for the sake of alms, unless he is meditating on the recollection of the Tathagata. If, however, he does preach the Dharma to women, he does not do so even for the sake of Dharma-attachment <note>meaning he teaches without being seduced by the process of teaching or the interaction itself</note>."

<summary>In this chapter, the Buddha instructs Manjushri on the four methods of conduct and association for Bodhisattvas who wish to teach the Lotus Sutra during the difficult final age.</summary>

Then <term>Manjushri</term> <gloss>the Bodhisattva of Wisdom</gloss>, the Ever-Young <note>original: "kumārabhūta"; a title indicating his youthful appearance and high spiritual status</note>, spoke to the Blessed One as follows: "O Blessed One, it is difficult, truly most difficult, what these <term>Bodhisattvas</term> <gloss>beings dedicated to awakening</gloss> <term>Mahasattvas</term> <gloss>great beings</gloss> have undertaken out of reverence for the Blessed One. How, O Blessed One, should this <term>Dharma-paryaya</term> <gloss>way of the Teaching</gloss> be proclaimed by these Bodhisattvas Mahasattvas in the future time, in the final age?"

When he had spoken thus, the Blessed One said to Manjushri the Ever-Young: "A Bodhisattva Mahasattva who is established in four qualities, Manjushri, should proclaim this Dharma-paryaya in the future time, in the final age. Which four? Here, Manjushri, a Bodhisattva Mahasattva who is established in his sphere of conduct and his sphere of activity <note>original: "ācāra-gocara"</note> should proclaim this Dharma-paryaya in the future time, in the final age.

And how, Manjushri, is a Bodhisattva Mahasattva established in his sphere of conduct and sphere of activity? When, Manjushri, a Bodhisattva Mahasattva is patient, disciplined, and has reached the stage of self-control; when his mind is free from fear, alarm, or anxiety; and when he is free from envy. And when, Manjushri, a Bodhisattva Mahasattva does not practice by clinging to any phenomenon <note>original: "dharma"</note>, but observes the true nature of things as they are. That which is non-clinging and non-conceptualizing regarding these phenomena is called the sphere of conduct <note>original: "ācāra"</note> of a Bodhisattva Mahasattva.

<margin>K 276 W 236</margin>
And what, Manjushri, is the sphere of activity <note>original: "gocara"</note> of a Bodhisattva Mahasattva? When a Bodhisattva Mahasattva does not serve kings, nor serve, associate with, honor, or visit princes, royal ministers, or royal officials. He does not serve, associate with, or honor followers of other traditions—itinerant mendicants, wanderers, <term>Ajivikas</term> <gloss>a sect of fatalist ascetics</gloss>, or <term>Nirgranthas</term> <gloss>Jain ascetics</gloss>—nor those who are devoted to secular poetry and literature. He does not serve, associate with, or honor those who keep the spells of the materialists <note>original: "Lokayata-mantra-dharakan"</note>, nor does he associate with materialists <note>original: "Lokayatikas"</note>.

He does not associate with <term>Chandalas</term> <gloss>outcastes</gloss>, pugilists, swine-breeders, poultry-breeders, <margin>N 181</margin> deer-hunters, butchers, actors, dancers, or wrestlers. He does not visit other places used by others for amusement and play. He does not associate with such people, except that when they come to him, he preaches the Dharma to them at the appropriate time, doing so without dependence or attachment.

Furthermore, he does not serve, associate with, or honor monks, nuns, laymen, or laywomen who belong to the vehicle of the Disciples <note>original: "Shravaka-yana"</note>, nor does he associate with them. He does not frequent the same places as they do, whether in a walking path or a monastery, except that when they come to him, he preaches the Dharma to them at the appropriate time, doing so without dependence. This, Manjushri, is the sphere of activity of a Bodhisattva Mahasattva.

<margin>K 277</margin>
Furthermore, Manjushri, a Bodhisattva Mahasattva does not repeatedly teach the Dharma to women by taking up any signs of attraction, nor does he desire to see women frequently. He does not visit the homes of others, nor does he think he must frequently converse with young girls, maidens, or daughters-in-law, nor does he exchange greetings with them. # १३ सुखविहारपरिवर्तः । <gloss>13. Chapter on Peaceful Practices</gloss>

->१३ सुखविहारपरिवर्तः ।<-

Then, the Bodhisattva-Mahasattva <note>original: "kumārabhūta", often translated as Prince or Youth, here referring to Manjushri</note> Manjushri asked the Lord: "O Lord, it is difficult, truly difficult, for these Bodhisattvas-Mahasattvas to endure what they have for the sake of reverence for the Lord. O Lord, how should these Bodhisattvas-Mahasattvas preach this Dharma-discourse <note>original: "dharmaparyāya"</note> in the final age, in the final time?" 

When this was said, the Lord replied to the youth Manjushri: "Manjushri, a Bodhisattva-Mahasattva should preach this Dharma-discourse in the final age, in the final time, by being established in four dharmas. In which four? Here, Manjushri, a Bodhisattva-Mahasattva should preach this Dharma-discourse in the final age, in the final time, by being established in proper conduct and proper associations <note>original: "ācāragocara"</note>. And how, Manjushri, is a Bodhisattva-Mahasattva established in proper conduct and proper associations? 

When, Manjushri, a Bodhisattva-Mahasattva is patient, disciplined, having reached the stage of the disciplined, with a mind not afraid or terrified, and free from jealousy; when, Manjushri, a Bodhisattva-Mahasattva does not linger on any dharma, but views the true nature <note>original: "svalakṣaṇa"</note> of all phenomena as it really is. This lack of attachment and lack of conceptualization in these dharmas, Manjushri, is called the conduct of the Bodhisattva-Mahasattva. And what, Manjushri, is the association of the Bodhisattva-Mahasattva?

<margin>K 276</margin>
W 236
When, Manjushri, a Bodhisattva-Mahasattva does not associate with, serve, wait upon, or approach kings, princes, high royal officials, or men of the king. He does not associate with, serve, or wait upon other sectarians, wandering ascetics, mendicants, or Jains <note>original: "nirgrantha"</note>. He does not associate with or wait upon those who are devoted to poetry and secular sciences, nor does he associate with, serve, or wait upon those who hold the mantras of the Materialists <note>original: "lokāyata"</note> or the Materialists themselves, and he does not engage in conversation with them. He does not associate with outcastes <note>original: "caṇḍāla"</note>, those who practice violent sports, butchers, poultry farmers, hunters, 

<margin>N 181</margin>
meat-sellers, actors, dancers, acrobats, or wrestlers. He does not approach other places of amusement for people, and he does not engage in conversation with them. If he approaches them on occasion to preach the Dharma, he does so without relying on them. He does not associate with, serve, or wait upon monks, nuns, laymen, or laywomen of the Hearer-vehicle <note>original: "śrāvakayāna"</note>, and he does not engage in conversation with them. He does not associate with them in the same place, whether while walking or dwelling. If he approaches them on occasion to preach the Dharma, he does so without relying on them. This, Manjushri, is the association of the Bodhisattva-Mahasattva."

<margin>K 277</margin>
Furthermore, Manjushri, a Bodhisattva-Mahasattva does not preach the Dharma to the community of women <note>original: "mātṛgrāma"</note> by seizing upon any signs of attachment, nor is he habitually desirous of seeing the community of women. He does not approach families; he does not think that a young girl, a maiden, or a young bride is to be spoken to habitually, nor does he offer them polite greetings. He does not preach the Dharma to a eunuch, he does not converse with him, nor does he offer him polite greetings. He does not enter a house alone for the sake of alms, unless he is cultivating the mindfulness of the Tathagata <note>original: "tathāgatānusmṛti"</note>. If, however, he preaches the Dharma to the community of women, he does not do so out of desire for the Dharma <note>original: "dharmasaṃrāga"</note>—

स्वरक्षार्थं च । एतादृशो वः युष्माकं चमसः अदनसाधनभूतः संग्रामो मा सुस्रोत् माऽपगच्छतु । तं वहेतेति मन्त्रद्रष्टा ऋषिर्ब्रूते ।

इमं यज्ञं विततं विश्वकर्मणा देवा यन्तु सुमनस्यमानाः ॥ ५ ॥

4. Make ye a pen (vrajá), for that is men-protecting for you; sew ye coats-of-mail (várman), abundant, broad; make ye strongholds of metal, unattackable (ádhṛṣṭa); let not your bowl leak (sru); make it strong.

5. Of the sacrifice the eye, beginning, and face; with voice, with hearing, with mind do I make oblation; to this sacrifice, extended by the all-working one, let the gods come [ā-i], with favoring minds.

6. They that are priests (ṛtvij) of the gods, and that are worshipful, for whom the oblation (havyá) is made the portion — coming to this sacrifice together with their spouses, let the gods, as many as they are (yā́vant), revel on the oblation.

<meta>continues from previous page: this text continues the commentary on the Vedic sacrifice and the protective nature of the ritual vessels.</meta>

...for the sake of one's own protection. May such a vessel <note>original: "camasa"</note> of yours, which is the means of consuming <note>food or sacrificial offerings</note>, never slip away from you during battle. The seer <note>term: rishi</note> who perceives the mantra says: "Carry that vessel forward."

### Hymn 58, Verse 5

I offer with speech, with hearing, and with the mind, the eye of the sacrifice, its beginning, and its face. 
May the gods, being well-disposed, come to this sacrifice extended by the All-Maker <note>term: Vishvakarman</note>. || 5 ||

Word-for-word analysis:
The sacrifice’s; eye; beginning; face; and; with speech; with hearing; with the mind; I offer.
This; sacrifice; extended; by the All-Maker; toward; gods; may they come; being well-disposed. || 5 ||

This verse has been explained previously <note>referring to Atharva Veda 2.35.5</note>. I offer the senses such as the eye and the mind in relation to the sacrifice; I make them devoted to it. The gods, acting as if they are of good mind <note>well-disposed</note>, should come to and attain this mental sacrifice which has been stretched out and expanded by the All-Maker <note>term: Vishvakarman</note>, the creator of the universe. This is the summarized meaning.

### Hymn 58, Verse 6

Those who are the officiating priests <note>term: ritvijah</note> of the gods, and those who are worthy of sacrifice, to whom the portion of the oblation is made; 
may all those gods, as many as they are, coming to this sacrifice together with their wives, rejoice in the light. || 6 ||

Word-for-word analysis:
Who; of the gods; officiating priests; who; and; worthy of sacrifice; to whom; oblation; is made; the portion.
This; sacrifice; together; with wives; toward; having come; as many as; gods; in light; may they rejoice. || 6 ||

Among the gods, those who are the officiating priests <note>term: ritvijah</note> are those who perform the sacrifice at the proper time <note>term: ritu</note>. And those who are worthy of sacrifice <note>term: yajniyah</note> are those to whom the sacrifice is offered. For both these types of gods, the oblation <note>term: havya</note> is prepared and given as their allotted portion. As many as there are gods of such measure, may those great gods, along with their respective wives such as Indrani and others, come to this sacrifice and rejoice; may they be satisfied by the acceptance of the oblation.

This concludes the fourth hymn in the seventh section <note>term: anuvaka</note>.

The hymn beginning with "You, O Agni, are the protector of vows" is used in the offering of clarified butter <note>term: ajya</note> or in the ritual of placing peaceful fuel <note>term: shantasamidhadhane</note> when there is a transgression or omission in the New Moon or Full Moon sacrifices. This is stated by Kaushika in the rules of the collection <note>term: Samhitavidhi</note>—

And for our own protection. May this cup of yours, which is the instrument of consumption, not slip away, may it not depart from the battle. The sage who envisioned the mantra says, "Carry it."

I offer the eye of the sacrifice, its opening, and its face, with speech, with hearing, and with the mind. May the gods, being well-disposed, approach this sacrifice spread out by the <term>Vishvakarman</term> <gloss>All-Maker/Creator of the Universe</gloss>. (5)

Of the sacrifice. Eye. Beginning. Face. And. With speech. With hearing. With the mind. I offer. This. Sacrifice. Spread out. By the All-Maker. Approach. May the gods. Being well-disposed. (5)

This stanza has been explained previously (Atharvaveda 2.35.5). I offer the senses, beginning with the eye, and the mind as being connected to the sacrifice, and I make them inclined toward it. May the gods, being well-disposed, meaning acting as if they have good intentions, approach this mental sacrifice—this sacrifice spread out by the All-Maker, the creator of the world—and may they reach it. This is the summary.

Those who are the officiating priests of the gods, those who are worthy of the sacrifice, and those for whom the sacrificial portion is prepared as an offering. May all the gods, together with their consorts, approach this sacrifice and delight in its brilliance. (6)

Those. Of the gods. Officiating priests. Those. And. Worthy of sacrifice. Those for whom. The sacrificial offering. Is made. As a portion. This. Sacrifice. Together. With consorts. Approach. Come. As many as. Gods. With brilliance. May they delight. (6)

Among the gods, those who are the <term>ritvij</term> <gloss>officiating priests</gloss> are those who perform the sacrifice at the proper time. Those who are <term>yajniya</term> <gloss>worthy of sacrifice</gloss> are those to whom the sacrifice is owed. For both of these groups of gods, the <term>bhagadheya</term> <gloss>share/portion</gloss>, in the form of an oblation, is prepared and given. May as many gods as exist, those who are great in their brilliance, come together with their respective consorts, such as <term>Indrani</term> <gloss>the wife of Indra</gloss> and others, approach this sacrifice, and find satisfaction through the acceptance of the offering.

Thus ends the fourth hymn of the seventh <term>anuvaka</term> <gloss>section/chapter</gloss>.

The hymn beginning with "You, Agni, are the protector of vows" is prescribed for use during the omission of the <term>darshapurnamasa</term> <gloss>new and full moon sacrifices</gloss>, in the offering of clarified butter, or in the peaceful depositing of sacred fuel. It is indeed codified by Kausika in the <term>Samhitavidhi</term> <gloss>ritual manual of the collection</gloss>—

Atharvaveda Commentary [Hymn 58, Verse 5]

And for the sake of protection. May this cup of yours, which is the instrument of consumption, may this battle not slip away, may it not depart. The seer who envisions the mantra says that they should carry it.

I offer into the sacrifice, which has the eye as its beginning and face, through speech, hearing, and the mind. May the gods, being of good mind, come to this sacrifice which has been extended by <term>Viśvakarman</term> <gloss>the all-creating deity/the creator of the world</gloss>. (5)

This verse has already been explained previously (A 2, 35, 5). I offer the senses, such as the eye, as being connected to the sacrifice, meaning I make them inclined toward it. May the gods, acting as if they are of good mind, come and reach this mental sacrifice which has been extended and spread out by <term>Viśvakarman</term> <gloss>the all-creating deity</gloss>. This is the summary.

Those who are the priests of the gods, and those who are worthy of sacrifice, and those for whom the offering is made as their portion. May all the gods, having come with their wives to this sacrifice, take delight in the splendor. (6)

Those who are the priests among the gods, who are the performers of sacrifice at the proper time. And those who are worthy of sacrifice, those who are to be worshipped. For both these groups of gods, the <term>havya</term> <gloss>oblation</gloss> is prepared and given as their <term>bhāgadheya</term> <gloss>allotted portion</gloss>. May all the gods, however many there are, being great in their splendor, come to this sacrifice along with their wives, such as <term>Indrāṇī</term> <gloss>Indra's wife</gloss> and others, and take delight, becoming satisfied by the acceptance of the offering.

Thus ends the fourth hymn in the seventh <term>anuvāka</term> <gloss>section</gloss>.

The hymn beginning "You, O Agni, are the protector of vows" is prescribed for use during the <term>darśa</term> <gloss>new moon</gloss> or <term>pūrṇamāsa</term> <gloss>full moon</gloss> rituals, in the event of an error, or during the offering of clarified butter, or during the peaceful placement of sacred firewood. Indeed, it is codified by <term>Kauśika</term> <gloss>the author of the Kausika-sutra</gloss> in the <term>Saṃhitā-vidhi</term> <gloss>rules for the collection of hymns</gloss>.

<summary>This page provides a commentary on verses 5 and 6 of the 58th hymn of the Atharvaveda, detailing the ritual significance of the sacrifice and the invocation of the gods and their consorts. It concludes with the end of the fourth hymn of the seventh section and a note on the liturgical application of a subsequent hymn.</summary>

"I offer with the eye of the sacrifice, the beginning, the face, and with speech, hearing, and mind.
May the gods, acting with a good mind, come to this sacrifice extended by the Creator of all." 5

This verse was explained previously (AV 2.35.5). I offer the senses, such as the eye, as being related to the mental sacrifice; I make them favorable to it. May the gods, thinking well, come to this mental sacrifice extended by the World-Creator—the Creator of all.

Come to this sacrifice together with the wives; may the gods, great in splendor, rejoice." 6

May as many gods as there are, the great ones, along with their respective wives—Indrani and others—come to this sacrifice and rejoice by accepting the oblation.

This is the fourth hymn of the seventh <term>anuvāka</term>.

For both of these groups of gods, the <term>bhagadheya</term> <gloss>share/portion</gloss>, in the form of an oblation, is prepared and given. May as many gods as exist, those who are great in their brilliance, come together with their respective consorts, such as <term>Indrani</term> <gloss>the wife of Indra</gloss> and others, approach this sacrifice, and find satisfaction through the acceptance of the offering.

Thus ends the fourth hymn of the seventh <term>anuvaka</term> <gloss>section/chapter</gloss>.

The hymn beginning with "You, Agni, are the protector of vows" is prescribed for use during the omission of the <term>darshapurnamasa</term> <gloss>new and full moon sacrifices</gloss>, in the offering of clarified butter, or in the peaceful depositing of sacred fuel. It is indeed codified by Kausika in the <term>Samhitavidhi</term> <gloss>ritual manual of the collection</gloss>—

<summary>This page provides a commentary on verses 5 and 6 of the 58th hymn of the Atharvaveda, detailing the ritual significance of the sacrifice and the involvement of the gods and their consorts.</summary>

<header>खाण्डवदहन प० । अध्याय २२७ । २२८ । ] ॥ आदिपर्व्व ॥</header>
<sig>३ ज</sig>

तच्छरैरर्जुनो वर्षं प्रतिजघ्ने ऽत्यमर्षितः । विफलं क्रियमाणं तत्समवेक्ष्य शतक्रतुः ।
भूयः संवर्द्धयामास तद्वर्षं पाकशासनः ।
सोऽसृजद्वर्षं महावेगैरिषुभिः पाकशासनः । विलयं गमयामास हर्षयन्नितरं तथा । <margin>८२८</margin>
<margin>पाय</margin> तत उत्पाद्य पाणिभ्यां मन्दराच्छिखरं महत् । सद्रुमं व्यसजच्चक्रो जिघांसुः पाण्डुनन्दनं ।
ततोऽर्जुनो वेगवद्भिर्ज्वलिताग्रैः शिखण्डिभिः । शरैर्विध्वंसयामास गिरेः शृङ्गं सहस्रधा ।
गिरेर्विध्वंस्यमानस्य तस्य रूपं तदा बभौ । सार्कचन्द्रग्रहस्येव नभसः परिशीर्य्यतः ।
तेनाभिपतता दावं शैलेन महता भृशं । शृङ्गेण निहतास्तत्र प्राणिनः खाण्डवालयाः ।
इत्यादिपर्व्वणि खाण्डवदहनपर्व्वणि देवकृष्णार्जुनयुद्धे सप्तविंशत्यधिकद्विशततमोऽध्यायः ॥ २२७ ॥
॥ वैशम्पायन उवाच ॥ तथा शैलनिपातेन भीषिताः खाण्डवालयाः । दानवा राक्षसा नागास्तरवश्च वनौकसः । <margin>८२९</margin>
द्विपाः प्रभिन्नाः शार्दूलाः सिंहाः केसरिणस्तथा । समुद्विग्ना विसृज्युस्त्यान्या भूतजातयः ।
तं दावं समुदैक्षन्त क्रुद्धाश्चाभ्युद्यतायुधाः । उत्पातनादशब्देन सञ्चारित इव स्थितः ।
ते वनं प्रसमीक्ष्याथ दह्यमानमनेकधा । कृष्णमभ्युद्यतास्त्रञ्च नादं मुमुचुरुणं ।
तेन नादेन रौद्रेण नादेन च विभावसोः । ररास गगनं कृत्स्नमुत्पातजलदैरिव ।
ततः कृष्णेन महाबाहुः क्षेतेजोभास्वरं महत् । चक्रं व्यसजदत्युग्रं तेषां नाशाय केशवः । <margin>८३०</margin>
तेनात्ता जातयः क्षुद्राः सदानवनिशाचराः । निकृत्ताः शतशः सर्व्वे निपेतुरनलं क्षणात् ।
तत्रादृश्यन्त ते दैत्याः कृष्णचक्रविदारिताः । वसारुधिरसंपृक्ताः सन्ध्यायामिव तोयदाः ।
पिशाचानर्चिषे नागान् पशूंश्चैव सहस्रशः । निघ्नंश्चरति वार्ष्णेयः कालवत्तञ्च भारत ।
चित्रं चित्रं पुनश्चक्रं कृष्णस्यामित्रघातिनः । छित्त्वा नैकानि सत्त्वानि पाणिमेति पुनः पुनः ।
तथातु निघ्नतस्तस्य पिशाचोरगराक्षसान् । बभूव रूपमत्युग्रं सर्व्वभूतात्मनस्तदा । <margin>८३१</margin>
समेतानान्तु सर्व्वेषां देवतानाञ्च सर्व्वशः । विजेता नाभवत्कश्चित्कृष्णपाण्डवयोर्मृधे ।
तयोर्बलमपरित्रातुं तञ्च दावं यदा सुराः । नाशक्नुवन् शमयितुं तदाऽभवन् पराङ्मुखाः ।
शतक्रतुस्तु संप्रेक्ष्य विमुखानमरांस्तथा । बभूव मुदितो राजन् प्रशंसन् केशवार्जुनौ ।
निवृत्तेष्वथ देवेषु वागुवाचाशरीरिणी । शतक्रतुं समाभाष्य महागम्भीरनिस्वना ।
न ते सखा संनिहितस्तक्षको भुजगोत्तमः । दाहकाले खाण्डवस्य कुरुक्षेत्रं गतो ह्यसौ । <margin>८३२</margin>
न च शक्या युधा जेतुं कथञ्चिदपि वासव । वासुदेवार्जुनौवेतौ निबोध वचनान्मम ।
नरनारायणौवेतौ पूर्व्वदेवौ दिविश्रुतौ । भवानप्यभिजानाति यद्वीर्य्यं यत्पराक्रमौ ।
नैतौ शक्या दुराधर्षौ विजेतुमजितौ युधि । अपि सर्व्वेषु लोकेषु पुराणऋषिसत्तमौ ।
पूजनीयतमावेतावपि सर्व्वैः सुरासुरैः । यक्षराक्षसगन्धर्व्वनरकिन्नरपन्नगैः ।
तस्मादितः सुरैः सार्द्धं गन्तुमर्हसि वासव । दिष्टं चाप्यनुपश्यैतत् खाण्डवस्य विनाशनं । <margin>८३३</margin>
इति वाक्यमुपश्रुत्य तथ्यमित्यमरेश्वरः । क्रोधमर्षं समुत्सृज्य संप्रतस्थे दिवं तदा ।

<vocab>Mahābhārata, Ādiparva, Khāṇḍavadahana, Arjuna, Kṛṣṇa, Indra, Takṣaka, Vaisampāyana, Nara-Nārāyaṇa</vocab>
