# The Latter Cloud <note>original: Uttaramegha</note>

<margin>The term for women with parted hair signifies married women whose husbands are alive. The Amarakosha <note>an ancient Sanskrit thesaurus</note> states: "Nari, Simantini, and Vadhu are synonyms."</margin>

Presented by a friend <note>original: suhṛdupanataḥ</note>; having arrived through the medium of a friend. The word "friend" is used to remove any suspicion of a deceptive message. The news of her beloved <note>original: kāntodantaḥ</note>; news is defined by the Amarakosha as "varta, pravritti, vrittanta, and udanta." It is slightly less than an actual reunion <note>original: saṃgamāt kiṃcidūnaḥ</note>, meaning it brings almost as much joy as the physical presence of the lover.

Now he delivers the message:

O Long-lived One, at my request and to do a favor for yourself, speak thus to her: "Your companion, residing in the hermitages of Ramagiri, being separated from you but still alive, asks after your welfare, O fragile one. For living beings whose misfortunes are easily met, this is the very first thing to be declared." (41)

Detailed explanation: O Long-lived One <note>original: āyuṣman</note>. The suffix denotes praise, implying a life made worthy by helping others. At my request <note>original: mama vacanāt</note> and to favor yourself <note>original: ātmanopकर्तुं</note>; meaning to make yourself successful through an act of charity. Although the self is the object of the act of favoring, the use of the genitive case <note>belonging to the self</note> is not incorrect, as seen in the works of Bharavi: "That wealth is useful which serves others," and Sri Harsha: "To favor the virtuous, to see wealth, and to travel through the sky." Thus, the grammarian Natha’s comment that the second case is seen elsewhere is merely a personal opinion. 

Speak thus to that beloved: "O fragile one <note>original: abale</note>, your companion <note>original: sahacaraḥ</note>, your husband, staying in the hermitages of Ramagiri <note>Chitrakoota</note>, being not dead <note>original: avyāpannaḥ</note>, asks after your well-being." He gives the reason for the inquiry: though suffering from separation <note>original: viyuktḥ</note>, he survives. This verb "to ask" takes two objects here. Indeed, for living beings for whom disasters are easily obtained <note>original: sulabhavipadām</note>, this inquiry into welfare is the very first thing that must necessarily be addressed. The suffix used here denotes necessity.

With his slender limb, your slender limb; with his scorched limb, your scorched limb; with his tearful limb, your limb flowing with tears; with his limb filled with constant longing, your longing limb...

<note>
1. Long-lived one. 2. He should speak. 3. One/Single. 4. Separated (feminine), Appointed. 5. This is the first thing to be said for beings whose disasters are easy; for in perishable bodies, this is the first breath. 6. O fair-limbed one, and slender. 7. Flow of tears.
</note>

<summary>The Yaksha instructs the Cloud on how to approach his wife, explaining that news from a friend is nearly as joyful as a reunion. He emphasizes the importance of inquiring after welfare as the first priority for those suffering in separation.</summary>
<keywords>Meghaduta, Kalidasa, Ramagiri, Sanskrit commentary, Amarakosha, separation, welfare inquiry, poetic grammar</keywords>

The Cloud Messenger

<note>Glossary note: "The women who have parted their hair" (seamantini); the Amarakosha states, "A woman with parted hair is a bride."</note> <note>Glossary note: "Presented by a friend" (suhṛdupanata); obtained through a friend. The term friend is used to dispel any suspicion of infidelity. "News of the beloved" (kāntodanta); news of the lover. The Amarakosha states, "News, occurrence, story, and report are synonyms for udanta." It means that receiving this news is almost as joyful as the reunion itself, effectively providing the same happiness.</note>

Now he gives the message:

O long-lived one, at my request and for your own benefit as well,
Speak these words to her: Your companion, staying at the hermitage of Ramagiri,
Alive and well, asks after your welfare, O helpless one, though separated from you.
For those beings whose calamities come easily, this is the first thing to be spoken. <note>Verse 41</note>

<note>Glossary note: "To her" (tām); O long-lived one (āyuṣman). The suffix matup is used here for praise, meaning one whose life is worthy because it is spent helping others. "At my request" (vacanāt); at the request of my prayer. "And for your own benefit" (ātmana upakartum); to fulfill yourself through the act of helping another. Even though this acts as an object for the action of helping, the use of the genitive case 'atmana' is not contradictory, as it implies a relationship of intent. As Bharavi says: "That wealth is meaningful through which one helps others." Similarly, Sriharsha says: "To help the good, to see wealth, and to travel through the sky." Thus, the commentator's claim that there is some other rule here is essentially baseless.</note> Tell her, the beloved, this: O helpless one, your companion, your husband, staying in the hermitages of Ramagiri, or Chitrakuta, is alive. This means he is not dead. He explains the reason for his remaining alive: separated and suffering from the separation, he asks after your welfare. Because the verb 'to ask' (pricchati) implies an object, it here takes two. Indeed, for living beings, whose misfortunes arise so easily, this inquiry about welfare is the very first thing that must be asked.

Body against body, thin against thin,
Hot with burning heat against one burning,
Tearful with tears against one whose eyes are flowing,
Longing against one who is longing,

<summary>This page provides a grammatical and contextual commentary on verse 41 of the Uttaramegha, focusing on the message the Yaksha sends to his beloved via the cloud, emphasizing his survival and his desire to confirm her well-being.</summary>
<keywords>Meghaduta, Kalidasa, Sanskrit literature, Ramagiri, separation, message, commentary</keywords>

Uttaramegha.

Of those whose hair is parted <note>referring to young wives who traditionally mark their status by parting their hair</note>. "A woman whose hair is parted is a bride," according to the Amarakosha. [Brought by a friend] Having arrived, brought by a friend or through the mouth of a friend. The word "friend" is used to prevent any suspicion of infidelity. The news of the beloved is the news of the husband. "News, information, event, and report are synonymous with Udanta," according to the Amarakosha. It means that the news is slightly less than the reunion itself, but it is just as joyful.

Now, he delivers the message—

O long-lived one, tell her, by my words and for your own benefit,
Speak thus: "Your companion, residing in the hermitage of Ramagiri,
Alive and well, asks after your welfare, O helpless one, though separated from you;
For this is the first thing that must be spoken to living beings who are prone to misfortune." || 41 ||

Tell her. O long-lived one. The suffix 'matup' implies praise, meaning one whose life is worthy because of performing favors for others. By my words, that is, the request, and also for your own benefit—that is, to fulfill yourself by performing a kindness for others. Even though the self is the object of the act of helping, the use of the genitive case 'atmanah' is not incorrect, as in phrases like "he helps him." As Bharavi says, "That is true fortune by which one helps others." Similarly, Sriharsha says, "To help the righteous, to see fortune, to travel through the sky." Thus, the statement of the master—that this is a second case of the same usage—is an unnecessary statement. Tell her, your beloved, thus. What should you say? He says, O helpless one, your companion, your husband, residing in the hermitages of Ramagiri, also known as Chitrakuta, is alive—meaning not dead. He provides the reason for not being dead: although suffering from being separated, he asks after your welfare. The verb 'to ask' takes two objects due to the state of being distressed. Indeed, for living beings who easily meet with misfortune, this very question regarding welfare is the first thing that must be asked. The 'nyat' suffix is applied here to indicate necessity.

With a slender body against a slender body, with a fevered body against a fevered one,
With eyes full of tears against eyes full of tears, with an unceasing longing against one who is longing,

1. Long-lived one. 2. You should speak. 3. One. 4. Separated, appointed. 5. This is the first greeting for living beings who are prone to misfortune; this is the first address for creatures whose instruments are prone to decay. 6. O slender one, and the body. 7. Flowing with tears.

<summary>This page provides a scholarly commentary on verses from Kālidāsa's Meghadūta, specifically detailing the etymology of terms related to news of a beloved and interpreting the opening of the Yakṣa's message to his wife.</summary>
<keywords>Meghadūta, Kālidāsa, Sanskrit commentary, Ramagiri, separation, literary analysis</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>

For "women" <term>sīmantinīnām</term>. The Amarakosha says: "Woman, simantini, vadhu." "News" <term>udantaḥ</term> of a "lover" <term>kāntasya</term> that has "arrived through a friend" <term>suhṛd-upanataḥ</term>. The word "friend" is used to remove any doubt of deception. The Amarakosha states: "Varta, pravritti, vrittanta, and udanta mean news." Such news is "only slightly less" <term>kiñcid-ūnaḥ</term> than an actual "meeting" <term>saṅgamāt</term>; that is, it brings almost the same amount of joy.

Now he gives the message:

->O long-lived one, for my sake and to benefit yourself, you should say to her: 'Your companion is alive at the hermitage of Ramagiri and asks of your welfare, O frail one'; for this is the first thing to be asked of living beings whose misfortunes are easily come by. 41<-

"O long-lived one" <term>āyuṣman</term>. This is used as praise, meaning one whose life is worthy because he helps others. To "benefit" <term>upakartum</term> "yourself" <term>ātmanaḥ</term> and "from my word" <term>mama vacanāt</term> <gloss>at my request</gloss>. This means fulfilling yourself by helping another. Even though the act of helping usually takes the second case, the sixth case <term>ātmanaḥ</term> is used here to show a general relationship, which is not incorrect. As Bharavi says: "That fortune is helpful by which one helps others." And Shriharsha: "To help the good, to see fortune, to go through the sky." "Say" <term>brūyāḥ</term> to that beloved as follows: "Your companion" <term>tava sahacaraḥ</term> <gloss>husband</gloss> "staying at the hermitage of Ramagiri" <term>rāmagiri-āśrama-sthaḥ</term> is "not dead" <term>avyāpannaḥ</term>. He gives the reason for his survival: "Though separated" <term>viyuktaḥ</term> and thus miserable, "he asks of your welfare" <term>kuśalam pṛcchati tvām</term>. For "living beings" <term>prāṇinām</term> for whom "misfortune is easily come by" <term>sulabha-vipadām</term>, "this very thing" <term>etad eva</term> <gloss>welfare</gloss> is the "first thing to be asked" <term>pūrva-ābhāṣyam</term>.

->He, with his body, joins your body; his thin body to your thin one; his body heated by the fire of separation to your intensely heated one; his tearful body to your tear-drenched one; his body of endless longing to your longing one. 42<-

<margin>1. O long-lived one 2. he should say 3. one 4. separated 5. first to be spoken/shined; for beings with perishable organs, this is the first speech 6. O beautiful one; thin and 7. with a flow of tears</margin>

<summary>The Yaksha instructs the cloud to deliver the message that he is alive at Ramagiri. He emphasizes that for those in distress, simply asking about welfare is the most important first step in communication.</summary>
<keywords>welfare, long-lived, Ramagiri, companion, misfortune, body, separation, greeting</keywords>

# The Latter Cloud

<margin>Married women</margin> <note>original: "sīmantinīnām"</note>. According to the Amarakosa <note>a famous Sanskrit thesaurus</note>: "Woman, married woman, bride." <margin>Brought by a friend</margin> <note>original: "suhṛdupanataḥ"</note>. This means received from a friend or through the mouth of a friend. The word "friend" is used here to prevent any suspicion of a secret lover during their separation. The news <note>original: "udantaḥ"</note> of her beloved. According to the Amarakosa: "News, report, account, and tidings are synonyms." It is "slightly less" <note>original: "kiṃcidūnaḥ"</note> than an actual meeting with the beloved, meaning it brings almost as much joy as his physical presence.

Now he delivers the message:

"O long-lived one! On my behalf and to benefit yourself, speak thus to her: 'Your companion, staying in the hermitages of Ramagiri, is alive. Separated from you, he asks after your welfare, O fragile one! For this is the very first thing to be said to living beings for whom calamities are so common.'" — Verse 41

Regarding the phrase "O long-lived one" <note>original: "āyuṣman"</note>: the suffix implies praise, meaning "one whose life is praiseworthy because of service to others." "On my behalf" <note>original: "mama vacanāt"</note> refers to my request. "To benefit yourself" <note>original: "ātmana upakartum"</note> means to make your own life meaningful through helping others. Although "yourself" is the object of the act of helping, the use of the genitive case <note>a grammatical case indicating possession or relation</note> is not incorrect, as it merely expresses a general relation. As Bharavi <note>a famous 6th-century poet</note> says: "That wealth is beneficial which belongs to others." Similarly, Sriharsha <note>the poet of the Naishadha Charita</note> writes: "To benefit the virtuous, to see the Goddess of Fortune, to travel through the sky." Therefore, the statement of the commentator Natha <note>an earlier commentator on Kalidasa</note> that the second case <note>accusative</note> is sometimes seen elsewhere is simply his own opinion.

Speak "thus" to my beloved. What should be said? "O fragile one <note>original: "abale"</note>, your companion and husband resides in the hermitages of Ramagiri." "Alive" <note>original: "avyāpannaḥ"</note> means he has not died. He gives the reason for not dying: "Separated" <note>original: "viyuktaḥ"</note>, meaning though he suffers from separation, he "asks after your welfare" <note>original: "kuśalaṃ pṛcchati"</note>. Because of the nature of the verb "to ask," it takes two objects. Indeed, for living beings whose "calamities are common" <note>original: "sulabhavipadām"</note>—meaning misfortunes occur without effort—this very welfare is the "first thing to be said" <note>original: "pūrvābhāṣyam"</note> or the first thing that must necessarily be asked. The suffix used here denotes necessity.

With his body, your slender body; with his deeply burning body, your burning body; with his tearful body, your body flowing with tears; with his incessantly longing body, your longing body...

<margin>1. Long-lived one. 2. He should speak. 3. One. 4. Separated (feminine), joined. 5. First to be said to those for whom calamities are common; for in the case of perishable instruments of living beings, this is the first breath. 6. O fair-bodied one, and slender. 7. Flowing with tears.</margin>

<summary>This page contains a Sanskrit commentary on verse 41 of the Meghaduta, where the Cloud messenger is instructed on how to approach the Yaksha's wife. It explains the grammatical nuances of the address and emphasizes that checking on someone's welfare is the essential first step in communication between mortals.</summary>
<keywords>Meghaduta, Kalidasa, Mallinatha, Sanskrit grammar, Ramagiri, welfare, separation, Amarakosa, Bharavi, Sriharsha</keywords>

# Uttaramēghaḥ |

Of women with divided hair <note>a reference to the practice of parting the hair as a sign of being a wife</note>. "A woman with a part in her hair is a bride" <note>original: 'nārī sīmantinī vadhūḥ'</note>, says the <term>Amara</term> <gloss>Amara-kośa, a standard Sanskrit thesaurus</gloss>. [Brought by a friend] Brought near or obtained through a friend. The word "friend" <term>suhṛt</term> is used to remove doubts regarding separation. News of the lover is the "lover's tidings" <term>kāntōdantaḥ</term>. "Tidings, occurrences, reports, and news are <term>udanta</term>" <note>original: 'vārtā pravṛttirvṛttānta udantaḥ syāt'</note>, says the <term>Amara</term>. The meaning is that it is almost as joyful as a meeting, or contact with the lover, though slightly less than the actual event.

Now he gives the message—

"O long-lived one, at my request and for your own benefit,
Speak thus to her, your companion, who dwells in the hermitage of Ramagiri:
'I am alive and well, though separated from you, and I ask after your welfare, O helpless one;
For those in distress, this is the first thing to be said.'" <41>

"To her" <note>referring to the beloved</note>. "O long-lived one" <term>āyuṣman</term>. The suffix <term>matup</term> <gloss>denoting possession</gloss> is used here for praise, meaning one whose life is worthy because of the benefit done to others. "At my request" <term>mama vacanāt</term>, meaning a request for a favor, "and for your own benefit," meaning to fulfill yourself through the act of helping others. Even though the act of helping is the object of the action, the genitive case <term>ātmanaḥ</term> is not contradictory when intending a relationship, as in "he does a favor for himself." As the poet <term>Bhāravi</term> says: "That is wealth, through which one does a favor to others." Likewise, <term>Śrīharṣa</term> says: "To do a favor to the good, to see wealth, to go through the sky." Thus, the statement of the teacher <term>Nātha</term>—"sometimes, because of the observation of a second, everything is as such"—is a statement of necessity. Speak thus to that beloved. What should you say? "O helpless one, your companion, your husband, dwells in the hermitages of Ramagiri, the mountain of paintings. I am not dead." He provides the reason for being alive: "Being separated from you and suffering, I ask about your welfare." Because of the state of distress, the verb "to ask" <term>pṛcchati</term> takes two objects. Indeed, for living beings who are prone to sudden misfortune, this greeting is the very first thing that must be asked. The suffix <term>ṇyat</term> is used in the sense of necessity.

"With a body, a very thin body pressed against a thin body;
With eyes full of tears, and an unrestrained longing for one who is longing;"

<note>1. Long-lived one. 2. You should speak. 3. One. 4. Separated from you, appointed. 5. This is the first thing to be asked for beings prone to misfortune; this is the first greeting for those whose means are decaying. 6. O slender one, and thin. 7. With liquid tears.</note>

<meta>continues from previous page: Mallinātha's commentary on the preceding verse, explaining "the news of a husband, brought by a friend, is to women little less than union with him."</meta>
<header>The Latter Cloud.</header>

of women whose hair is parted, that is, married women. "<term>Nārī</term>, <term>sīmantinī</term>, <term>vadhū</term> <gloss>all words for a woman or wife</gloss>," says Amara. **"Brought by a friend"**: brought, that is, received, through the mouth of a friend. The word "friend" is there to rule out any suspicion of deception. The news of the beloved is <term>kāntodanta</term> <gloss>tidings of the husband</gloss>. "<term>Vārtā</term>, <term>pravṛtti</term>, <term>vṛttānta</term> and <term>udanta</term> <gloss>all words for news</gloss>," says Amara. "A little less than union": only slightly less than contact with the beloved; the meaning is that it gives joy almost as union does.

Now he delivers the message:

O long-lived one, at my word, and to do a kindness to yourself,
say this to her: "Your companion, dwelling in the hermitages of Rāmagiri,
not dead, but parted from you, asks after your welfare, O tender one;
for creatures to whom misfortune comes so easily, this is the first thing to be said." ‖ 41 ‖

**"Her"**: O long-lived one. The suffix <term>matup</term> <gloss>a possessive suffix</gloss> is used here in the sense of praise; the meaning is, one whose life is to be praised for helping others. **"At my word"**: at my word, that is, my words of entreaty; and also "to do a kindness to yourself," your own self. The meaning is: to make yourself fulfilled by helping another. Although the self is the object of the act of helping, the genitive <term>ātmanaḥ</term> <gloss>"of yourself"</gloss> is not wrong when only a general relation is meant, just as in "he does a kindness to him." <note>Mallinātha defends Kālidāsa's grammar: the verb "to help" normally takes an accusative object, but a genitive is allowed when the speaker expresses a mere relation.</note> As Bhāravi says: "That is true wealth by which one does kindness to others." And likewise Śrīharṣa: "To do kindness to the good, to behold Lakṣmī, to travel through the sky." And so the dictum of Nātha, "somewhere a certain accusative, because it is not seen, so for all," is no dictum at all. <note>This sentence is partly garbled in the OCR; the sense appears to be that a contrary grammatical rule cited from an earlier commentator carries no authority.</note> Say thus to her, your beloved. Say what? He tells it: "O tender one, your companion," your husband, "dwelling in the hermitages of Rāmagiri," that is, staying in the hermitages of Citrakūṭa, <term>rāmagiryāśramasthaḥ</term>. **"Not dead"**: <term>avyāpannaḥ</term> means not dead. He gives the reason for his not having died: **"parted,"** having suffered separation and being in grief, he asks you about your welfare. Because the verb "to ask" belongs to the class beginning with "to milk," it takes two objects. <note>A rule of Pāṇini's grammar: verbs of the <term>duh</term> <gloss>"to milk"</gloss> group, including "ask," govern a double accusative, here "you" and "welfare."</note> For indeed, for creatures whose misfortunes arrive without any effort, "this alone," welfare alone, is **"the first thing to be said,"** that which must necessarily be asked first. The suffix <term>ṇyat</term> is used in the sense of necessity, by the rule "and the <term>kṛtya</term> suffixes." <note>Rāmagiri, the "Mountain of Rāma," is where the exiled yakṣa of the poem lives; Mallinātha identifies it with Citrakūṭa.</note>

With his limbs, so thin and fiercely burning, your limbs, so thin and burning;
with his tearful one, yours dissolved in tears; with his yearning, yours ceaselessly yearning;

1 "long-lived one" (another form). 2 "let him say." 3 "one." 4 "parted from you" (feminine); "appointed." 5 another reading of the last line: "for creatures to whom misfortune comes so easily, this alone; for beings whose senses are failing, this is the first comfort." <note>The second half of this variant is garbled in the OCR; the rendering is tentative.</note> 6 "O slender one"; "and thin." 7 "with flowing tears."

<summary>This page of the Meghadūta, with Mallinātha's Sanskrit commentary, gives verse 41 of the Latter Cloud, where the exiled yakṣa begins dictating his actual message to his wife, and opens the next verse on their shared suffering. The commentary explains vocabulary from the Amarakośa, justifies points of grammar with citations from Bhāravi and Śrīharṣa, and identifies Rāmagiri with Citrakūṭa.</summary>

अखण्डितं प्रेम लभस्व पत्यु-
रित्युच्यते ताभिरुमा स्म नम्रा ।
तया तु तस्यार्धशरीरभाजा
पश्चाकृताः स्निग्धजनाशिषोऽपि ॥ २८ ॥

अखण्डतमिति ॥ नम्रा प्रणता उमा ताभिः सतीभिः पत्युः शिवस्य अखण्डतम् अक्षतं प्रेम लभस्व प्राप्नुहि इति उच्यते स्म अभिहिता । लट् स्म इति भूतार्थे लट् । तस्य हरस्य । अर्ध शरीरस्यार्धशरीरम् । अर्ध नपुंसकं इति समासः । तदजतीति अर्धशरीरभाजा तया गौर्या तु स्निग्धजनाशिषः बन्धुजनाशीर्वादाः अपि पश्चाकृताः अधरकृताः । ततोऽप्यधिकफललाभादिति भावः ॥

इच्छाविभूत्योरनुरूपमद्रि-
स्तस्याः कृती कृत्यमशेषयित्वा ।
सभ्यः सभायां सुहृदास्थितायां
तस्थौ वृषाङ्गागमनप्रतीक्षः ॥ २९ ॥

इच्छेति ॥ कृती कुशलः । सभायां साधुः सभ्यः । सभाया यः इति यप्रत्ययः । अद्रिः हिमवान् इच्छाविभूत्योः उत्साहैश्वर्ययोः अनुरूपं सदृशं यथा तथा तस्याः पार्वत्याः कृत्यं कर्तव्यम् अशेषयित्वा शेषं निःशेषं कृत्वा । समाप्येत्यर्थः । अशेषशब्दात्करोतीति ण्यन्तात् क्त्वाप्रत्ययः । सुहृदास्थितायां बन्धुजनाक्रान्तायां सभायां संसदि [ वृषाङ्गागमनप्रतीक्षः ] वृषाङ्कस्य हरस्यागमनं प्रतीक्षत इति तथोक्तः सन् । कर्मण्यण् इत्यण् । तस्थौ स्थितः ॥

तावन्भवस्यापि कुबेरशैले
तत्पूर्वपाणिग्रहणानुरूपम् ।
प्रसाधनं मातृभिराहताभि-
न्यस्तं पुरस्तात्पुरशासनस्य ॥ ३० ॥

तावदिति ॥ तावत् । यावद्गौरीप्रसाधनं क्रियते तत्काल एवेत्यर्थः । कुबेरशैले कैलासे । [ तत्पूर्वपाणिग्रहणानुरूपम् ] तदेव पूर्वं तत्पूर्वं तच्च तत्पाणिग्रहणं तस्यानुरूपं प्रसाधनं अलङ्कारसामग्री । आहताभिः सादरभिः । कर्तरि क्तः । मातृभिः ब्राह्मीप्रभृतिभिः सप्तमातृकाभिः । पुरं शास्तीति पुरशासनस्तस्य पुरशासनस्य । कर्तरि ल्युट् । भवस्यापि पुरस्तात् अग्रे न्यस्तं निक्षिप्तम् ॥

१ असो. २ क्ष्मात्. ३ बंधु. ४ आगमन प्रतीक्ष. ५ वरस्य. ६ स्मर.

Then at her mother's hest, the maid adored The spirit of each high ancestral lord, Nor failed she next the noble dames to greet, And give due honour to their reverend feet. They raised the maiden as she bowed her head: "Thine be the fulness of his love!" they said. Half of his being, blessing high as this Can add no rapture to her perfect bliss. Well-pleased HIMÁLAYA viewed the pomp and pride Meet for his daughter, meet for ŚIVA'S bride; Then sought the hall with all his friends to wait The bridegroom's coming with a monarch's state.

Meanwhile by heavenly matrons' care displayed Upon KUVERA'S lofty mount were laid The ornaments of ŚIVA, which of yore At his first nuptials the bridegroom wore. He laid his hand upon the dress, but how Shall robes so sad, so holy, grace him now? His own dire vesture took a shape as fair As gentle bridegroom's heart could wish to wear.

Mapping: 'Then at her mother's hest ... reverend feet' = VII.27 (context); 'They raised the maiden ... perfect bliss' = VII.28; 'Well-pleased HIMÁLAYA ... monarch's state' = VII.29; 'Meanwhile by heavenly matrons' care ... the bridegroom wore' = VII.30; 'He laid his hand ... wish to wear' = VII.31 (context; Griffith's couplet is loose). PG markup ['S]IVA rendered as ŚIVA.

Commentary: "Unbroken," etc. Umā, being humble, was addressed by those virtuous women who said, "May you obtain the unbroken, unblemished love of your husband, Shiva." The use of the imperfect tense is indicated by the particle *sma*. "Him," meaning Hara (Shiva). "Half of the body," meaning *ardhaśarīra*, formed by the compound *ardha* (half) in the neuter gender. By her, Gauri (Pārvatī), who has become one who shares half the body of him, the blessings of her dear ones were made secondary, or placed below, because she had gained a fruit even greater than those blessings.

The mountain king, having skillfully completed all the tasks of her (Pārvatī) according to his own desires and resources, sat in the assembly occupied by his friends, waiting for the arrival of the bull-emblemed one. || 29 ||

Commentary: "Desire," etc. A *kṛtī* is one who is skillful. A *sabhya* is one who is worthy of the assembly. The mountain, Himavān, having completed every remaining task of Pārvatī in a manner appropriate to his own desires and wealth—that is, his enthusiasm and majesty—stood (remained) in the assembly occupied by his friends, waiting for the arrival of Hara, whose emblem is the bull.

Meanwhile, on the mountain of Kubera <note>Mount Kailāsa</note>, the accessories for decoration, appropriate for that former marriage ceremony, were brought by the Mothers <note>the seven divine mothers, such as Brāhmī</note> who had been summoned, and were placed before the City-Subduer <note>Shiva, the destroyer of Tripura</note>. || 30 ||

Commentary: "Meanwhile," etc. While Gauri's adornment was being performed, at that very moment, on the mountain of Kubera (Kailāsa), the items for decoration, matching that previous wedding ceremony, were brought by the Mothers who had been respectfully summoned, and were placed before the destroyer of the city (Shiva).

७३०

ऋक्षाः सिंहा वराहाश्च महिषा वारणा मृगाः । तेन शब्देन दिन्त्रस्ता जग्मुर्भीता दिशो दश ॥
शिखरं तत्त्रिकूटस्य प्रांशु चैकं दिविस्पृशम् । समन्तात्पुष्पसंछन्नं महारजतसंनिभम् ॥ १८
शतयोजनविस्तीर्णं विमलं चारुदर्शनम् । श्लक्ष्णं श्रीमन्महच्चैव दुष्प्रापं शकुनैरपि ॥ १९
मनसापि दुरारोहं किं पुनः कर्मणा जनैः । निविष्टा तत्र शिखरे लङ्का रावणपालिता ॥ २०
शतयोजनविस्तीर्णा त्रिंशद्योजनआयता । सा पुरी गोपुरैरुच्चैः पाण्डराम्बुदसंनिभैः ॥ २१
काञ्चनेन च सालेन राजतेन च शोभिता । प्रासादैश्च विमानैश्च लङ्का परमभूषिता ॥ २२
घनैरिवातपापाये मध्यं वैणवमं पदम् । यस्यां स्तम्भसहस्रेण प्रासादः समलंकृतः ॥ २३
कैलासशिखराकारो दृश्यते स्मिवोल्लिवन् । चैत्यः स राक्षसेन्द्रस्य बभूव पुरभूषणम् ॥ २४
शतेन रक्षसां नित्यं यः समग्रेण दृश्यते । मनोज्ञां काननवतां पर्वतैरुपशोभिताम् ॥ २५
नानाधातुविचित्रैश्च उद्यानैरुपशोभिताम् । नानाविहगसंघुष्टां नानागणनिषेविताम् ॥ २६
नानाकुसुमसंछन्नां नाना राक्षससेविताम् । तां समृद्धां समुद्रार्थां लक्ष्मीवाँल्लक्ष्मणाग्रजः ॥ २७
रावणस्य पुरीं रामो ददर्श सह वानरैः । तां महागृहसंबाधां दृष्ट्वा लक्ष्मणपूर्वजः ॥ २८
नगरीममरप्रख्यां विस्मयं प्राप वीर्यवान् ॥

तां रत्नपूर्णां बहुसंविधानां प्रासादमालाभिरलंकृतां च ।
पुरीं महायन्त्रकवाटमुख्यां ददर्श रामो महता बलेन ॥ २९

इत्यार्षे श्रीमद्रामायणे वाल्मीकीये आदिकाव्ये चतुर्विंशतिसहस्रिकायां संहितायाम्
युद्धकाण्डे लङ्कादर्शनं नाम एकोनचत्वारिंशः सर्गः

---

### चत्वारिंशः सर्गः
**रावणसुग्रीवनियुद्धम्**

ततो रामः सुवेलाग्रं योजनद्वयमण्डलम । आरुरोह सुग्रीवा हरियूथपसंवृतः ॥ १
स्थित्वा मुहूर्तं तत्रैव दिशो दश विलोकयन् । त्रिकूटशिखरे रम्ये निर्मितां विश्वकर्मणा ॥ २
ददर्श लङ्कां सुन्यस्तां रम्यकाननशोभिताम् । तस्यां गोपुरशृङ्गस्थं राक्षसेन्द्रं दुरासदम् ॥ ३
श्वेतचामरपर्यन्तं विजयच्छत्रशोभितम् । रक्तचन्दनसंलिप्तं रत्नाभरणभूषितम् ॥ ४
नीलजीमूतसंकाशं हेमच्छादिताम्बरम् । ऐरावतविपाणामैरुत्कृष्टकिणवक्षसम् ॥ ५
शशलोहिनरागेण संवीतं रक्तवाससा । सन्ध्यातापेन संवीतं मेघराशिमिवाम्बरे ॥ ६
पश्यतां वानरेन्द्राणां राघवस्यापि पश्यतः । दर्शनाद्राक्षसेन्द्रस्य सुग्रीवः सहसोत्थितः ॥ ७

<note>१. इदमर्धम् क. नास्ति ।</note>

And they, endowed with great impetuosity, went on, oppressing the earth with their battle-array; and clouds of dust suddenly arose from the the march of the soldiery. And bears, and lions, and buffaloes, and elephants, and deer, and birds, overwhelmed with affright, made for the ten cardinal points. The graceful and lovely summit of Trikuta was entire, elevated, sky-piercing, of golden splendour, measuring an hundred yoyanas, clear-shining, level, inaccessible even to fowls, and incapable of being ascended even in thought—not to say of actual ascension by people. Lanka, ruled by Ravana, was situated on its top,—ten yoyanas in width and twenty in length. And that city was graced with lofty ornamented gateways resembling pale clouds, and golden and silvern walls; and Lanka was adorned with palaces and piles; like the sky graced with clouds on the approach of the rainy season. And that palace, which was adorned with thousands of pillars, and which, as if piercing the heavens, looked like a peak of Kailaça—was the residence of the Sovereign of the Rakshasas—the ornament of the city, (ever guarded by full hundreds of Rakshasas. And Lakshmana's auspicious and puissant elder brother, beholding that flourishing and wealthy city resembling the celestial regions,—charming to the mind, made of gold, graced with mountains, and decked out with mountains containing various metals,—resonant with the notes of various birds; abounding in various beasts,—furnished with various kinds of flowers,—and inhabited by various orders of Rakshasas,—was struck with astonishment. And Rama, surrounded by his mighty forces, saw that palace, filled with diverse kinds of gems, adorned with rows of edifices, and having huge engines and gateways.

SECTION XL.

Then Rama, accompanied by the monkey-leaders, along with Sugriva, ascended the top of Suvela, measuring a circumference of two yoyanas. And staying there for a while and looking at the ten cardinal points, he saw Lanka finely placed on the charming summit of Trikuta,—graced with elegant groves; and (he also saw) the unconquerable lord of Rakshasas, stationed at the top of the gateway, fanned with white chamaras; graced with the umbrella betokening victory; smeared with red sandal; adorned in red ornaments; resembling masses of sable clouds; and apparelled in golden attire,—his breast bearing scars from the tusk-ends of Airavata; covered with a sheet hued like the blood of hares; and appearing like clouds lighted up by the evening sun. And on seeing the Rakshasa-chief, Sugriva suddenly rose up in the sight of the lords of monkeys as well as Raghava. And influenced by wrath, he, mustering strength and vigor, rising from the brow of the mountain, bounded to the gateway.

# The Beautiful City of Lanka
### From the War Book of the Valmiki Ramayana

The bears, lions, boars, buffaloes, elephants, and deer were terrified by that sound and fled in fear in all ten directions. There was a single, lofty peak of Mount Trikuta that touched the sky, covered all over with flowers and shining like great silver. It was a hundred <term>yojanas</term> <gloss>a measurement of distance, roughly eight miles</gloss> wide, pure and beautiful to behold. It was smooth, majestic, and massive, unreachable even by birds. It was difficult to ascend even in thought, let alone by the actions of men. Situated upon that peak was the city of Lanka, ruled by Ravana. 

It was a hundred <term>yojanas</term> wide and thirty <term>yojanas</term> long. That city was adorned with high gateways that looked like white clouds. It was beautified by a golden wall and a silver wall, and Lanka was highly decorated with palaces and celestial mansions. Like the sky at the end of the hot season filled with clouds, the city stood grand. There, a palace decorated with a thousand pillars stood out, resembling the peak of Mount Kailasa and appearing to scrape the sky. This <term>caitya</term> <gloss>shrine or sacred palace</gloss> of the Lord of the Rakshasas was the jewel of the city. 

It was constantly guarded by a full hundred Rakshasas. Rama, the prosperous elder brother of Lakshmana, together with the monkeys, beheld that charming city of Ravana, which possessed many forests, was graced by mountains of various colorful minerals, and adorned with gardens. It was filled with the songs of various birds and frequented by various groups of beings. It was covered with various flowers and inhabited by various Rakshasas. Seeing that city, crowded with great houses and resembling the city of the gods, the heroic elder brother of Lakshmana was filled with wonder.

Rama, with his great army, gazed upon that city filled with gems, possessing many arrangements, decorated with rows of palaces, and featuring great mechanical engines at its main gates.

Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled The Sight of Lanka, in the War Book of the glorious Ramayana of Valmiki, the first epic poem, a collection of twenty-four thousand verses.

---

### Chapter 40
**The Duel Between Ravana and Sugriva**

Then Rama, surrounded by Sugriva and the leaders of the monkey troops, climbed the peak of Mount Suvela, which had a circumference of two <term>yojanas</term>. Standing there for a moment and looking in all ten directions, he saw the well-constructed city of Lanka on the lovely peak of Trikuta, built by Vishvakarman <note>the divine architect of the gods</note> and graced by beautiful forests. 

On a tower of the gateway, he saw the invincible Lord of the Rakshasas. He was flanked by white fly-whisks and graced by a victorious parasol. He was anointed with red sandalwood and adorned with jeweled ornaments. Appearing like a dark rain-cloud, he wore garments embroidered with gold. His chest bore prominent scars from the tusks of Airavata <note>the divine elephant of Indra</note>. He was wrapped in a red robe with the hue of a rabbit's blood, looking like a mass of clouds in the sky illuminated by the heat of the twilight. 

As the leaders of the monkeys and Rama were watching, Sugriva suddenly sprang up at the sight of the Lord of the Rakshasas.

### Fortieth Chapter
**The Duel Between Rāvaṇa and Sugrīva**

Then Rāma, surrounded by Sugrīva and the leaders of the monkey army, ascended the summit of Mount Suvela, which measured two <term>yojanas</term>. 1

### The Duel between Ravana and Sugriva

He was dressed in red silk, like the color of the sun at twilight, resembling a mass of clouds in the sky. 6
While the monkey kings and Rama were looking on, Sugriva, upon seeing the demon king, suddenly stood up. 7

### Śrīmad Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa, Yuddhakāṇḍa

730

Bears, lions, boars, buffaloes, elephants, and deer were terrified by that sound and fled in fear toward the ten directions. There was a tall peak of Mount <term>Trikūṭa</term> <gloss>Three-peaks</gloss> that touched the heavens. It was covered all over with flowers and shone like great silver. It was a hundred <term>yojanas</term> <gloss>a measure of distance, about 8-9 miles</gloss> wide, pure and beautiful to behold, smooth, majestic, and so vast that it was inaccessible even to birds. It was impossible to climb even in thought, much less by the actions of men. Situated on that peak was the city of Lanka, protected by Ravana. It was a hundred <term>yojanas</term> wide and thirty <term>yojanas</term> long. That city, with its high gate-towers resembling white clouds, was adorned with a golden wall and silver <note>ornamentation</note>. Lanka was superbly decorated with palaces and celestial mansions, appearing like the sky filled with thick clouds at the end of the summer heat. In that city, a palace adorned with a thousand pillars, shaped like a peak of Mount Kailas and seemingly scraping the sky, served as the ornament of the city for the King of the Rākṣasas. That place was guarded constantly by a full hundred Rākṣasas. The glorious Rama, elder brother of Lakshmana, along with the monkeys, beheld that prosperous city of Ravana, which reached to the sea, was full of forests, graced by mountains with various colorful minerals, adorned with gardens, filled with the sounds of various birds, and inhabited by diverse groups of beings. It was covered with various flowers and served by various Rākṣasas. Seeing that city crowded with great houses, looking like the city of the gods, the powerful Rama, elder brother of Lakshmana, was filled with wonder. Rama, with his great army, gazed upon that city filled with gems and various arrangements, decorated with rows of palaces and featuring great mechanical gates.

Thus ends the thirty-ninth canto, titled "The Sight of Lanka," in the Yuddhakāṇḍa of the glorious Rāmāyaṇa of Vālmīki, the first epic poem, a compendium of twenty-four thousand verses.

### Canto Forty
**The Duel Between Ravana and Sugriva**

Then Rama, accompanied by Sugriva and the leaders of the monkey hosts, ascended the summit of Mount Suvela, which had a circumference of two <term>yojanas</term>. After standing there for a moment and looking toward the ten directions, he saw Lanka, built by <term>Viśvakarmā</term> <gloss>the divine architect</gloss> on the lovely peak of Trikūṭa, well-laid out and graced with beautiful forests. He saw the King of the Rākṣasas, difficult to approach, standing on the top of a gate-tower. He was flanked by white fly-whisks and graced by the parasol of victory. He was anointed with red sandalwood and adorned with jeweled ornaments. Looking like a dark rain-cloud, he wore clothing covered in gold. His chest bore the prominent scars inflicted by the tusks of Airavata <note>the divine elephant of Indra</note>. He was wrapped in a red cloth with the hue of a rabbit's blood, looking like a mass of clouds in the sky bathed in the glow of twilight. While the monkey leaders were looking and while Rama was looking, Sugriva suddenly sprang up at the sight of the King of the Rākṣasas.

reference_meta.located: Karṇaparvan 8.22.58–61 (end of adhyāya 22: Karṇa's boast; Duryodhana grants the carts and cars; turns to Śalya) and 8.23.1–2ab (Duryodhana humbly approaches Śalya); printed page 174; edition's concordance line: Calcutta 8.1318, Bombay 8.31.68, Kumbhakonam 8.22.72
reference_meta.coverage_note: Ganguli follows the vulgate (Bombay/Calcutta) numbering: BORI 8.22 = Ganguli Karna Parva Section XXXI, BORI 8.23 = Ganguli Section XXXII (offset of 9 adhyāyas here). Context added: one sentence before 8.22.58 ('Thou wilt then see...') and the rest of Duryodhana's vocative string after 8.23.2ab (to '...hostile troops with fear,'). Ganguli's 'The very gods and Asuras are not able to advance against me... of human origin?' after 8.22.58 has no counterpart on this page (vulgate-only lines, not in the critical text); Ganguli also expands 8.22.59–60 (cars with steeds, vulturine feathers). The critical apparatus has no reference. The Project Gutenberg text prints section headings as bare numerals ('32' = Section XXXII), kept as printed.

reference_text: For here these groups of gods are entering into you. Some being afraid are praying with joined hands, and the groups of great sages and Siddhas are saying 'Welfare!' and praising you with abundant (hymns) of praise. The Rudras, and Adityas, the Vasus, the Sadhyas, the Visvas, the two Asvins, the Maruts, and the Ushmapas, and the groups of Gandharvas, Yakshas, demons, and Siddhas are all looking at you amazed. Seeing your mighty form, with many mouths and eyes, with many arms, thighs, and feet, with many stomachs, and fearful with many jaws, all people, and I likewise, are much alarmed, O you of mighty arms! Seeing you, O Vishnu! touching the skies, radiant, possessed of many hues, with a gaping mouth, and with large blazing eyes, I am much alarmed in my inmost self, and feel no courage, no tranquillity. And seeing your mouths terrible by the jaws, and resembling the fire of destruction, I cannot recognise the (various) directions, I feel no comfort. Be gracious, O lord of gods! who pervadest the universe. And all these sons of Dhritarâshtra, together with all the bands of kings, and Bhishma and Drona, and this charioteer's son likewise, together with our principal warriors also, are rapidly entering your mouths, fearful and horrific by (reason of your) jaws. And some with their heads smashed are seen (to be) stuck in the spaces between the teeth. As the many rapid currents of a river's waters run towards the sea alone, so do these heroes of the human world enter your mouths blazing all round. As butterflies, with increased velocity, enter a blazing fire to their destruction, so too do these people enter your mouths with increased velocity (only) to their destruction. Swallowing all these people, you are licking them over and over again from all sides, with your blazing mouths. Your fierce splendours, O Vishnu! filling the whole universe with (their) effulgence, are heating it.

एव ह्येभ्यः सर्वेभ्यः परः प्रतिपाद्यत इति युक्तं न प्रत्येकमेषां परत्वप्रतिपादनम् । कस्मात् । प्रयोजनाभावात् । नहीतरेषु परत्वेन प्रतिपन्नेषु किञ्चित्प्रयोजनं दृश्यते श्रूयते वा । पुरुषे त्विन्द्रियादिभ्यः परस्मिन्सर्वार्थवातातीते प्रतिपन्ने दृश्यते प्रयोजनं मोक्षसिद्धिः । तथाच श्रुतिः—‘निचाय्य तन्मृत्युमुखात्प्रमुच्यते’ (कठ० ३।१५) इति । अपिच परप्रतिषेधेन काष्ठाशब्देन च पुरुषविषयमादरं दर्शयन्पुरुषप्रतिपत्तयैव पूर्वोत्तरप्रवाह इति दर्शयति—आख्यानायेति । आख्यानपूर्वकाय सम्यग्दर्शनायेत्यर्थः । सम्यग्दर्शनार्थमेव हीदमाख्यानमुपदिश्यते न त्वाख्यानमेव स्वप्रधानम् ॥ १४ ॥

**आत्मशब्दाच्च ॥ १५ ॥**

इतश्च पुरुषप्रतिपत्तयैवेमिन्द्रियादिप्रवाहोक्तिः । यत्कारणम् ‘एष सर्वेषु भूतेषु गूढोत्मा न प्रकाशते । दृश्यते त्वग्र्यया बुद्ध्या सूक्ष्मया सूक्ष्मदर्शिभिः’ (कठ० ३।१२) इति प्रकृतं पुरुषमात्मत्याह । अतःश्रुतानात्मत्वमितरेषां विवक्षितमिति गम्यते तस्यैव च दुर्विज्ञानतां संस्कृतमतिगम्यतां च दर्शयति । तद्विज्ञानायैव ‘यच्छेद्वाङ्मनसी प्राज्ञः’ (कठ० ३।१३) इत्याख्यानं विदधाति । तद्व्याख्यातम ‘आनुमानिकमप्येकेषाम्’ (ब्र० सू० १।४।१) इत्यत्र । एवमनेकप्रकार-

किञ्चित्सा काष्ठा’ इति वेदः परनिषेधलिङ्गेन सर्वभावाधिवलिङ्गेन च पुरुषे तात्पर्यं दर्शयन्पूर्वसात्पूर्वस्मादपरस्यापरस्य परत्वोक्तिस्तदर्थेति दर्शयतीलाह—अपिचेति । अर्थादीनामपिराध्यानाय तत्सपरत्वाधानपूर्वकं पुरुषदर्शनायैव स्वतः प्रयोजनाभावादिति सूत्रं योजयति—आख्यानायेति ॥ १४ ॥ आत्मशब्दाच्चेति । किंच ‘तद्विष्णोः परमं पदं, पुरुषात् परं किञ्चित्’ इत्युपक्रमोपसंहारयोरैकरूप्याल्लक्ष-फलवदेकपुरुषपरत्वेनैकवाक्यत्वनिश्चये सति वाक्यभेदफलभेदकल्पना न युक्ता गौरवादित्याह—अपिचेति ॥ १५ ॥

**न्यायनिर्णयः**

कस्मादिति । तात्पर्यमेयरनिनिष्फलभावाज्ञानादीपरत्वात् तन्मेयेतेति मत्वाह—प्रयोजनेति । कथं प्रयोजनाभावोक्तिरित्याशङ्कान्वयव्यतिरेकसिद्धं शास्त्रसिद्धं वा फलमिति विकल्प्याहं निराह—नेतीति । द्वितीयं प्रत्याह—श्रूयते चेति । प्रकरणस्यास्य वस्तुपरत्वदृष्टेरुपास्तिविधिपरत्वायोगत्परमपुरुषार्थेतत्त्वधीपरत्वे च संभवतीन्द्रियाण्युपस्थीनस्मृतिसिद्धान्तान्तरपुमर्थपरत्वायोगान्न प्रत्येकंमधीपरत्वसिद्धि रित्यर्थः । पुरुषस्य परत्वधीरापि न फलवती परत्वधीतवादयोदिपरत्वधीत्वनुमानात्कथं त्वन्यतेऽपि पुरुषार्थे-हेतुफलत्वमित्याशङ्कनार्थशून्यतोपलक्षितानबच्छिन्नातिविषयत्वात्पुरुषपरत्वेष्टेरनध्वंसत्वमनुभवसिद्धमित्याह—पुरुषे त्विति । अज्ञानमिथ्याशान्तेर्दृष्टफलत्वाष्टे सत्यदृष्टकल्पना न युक्तेति मत्वाह—दृश्यते इति । विद्वदनुभवे विप्रतिपन्नं प्रति पुरुषपरत्वदृष्टेष्टफलत्वे श्रुतिमाह—तथाचेति । इतश्चास्य संदर्भस्य सर्वतात्पर्यत्वेन पुरुषप्रमितिपरत्वेत्याह—अपिचेति । पुरुषात्परमिति निषेधलिङ्गेन सा काष्ठेति काष्ठाशब्देन बाधाधिवेन परत्वोक्तिलेन च पुरुषविषयमादरं दर्शयन्वेद इति यावत् । पूर्वोपरप्रवाहोक्तिः पूर्वसात्पूर्वस्मादपरस्य परत्वोक्तिः । ध्यानविधेरिहाभावात्परपुरुषमितेर्ध्यानाथता कथं श्रुतेतलाशङ्कय सूत्रावयवं व्याचष्टे—आख्यानेति । निर्गुणब्रह्मप्रमितिरपि ध्यानाथा ब्रह्मस्थितत्वात्सुगुणमभिवदतिदिश्याशङ्क ततस्तु तमित्यादिश्रुतिविरोधमाह—सम्यगिति ॥ १४ ॥ सर्वसात्परत्वेन पुरुषस्यैवात्र प्रतिपाद्यत्वे हेत्वन्तरमाह—आरमेति । सूत्रस्थं चशब्दं व्याकरोति—इतश्चेति । तदेव स्फुटयन्नात्मशब्दं विभजते—यदिति । आत्मनोऽप्रकाशमानत्वं स्वाभाविकमिति शङ्कां वारयति—दृश्यते त्विति । तस्यां श्रुतावेव आत्मत्वेत्याह—प्रकृतमिति । सूत्रगतपदव्याख्या विवक्षितमर्थमाह—अतश्चेति । अवशिष्टपूर्वार्थसाधनाह—तस्येति । उत्तरार्थतात्पर्यमाह—संस्कृतति । चशब्दसूचित हेत्वन्तरमाह—तदिति । वागादिनियमनमात्रं मन्त्रे प्रतीतं न तु ध्यानविधिरित्याशङ्क—तव्याख्यातमिति । अज्ञातार्थपनस्त्वाभ्यादागमस्यात्मनश्च श्रुत्यैव दुर्ज्ञानत्वेर्विस्तृतत्व तसादाददीनां च सुगमत्वादेषां परत्वोक्तिरपि तात्पर्यवेधमितेत्यर्थः—एवमिति । उपक्रमोप-

To this we reply as follows.

We must assume that the whole passage aims at intimating only that the person is higher than everything. Any information as to the relative superiority of the preceding members of the series would be devoid of all purpose ; for of the knowledge derived from such observation a use is neither to be seen nor declared by scripture. Of the knowledge, on the other hand, of the person being higher than the senses and everything else, raised above all evil, we do see a purpose, viz. the accomplishment of final release. And so scripture also says, ' He who has perceived that is freed from the jaws of death' (I, 3, 15). Moreover, the text by declaring that nothing is higher than the person and that he is the highest goal intimates reverence for the person, and thereby shows that the whole series of objects is enumerated only to the end of giving information about the person. — ' For the purpose of pious meditation,' i.e. for the purpose of perfect knowledge which has pious meditation for its antecedent. For the passage under consideration does not teach pious meditation by itself.

15. And on account of the word ' Self.'

The above conclusion is confirmed by the circumstance that the person under discussion is called the Self in I, 3, 12, 'That Self is hidden in all beings and does not shine forth, but it is seen by subtle seers through their sharp and subtle intellect.' From this we conclude that the text wishes to represent the other beings enumerated as the Non-Self. The passage quoted, moreover, indicates that the person is hard to know, and to be reached by sharp minds only. — Again, the passage (I, 3, 13), 'A wise man should keep down speech and mind,' enjoins pious meditation as a means of the knowledge of the highest person, as we have explained under I, 4, i. — It thus follows that scripture indicates various excellences in the case of the purusha only, and not in that of the other beings enumerated.— The passage, moreover, ' He reaches the end of his journey and that is the highest place of Vish/m,' suggests the question as to who is the end of the journey and so on, and we therefore conclude that the enumeration of the senses, objects, &c., has merely the purpose of teaching the highest place of Vish;/u (not of teaching anything about the relation of the senses, objects, and so on).

For in this way, the one who is higher than all of these is presented, and it is correct that the focus is not on the superiority of each individual element. Why so? Because there is no purpose in doing so. No purpose is seen or heard of in the scriptures regarding the individual superiority of the other elements <note>such as the senses and mind</note>. However, regarding the <term>Purusha</term> <gloss>the Supreme Person or Consciousness</gloss>, who is higher than the senses and the rest, and who transcends the entire realm of objects, a purpose is seen: the attainment of <term>Moksha</term> <gloss>liberation</gloss>. Thus says the <term>Shruti</term> <gloss>scripture</gloss>: Having perceived That, one is released from the jaws of death <note>Katha Upanishad 3.15</note>. Moreover, by denying anything higher than the <term>Purusha</term> and by using the word <term>Kastha</term> <gloss>the ultimate goal/pinnacle</gloss>, the scripture shows its primary regard for the <term>Purusha</term>. It shows that the progression of preceding and succeeding elements is for the sake of realizing the <term>Purusha</term>. As for the phrase for the sake of the story: it means for the sake of right knowledge which is preceded by the story. This story is taught only for the purpose of right knowledge, and the story itself is not the primary objective.

**And because of the word Atman. (15)**

For this reason also, the description of the sequence of the senses and so on is intended only for the realization of the <term>Purusha</term>. The reason is that the scripture refers to the <term>Purusha</term> under discussion as the <term>Atman</term> <gloss>the Self</gloss>, saying: This Self, hidden in all beings, does not shine forth; but it is seen by subtle seers through their sharp and subtle intellect <note>Katha Upanishad 3.12</note>. From this, it is understood that the others <note>senses, objects, mind</note> are not intended to be regarded as the Self. It also shows the difficulty of knowing Him and that He is attainable by a refined intellect. For the very purpose of knowing Him, the scripture prescribes the method: The wise man should restrain speech in the mind <note>Katha Upanishad 3.13</note>. This was already explained under the section Beginning with the Inference <note>Brahma Sutra 1.4.1</note>. Thus, in various ways...

->**Bhamati**<-

Furthermore, the Veda, by the sign of denying anything beyond <note>There is nothing beyond the Purusha</note> and by the sign of the <term>Purusha</term> being the goal of all things, shows that the intent is on the <term>Purusha</term>. It shows that the mention of the superiority of one element over another is for that purpose; this is stated in the phrase moreover. Because objects and the rest have no independent purpose, the author connects the sutra by saying for the sake of the story, meaning for the sake of the vision of the <term>Purusha</term> preceded by those superiorities. **And because of the word Atman.** Since there is a consistency between the beginning and the end in phrases like That is the supreme step of Vishnu and There is nothing higher than the Purusha, it is certain that the whole passage forms a single sentence focused on the one <term>Purusha</term>. Therefore, it is not proper to imagine a split in the sentence or a split in the results, as that would be unnecessarily complex.

->**Nyaya Nirnaya**<-

To the question "Why?", the author replies "Because of the lack of purpose," thinking that since there is no result from knowing the superiority of the senses and so on, it cannot be the intended meaning. To the doubt that there might be a purpose, he denies it by saying "No." To the second alternative <note>that a result is heard in scripture</note>, he says "nor is it heard." Since this context is seen to concern the nature of reality and not injunctions for meditation, and since it is possible for it to concern the knowledge of the Supreme Goal, it is not proper to assume it concerns the superiority of individual senses. One might object that the knowledge of the <term>Purusha's</term> superiority is also not fruitful. He replies "But in the <term>Purusha</term>," stating that the vision of the <term>Purusha</term> as higher than the senses—characterized by the absence of objects and being unconditioned—is experienced as the destruction of ignorance. He says "It is seen," meaning the removal of ignorance and false knowledge is a visible result. For those who disagree with the experience of the wise, he cites the <term>Shruti</term>: "Thus." He adds "Moreover" to show this is the total intent of the context. The Veda shows its regard for the <term>Purusha</term> by the word <term>Kastha</term> <gloss>pinnacle</gloss>. The "progression" refers to the superiority of each succeeding element over the preceding one. He explains the part of the sutra "for the sake of the story" to counter the idea that it refers to an injunction for meditation. **And because of the word Atman.** He explains the "and" in the sutra with "For this reason." He clarifies the word <term>Atman</term> by saying "Which." He removes the doubt that the non-manifestation of the Self is natural by saying "But it is seen." He shows that the difficulty of knowing the Self is due to the excellence of the intent regarding the beginning and end of the text.

<summary>Shankara argues that the hierarchical progression of the senses and mind in the Katha Upanishad is not to teach their individual importance, but to guide the seeker toward the Supreme Purusha (Self), which is the only source of liberation.</summary>

# Brahma Sutra Bhashya | [Adhyaya 3, Pada 3, Adhikarana 7, Sutra 14]

It is the Supreme Being alone that is presented as superior to all of these; therefore, it is appropriate that each one is not declared superior. Why? Because there is no purpose. For no purpose is seen or heard in the superiority of the others being established. However, when the Person <term>purusha</term> <gloss>the Conscious Subject</gloss> is understood as being beyond the senses and the rest, and beyond all objective phenomena, a purpose is seen: the attainment of liberation <term>moksha</term> <gloss>release</gloss>. And so the scripture says: "By discerning this, one is released from the mouth of death" (Katha Upanishad 3.15). Moreover, by showing reverence for the subject of the Person through the denial of anything else and the use of the word 'limit' <term>kastha</term> <gloss>the final point or limit</gloss>, the text shows that the sequence from the former to the latter is for the realization of the Person. The phrase "for the sake of the narrative" means for the sake of the correct knowledge preceded by a narrative. This narrative is indeed taught only for the sake of correct knowledge, not because the narrative itself is the primary focus. 14

**And because of the word 'Self'. 15**

For this reason also, the description of the sequence of the senses and the rest is meant for the realization of the Person. The reason is that the text refers to the Person under discussion as the Self: "This Self, hidden in all beings, does not shine forth. But it is seen by the subtle seers through their sharp and subtle intellect" (Katha Upanishad 3.12). Hence, it is understood that it is not intended for the others to be the Self. It also shows that the Person is difficult to know and requires a refined mind to be understood. For the sake of that knowledge, the text prescribes the narrative: "The wise man should restrain his speech into the mind" (Katha Upanishad 3.13). **Bhamati**

The Veda, by the sign of the negation of others and the sign of being the substrate of all things, shows the purport lies in the Person. Thus, he says 'Moreover' <term>apica</term>, to show that the statement of superiority of each subsequent one over the previous one is intended for that purpose. He connects the sutra 'for the sake of the narrative' by explaining that the superiority of one over the other is for the sake of seeing the Person, as there is no independent purpose in the others. 14 'And because of the word Self'. Furthermore, because of the consistency between the opening and closing statements—"That is the highest abode of Vishnu" and "There is nothing superior to the Person"—it is certain that the whole passage aims at a single Person. Thus, it is not appropriate to assume a difference in sentences or a difference in results, as it would be cumbersome. 15

**Nyaya Nirnaya**

'Why?' He considers that the purport is not meant for the others because they lack the capacity to produce the desired result. 'No purpose'—he asks how the absence of purpose is stated, and he differentiates between fruit established by logical analysis and fruit established by scripture. He says 'No' to the first. He replies to the second, 'is heard'. Since this passage is seen to concern the nature of reality, it is not suited for the injunction of meditation; it concerns the knowledge of the ultimate goal of human life. Since the inner self is the goal, the senses do not have independent status as the goal, so the knowledge of each one's superiority is not the aim. If the knowledge of the Person's superiority were also fruitless, how could there be a causal relationship to the human goal? He says 'However, in the Person' because, as the subject of the ultimate, the knowledge of the Person is not empty and is experiential. 'Is seen'—he maintains that since the cessation of ignorance and false knowledge is a visible fruit, it is not right to imagine an unseen one. Regarding the experience of the wise, he cites the scripture 'And so'. He says 'Moreover' because the entire context aims at the knowledge of the Person. 'Superior to the Person'—the Veda shows reverence for the Person by the sign of negation and the word 'limit' as a boundary. The sequence of former to latter is the statement of the superiority of the latter over the former. Since there is no injunction for meditation here, how can the knowledge of the Person be for meditation? He explains the part of the sutra: 'for the sake of the narrative'. The knowledge of the attributeless Brahman is also for the sake of meditation as it resides in Brahman, but he clarifies that it is consistent with the scripture 'Then he who...'. 14 He gives another reason for the Person being the only subject here: 'And because of the word Self'. He explains the word 'and' in the sutra: 'For this reason also'. Explaining clearly, he breaks down the word 'Self'. He refutes the doubt that the non-manifestation of the Self is natural: 'But it is seen'. He says 'under discussion' because of the Selfhood in that scripture. He states the intended meaning of the sutra: 'Hence'. He explains the rest of the earlier meaning: 'of that'. He states the purport of the later part: 'refined mind'. He gives the other reason indicated by the word 'and': 'That'. Regarding the doubt that only the restraint of speech is mentioned in the mantra, not an injunction for meditation, he says 'That has been explained'. The meaning is that since the Self is difficult to know by scripture itself, and the senses are easy to know, the declaration of their superiority is a device for the purport. <summary>This page continues the commentary on the Brahma Sutras, arguing that the sequence of elements (senses, mind, intellect, etc.) in the Katha Upanishad is not an end in itself, but a means to lead the seeker toward the realization of the Supreme Person (Purusha) as the ultimate Self. It emphasizes that realization of the Person is the sole purpose of these narratives and that the text consistently points to the Person as the highest reality.</summary>

# Brahma Sutra Bhashya | [Adhyaya 3, Pada 3, Adhikarana 7, Sutra 14

For it is indeed the Supreme Being that is taught as higher than all of these; therefore, it is reasonable that the superiority of each one is not being established. Why? Because there is no purpose. For no purpose is seen or heard if superiority is established in the others. However, when the Purusha <note>original: "पुरुष" <gloss>the Self or Supreme Person</gloss></note> is understood as higher than the senses and the rest, and as surpassing all objects, a purpose is seen, namely, the attainment of liberation. And so the Shruti <note>original: "श्रुति" <gloss>scriptural revelation</gloss></note> says: "Having perceived Him, one is liberated from the mouth of death" (Katha Upanishad 3.15). Furthermore, by showing regard for the subject of the Purusha through the negation of the others and through the word *kashtha* <gloss>limit or culmination</gloss>, it indicates that the entire progression from the earlier to the later is for the sake of the realization of the Purusha. This is meant for *akhyana* <gloss>narrative or instruction</gloss>. The meaning is that the narrative exists for the sake of right knowledge. For this narrative is taught solely for the sake of right knowledge, and not that the narrative itself is the primary object. 14

**Due to the word *Atman* also. 15**

From this also it is evident that the statement of the progression of the senses and the rest is solely for the realization of the Purusha. For the reason that it says "This *Atman* <gloss>Self</gloss> hidden in all beings does not shine forth; but it is seen by the subtle, sharp intellect of those who see the subtle" (Katha Upanishad 3.12), it calls the Purusha under discussion the *Atman*. Thus, it is understood that the quality of being the *Atman* is intended to be excluded in the others. It also shows that the Purusha is difficult to know and to be realized by those whose minds are refined. It provides the narrative "The wise man should restrain his speech in the mind" (Katha Upanishad 3.13) for the sake of knowing Him. That has been explained in the section "Even that which is inferred by some" (Brahma Sutra 1.4.1). In this way, of many types—

**Bhamati**

...the limit of something—the Veda, by the indicator of negation of the others and by the indicator of it being the basis of all beings, shows that the purport is in the Purusha. Therefore, it indicates that the statement of superiority of the later over the earlier is for that purpose, he says "Furthermore." He links the Sutra to the fact that because there is no purpose in the others, and the sequence of superiority is for the sake of the realization of the Purusha, thus the narrative is for the sake of instruction. 14. "Due to the word Atman also": Furthermore, because there is uniformity in the opening and the conclusion, such as "That is the supreme step of Vishnu" and "There is nothing higher than the Purusha," upon establishing a unity of meaning focused on the one Purusha, it is not reasonable to assume a difference in sentences or a difference in results, as it would be unnecessarily complex, he says "Furthermore." 15

**Nyaya Nirnaya**

Why? Because the purport is not established regarding the fruitlessness of the others. He thinks, since there is no such fruit, it is not established, and says "Because there is no purpose." How can there be an assertion of a lack of purpose? He considers the alternative of whether the result is established by logic or by scripture, and says "Not so." He replies to the second: "It is also heard." Since the context is seen to be focused on the reality, it cannot be for the sake of a command for meditation. If it is focused on the highest human goal, the knowledge of the truth, then the explanation is possible. The purpose is not to establish the superiority of each one, as that would contradict the logic of the senses and the established doctrine of the human goal. The realization of the superiority of the Purusha is not fruitless. If it were fruitless, one would have to infer the fruit based on the text. Why should the Purusha be the goal if there is no other purpose? He says "However, for the Purusha," because he is the limitless object characterized by being free from all worldly concepts; thus, the absence of destruction is a matter of experience. He sees that for one who has destroyed ignorance and false knowledge, the fruit is seen, so it is not reasonable to imagine an unseen result, and says "It is seen." Regarding the doubt of the wise experience, he cites the Shruti for the result of the vision of the superiority of the Purusha: "And so." From this, because the entire context has this as its purport, he says "Furthermore." The negation "higher than Purusha" is an indicator of the limit, and the word *kashtha* is the boundary; thus, the Veda shows regard for the Purusha. The statement of the progression from the earlier to the later is the statement of the superiority of the later over the earlier. Since there is no command for meditation here, how can the knowledge of the supreme Purusha be for the sake of meditation? He raises this doubt and explains the part of the Sutra: "For the sake of narrative." Even the realization of the attributeless Brahman is for the sake of meditation because it is the state of Brahman. He points to the objection of contradiction with the Shruti "From that, Him..." and says "Right knowledge." 14. He gives another reason why the Purusha alone is to be established here as superior: "Due to the word Atman." He explains the word *cha* <gloss>and</gloss> in the Sutra: "From this also." Clarifying that, he analyzes the word *Atman*: "That which." He wards off the doubt that the non-shining of the Atman is natural: "But it is seen." He says it is "under discussion" because the Atman quality is in that very Shruti. He explains the intended meaning of the words in the Sutra: "Thus also." He performs the task of establishing the remaining meaning: "Of Him." He states the purport of the latter part: "Refined." He states the other reason indicated by the word *cha*: "That." He objects that only the restraint of speech and mind is apparent in the mantra, not a command for meditation: "That has been explained." The meaning is that since the Atman is difficult to know by scripture itself, and the rest are easy to understand, the statement of their superiority is also intended as the primary focus. In this way, the excess of the opening and the conclusion.

The knowledge of the attributeless Brahman is also for the sake of meditation as it resides in Brahman, but he clarifies that it is consistent with the scripture 'Then he who...'. 14 He gives another reason for the Person being the only subject here: 'And because of the word Self'. He explains the word 'and' in the sutra: 'For this reason also'. Explaining clearly, he breaks down the word 'Self'. He refutes the doubt that the non-manifestation of the Self is natural: 'But it is seen'. He says 'under discussion' because of the Selfhood in that scripture. He states the intended meaning of the sutra: 'Hence'. He explains the rest of the earlier meaning: 'of that'. He states the purport of the later part: 'refined mind'. He gives the other reason indicated by the word 'and': 'That'. Regarding the doubt that only the restraint of speech is mentioned in the mantra, not an injunction for meditation, he says 'That has been explained'. The meaning is that since the Self is difficult to know by scripture itself, and the senses are easy to know, the declaration of their superiority is a device for the purport. In all cases of offences, punishment for offences committed for the first time shall be the first amercement; twice as much for offences committed for a second time; thrice as much for the third time; and for offences committed for the fourth time, the king may impose any punishment he likes.

When a prostitute does not yield her person to any one under the orders of the king, she shall receive 1000 lashes with a whip or pay a fine of 5,000 panas.

When having received the requisite amount of fees, a prostitute dislikes to yield her person, she shall be fined twice the amount of the fees.

When, in her own house, a prostitute deprives her paramour of his enjoyment, she shall be fined eight times the amount of the fees unless the paramour happens to be unassociable on account of disease and personal defects.

When a prostitute murders her paramour, she shall be burnt alive or thrown into water.

When a paramour steals the jewellery or money of, or deceives to pay the fees due to, a prostitute, he shall be fined eight times that amount.

Every prostitute shall supply information to the superintendent as to the amount of her daily fees (bhoga), her future income (áyati), and the paramour (under her influence).

The same rules shall apply to an actor, dancer, singer, player on musical instruments, a buffoon (vágjivana), a mimic player (kusílava), rope-dancer (plavaka), a juggler (saubhika), a wandering bard or herald (chárana), pimps, and unchaste women.

When persons of the above description come from foreign countries to hold their performances, they shall pay 5 panas as license fee (prekshávetana).

Every prostitute (rúpájivá) shall pay every month twice the amount of a day's earning (bhogadvigunam) to the Government.

Those who teach prostitutes, female slaves, and actresses, arts such as singing, playing on musical instruments, reading, dancing, acting, writing, painting, playing on the instruments like vina, pipe, and drum, reading the thoughts of others, manufacture of scents and garlands, shampooing, and the art of attracting and captivating the mind of others shall be endowed with maintenance from the State.

They (the teachers) shall train the sons of prostitutes to be chief actors (rangopajívi) on the stage.

The wives of actors and others of similar profession who have been taught various languages and the use of signals (sanja) shall, along with their relatives, be made use of in detecting the wicked and murdering or deluding foreign spies.

[Thus ends Chapter XXVII, "The Superintendent of Prostitutes" in Book II, "The Duties of Government Superintendents," of the Arthasástra of Kautilya. End of the forty-eighth chapter from the beginning.]

# 44 Section: The Superintendent of Courtesans

By the King’s order, a courtesan refusing to associate with a man shall receive one thousand lashes with a whip <note>original: "shifa-sahasram"</note>; or she shall pay a fine of five thousand <term>panas</term> <gloss>the standard copper coin of the era</gloss>.

If she harbors hatred toward a man after receiving payment, she shall be fined twice the amount of the payment.

If she prevents a man from staying or withholds his dues, she shall pay eight times the amount of the payment, unless the man suffers from disease or personal defects.

If a courtesan causes the death of a man out of excessive passion, she shall be burned alive or drowned in water.

Anyone who steals the jewelry or the payment of a courtesan shall be fined eight times the value.

A courtesan shall report her earnings, her future income, and the identity of her clients to the authorities.

By these rules, the conduct of the wives of actors, dancers, singers, musicians, storytellers, bards, rope-dancers, jugglers, and wandering performers, as well as secret prostitutes, is explained.

Those among them who are traveling performers shall pay five <term>panas</term> as a performance tax for each show.

Prostitutes who live by their beauty <term>rupajiva</term> <gloss>those not in the state service but living independently</gloss> shall pay one-fifteenth of their monthly income to the state.

The teachers shall instruct the courtesans, female slaves, and stage performers in the arts of singing, playing instruments, recitation, dancing, acting, writing, painting, playing the lute <term>veena</term>, flute, and drum, reading the thoughts of others, preparation of perfumes and garlands, the art of seduction, massage, and the specialized knowledge of the courtesan's craft.

The state shall provide a livelihood for these teachers from the royal treasury. The sons of courtesans and chief stage performers shall be trained as lead performers and in all types of rhythmic timing <term>tala</term>.

Women who are skilled in signs and foreign languages shall be employed to detect foreign spies, to assassinate enemies, or to cause negligence among the enemy's forces, while appearing to be relatives or servants.

Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, The Superintendent of Courtesans, in the section concerning the Activity of Superintendents. It is the forty-eighth chapter from the beginning of the work.

[अ०९श्लो०३०-३१]

श्री० टी०—यदि भक्तेभ्य एव मोक्षं ददासि नामक्तेभ्यस्तर्हि तवापि किं रागद्वेषादिकृतं वैषम्यमस्ति नेत्याह—सम इति। समोऽहं सर्वेष्वपि भूतेषु अतो मे मम प्रियश्च द्वेष्यश्च नास्त्येव। एवं सत्यपि ये मां भजन्ति ते भक्ता मयि वर्तन्ते। अहमपि तेषु अनुग्राहकतया। अयं भावः—यथाऽग्नेः स्वसेवकष्वेव तमःशीतादिदुःखमपाकुरुवतोऽपि न वैषम्यं, यथा वा कल्पवृक्षस्य, तथैव भक्तपक्षपातिनोऽपि मम नास्त्येव वैषम्यं किं तु मद्भक्तेरायं महिमेति ॥ २९ ॥

म० टी०—किं च मद्भक्तेरायं महिमा यत्समेऽपि वैषम्यमापादयति, शृणु तन्महिमानम्—

> अपि चेत्सुदुराचारो भजते मामनन्यभाक् ॥
> साधुरेव स मन्तव्यः सम्यग्व्यवसितो हि सः ॥३०॥

यः कश्चित्सुदुराचारोऽपि चेदजामिलादिरिवानन्यभाक्सन्मां भजते कुतश्चिद्भाग्योदयात्सेवते स प्रागसाधुरपि साधुरेव मन्तव्यः। हि यस्मात्सम्यग्व्यवसितः साधुनिश्चयवान्सः ॥ ३० ॥

श्री० टी०—अपि च मद्भक्तेरवितर्क्यः प्रभाव इति दर्शयन्नाह—अपि चेदिति। अत्यन्तं दुराचारोऽपि नरो यदि पृथक्त्वेन देवतान्तरभक्तिमकुर्वन्नामेव श्रीनारायणं भजते तर्हि साधुः श्रेष्ठ एव स मन्तव्यः। यतोऽसौ सम्यग्व्यवसितः परमेश्वरभजनेनैव कृतार्थो भविष्यामीति शोभनमध्यवसायं कृतवान् ॥ ३० ॥

म० टी०—अस्मादेव सम्यग्व्यवसायात्स हित्वा दुराचारताम्—

> क्षिप्रं भवति धर्मात्मा शश्वच्छान्तिं निगच्छति ॥
> कौन्तेय प्रतिजानीहि न मे भक्तः प्रणश्यति ॥ ३१ ॥

चिरकालमधर्मात्माऽपि मद्भजनमहिम्ना क्षिप्रं शीघ्रमेव भवति धर्मात्मा धर्मानुगतचित्तो दुराचारत्वं झटित्येव त्यक्त्वा सदाचारो भवतीत्यर्थः। किं च शश्वन्नित्यं शान्तिं विषयभोगस्पृहानिवृत्तिं निगच्छति नितरां प्राप्नोत्यतिनिर्वेदात्। काश्चिन्मद्भक्तः प्रागभ्यस्तं दुराचारवमत्यजन्न भवेदपि धर्मात्मा, तथा च स नश्येदेवेति नेत्याह भक्तानुकम्पापरवशतया कुपित इव भगवान्—नैतदाश्चर्यं मन्वीथा हे कौन्तेय निश्चितमेवेदशं मद्भक्तेर्माहात्म्यम्। अतो विप्रतिपन्नानां पुरस्तादपि त्वं प्रतिजानीहि सावज्ञं सगर्वं च प्रतिज्ञां कुरु न मे वासुदेवस्य भक्तोऽतिदुराचारोऽपि प्राणसंकटमापन्नोऽपि सुदुर्लभयोग्यः सन्प्रार्थ्यमानोऽपि अतिमूढोऽशरणोऽपि न प्रणश्यति किं तु कृतार्थ एव
