"With the tongue," etc. By extending the tongue outward like the lower beak of a bird, draw in the air and perform the <term>puraka</term> <gloss>inhalation</gloss> slowly. Perform the <term>kumbhaka</term> <gloss>breath retention</gloss> as mentioned previously regarding the <term>Suryabhedana</term> <gloss>Sun-piercing breath</gloss>. The wise one, possessing good intellect, should slowly exhale the air through the openings of the nostrils. 57.

Describing the virtues of <term>Shitali</term>. "Tumors," etc. Tumors, enlarged spleen, and other such diseases, fever, bilious disorders, hunger, thirst, and toxins resulting from snakebites and similar poisons—this <term>kumbhaka</term> known as <term>Shitali</term> destroys them completely. 58.

<column-break/>

-> Vernacular Translation <-

"Will become," etc. The body gains strength, and through this practice, one becomes like an Indra among yogis upon the earth, free from all disturbances. The fruit mentioned here is certain. 56.

Now, the fourth <term>kumbhaka</term>, <term>Shitali</term>, is described. "With the tongue," etc. Extending the tongue outside the lips like the lower beak of a bird, draw in the air, perform inhalation, and then perform the <term>kumbhaka</term> practice as previously mentioned for <term>Suryabhedana</term>. Then, one whose intellect is fine should slowly exhale the air through the nasal passages. 57.

The virtues of <term>Shitali</term> are described. "Tumors," etc. Diseases such as tumors and enlarged spleen, fever, bilious disorders, the desire for food, the desire for water, the poison of snakebites, and other poisons—all of these are removed by this <term>kumbhaka</term> called <term>Shitali</term>. 58.

<summary>This page describes the Shitali pranayama technique, explaining the physical practice and its therapeutic benefits, such as alleviating fever, digestive issues, and poisoning.</summary>
<keywords>Shitali Kumbhaka, Hatha Yoga, Pranayama, Respiratory health, Traditional medicine, Svatmarama</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page: the root verse 56 completes the description of the Sītkārī breath-retention begun on the previous page</meta>

**Root text** <note>original: "mū°", short for <term>mūla</term> <gloss>the root verses of Svātmārāma, as distinct from the commentary</gloss></note> . . . and strength of body arises, free from every affliction.
By this method, truly, he becomes a lord among yogis on the face of the earth. ॥ 56 ॥

### Now the Śītalī ॥ <note><term>Śītalī</term> <gloss>"the cooling one"</gloss>, a breath-retention practised by drawing air in over the tongue.</note>

Drawing in the air with the tongue, let the wise one perform the breath-retention as before,
and then slowly expel the breath through the two nostrils. ॥ 57 ॥

Abdominal swellings, disorders of the spleen and other diseases, fever, bile, hunger and thirst,
and poisons: this breath-retention called Śītalī destroys them all. ॥ 58 ॥

---

->॥ Commentary ॥<- <note>This is the Sanskrit commentary printed with the root text, generally identified as Brahmānanda's <term>Jyotsnā</term> <gloss>"Moonlight"</gloss>.</note>

"Bhavet" ॥ Strength <note>original: "sattvam", glossed as "balam", strength</note> of the body <note>"dehasya" glossed as "śarīrasya"</note> also arises. By this method just stated, that is, the method of practice, the lord of yogis, meaning one who is like Indra among yogis, becomes truly free from all afflictions on the face of the earth. Following the maxim "every statement carries an emphasis" <note>original: "sarvaṃ vākyaṃ sāvadhāraṇam"</note>, the meaning is that the fruit which has been stated is indeed true. ॥ 56 ॥

He now describes the Śītalī breath-retention ॥ "Jihvayā" <note>"with the tongue"</note>. With the tongue put out beyond the lips, shaped like the lower half of a bird's beak, drawing in the air: the meaning is "having slowly made the inhalation" <note><term>pūraka</term> <gloss>the in-breath</gloss></note>. "As before" means as in the Sūryabhedana: the words "having carried out the performance of the retention" <note><term>kumbha</term>, that is <term>kumbhaka</term> <gloss>holding of the breath</gloss></note> are to be supplied. "The wise one": one whose understanding is excellent. Through the two openings of the nose, that is, through the cavities of the nostrils, "śanakaiḥ", meaning simply "slowly". <note>The commentator explains the grammar: by Pāṇini's rule beginning "avyaya-sarvanāmnām", the suffix <term>akac</term> is inserted into the adverb "śanaiḥ", giving the form "śanakaiḥ" with the same meaning.</note> Let him expel <note><term>recaka</term> <gloss>the out-breath</gloss></note> the breath, that is, the air. ॥ 57 ॥

He states the benefits of the Śītalī ॥ "Gulma". Gulma and plīha, abdominal swelling and disease of the spleen, are particular diseases; those disorders which begin with these two are "gulma, plīha and the rest". Fever: the disease called fever. Bile: disorders of the bile. Hunger: the desire to eat. Thirst: the desire to drink water. Poisons: the disorders produced by the venom of snakes and the like. "Called Śītalī" <note>original: "śītalī-nāma"</note>: here "nāma" is an indeclinable carrying the sense "well known as". This breath-retention just described "nihanti", destroys, that is, destroys utterly. The word "kumbha" in the femin- <note>The sentence breaks off at the foot of the page; the commentator is explaining why the feminine form "kumbhikā" is used.</note>

---

->॥ Vernacular explanation ॥<- <note>original: "bhāṣā", a paraphrase in the Hindi of the period, printed beneath the Sanskrit commentary</note>

"Bhavet" ॥ Strength comes to the body, and by this method of practice that has been described, one who is like Indra among yogis becomes free from all afflictions on the earth. The fruit that has been stated here is true. ॥ 56 ॥

Now we describe the fourth, the Śītalī breath-retention ॥ "Jihvayā". Putting one's tongue out beyond the lips like the lower half of a bird's beak, drawing in the air and making the inhalation, one should then carry out the breath-retention just as was described earlier for the Sūryabhedana. Then he whose understanding is fine should slowly, slowly expel the air through the openings of the nose. ॥ 57 ॥

We describe the benefits of the Śītalī ॥ "Gulma". Abdominal swelling and disease of the spleen, and the diseases that begin with these; and fever, and disorders of the bile; and the desire to eat, the desire to drink water; and the venom of snakebite and other poisons as well: all these the breath-retention named Śītalī removes. ॥ 58 ॥

<summary>This page of the Haṭhayogapradīpikā (verses 2.56 to 2.58) closes the account of the Sītkārī breath-retention and teaches the Śītalī, in which air is drawn in over a protruding tongue, held, and released through the nose. It lists the ailments Śītalī is said to cure, with a Sanskrit commentary and a Hindi paraphrase explaining each word.</summary>

reference_text: The following is stated in the Vinaya. «An engineer might construct a mechanical doll (with the form of) a beautiful young woman. It was not a real woman, (but the workmanship was so perfect) that it appeared as a real beauty, and an artist painter (really) fell in love with it. Just so is it that phenomena, although having no separate reality of their own, are nevertheless efficient producers either of moral pollution or moral purification for simple people». We find in the Ratnakutasutra the following (story). «At that time there were five hundred monks who did not understand the preaching of the Buddha. They did not go deep into it. They had no fervour for it. They then stood up from their seats and went away. The Buddha on this occasion produced a magical vision of two recluses on the path by which the monks were receding. The five hundred monks then reached the place where the two apparitional recluses were standing. Having met them they spoke unto them. «Where are both the Reverend Fathers going»? The magical monks answered. «We are retiring to the woods. There we will live enjoying the delightful feeling of trance. We cannot penetrate the doctrine taught by the Buddha, we cannot go deep into it. We feel no devotion, we fear it, we are trembling before it». Then the five hundred monks spoke. «Neither we can penetrate into the doctrine taught by the Buddha, nor can we go deep into it, nor are we devoted to it. We fear, we tremble, we have got quite in a tremble. Therefore we too will go to the woods and live there enjoying the delightful feeling of trance». The magical monks spoke. «Therefore, O Reverends, we shall be united, we shall not quarrel. Above all duties for the monk, not to quarrel is the paramount!» «Whom do the Reverends think to get rid of»? They answered. «We think to get rid of covetousness, of hatred and of infatuation». The two magical monks spoke. «But are the Reverends (really) possessed of those covetousness, hatred and infatuation which they want to forsake ?»

Likewise, in the <term>Ratnakūṭa Sūtra</term> <gloss>The Jewel-Heap Scripture</gloss> <note>original: "Arya-Ratnakūṭa-Sūtra"</note>:

Then it happened that those five hundred <term>bhikṣus</term> <gloss>monks</gloss>, because they did not enter into, dive into, or feel conviction toward the Lord’s teaching of the <term>Dharma</term> <gloss>Universal Law/Truth</gloss>, rose from their seats and departed.

Then the Lord, at that moment, magically produced two monks on the path where those monks were traveling.

Then those five hundred monks approached the place where the two <term>nirmitakas</term> <gloss>magically created forms</gloss> were. Having approached, they said: "Where are you venerable ones going?"

For we do not enter into, dive into, or feel conviction toward the Dharma that the Lord teaches; we stand aloof, we are terrified, we have fallen into great fear."

Then those five hundred monks said: "Venerable ones, we also do not enter into, dive into, or feel conviction toward the Lord’s teaching of the Dharma; we stand aloof, we are terrified, we have fallen into great fear. Therefore, we too shall dwell in the forest retreats in the pleasant states of meditative absorption."

The two created monks said: "In that case, venerable ones, let us harmonize and not dispute. For the qualities of a <term>śramaṇa</term> <gloss>ascetic/seeker</gloss> are defined by non-dispute." <unclear>6 lines of text, not transcribed</unclear>. <summary>This page recounts a narrative from the Ratnakūṭa Sūtra where the Buddha uses magically created monks to guide five hundred followers who were unable to accept his direct teachings. The passage emphasizes the importance of non-dispute and the primary goal of overcoming the three poisons of lust, hatred, and delusion.</summary>

<keywords>Ratnakūṭa Sūtra, bhikṣu, nirmitaka, dhyāna, avivāda, śramaṇa, three poisons, meditation, Buddhist ethics</keywords>

Likewise, in the <term>Ratnakūṭa Sūtra</term> <gloss>The Heap of Jewels Scripture</gloss> <note>original: "Ratnakūṭasūtra"; see the same text cited below regarding chapter 17, verse 33</note>: At that time, those five hundred <term>bhikṣus</term> <gloss>monks</gloss> <note>The Tibetan translation adds "who had attained meditative absorption"</note>, not penetrating, not diving into, and not finding faith in the Lord's teaching of the <term>Dharma</term> <gloss>the Buddha's Law</gloss>, rose from their seats and departed.

Then the Lord, at that moment, magically produced two <term>bhikṣus</term> <gloss>monks</gloss> on the path by which those monks were traveling.

Then those five hundred monks approached the place where those two <term>nirmitakas</term> <gloss>magically created beings</gloss> were. Having approached, they said: "Where are you venerable ones going?"

The two created monks replied: "We are going to the forest retreats. There we shall dwell in the comfortable state of the bliss of <term>dhyāna</term> <gloss>meditative absorption</gloss>. For as for the <term>Dharma</term> which the Lord teaches, we do not penetrate it, we do not dive into it, we do not find faith in it; we are alienated, we feel terror, and we are falling into panic."

Then those five hundred monks said this: "Venerable ones, we also do not penetrate, dive into, or find faith in the Lord's teaching of the <term>Dharma</term>. We are alienated, we are terrified, and we are falling into panic. Therefore, we too shall dwell in the forest retreats in the comfortable state of the bliss of meditation."

The two created monks said: "In that case, venerable ones, we shall agree and not dispute. For the qualities of a <term>śramaṇa</term> <gloss>ascetic seeker</gloss> consist primarily of <term>avivāda</term> <gloss>freedom from dispute</gloss>." <unclear>******</unclear> <note>See below at folio 100a; the text here is abbreviated</note> "For the sake of abandoning what, venerable ones, have you set out?"

They replied: "We have set out for the sake of abandoning lust, hatred, and delusion."

# First Chapter

As it is said in the *Āryaratnakūṭasūtra* <gloss>Noble Heap of Jewels Sutra</gloss>. Then, those five hundred monks, not comprehending, not penetrating, and not having faith in the teaching of the Dharma <gloss>truth/doctrine</gloss> of the Blessed One, rose from their seats and departed. Then the Blessed One created two monks on the path by which those monks were traveling.

Then those five hundred monks approached the path where those two monks—who were *nirmitaka* <gloss>magically created beings</gloss>—were traveling. Having approached, they said to them: "Where are you going, venerable ones?" The created ones replied: "We shall go to the forest dwellings; there we shall dwell in the happiness of meditative contact <gloss>states of deep trance</gloss>. For the Dharma that the Blessed One teaches, we do not comprehend, we do not penetrate, we do not have faith in; we become agitated, we experience distress." Then those five hundred monks said: "We also, venerable ones, do not comprehend, do not penetrate, do not have faith in the teaching of the Dharma of the Blessed One; we become agitated, we experience distress. Therefore, we shall dwell in the forest dwellings in the happiness of meditative contact." The created ones replied: "In that case, venerable ones, we shall live together; we shall not dispute. For the Dharma of a *śramaṇa* <gloss>ascetic/monk</gloss> is supreme in non-dispute." <unclear>******</unclear> "For the abandonment of what, venerable ones, have you undertaken this path?" They replied: "For the abandonment of attachment, aversion, and delusion, we have undertaken..."

# Chapter One

<margin>-12b]</margin>

As in the <term>Āryaratnakūṭasūtra</term> <gloss>The Noble Heap of Jewels Sūtra</gloss>: Then those five hundred monks, not understanding the teaching of the Dharma <gloss>truth/doctrine</gloss> of the Blessed One, not penetrating it, and not finding faith in it, rose from their seats and departed. Then the Blessed One created two monks on the path along which those monks were traveling.

Then those five hundred monks approached the path where those two created monks were. Having approached, they said to them, "Where are you going, venerable ones?" The created ones replied, "We are going to the forest dwellings; there we shall dwell in the happiness of meditative touch <note>a state of profound meditative absorption</note>. For the Dharma the Blessed One teaches, we do not descend into, do not penetrate, do not find faith in; we are uneasy and fall into terror." Then those five hundred monks said this, "We also, venerable ones, do not descend into the Blessed One's teaching of the Dharma, do not penetrate it, do not find faith in it; we are uneasy, we are terrified, and fall into terror. Therefore, we shall dwell in the forest dwellings in the happiness of meditative touch." The created ones replied, "Therefore, venerable ones, we shall associate together and will not dispute. For the Dharma of a <term>śramaṇa</term> <gloss>ascetic/monk</gloss> has non-dispute as its highest goal." <unclear>******</unclear> "For the sake of abandoning what have you, venerable ones, undertaken this practice?" They replied, "We have undertaken this for the sake of abandoning attachment, hatred, and delusion."

<header>सांख्यतत्त्ववृत्तिः ।</header>

स्रष्टः परः अनकान् महेश्वरः सर्वज्ञः सकलजगन्मातृ विधाता । सः कथं ज्ञातव्यः । अनुमानात् वा श्रमात् वा । तथा हि, विवादाध्यासितम् उपलब्धं साकारणं, बभूत्वा भावित्वात्, चित्रवत् इति अनुमानम् । ततः सामान्येन अवगतस्य योगेन विशेषतः ज्ञानम् । अपरस्य जीवस्य स्वानुभवात् एव सिद्धिः । तयोः परापरयोः विवेकज्ञानाय प्रकृतेः प्रवृत्तिः । तत्र परार्थता वक्ष्यते । स्वार्थता च, यं पुरुषं प्रति आत्मानं विवेकेन दर्शितवती, तं प्रति उदास्ते । अचेतनायाः प्रकृतेः कथं प्रवृत्तिः । दृष्टम् अचेतनानाम् अपि दुग्धादीनां फलादि-द्वारेण प्रवृत्तिः इति ॥ १ ॥

अथ के मोक्षाधिकारिणः इत्यत्र आह ॥

विरक्तस्य तत्सिद्धेः ॥ २ ॥

तथा च श्रुतिः 'पुत्रैषणायाश्च वित्तैषणायाश्च लोकैषणायाश्च व्युत्थाय अथ भिक्षाचर्यं चरन्ति' इति, 'शान्तो दान्त उपरतस्तितिक्षुः समाहितो भूत्वा आत्मनि एव आत्मानं पश्यति' ॥ २ ॥

यदि वैराग्यात् श्रवणानन्तरं मोक्षः तदा सर्वेषां गुरुपदेशानन्तरं मोक्षः स्यात्, न च एवं दृश्यते इत्यत्र आह ॥

न श्रवणमात्रात्तत्सिद्धिरनादिवासनायाः बलवत्वात् ॥ ३ ॥

न श्रवणानन्तरं मोक्षः, किन्तु अनादिवासनाया बलवत्वात् क्षिप्रं मुक्तिः, अन्यत्र चिरात् इति ॥ ३ ॥

युक्त्यन्तरम् आह ॥

बहुभृत्ववहा प्रत्येकम् ॥ ४ ॥

The higher [Self] is characterized by knowledge and divine power, and does not even in the least come in contact with the attributes of mundane existence; it is the Supreme, the great God, the omniscient, the creator, because he brings forth everything. How is this to be known? Either by inference or by concentration [i. e., Yoga]. The inference is as follows:

(1) The perceptible [world] which is the object of the dispute must have a cause,

(2) Since it exists after not having existed before,

(3) As is the case with a picture.

[The existence of the Self] in general having been conceived from this [inference], the cognition [of it] in particular [is obtained] by the Yoga. The existence of the lower [Self], i. e., of the empirical soul, is established by the fact that [everybody] is sensible of it. Now, the activity of Matter is for the sake of the discriminative knowledge of these two, i. e., of the higher and of the lower [Self]. As for this [activity of Matter], its being for the benefit of another [i. e., of the Self] will be stated [in III. 58]. And [what is declared in our aphorism, too, viz., that the agency of Matter] is for its own [liberation, must be understood as follows]: to which soul [Matter] has shown itself in its distinction, with that it has nothing to do any more. [“But,” some one may ask,] “how can non-intellectual Matter be active?” [To this question we reply:] We see that non-intellectual trees, also, are active through [the production of] fruits, etc.

“But then, who are those privileged [to attain] to liberation?” With regard to this [question the author] declares:

2. Because this falls to him [only] who has become indifferent.

And thus Scripture says: “And having risen above the desire for sons, above the desire for wealth and above the desire for [other] worlds, they then wander about as mendicants” (Bṛihadâr. Up. 4. 4. 22), “Having become quiet, subdued, satisfied, patient and collected, he sees himself in the Self only” (l. c. 4. 4. 23).

“If liberation takes place in consequence of indifference immediately after the hearing [of the truth], then all would be liberated immediately after the teacher’s instruction; and, as we see, this is not the case.” With reference to this [objection the author] says:

3. It does not take place in consequence of the mere hearing, [but] of the aptitude of the beginningless disposition.

Liberation is not [obtained] immediately after the hearing [of the truth]; but whose beginningless disposition is apt, to him [alone] liberation comes quickly [after the instruction], to another late.

[The author] mentions another reason:

4. Or, as many servants belong to a single [master].

As, among many servants of a single [master], on account of good service or offence, some are set at liberty, some enjoy the benevolence [of their master] and some are imprisoned, just so Matter is single, and Souls are many. Those who possess a clear discriminative knowledge [obtain liberation] quickly; those who practise devotion only, in the course of time; the others never.

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>The supreme, unique Great Lord <term>Maheshvara</term> <gloss>an epithet for the divine principle or a supreme deity</gloss> is all-knowing, the mother and creator of the entire world. How is he to be known? Either through inference or through dedicated exertion. For instance, there is the following inference: this perceptible world, which is a subject of dispute, must have a cause, because it comes into existence after having not existed, just like a painting. From there, one gains specific knowledge through <term>yoga</term> <gloss>disciplined practice</gloss> of that which was previously understood only in a general sense. As for the other, the individual soul <term>jiva</term>, its proof comes from personal experience alone. 

The activity of Nature <term>prakriti</term> is for the sake of the knowledge of the distinction between these two, the higher and the lower. In this context, it will be stated that her activity is for the sake of another. There is also an element of self-interest: she becomes indifferent toward that person <term>purusha</term> to whom she has revealed her true nature through the knowledge of distinction. How can unconscious Nature exhibit activity? It is observed that even unconscious things, such as milk, exhibit activity for the sake of a result <note>referring to the classic analogy of milk flowing for the sake of the calf</note>.

Now, regarding who is eligible for liberation <term>moksha</term>, it is said:

Success comes to one who is dispassionate.

As the scripture <term>shruti</term> <gloss>sacred revealed text</gloss> states: Having risen above the desire for sons, the desire for wealth, and the desire for worlds, they then live the life of a mendicant. Also: Having become peaceful, self-controlled, withdrawn, patient, and concentrated, one sees the Self within the self.

If liberation occurs after hearing the teachings due to dispassion, then everyone should be liberated immediately after receiving a teacher's instruction. Since this is not observed to happen, it is said:

Success is not achieved by mere hearing, because beginningless impressions are powerful.

Liberation does not follow immediately after hearing. Rather, because beginningless mental impressions <term>vasana</term> <gloss>latent tendencies or subconscious inclinations</gloss> are powerful, liberation may be swift for some and delayed for others.

Another reasoning is stated:

Because of the many tasks, each one...

<header>Sāṃkhyatattvavṛttiḥ</header>

The supreme <term>Maheśvara</term> <gloss>the Great Lord</gloss> is omniscient, the mother of the entire universe, and the creator. How is He to be known? Through inference or through scriptural authority? For example, the inference is as follows: the object under dispute, which is perceived, must have a cause, because it comes into existence and will cease to exist, like a painting. From this, what is understood in general is known in particular through <term>yoga</term> <gloss>meditation/disciplined union</gloss>. For the individual soul, realization comes from one's own experience. The activity of <term>prakṛti</term> <gloss>primordial nature</gloss> is for the purpose of discriminating between these two, the supreme and the individual. Its purpose for another will be explained later. And its purpose for itself: it remains indifferent toward that <term>puruṣa</term> <gloss>conscious spirit</gloss> to whom it has already revealed itself through discrimination. How can <term>prakṛti</term>, which is unconscious, be active? It is observed that even unconscious things, such as milk, act for a purpose, such as the nourishment of a calf.

Now, regarding who is eligible for liberation, the text says:

**Through detachment, that is accomplished.**

And so the scripture says: "Rising above the desire for sons, the desire for wealth, and the desire for worldly status, they then wander, living on alms." Also: "Having become peaceful, self-controlled, retired from sensory objects, patient, and collected, one sees the Self within the Self."

If liberation followed immediately after hearing the teachings due to detachment, then everyone would attain liberation after the guru's instruction, but this is not observed. Regarding this, the text says:

**Not by hearing alone is that accomplished, due to the strength of beginningless tendencies.**

Liberation does not occur immediately after hearing; rather, due to the strength of beginningless tendencies, for some liberation is swift, while for others it is delayed.

The text offers another reason:

**Like many streams, each one flows.**

Sāṃkhyatattvavṛttiḥ

The supreme Lord is omniscient, the mother and creator of the entire world. How is He to be known? By inference or by effort? For instance, the inference is that this world, which is the subject of debate and is perceived to have form, must have a cause, because it arises and ceases, just like a painting. From there, what is generally understood becomes known specifically through <term>yoga</term> <gloss>spiritual discipline/union</gloss>. For the individual soul, realization comes from one's own experience. The activity of <term>prakṛti</term> <gloss>primordial nature</gloss> is for the purpose of discriminating between these two: the supreme and the individual. Its purpose for the sake of others will be described. As for its purpose for itself, once it has revealed itself through discrimination to the <term>puruṣa</term> <gloss>self/consciousness</gloss> for whom it acted, it remains indifferent to him. How can inanimate nature act? It is observed that even inanimate things like milk act toward an end, such as the nourishment of a calf. || 1 ||

Now, concerning who is entitled to liberation, it says:

Due to the attainment of detachment. || 2 ||

And the <term>śruti</term> <gloss>Vedic scripture</gloss> says, "Having renounced the desire for sons, the desire for wealth, and the desire for worldly status, they then live the life of a mendicant," and "Having become peaceful, self-controlled, withdrawn, patient, and concentrated, one sees the Self within the Self." || 2 ||

If liberation followed immediately after hearing the teachings due to detachment, then everyone would attain liberation after the teacher's instruction, yet this is not seen. In response, it says:

Liberation is not attained from mere hearing due to the strength of beginningless impressions. || 3 ||

Liberation does not occur immediately after hearing; rather, due to the strength of beginningless <term>vāsanā</term> <gloss>subconscious impressions</gloss>, liberation comes quickly for some and after a long time for others. || 3 ||

It offers another argument:

They are experienced individually, like many flows of water. || 4 ||

<summary>This page discusses the nature of divine creation and the necessity of discrimination between primordial nature and the self, while explaining why mere hearing of the truth does not immediately lead to liberation due to deep-seated subconscious impressions.</summary>

# The Sāṅkhyatattvavṛtti

The Supreme, the Great Lord, the All-knowing, the Mother of the entire universe, the Creator. How is He to be known? By inference or by scriptural testimony? Thus: that which is subject to debate and is perceived is found to have a cause, because it has come into being and will cease to be, just like a painting; this is the inference. From that, knowledge of the particular is obtained through <term>yoga</term> <gloss>union/meditative discipline</gloss>, after having understood the general. For the other—the individual soul—the proof comes from personal experience alone. It is for the sake of the discriminative knowledge of these two, the Supreme and the subordinate, that the <term>prakṛti</term> <gloss>Principal/Primordial Matter</gloss> acts. Regarding this, its purpose for another will be explained. As for its purpose for itself, toward that soul to whom it has shown itself through discrimination, it remains indifferent. How can the unconscious <term>prakṛti</term> act? It is seen that even unconscious things, such as milk and the like, act for the sake of fruit and so forth. || 1 ||

Now, it asks: who are the ones eligible for liberation?

# 2. Because of its attainment by the dispassionate.

And thus the <term>śruti</term> <gloss>scriptural revelation</gloss> says: "Having renounced the desire for sons, the desire for wealth, and the desire for worlds, they then practice mendicancy," and "Having become tranquil, self-controlled, retired, patient, and collected, one sees the Self in the Self." || 2 ||

If liberation occurs after hearing [the truth] due to detachment, then everyone should attain liberation after receiving the teacher’s instruction, but that is not seen to be the case. To this, it says:

# 3. Attainment does not come from hearing alone, because of the strength of beginningless impressions.

Liberation does not follow immediately after hearing, but due to the strength of beginningless <term>vāsanā</term> <gloss>subconscious impressions/habitual tendencies</gloss>, liberation is swift; elsewhere, it is delayed. || 3 ||

It provides another reason:

# 4. It is like the many servants, for each one.

The Supreme Lord, who is one, is all-knowing, the mother of the entire world, and the creator. How is He to be known? Through inference or through labor <note>spiritual practice or exertion</note>. For instance, there is the inference: "This perceived world, which is subject to dispute, has a cause, because it comes into being and passes away, just like a painting." the Supreme <note>original: "paraḥ"; the OCR's following word "anakān" is unclear and probably corrupt</note> is the Great Lord, all-knowing, the maker <note>original: "sakala-jagan-mātṛ", literally "the measurer" or "mother" of the whole world</note> and ordainer of the whole world. How is he to be known? By inference, or by <unclear>śramāt</unclear> <note>the reading "śramāt", "by toil", looks corrupt; "āgamāt", "by scripture", would be expected alongside inference</note>. For it is like this. The inference runs: "The perceived world under dispute has a cause, because it comes to be after not having been <note>the OCR reads "babhūtvā"; the sense requires "abhūtvā bhāvitvāt", "because of coming into being after not being"</note>, like a painting." After that, what has been understood in general through inference is known in its particulars through yoga. The other, the individual soul <note><term>jīva</term> <gloss>the embodied self</gloss></note>, is established simply by one's own experience. Nature <note><term>prakṛti</term> <gloss>primal matter, the unconscious source of the world</gloss></note> becomes active so that the difference between these two, the higher and the lower, may be known. Its acting for the sake of another will be explained later. And as to its acting for its own sake: towards whichever conscious being <note><term>puruṣa</term> <gloss>the spirit or witness</gloss></note> it has displayed itself through discrimination, towards him it ceases to act <note>original: "udāste", literally "sits apart, becomes indifferent"</note>. How can unconscious nature become active? Activity is observed even in unconscious things, such as milk, for the sake of a result such as the nourishment of a calf <note>the classic Sāṃkhya example: milk flows of itself to feed the calf</note>. ॥ 1 ॥

Next, to the question "Who are qualified for liberation?", he says:

Sūtra: Of the one who is free from passion, because for him it is accomplished. ॥ 2 ॥ <note>original: "viraktasya tatsiddheḥ"</note>

And so scripture says: "Having risen above the desire for sons, the desire for wealth and the desire for worlds, they then go about living as mendicants," and: "Having become calm, controlled, withdrawn, patient and collected, he sees the Self within the Self alone." <note>Both quotations come from the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad.</note> ॥ 2 ॥

If liberation follows upon hearing the teaching, because of dispassion, then everyone would be liberated after receiving a teacher's instruction; and that is not what we see. To this he says:

Sūtra: It is not accomplished by hearing alone, because of the strength of beginningless latent impressions. ॥ 3 ॥ <note>original: "na śravaṇamātrāt tatsiddhir anādivāsanāyā balavattvāt"; <term>vāsanā</term> <gloss>the residual impressions left by past actions and experiences</gloss></note>

He gives a further reason:

Sūtra: Or, as with one who has many servants, for each one separately. ॥ 4 ॥ <note>The OCR reads "bahubhṛtvavahā pratyekam", which appears to be a corruption of "bahubhṛtyavad vā pratyekam"; it is translated in that sense. The point of the image is explained on the next page.</note>

<margin>蘇註</margin>不知道而務學聞見日多而無以一之未免為累也孔子曰多聞擇其善者而從之多見而識之知之次也苟一日知道顧偽偽為無一非妄去妄復性是謂之損孔子謂子貢曰女以予為多學而識之者與曰然非與曰非也予一以貫之夫忘心以純復性無謂損矣而妄之不猶存以及其兼忘此心以純復性無餘然後去為而不失於無為矣人皆有欲取天下終事理之心故造事而求之心見於外而物惡之故難不可得聖人無為故無事其心見於外而物安之雖不取天下事理而為之而天下事理順安於是矣

<margin>呂註</margin>為學未聞道者也未聞道而求之不得不博故曰益為道者已聞道者也已聞道而為之不得不無為而已故曰損而又損者未免乎有為也并其損之者而損焉而後至於無為無為者寂然而不動之謂也無不為者感而遂通天下之故之謂也無為而至無為此之謂經學無憂謂之神神之為方也道之謂也至神其孰能與於此也由此觀之取天下常以無為及其有為不足以取天下可知已

<column-break/>

<margin>黃茂材註</margin>無所不知而後可以言學故學欲日益無所不為而後可以言道故道欲日損然益者可以進求而損者或難於強致唯至明者方能瞥地脫落乃至無為之地故能無所不為而應用不窮施於天下綽綽然矣

<margin>息齋註</margin>為學所以求知故日益為道所以去妄故日損知不極則損不全故日益者為日損之地也若損之又損妄去真全則無為矣至於無為則凡有為未嘗不無此又未易以損益論也及其無為之至雖天下之多而一貫之也若以有事而生事難暇前之一物尚膠纒乖錯而況天下之多乎

聖人無常心以百姓心為心善者吾善之不善者吾亦善之德善矣信者吾信之不信者吾亦信之德信矣聖人在天下惛惛為天下渾其心百姓皆注其耳目聖人

<margin>Su Commentary <note>Su Zhe, 1039 to 1112, a prominent Song Dynasty scholar</note></margin>Those who do not know the <term>Tao</term> <gloss>the Way</gloss> but devote themselves to learning will find that what they hear and see increases daily. Without a single principle to unify this knowledge, they cannot avoid it becoming a burden. Confucius said: Hear much, select what is good and follow it; see much and remember it. This is the second level of knowledge. If one day you know the Way, you will look back on worldly deceptions and realize that all is false. By removing the false and returning to your true nature, this is what is called "decreasing." Confucius asked his disciple Zigong: Do you think I am one who learns much and remembers it all? Zigong replied: Yes, is it not so? Confucius said: No, I permeate everything with a single principle. To forget the worldly mind and restore one's nature is called decreasing. As long as delusions remain, one must continue this process until even the act of forgetting is forgotten. When the mind is pure and nature is restored without remainder, one removes "doing" and reaches the state of "non-doing" <note>original: <term>wu wei</term></note>. People all have the desire to take hold of the world and manage its affairs. Because they create complications and seek external results, their intentions are visible, and things resist them; thus, they encounter difficulty and fail. The Sage practices non-doing, so his mind has no worldly affairs. His inner state is visible externally, and things are at peace with him. Though he does not strive to take the world or manage its affairs, the world and its affairs naturally follow and find peace.

<margin>Lü Commentary <note>Lü Huiqing, 1032 to 1111, a key political figure and philosopher</note></margin>To pursue learning is the path for those who have not yet heard the Way. Because they seek it without knowing it, they must be broad in their study; thus it is said to "increase." To pursue the Way is for those who have already heard it. Because they act upon what they know, they must practice non-doing; thus it is said to "decrease." To "decrease and further decrease" refers to those who have not yet escaped purposeful action. One must decrease even the act of decreasing itself to finally reach the state of non-doing. Non-doing means remaining silent and unmoving. "Doing nothing left undone" means that when stimulated, one resonates and connects with all circumstances under heaven. To reach non-doing through the act of non-doing is the constant path. Learning without worry is called divine. The direction of the divine is the Way. Who can attain such supreme divinity? From this we see that to take the world, one must always use non-doing. If one relies on purposeful action, it is clear that such a person is not fit to take the world.

<column-break/>

<margin>Huang Maocai Commentary <note>Huang Maocai, a Southern Song Dynasty scholar</note></margin>Only after one reaches a state of knowing everything can one speak of learning; therefore, learning desires a daily increase. Only after one reaches a state of doing nothing can one speak of the Way; therefore, the Way desires a daily decrease. However, "increase" can be pursued through progress, while "decrease" is often difficult to achieve through forced effort. Only those with supreme clarity can suddenly cast off worldly attachments and reach the realm of non-doing. Thus, they can leave nothing undone, and their applications are inexhaustible, spreading through the world with great ease.

<margin>Xizhai Commentary <note>Li Daochun, a 13th century Taoist master whose literary name was Xizhai</note></margin>The purpose of learning is to seek knowledge, hence the daily increase. The purpose of the Way is to remove delusion, hence the daily decrease. If knowledge is not perfected, the decrease will not be complete. Therefore, daily increase serves as the foundation for daily decrease. If one decreases and further decreases until delusion is gone and truth is whole, one reaches non-doing. Upon reaching non-doing, any purposeful action is itself non-doing. This state cannot easily be discussed in terms of mere increase or decrease. When non-doing reaches its peak, though the world is vast, it is unified by a single principle. If one uses busy-ness to create more business, life becomes difficult and lacks leisure. If even a single object can cause entanglement and error, how much more so the vastness of the world?

The Sage has no fixed heart <note>or mind</note> of his own; he takes the heart of the people as his heart. To those who are good, I am good. To those who are not good, I am also good. Thus, virtue is goodness. To those who are trustful, I give my trust. To those who are not trustful, I also give my trust. Thus, virtue is trust. The Sage lives in the world in a state of humble simplicity, making his heart harmoniously one with the world. The people all focus their ears and eyes upon him; the Sage

<summary>This page contains commentaries on Chapters 48 and 49 of the Tao Te Ching, focusing on the distinction between worldly learning (increase) and the pursuit of the Way (decrease). The text explains how reaching a state of non-doing allows a ruler or Sage to harmonize with the world and the hearts of the people.</summary>

<margin>Commentary by Su</margin> Not knowing but striving for learning, hearing and seeing more each day, yet having no way to unify it, one cannot avoid being burdened. Confucius said, "Hear much, choose what is good and follow it; see much and remember it; this is the second level of knowledge." If one day one comes to know the <term>Tao</term> <gloss>the Way</gloss>, looking back, all acts of pretense are false. To remove falsehood and restore one's nature is called "diminishing." Confucius asked Zigong, "Do you think I am one who learns much and remembers it?" Zigong replied, "Yes, is it not so?" Confucius said, "No, I unify it all with a single thread." When the mind is forgotten and becomes pure, and the nature is restored, this is called diminishing. If the false is not yet fully removed, even to the point of forgetting the act of forgetting, the mind cannot be pure and restore the nature without remainder. Only then can one act without losing the state of non-action. People all have the desire to seize the world and the reasoning behind things, so they initiate affairs and seek to control them. When the heart is revealed externally, things will dislike it, which makes success impossible. The sage performs non-action, so he has no affairs. When his heart is not revealed externally, things find peace. Although he does not seek to control the world or its reasoning, because he acts this way, the world and its reasoning become harmonious and peaceful.

<margin>Commentary by Lü</margin> Engaging in learning means one has not yet heard the <term>Tao</term>. Not having heard the <term>Tao</term>, one must be broad in seeking it, therefore it is said, "increase." Engaging in the <term>Tao</term> means one has already heard the <term>Tao</term>. Having heard the <term>Tao</term>, one must inevitably practice non-action, therefore it is said, "diminish." Diminishing and further diminishing still does not escape from having intentional action. One must also diminish the act of diminishing itself, and only then reach the state of non-action. Non-action refers to being silent and unmoved. "Doing nothing, yet leaving nothing undone" refers to the state where, upon being stimulated, one perfectly comprehends all the affairs of the world. To act through non-action to reach the ultimate non-action is what is meant by the constant. Learning that is free from worry is called spirit. The method of the spirit is the <term>Tao</term>. Who but the most divine can participate in this? Viewed from this perspective, one knows that to take the world, one must always use non-action; if one uses intentional action, it is not enough to take the world.

<column-break/>

<margin>Commentary by Huang Maocai</margin> Only after one knows everything can one speak of learning, so learning aims to increase day by day. Only after one can do anything can one speak of the <term>Tao</term>, so the <term>Tao</term> aims to diminish day by day. Yet, "increasing" is something one can pursue, while "diminishing" is perhaps difficult to force. Only those with the utmost clarity can instantly cast off their burdens and arrive at the state of non-action. Thus, they can act in such a way that nothing is left undone, and their applications are inexhaustible, governing the world with ease.

<margin>Commentary by Xizhai</margin> Engaging in learning is for the sake of seeking knowledge, thus it increases day by day. Engaging in the <term>Tao</term> is for the sake of removing falsehood, thus it diminishes day by day. If knowledge does not reach the limit, the diminishing will be incomplete; thus, the "increasing" is the foundation for the "diminishing." If one diminishes and diminishes again until falsehood is gone and the truth is complete, then one arrives at non-action. When one reaches non-action, there is nothing one does that is not non-action. This is not easily discussed in terms of increase or decrease. When it comes to the height of non-action, even though the world is vast, it is unified by a single thread. If one creates affairs through intentional action, it is hard to find a moment of peace. If even one thing creates entanglement and contradiction, how much more so with the complexity of the whole world?

The sage has no constant mind. He makes the hearts of the common people his own heart. To those who are good, I am good; to those who are not good, I am also good, for the <term>De</term> <gloss>Virtue/Power</gloss> of goodness is attained. To those who are trustworthy, I am trustworthy; to those who are not trustworthy, I am also trustworthy, for the <term>De</term> of trust is attained. <summary>This page contains classical commentaries on the early chapters of the Tao Te Ching, discussing the paradox of learning (which increases) versus practicing the Tao (which diminishes). <margin>Commentary by Su</margin> Not knowing yet striving for knowledge, seeing and hearing more each day without a way to unify it, one cannot avoid being burdened. Confucius said: "Hear much, select the good and follow it; see much and remember it; this is the second tier of knowledge." If one truly understands the Way, then one sees that all false actions are vanity. Removing vanity to return to one's true nature is what is meant by "diminishing." Confucius asked Zigong: "Do you think that I am a person who learns much and remembers it?" Zigong replied: "Yes, is it not so?" Confucius said: "No, I unify it all with a single thread." To forget the grasping mind in order to purely return to one's true nature, this is what is meant by diminishing. If one does not stop at forgetting the mind, but also lets go of that very forgetting to achieve a state of pure, natural existence with nothing left over, only then can one engage in action without losing the essence of non-action. People all have desires and the intent to grasp the affairs and principles of the world. Thus, they create affairs and seek them; their minds are revealed externally, and things resist them, making success impossible. The Sage practices non-action, so there are no affairs; his mind is not revealed externally, and things are at peace. Though he does not seek to grasp the affairs and principles of the world, they are practiced, and the affairs and principles of the world are then harmonious and at peace.

<margin>Commentary by Lü</margin> To study is to seek the Way without yet having heard it. If one has not heard the Way and seeks it, one must be broad in learning, hence it is said "to increase daily." To practice the Way is to have already heard it. If one has already heard the Way and acts upon it, one must inevitably arrive at non-action, hence it is said "diminish and diminish again" because one has not yet avoided having a sense of action. By diminishing even that sense of diminishing, one finally arrives at true non-action. Non-action is a state of stillness and lack of movement. "Doing nothing, yet leaving nothing undone" means responding to all things in the world and being connected to their fundamental patterns. To move from non-action to the ultimate state of non-action is what is meant by the classics. Learning without anxiety is called spirit. The method of the spirit is the Way. Who can reach this state of supreme spirit? Viewing it from this perspective, we can understand why those who seek to govern the world through constant, calculated action are insufficient to take possession of the world.

<column-break/>

<margin>Commentary by Huang Maocai</margin> Only after one knows everything can one speak of learning, hence learning seeks to increase daily. Only after one can do everything can one speak of the Way, hence the Way seeks to diminish daily. However, "increasing" allows one to advance in seeking, while "diminishing" may be difficult to force. Only the most enlightened can suddenly cast off their attachments and arrive at the realm of non-action. Thus, they are able to perform all actions, and their applications are inexhaustible, governing the world with ease and abundance.

<margin>Commentary by Xizhai</margin> The purpose of study is to seek knowledge, hence it increases daily. The purpose of the Way is to remove vanity, hence it diminishes daily. If knowledge does not reach its limit, then the diminishing is not complete; therefore, "increasing daily" is the ground for "diminishing daily." If one diminishes and diminishes again, removing vanity until the truth is complete, then one arrives at non-action. When one arrives at non-action, there is no action that is not also non-action. This can no longer be discussed in terms of mere increasing or diminishing. When one arrives at the peak of non-action, even though the world is vast, it is all unified by a single thread. If one creates affairs where there are none, one will find it difficult to manage; even a single object can become a tangled, erroneous mess, let alone the complexity of the entire world.

The Sage has no constant mind; he takes the minds of the people as his own. To those who are good, I am good; to those who are not good, I am also good; this is the goodness of virtue. To those who are trustworthy, I am trustworthy; to those who are not trustworthy, I am also trustworthy; this is the trustworthiness of virtue. The Sage exists in the world, appearing muddled and simple, blurring his mind for the sake of the world. The people all focus their ears and eyes upon him; the Sage

<summary>This page presents traditional commentaries on the concepts of "increasing learning" versus "diminishing to the Way" as described in the Tao Te Ching, emphasizing the transition from external intellectual pursuit to internal, effortless non-action.</summary>
<keywords>Tao Te Ching, Non-action, Sage, Knowledge, Virtue, Su, Lü, Huang Maocai, Xizhai</keywords>

<margin>Commentary by Su</margin>
If you do not know the Way and focus on learning, the things you hear and see increase daily, but there is no way to unify them, and you inevitably suffer the burden. Confucius said: "Hear much, select the good and follow it; see much and remember it. This is the second level of knowledge." If one day you know the Way, look back at your hypocrisy; there is nothing that is not delusion. To remove delusion and return to one's nature is called "decreasing." Confucius said to Zigong: "Do you think I have learned much and remembered it?" Zigong said: "Yes, is it not so?" Confucius said: "No, I unify it with a single thread." Forgetting the heart and purely returning to one's nature is what is called decreasing. If delusions still remain, one proceeds to forget both self and others, making the heart pure and returning to nature without remainder. Then, one removes action and does not lose the state of non-action. Everyone has the desire to take the world and occupy their heart with logic. Therefore, they create affairs and seek them. When the heart is revealed externally, things hate it. Therefore, it is difficult to obtain. The sage has no action, so he has no affairs. When his heart is revealed externally, things are at peace. Although he does not take the world's affairs, he acts for them, and the world's affairs are naturally harmonious and peaceful.

<margin>Commentary by Lü</margin>
Studying without having heard the Way is not yet having heard it. Not having heard the Way, you have to be broad in your studies to seek it. Therefore, it is called "increasing." One who practices the Way has already heard the Way. Having heard the Way, one has to do nothing but non-action. Therefore, it is called "decreasing." Decreasing and decreasing again is because you haven't yet avoided action. By even removing the "decreasing," one arrives at non-action. Non-action is what is called "still and motionless." "There is nothing that cannot be done" is what is called "responding and passing through all matters of the world." To arrive at non-action from non-action—this is what is called the classic. Learning without worry is what is called spirit. The method of spirit is the Way. Who can equal this ultimate spirit? Looking at it from this perspective, "To win the world, one should always be free of affairs; when one interferes, one is not fit to win the world"—this can be known.

<column-break/>

<margin>Commentary by Huang Mao-cai</margin>
Only after one knows everything can one speak of learning; therefore, learning desires to increase daily. Only after one does nothing can one speak of the Way; therefore, the Way desires to decrease daily. However, those who increase can progress, while those who decrease may find it difficult to force. Only the one with ultimate clarity can suddenly drop away everything and arrive at the land of non-action. Thus, he can do nothing that is not done, and his applications are inexhaustible. His governance of the world is effortless and ample.

<margin>Commentary by Xizhai</margin>
Learning is for seeking knowledge; therefore, it increases daily. The Way is for removing delusion; therefore, it decreases daily. If knowledge is not ultimate, then the decrease is not complete. Therefore, "increasing" is the place where "decreasing" occurs. If you decrease and decrease again, and delusion is removed while the truth is complete, then there is non-action. When you arrive at non-action, then even if there is action, there is never a time it is not without it. This is not easily discussed in terms of increase and decrease. When he arrives at non-action, even though the world is vast, he unifies it with a single thread. If you create affairs, you will have no time to rest. One thing alone is already gluey, tangled, and contradictory; how much more so is the complexity of the world?

To those who are faithful, I am faithful. To those who are not faithful, I am also faithful. Virtue is faithful. The sage is in the world, dim and murky. He muddies his heart for the world. <summary>This page details the necessity of shedding intellectual clutter and active interference to reach the "non-action" of the sage. It presents the sage as a mirror for the world, unburdened by fixed agendas or personal desires.</summary>

<keywords>Learning, the Way, non-action, sage, heart, virtue, faithfulness, Su, Lü, Huang Mao-cai, Xizhai</keywords>

<meta>This page contains commentaries on Chapter 48 and the beginning of Chapter 49 of the Tao Te Ching. The commentators include Su Zhe (Su Zhu), Lü Huiqing (Lü Zhu), Huang Maocai, and Xizhai (Li Jia).</meta>

<margin>Su's Commentary <note>Su Zhe, 1039–1112 AD, a prominent Song dynasty official and scholar.</note></margin> Those who do not know the <term>Dao</term> <gloss>the Way</gloss> but devote themselves to learning will find that what they hear and see increases daily. Without a single principle to unify this knowledge, they cannot avoid it becoming a burden. Confucius said: "Hear much, select what is good and follow it; see much and remember it. This is the second level of knowledge." <note>A reference to the Analects 7:27.</note> If one day a person knows the <term>Dao</term>, they will look back at their previous false actions and realize that none were not delusions. Removing delusions to return to one's true nature is called "decreasing." Confucius asked Zigong: "Do you think I am one who learns much and remembers it all?" Zigong replied: "Yes, is it not so?" Confucius said: "No, I unify it all with a single thread." <note>Reference to Analects 15:3. The "single thread" implies a unifying spiritual principle rather than an accumulation of facts.</note> Forgetting the mind to return purely to one's nature is what is meant by "decreasing." If delusions still remain, one must continue until both the delusions and the act of forgetting are themselves forgotten. Once the mind returns purely to nature without any remainder, then one eliminates "doing" <note>purposive, ego-driven action</note> and does not fail to reach <term>wu wei</term> <gloss>non-action or effortless action</gloss>. All people have the desire to take hold of the world and finish its affairs; thus, they create business and seek after things. When their intentions are visible externally, things <note>others, or the world at large</note> will dislike them, making success difficult. The Sage practices non-action and therefore has no "business" in his heart. When his heart is visible externally, things are at peace with him. Although he does not try to take hold of the world's affairs, the world's affairs naturally follow and find peace through him.

<margin>Lü's Commentary <note>Lü Huiqing, 1032–1111 AD, a key figure in the New Policies of the Song dynasty.</note></margin> Practicing learning is for those who have not yet heard the <term>Dao</term>. Seeking it without having heard it requires breadth, hence it is said "one gains daily." Practicing the <term>Dao</term> is for those who have already heard the <term>Dao</term>. Having heard it and acting upon it requires nothing more than non-action, hence it is said "one decreases daily." To "decrease and further decrease" means one has not yet escaped the realm of "doing." Only by decreasing even the act of decreasing does one arrive at <term>wu wei</term> <gloss>non-action</gloss>. Non-action refers to being still and unmoving. "Nothing left undone" refers to being moved and subsequently penetrating the causes of all under heaven. Arriving at non-action through the process of non-action is what is called the Constant. Learning without worry is called divine; the direction of the divine is what is called the <term>Dao</term>. As for the ultimate divine, who can compare to this? From this perspective, taking the world is always done through non-action. As for using "doing" <note>purposive action</note>, it is clear that this is insufficient to take the world.

<column-break/>

<margin>Huang Maocai's Commentary <note>A Southern Song dynasty scholar known for his work on the Laozi.</note></margin> Only after there is nothing one does not know can one speak of learning; therefore, learning desires a daily increase. Only after there is nothing one does not do can one speak of the <term>Dao</term>; therefore, the <term>Dao</term> desires a daily decrease. However, increase can be sought through progress, while decrease is sometimes difficult to achieve through force. Only the most enlightened can suddenly drop everything and reach the realm of non-action. Thus they can leave nothing undone, and their practical application is inexhaustible, applied to the world with great ease.

<margin>Xizhai's Commentary <note>Li Jia, also known by his pseudonym Xizhai.</note></margin> Practicing learning is the means to seek knowledge, so it increases daily. Practicing the <term>Dao</term> is the means to remove delusion, so it decreases daily. If knowledge is not ultimate, then the decrease will not be complete. Thus, daily increase serves as the foundation for daily decrease. If one decreases and further decreases until delusion is gone and truth is whole, then one reaches non-action. When one reaches non-action, then every instance of "doing" is never anything other than "non-doing." This state cannot easily be discussed in terms of increase or decrease. When non-action reaches its ultimate point, even with the vastness of the world, one unifies it with a single thread. If one uses "busyness" <note>interfering action</note> to create more business, then even a single object beforehand will be sticky, entangled, and wrong, let alone the vastness of the world.

# Chapter 49

The Sage has no fixed heart <note>or mind</note>; he takes the heart of the people as his own. Those who are good, I treat as good. Those who are not good, I also treat as good; thus, virtue is goodness. Those who are faithful, I trust. Those who are not faithful, I also trust; thus, virtue is trust. The Sage lives in the world in a state of convergence, making his heart muddled for the sake of the world. The people all focus their ears and eyes on him; the Sage <note>The text cuts off here and continues on the next page.</note>

<margin>Commentary by Su</margin>
If one studies without knowing the Way, knowledge and sight increase daily, but there is no way to unify them; this inevitably leads to a burden. Confucius said, "When hearing much, select the good and follow it; when seeing much, remember it. This is the second level of knowledge." If one truly knows the Way, one looks at falsehood as false. If one acts, it is not without a single thought of deception. Removing deception and returning to one's nature is what is meant by "decrease." When someone asked Confucius, "Do you consider me one who learns much and remembers it?" he replied, "Yes, is it not so?" Confucius said, "No. I unify it with one thread." To forget the heart in order to return purely to one's nature is "decrease." If one does not stop at forgetting the heart and returning to one's nature, but proceeds to forget even this, then the heart is pure and the nature is restored without remainder. Then, one removes the "acting," and one does not fail to reach "non-action." People all have desires to take hold of the world and the reasoning of things. Thus, they create affairs and seek them. When the heart manifests externally, things resent it; thus, it is difficult and cannot be attained. The sage practices non-action; thus, there are no affairs. When his heart manifests externally, things are at peace. Even if he does not take hold of the world and its reasoning, and yet handles them, the reasoning of the world is then compliant and peaceful.

<margin>Commentary by Lü</margin>
Learning is for those who have not yet heard of the Way. Because those who have not heard of the Way seek it, they cannot help but be extensive; hence, it is said, "Increase." Practicing the Way is for those who have already heard of the Way. Because those who have already heard of the Way practice it, they cannot help but be in non-action; hence, it is said, "Decrease." To say "decrease and decrease again" means one has not yet avoided having action. To reach the point of forgetting even the act of decreasing, one arrives at non-action. Non-action means to be silent and unmoving. "Nothing left undone" means to respond and penetrate the causes of the world. To be in non-action and arrive at the ultimate non-action is what is called "the constant." If study has no worry, it is called spirit. The function of spirit is what is called the Way. Who can participate in this ultimate spirit? Looking at it this way, one knows that to take the world, one must always use non-action. If one uses action, one is not enough to take the world.

<column-break/>

<margin>Commentary by Huang Maocai</margin>
Only when there is nothing one does not know can one speak of learning; thus, learning wishes to increase daily. Only when there is nothing one does not do can one speak of the Way; thus, the Way wishes to decrease daily. However, "increase" can be pursued through advancement, while "decrease" is perhaps difficult to force. Only the extremely bright can suddenly cast off their attachments and arrive at the ground of non-action. Thus, they can do nothing that is not done, and their application in the world is inexhaustible and abundant.

<margin>Commentary by Xizhai</margin>
Learning is the means to seek knowledge; thus, it increases daily. Practicing the Way is the means to remove deception; thus, it decreases daily. If knowledge is not extreme, the decrease is not complete; thus, "increasing daily" is the ground for "decreasing daily." If one decreases and decreases again, deception is removed and the true is complete, then there is non-action. Once one reaches non-action, whatever is done is never "not-non-action." This is not something that can be easily discussed in terms of increase or decrease. When one arrives at the ultimate non-action, even though the world is vast, one unifies it with a single thread. If one creates affairs where there are none, one is hard-pressed. If even a single thing from before is still tangled and erroneous, how much more so for the multitude of things in the world?

The sage has no constant heart. He takes the heart of the common people as his heart. To those who are good, I am good; to those who are not good, I am also good, so that virtue becomes good. To those who are trustworthy, I am trustworthy; to those who are not trustworthy, I am also trustworthy, so that virtue becomes trustworthy. The sage, in the world, is muddled and makes his heart unrefined for the world. The common people all fasten their ears and eyes upon him. The sage

<summary>This page explores the transition from the accumulation of knowledge (increasing) to the shedding of attachments (decreasing) as the path to non-action, emphasizing that the sage harmonizes with the world by aligning his heart with the hearts of the people.</summary>
<keywords>Learning, the Way, non-action, sage, decrease, daily increase, constant heart, common people</keywords>

<margin>Commentary by Su</margin> Not knowing but striving for learning, hearing and seeing more each day, yet having no way to unify it, one cannot avoid being burdened. Confucius said, "Hear much, choose what is good and follow it; see much and remember it; this is the second level of knowledge." If one day one comes to know the <term>Tao</term> <gloss>the Way</gloss>, looking back, all acts of pretense are false. To remove falsehood and restore one's nature is called "diminishing." Confucius asked Zigong, "Do you think I am one who learns much and remembers it?" Zigong replied, "Yes, is it not so?" Confucius said, "No, I unify it all with a single thread." When the mind is forgotten and becomes pure, and the nature is restored, this is called diminishing. If the false is not yet fully removed, even to the point of forgetting the act of forgetting, the mind cannot be pure and restore the nature without remainder. Only then can one act without losing the state of non-action. People all have the desire to seize the world and the reasoning behind things, so they initiate affairs and seek to control them. When the heart is revealed externally, things will dislike it, which makes success impossible. The sage performs non-action, so he has no affairs. When his heart is revealed externally, things find peace. Although he does not seek to control the world or its reasoning, because he acts this way, the world and its reasoning become harmonious and peaceful.

<margin>Commentary by Lü</margin> Engaging in learning means one has not yet heard the <term>Tao</term>. Not having heard the <term>Tao</term>, one must be broad in seeking it, therefore it is said, "increase." Engaging in the <term>Tao</term> means one has already heard the <term>Tao</term>. Having heard the <term>Tao</term>, one must inevitably practice non-action, therefore it is said, "diminish." Diminishing and further diminishing still does not escape from having intentional action. One must also diminish the act of diminishing itself, and only then reach the state of non-action. Non-action means there is no intentional action, which is called being silent and unmoved. "Doing nothing, yet leaving nothing undone" refers to the state where, upon being stimulated, one perfectly comprehends all the affairs of the world. To act through non-action to reach the ultimate non-action is what is meant by the constant. Learning that is free from worry is called spirit. The method of the spirit is the <term>Tao</term>. Who but the most divine can participate in this? Viewed from this perspective, one knows that to take the world, one must always use non-action; if one uses intentional action, it is not enough to take the world.

<column-break/>

<margin>Commentary by Huang Maocai</margin> Only after one knows everything can one speak of learning, so learning aims to increase day by day. Only after one can do anything can one speak of the <term>Tao</term>, so the <term>Tao</term> aims to diminish day by day. Yet, "increasing" is something one can pursue, while "diminishing" is perhaps difficult to force. Only those with the utmost clarity can instantly cast off their burdens and arrive at the state of non-action. Thus, they can act in such a way that nothing is left undone, and their applications are inexhaustible, governing the world with ease.

<margin>Commentary by Xizhai</margin> Engaging in learning is for the sake of seeking knowledge, thus it increases day by day. Engaging in the <term>Tao</term> is for the sake of removing falsehood, thus it diminishes day by day. If knowledge does not reach the limit, the diminishing will be incomplete; thus, the "increasing" is the foundation for the "diminishing." If one diminishes and diminishes again until falsehood is gone and the truth is complete, then one arrives at non-action. When one reaches non-action, there is nothing one does that is not non-action. This is not easily discussed in terms of increase or decrease. When it comes to the height of non-action, even though the world is vast, it is unified by a single thread. If one creates affairs through intentional action, it is hard to find a moment of peace. If even one thing creates entanglement and contradiction, how much more so with the complexity of the whole world?

The sage has no constant mind. He makes the hearts of the common people his own heart. To those who are good, I am good; to those who are not good, I am also good, for the <term>De</term> <gloss>Virtue/Power</gloss> of goodness is attained. To those who are trustworthy, I am trustworthy; to those who are not trustworthy, I am also trustworthy, for the <term>De</term> of trust is attained. reference_text: Kung-nî said, 'Once when I was sent on a mission to Khû, I saw some pigs sucking at their dead mother. After a little they looked with rapid glances, when they all left her, and ran away. They felt that she did not see them, and that she was no longer like themselves. What they had loved in their mother was not her bodily figure, but what had given animation to her figure. When a man dies in battle, they do not at his interment employ the usual appendages of plumes: as to supplying shoes to one who has lost his feet, there is no reason why he should care for them;—in neither case is there the proper reason for their use. The members of the royal harem do not pare their nails nor pierce their ears; when a man is newly married, he remains (for a time) absent from his official duties, and unoccupied with them. That their bodies might be perfect was sufficient to make them thus dealt with;—how much greater results should be expected from men whose mental gifts are perfect!

The reasoning in this northern passage is subtle and profound.

<margin>Feeding at the breast</margin>
Consider a child nursing from its dead mother. After a short while, the child's eyes seem to cast everything aside and 
<margin>Because the blinking of the eyes can no longer be seen</margin>
the child gets up and departs, for the mother no longer notices the child. The child finds no likeness there. That which makes the child love the mother is not 
<margin>The stiffness of the corpse no longer resembles a living person</margin>
<margin>When the physical form is insufficient to be loved, then it is not loved</margin>
love for her physical form, but love for that which animated her form. When those who die in battle 
<margin>Those killed in battle have no further use for military power, so they are not provided with concubines</margin>
are buried, they are not provided with the burial finery of handmaidens. For those whose feet have been amputated, there is no reason to love their shoes, as they have lost 
<margin>The foot is the basis of the shoe</margin>
<margin>Another metaphor is set: The selection of imperial consorts does not require a complete physical form; this illustrates the deficiency of the most honored station</margin>
the foundation for them. The various attendants of the Son of Heaven <note>The Emperor</note> do not trim their nails and do not pierce their ears. Those who have just taken 
<margin>They are not kept in official service for fear of callousing their hands and feet, which would prevent them from forming a new marriage bond</margin>
a wife stay outside the palace and are no longer sent on labor service. If keeping the physical form 
<margin>A complete form is still enough to move others</margin>
whole is enough to make a person stand out, how much more so for one whose 
Virtue <note>original: "de"</note> is complete?
What follows is also the meaning.

<summary>Zhuangzi uses metaphors of a nursing child and palace rituals to argue that true value lies in the animating spirit and internal virtue rather than the physical body. He illustrates that even worldly authorities recognize the importance of physical wholeness, suggesting that spiritual wholeness is even more significant.</summary>
<keywords>Zhuangzi, Virtue, physical form, burial customs, imperial attendants, Sign of Full Virtue, De Chong Fu, philosophy of spirit</keywords>

### The subtle principles of the northern section

<margin>Feeding on breast milk</margin>
When one feeds a child at the breast of its dead mother, after a short time the child will notice that the mother is different and will leave her. 
<margin>This means the movement of the eyes does not perceive her anymore</margin>
It rises and does not see her anymore. It does not recognize the likeness of its mother. That which you loved in your mother, it was not
<margin>The stiffening of the body is not like the person anymore</margin>
<margin>If the body is not worth loving, then nothing is worth loving</margin>
the love of her physical form. It was the love of that which animated her form. For those who die in battle, the funeral rites
<margin>Those who die in battle lack martial virtue, so they are not honored with the sacrifice of concubines</margin>
are performed without killing concubines to provide for them in the afterlife. In all these cases, the failure to act stems from the fact that they have lost their original nature.
<margin>Often using the feet as the root</margin>
<margin>Another metaphor: choosing imperial consorts should not exhaust their physical perfection, as it would cause a loss of the utmost dignity</margin>
As for the consorts of the Son of Heaven, they do not cut their nails nor pierce their ears. When one takes a wife,
<margin>They are not assigned official duties for fear of callousing their hands and feet, which would prevent them from fulfilling the duties of a new marriage</margin>
she is kept in the outer quarters. She is not allowed to be employed again. If the form remains complete, it is still sufficient to fulfill the 
<margin>One whose form is complete is still sufficient to move people</margin>

# The subtleties of the principles in the Northern section

<margin>Feeding at the breast</margin>
The child feeding at the breast of its dead mother, after a short while, looks as if it has lost her, and <margin>This means that at the blink of an eye, the mother is gone</margin>
rising, it does not see her. It does not find anyone who resembles her. That which you loved in your mother was <margin>The stiffening of the body no longer resembles her</margin>
<margin>If the form is not worth loving, then there is nothing left to love</margin>
not her physical form, but that which moved her form. When men die in battle, they are buried; <margin>When they die in battle, there is no value in physical strength, therefore one does not provide them with concubines</margin>
yet one does not provide them with concubines to be killed as funerary offerings. The fetus, in its repeated states, has no conscious intention; to love it is to lose <margin>Repeatedly returning to the foundation/root</margin>
<margin>Another metaphor: To select concubines without exhausting their complete form, so as to avoid inflicting harm on the supreme nobility</margin>
its foundation. Those who are the concubines of the Son of Heaven do not have their nails trimmed, nor their ears pierced. Those who take <margin>They are not placed in official labor, for fear of callousing their hands and feet, which would make them unfit for the intimate duties of the newlywed</margin>
wives are stopped at the outer gates. Even when one is not permitted to employ them again, if the form is complete, it is still sufficient to move <margin>Those whose form is complete are still sufficient to move others</margin>
the mind.
The mind below is again this.

<margin>Eating milk.</margin>
The child feeds on its dead mother. After a short while, the pupils of its eyes seem to abandon it <note>original: "眸若皆棄之"</note> and
<margin>Meaning the movement of the eyes no longer sees the self.</margin>
rise up, and he is no longer there. You cannot classify this. What you love about the mother
<margin>The stiffening of the body is not like the self.</margin>
<margin>If the form is not worth loving, then nothing is worth loving.</margin>
is not her form; you love what directs that form. Those who die in battle, their people
<margin>Dying in battle means no martial pride, therefore they are not provided with a concubine.</margin>
are buried, but they do not use concubines to be killed or provided. Those who have a fetus are not <note>unclear> repeatedly  without purpose, for they all do not love it for
<margin>Repeatedly taking the feet as the root.</margin>
<margin>Also setting up a metaphor; selecting palace maids does not exhaust their complete form, thus causing harm to the most honored.</margin>
its roots. As for the attendants of the Son of Heaven, they do not trim their nails, they do not pierce their ears. Those who take wives
<margin>Not in official service, for fear of callousing their hands and feet, which would prevent them from fulfilling new marriage duties.</margin>
stop at the outside; they do not require the form to be made whole, yet it is enough to make
<margin>Those with complete form are still enough to move others.</margin>

Under the intention is yet more.

# This Section Contains Subtle and Profound Principles

<margin>Nursing</margin>
A child who nurses from its mother after she has died will, after a short while, look at her with a fixed gaze and then <margin>Thinking her eyes no longer blink or see him</margin> get up and leave her. This is because the child no longer finds his own kind in her. <margin>The stillness of the form no longer resembles himself</margin> What he loved about his mother was <margin>If the form is not enough to be loved, then it is truly not loved</margin> not her physical form, but that which animated her form. When a man dies in battle <margin>Dying in battle means his martial prowess is gone, so he is not provided with concubines for the burial</margin> and is buried, he is not provided with the burial finery of concubines. A man whose feet have been amputated <margin>The feet are the root of the body</margin> has no reason to love his shoes. In both cases, the root is gone. <note>The text uses these analogies to show that once the essence or function is lost, the physical shell or its accessories lose their value.</note> <margin>Another metaphor: In selecting ladies-in-waiting, the emperor does not seek to exhaust the perfection of their physical forms; thus the most high should disregard physical defects.</margin> The ladies-in-waiting of the Son of Heaven do not trim their nails and do not pierce their ears. A man who has just <margin>Remaining outside of official service for fear that laboring with hands and feet would make him unfit for the wedding chambers</margin> taken a wife remains outside of official duties and is no longer sent on exhausting tasks. If keeping the physical form whole is enough to be treated with such consideration, <margin>One with a whole form is still able to move people</margin> how much more should this apply to one whose inner virtue is whole?
The meaning continues below.
