<summary>Zhuangzi uses analogies of a nursing child, a fallen warrior, and an amputee to argue that essence and spirit are more important than the physical body. He concludes that if people value physical wholeness in servants and newlyweds, they should value spiritual wholeness even more.</summary>
<keywords>Zhuangzi, Signs of Full Virtue, essence vs. form, burial customs, physical wholeness, inner virtue</keywords>

# The Subtle Principles of the Northern Section

<margin>Feeding on milk</margin>
When a child feeds at the breast of its dead mother, after a short while, it will look at her <margin>meaning the blinking of the eyes shows she is no longer there</margin>
and abandon her, rising up without looking at her any longer. This is because it does not recognize a kinship. The reason you loved your mother was <margin>the stiff body is no longer kin</margin>
<margin>if the form is not worth loving, then the essence is not worth loving</margin>
not because of her physical form, but because of that which animated her form. Those who die in battle are buried by others <margin>those who die in battle lack martial virtues, so one does not reward them with concubines</margin>
who do not sacrifice concubines to accompany them in death. A pregnant woman who miscarries <margin>repeatedly using the foot as a root</margin>
<margin>another metaphor: selecting concubines does not exhaust the wholeness of the form; this would be to impose a loss upon the supreme status</margin>
does not care for the fetus; all have abandoned the root. For the various consorts of the Son of Heaven, they do not trim their nails nor pierce their ears. When taking a wife, <margin>they are not engaged in official labor for fear of callousing their hands and feet, which would prevent them from fulfilling their duties in a new marriage</margin>
one remains on the outside and may not employ her, for if the form remains whole, it is still sufficient to move the <margin>those whose forms are whole are still sufficient to move others</margin>
intent.
Below the intent is the [true] reality.

Because there was some rice left about the holes of the rats, you sent away your younger sister, which was unkind; when your food, whether raw or cooked, remains before you not all consumed, you keep on hoarding it up to any extent.' Lâo-ȝze looked indifferent, and gave him no answer.

Next day Khî again saw Lâo-ȝze, and said, 'Yesterday I taunted you; but to-day I have gone back to a better mood of mind. What is the cause (of the change)?' Lâo-ȝze replied, 'I consider that I have freed myself from the trammels of claiming to be artfully knowing, spirit-like, and sage. Yesterday if you had called me an ox, you might have done so; or if you had called me a horse, you might have done so. If there be a reality (corresponding to men's ideas), and men give it a name, which another will not receive, he will in the sequel suffer the more. My manner was what I constantly observe;—I did not put it on for the occasion.'

Shih-khăng Khî sidled away out of Lâo's shadow; then he retraced his steps, advanced forward, and asked how he should cultivate himself.

Drinking without limit <note>meaning to be completely immersed in the Tao</note>, <term>Laozi</term> <gloss>Old Master</gloss> remained indifferent and did not respond. The next day, Shi Chengqi appeared again and said:

### Discussion

Yesterday I had a stinging criticism for you, but today my heart has truly turned away from it. Why is this so? 

<margin>Turning away is like feeling regret.</margin>

<term>Laozi</term> said: Regarding those of clever wisdom and divine holiness, I thought I had broken free from such things. Yesterday, if you had called me an ox, I would have called myself an ox. If you had called me a horse, I would have called myself a horse. 

<margin>The word "stopped" is used here for stylistic effect.</margin>
<margin>Falling short.</margin>
<margin>The word "method" is used here for stylistic effect.</margin>

If the reality is present and someone gives it a name, to refuse that name is to invite disaster twice over. 

<margin>To be like this always.</margin>
<margin>To struggle with them a second time brings disaster upon oneself.</margin>

My submission is a constant submission. I do not submit because there is something to submit to. 

<margin>It is not that one acts because one thinks one should act; submission here is like "holding to the breast" or internalizing.</margin>

Shi Chengqi moved with a side-long gait like a shadow, avoiding his own reflection, and walked with careful steps.

<margin>Sentence structure note.</margin>
<margin>What I have practiced.</margin>
<margin>The appearance of moving with the body turned sideways.</margin>

<summary>Shi Chengqi returns to Laozi to express his change of heart, and Laozi explains the freedom found in being indifferent to names and labels. The passage emphasizes natural submission to reality rather than social status or intellectual vanity.</summary>

Formerly I found fault with you. Now my heart has changed and settled. Why is this? Laozi said, As for those who are clever, wise, or holy, I consider myself free from such things. Drinking without limit. Laozi stood blankly and did not respond. Shicheng Qi came to see him again the next day and said:
Discourse
"In the past, I had criticisms for you. Now my heart is corrected and calmed. Why is this?" Lao
zi said: "As for those who are cleverly wise and divine, I consider myself free from them. In the past,
you called me an ox, and I said it was an ox. You called me a horse, and I said it was a horse.
If there is the reality, and people give it a name, and I do not accept it, I would only receive a second disaster. I wear it like a garment. My wearing it is not because I hold on to a garment." Shicheng Qi stood straight, avoiding shadows and walking.

Drinking from the shoreless <note>boundless</note> stream, Laozi remained indifferent and did not respond. The next day, Shi Chengqi saw him again and said:

### Commentary

"In the past, I had a critical <note>literally: piercing</note> view of you. Now, my mind is truly set back <note>changed or retracted</note>. Why is this so?" 

Laozi said: "As for those people of clever wisdom and divinity, I consider myself to have escaped such things. Previously, if you called me an ox, I would have called myself an ox. If you called me a horse, I would have called myself a horse. If the reality exists and a person gives it a name, yet one does not accept it, they will receive double the disaster. Therefore he does not censure men, and men do not censure him. The perfect man does not seek to be heard of; how is it that you delight in doing so?'

Confucius said, 'Excellent;' and thereupon he took leave of his associates, forsook his disciples, retired to the neighbourhood of a great marsh, wore skins and hair cloth, and ate acorns and chestnuts. He went among animals without causing any confusion among their herds, and among birds without troubling their movements. Birds and beasts did not dislike him; how much less would men do so!

5. Confucius asked Ȝze-sang Hû, saying, 'I was twice driven from Lû; the tree was felled over me in Sung; I was obliged to disappear from Wei; I was reduced to extreme distress in Shang and Kâu; and I was kept in a state of siege between Khăn and Ȝhâi. I have encountered these various calamities; my intimate associates are removed from me more and more; my followers and friends are more and more dispersed;—why have all these things befallen me?'

5. Confucius, having gone to Khû, was lodging in the house of a seller of Congee at Ant-hill. On the roof of a neighbouring house there appeared the husband and his wife, with their servants, male and female. Ȝze-lû said, 'What are those people doing, collected there as we see them?' Kung-nî replied, 'The man is a disciple of the sages. He is burying himself among the people, and hiding among the fields. Reputation has become little in his eyes, but there is no bound to his cherished aims. Though he may speak with his mouth, he never tells what is in his mind. Moreover, he is at variance with the age, and his mind disdains to associate with it; -- he is one who may be said to lie hid at the bottom of the water on the dry land. Is he not a sort of Î Liâo of Shih-nan?' Ȝze-lû asked leave to go and call him, but Confucius said, 'Stop. He knows that I understand him well. He knows that I am come to Khû, and thinks that I am sure to try and get the king to invite him (to court). He also thinks that I am a man swift to speak. Being such a man, he would feel ashamed to listen to the words of one of voluble and flattering tongue, and how much more to come himself and see his person! And why should we think that he will remain here?' Ȝze-lû, however, went to see how it was, but found the house empty.

6. The Border-warden of Khang-wû, in questioning Ȝze-lâo, said, 'Let not a ruler in the exercise of his government be (like the farmer) who leaves the clods unbroken, nor, in regulating his people, (like one) who recklessly plucks up the shoots. Formerly, in ploughing my corn-fields, I left the clods unbroken, and my recompense was in the rough unsatisfactory crops; and in weeding, I destroyed and tore up (many good plants), and my recompense was in the scantiness of my harvests. In subsequent years I changed my methods, ploughing deeply and carefully covering up the seed; and my harvests were rich and abundant, so that all the year I had more than I could eat.'

10. Confucius said, 'The minds of men are more difficult of approach than (the position defended by) mountains and rivers, and more difficult to know than Heaven itself. Heaven has its periods of spring and autumn, of winter and summer, and of morning and evening; but man's exterior is thickly veiled, and his feelings lie deep. Thus the demeanour of some is honest-like, and yet they go to excess (in what is mean); others are really gifted, and yet look to be without ability; some seem docile and impressible, but yet they have far-reaching schemes; others look firm, and yet may be twisted about; others look slow, and yet they are hasty. In this way those who hasten to do what is right as if they were thirsty will anon hurry away from it as if it were fire. Hence the superior man looks at them when employed at a distance to test their fidelity, and when employed near at hand to test their reverence. By employing them on difficult services, he tests their ability; by questioning them suddenly, he tests their knowledge; by appointing them a fixed time, he tests their good faith; by entrusting them with wealth, he tests their benevolence; by telling them of danger, he tests their self-command in emergencies; by making them drunk, he tests their tendencies; by placing them in a variety of society, he tests their chastity: -- by these nine tests the inferior man is discovered.'

11. When Khao-fu, the Correct, received the first grade of official rank, he walked with head bowed down; on receiving the second, with bent back; on receiving the third, with body stooping, he ran and hurried along the wall: -- who would presume not to take him as a model? But one of those ordinary men, on receiving his first appointment, goes along with a haughty stride; on receiving his second, he looks quite elated in his chariot; and on receiving the third, he calls his uncles by their personal names; -- how very different from Hsü (Yû) in the time (of Yâo of) Thang!

Of all things that injure (men) there is none greater than the practising of virtue with the purpose of the mind, till the mind becomes supercilious. When it becomes so, the mind (only) looks inwards (on itself), and such looking into itself leads to its ruin. This evil quality has five forms, and the chief of them is that which is the central. What do we mean by the central quality? It is that which appears in a man's loving (only) his own views, and reviling whatever he does not do (himself).

When the mind is enslaved by the appearance of the eyes and lashes, virtue becomes even more of a pretense <margin>The more one forces it through the senses, the further virtue is falsified</margin>. If one looks inward from this state, the mind remains in constant turmoil and can never achieve true virtue or advance toward the Dao <margin>Looking inward with a cluttered mind prevents spiritual progress</margin>.

There may be similarity in understanding without similarity in outward form. There may also be similarity in form without similarity in understanding. The Sage embraces similarity of understanding and pays no regard to similarity of form. The world in general is attracted by similarity of form, but remains indifferent to similarity of understanding. Those creatures that resemble them in shape they love and consort with; those that differ from them in shape they fear and keep at a distance. The creature that has a skeleton seven feet long, hands differently shaped from the feet, hair on its head, and an even set of teeth in its jaws, and walks erect, is called a man. But it does not follow that a man may not have the mind of a brute. Even though this be the case, other men will still recognise him as one of their own species in virtue of his outward form. Creatures which have wings on the back or horns on the head, serrated teeth or extensile talons, which fly overhead or run on all fours, are called birds and beasts. But it does not follow that a bird or a beast may not have the mind of a man. Yet, even if this be so, it is nevertheless assigned to another species because of the difference in form. P'ao Hsi, Nü Kua, Shen Nung and Hsia Hou had serpents' bodies, human faces, ox-heads and tigers' snouts. Thus, their forms were not human, yet their virtue was of the saintliest. Chieh of the Hsia dynasty, Chou of the Yin, Huan of the Lu State, and Mu of the Ch'u State, were in all external respects, as facial appearance and possession of the seven channels of sense, like unto other men; yet they had the minds of savage brutes. Howbeit, in seeking perfect wisdom, men attend to the outward form alone, which will not bring them near to it.

When the Yellow Emperor fought with Yen Ti on the field of P'an-ch'uan, his vanguard was composed of bears, wolves, panthers, lynxes and tigers, while his ensign-bearers were eagles, ospreys, falcons and kites. This was forcible impressment of animals into the service of man. The Emperor Yao entrusted K'uei with the regulation of music. When the latter tapped the musical stone in varying cadence, all the animals danced to the sound of the music. When the strains of the Shao were heard on the flute, the phoenix itself flew down to assist. This was the attraction of animals by the power of music.

It also describes how legendary kings like the Yellow Emperor and Yao commanded or harmonized with animals through power and music.</summary>
<keywords>Yellow Emperor, Flame Emperor, Banquan, virtue, appearance vs reality, Fuxi, Shennong, music, phoenix, legendary beasts</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page: ...this is called a human, yet</meta> it may not be without a beast's heart. Although one may possess a beast's heart, if one's outward form appears human, one is treated with affection. It is said that those who wear horns, divide their teeth, spread their claws, soar aloft, or crouch and scuttle are called birds and beasts. They may not be without a human heart, yet although they possess a human heart, if their outward form appears animal, one is treated with alienation. Fuxi, Nuwa, Shennong, and the rulers of the Xia dynasty had the bodies of snakes, human faces, heads of oxen, and noses of tigers. They possessed forms that were not human, yet they held the virtues of the great sages. Jie of Xia, Zhou of Shang, Huan of Lu, and Mu of Chu had faces, features, and seven orifices exactly like those of humans, yet they possessed the hearts of birds and beasts. If the masses rely on a single outward appearance to seek the highest wisdom, they will never come near to it.

The Yellow Emperor fought the Flame Emperor on the plains of Banquan. He commanded bears, grizzly bears, wolves, leopards, <term>pixiu</term> <gloss>mythical beasts</gloss>, and tigers as his vanguard, and used eagles, <term>he</term> <gloss>long-tailed pheasants</gloss>, hawks, and kites as his banners. This is how he used force to command birds and beasts. When Yao commanded Kui to oversee music, striking stones and beating stones, all the beasts followed the dance. When the <term>Xiaoshao</term> <gloss>the legendary music of Emperor Shun</gloss> was performed in nine movements, the phoenix came to perform ceremonies.

<margin>Both of these meanings are possible.</margin>
<margin>Liezi, Yellow Emperor.</margin>

<summary>This passage contrasts external appearance with internal morality, arguing that outward form does not determine the presence of a human or beastly nature. It cites the legendary sage-kings and tyrannical rulers as evidence, concluding that true wisdom cannot be judged by physical form.</summary>
<keywords>Fuxi, Nuwa, Yellow Emperor, Flame Emperor, outward appearance, human heart, beastly nature, virtue</keywords>

<meta>The text continues a discourse on the nature of internal character versus outward appearance, arguing that physical form does not dictate one's humanity or virtue.</meta>

<margin>Both these points are acceptable</margin>
<margin>Liezi, Yellow Emperor</margin>

One may definitely have the heart of a beast, yet because of one's appearance, one is treated with the closeness reserved for one's own kind. The traditions state that those with horns, teeth, claws, who fly, walk, crouch, or run are called birds and beasts. They do not necessarily lack the heart of a human, yet because of their appearance, they are treated with alienation. Fuxi, Nüwa, Shennong, and the sovereigns of the Xia dynasty had bodies like snakes, human faces, ox heads, and tiger noses. They possessed forms that were not human, yet they held the virtues of the great sages. Jie of Xia, Zhou of Shang, Huan of Lu, and Mu of Chu all possessed the features and seven orifices exactly the same as any human, yet they harbored the hearts of beasts. For the common people to rely solely on outward appearance to seek supreme wisdom is to remain far from the truth. The Yellow Emperor fought the Flame Emperor on the plains of Banquan. He commanded bears, brown bears, wolves, leopards, <term>pixiu</term> <gloss>mythical fierce beasts</gloss>, and tigers as his vanguard, while vultures, pheasants, eagles, and kites served as his banners. This was a case of using strength to command birds and beasts. When Yao appointed Kui to oversee music, striking stones and beating percussion instruments, a hundred beasts danced in sequence. When the <term>Xiaoshao</term> <gloss>a legendary ancient musical composition</gloss> was played in nine movements, the phoenix came to perform its rites.

<summary>This passage contrasts external appearance with internal moral character, citing mythological sage-kings with non-human features alongside tyrannical rulers with human forms to argue that human nature is defined by virtue rather than physical shape.</summary>

IV. Jeh yueh.

1 O sun, O moon,
Which enlighten this lower earth!
Here is this man,
Who treats me not according to the ancient rule.
How can he get his mind settled?
Would he then not regard me?

2 O sun, O moon,
Which overshadow this lower earth!
Here is this man,
Who will not be friendly with me.
How can he get his mind settled?
Would he then not respond to me?

3 O sun, O moon,
Which come forth from the east!
Here is this man,
With virtuous words, but really not good.
How can he get his mind settled?
Would he then allow me to be forgotten?

4 O sun, O moon,
From the east which come forth!
O father, O mother,
There is no sequel to your nourishing of me.
How can he get his mind settled?
Would he then respond to me, contrary to all reason?

Kung Mengtse said to Motse: "There is only righteousness and unrighteousness, but no such thing as propitiousness or unpropitiousness." Motse said: The ancient sage-kings all regarded the ghosts and spirits as intelligent and in control of calamity and blessing. They held there was propitiousness and unpropitiousness and thereby the government was well administered and the country was secure. From Chieh and Chow down they all regarded the ghosts and spirits as unintelligent and not in control of calamity and blessing. They held there was no propitiousness and unpropitiousness, and thereby the government became disorderly and the country in danger. So, the book of the ancient kings "Chitse" says, "Pride brings calamity." That is to say, the evil act will be punished and the good act will be rewarded.

Motse said to Kung Mengtse: According to the ceremonial, for the death of the ruler, the parents, the wife, and the first-born son, there shall be mourning for three years. For the elder uncle, younger uncle, elder brother, younger brother, and first cousins within the family, five months. And for the aunt, the sister, the uncle on mother's side, and the nephew on sisters side, there will be mourning of several months for each. Many also use the intervals between periods of mourning to read the Three Hundred Poems according to rhymes, to play them on the string instruments, to sing them, and to dance to them. If your counsel should be followed when can the gentleman attend to government, the common man to work? Kung Mengtse said: "When the country is in chaos it should be put in order; when it is in order, ceremonials and music may be pursued. When the country is poor work should be attended to; when it is rich, ceremonials and music may be pursued." Motse said: A country may be orderly. But it is because it is being well governed that it is orderly. As soon as good administration is abandoned, order disappears also. A country may be rich. But it is because work is being attended to that it is rich. As soon as work is abandoned, wealth disappears also.

The sophists common to-day say: "Ch'ie and Chou were the legal rulers of the empire; T'ang and Wu rebelled and took it by force." This is not so. If by being Emperor is meant that Ch'ie and Chou possessed the registers and census records of the empire at that time, then yes. If it means that they themselves possessed the empire, then no. If it means that the empire could be said to be in the hands of Ch'ie and Chou, then no. In ancient times the Emperor had a thousand officials, and the feudal princes a hundred officials. By being king is meant to have his command performed through the states of China through these thousand officials. By being prince is meant to have his command performed throughout his borders through those hundred officials, and although his state be not at peace, yet not to be cast aside, displaced and ruined. The descendants of the Sage-Kings inherited the empire; the authority and the registers were in their hands. But if the Imperial Clan of the Empire had not a man of ability, it was unfit for its position. On the one hand his subjects hated him, and on the other the feudal princes revolted. Near the capital, those within his own borders were not united; at a distance, the feudal princes did not obey. His commands were not performed within his own borders. The feudal princes even invaded and sliced off some of his territory; they attacked and chastised him. When such was the situation, although he had not yet fallen, I say that he did not truly possess the empire. When the Sage-Kings died, those who possessed the authority and registers became weak, and became unable to control the empire.

When the country has no real prince, if there is a feudal noble who has ability, and if his virtue is illustrious and his majesty is great, none of the people of the country will be unwilling to take him for prince and leader; then if he should seek out and kill this isolated and wasteful tyrant, he would not injure anyone, he would be a blameless subject. If he put to death the prince of a tyrannous state, it would be the same as killing an ordinary individual. A person like this can be said to be able to wield the empire. He who is able to wield the empire can be called a King. T'ang and Wu did not capture the empire; they cultivated their ways (Tao); they carried out the principle of justice (Yi); they exalted the common benefit of the Empire; they did away with the common sources of injury to the empire; and so the empire turned to them. Ch'ie and Chou did not resign the empire; they perverted the virtue of Yu and T'ang; they confused the distinctions of the rules of proper conduct (Li) and justice (Yi); their bestial actions heaped up misfortune for them, completed their evil destiny, and the empire dismissed them. He to whom the empire turns is called King; he whom the empire dismisses, is ruined. Hence the fact that Ch'ie and Chou did not possess the empire and that T'ang and Wu did not murder their prince is clear from this argument.

# Correct Discourse

In ancient times, the Son of Heaven <note>the Emperor</note> had a thousand officials and the feudal lords had a hundred officials. When a ruler used these thousand officials to ensure his orders were carried out across all the Chinese states, he was called a King. When a ruler used these hundred officials to ensure his orders were carried out within his own borders, even if the state was not entirely stable, it did not reach the point of collapse or ruin <gloss>the original text uses a word read as "fall" or "losing one's legacy"</gloss>; such a person was called a Lord.

Consider the son of a Sage King. After inheriting the world and holding the official records of land and population, he becomes the head of the Great House of the world. However, if he is untalented and lacks integrity <gloss>literally "not hitting the mark," meaning not upright</gloss>, then internally the common people will hate him, and externally the feudal lords will rebel against him. Those nearby within his borders will not be unified, and the distant feudal lords will not obey. His orders will not even be carried out within his own territory. In extreme cases, the feudal lords will seize and diminish his lands or launch military attacks against him. In such a state, even if he has not yet perished, I say he no longer possesses the world.

When a Sage King dies and his successor is weak and incapable of managing affairs <gloss>literally "tired" or "weak," meaning unable to hold things together</gloss>, he cannot bind the world to him. If the world is without a true ruler, and there is a feudal lord whose virtue is bright and whose prestige has accumulated so that all the people within the four seas wish to have him as their ruler and teacher—yet a violent state remains arrogant and willful—then that lord must punish them. He will certainly not harm innocent people. Punishing the ruler of a violent state is like punishing a solitary fellow <gloss>meaning a man who has lost all support and stands alone</gloss>. One who acts like this can be said to know how to employ the world.

Knowing how to employ the world is what is meant by being a King. Tang and Wu <note>Founders of the Shang and Zhou dynasties</note> did not "take" the world. They cultivated their Way, practiced righteousness, shared benefits with the world, and eliminated the common harms of the world, and thus the world turned to them. Jie and Zhou <note>Last rulers of the Xia and Shang dynasties, cited as tyrants</note> did not "lose" the world <gloss>literally "leave" the world</gloss>; rather, they turned against the virtue of Yu and Tang, disrupted the distinctions of ritual and righteousness, acted like birds and beasts, accumulated wickedness, and so their subjects abandoned them.

<margin>1. The word for "followed" should be read as "fallen," meaning to lose one's legacy.</margin>
<margin>2. "Not middle" means not upright or correct.</margin>
<margin>3. "Tired" refers to being weak and unfit for duty; "suspend" means to bind or connect.</margin>
<margin>4. "Violent states" refers to rulers like Jie and Zhou; "singularly extravagant" means acting with total license; "how" here functions like "then."</margin>
<margin>5. "Solitary fellow" refers to one whom the whole world refuses to help, leaving him like a single man.</margin>
<margin>6. This implies the world abandoned them of its own accord.</margin>

<summary>Xunzi defines true kingship not by hereditary right or the possession of records, but by the ability to maintain order through ritual and the support of the people. He argues that tyrants like Jie and Zhou did not simply lose their empires but were abandoned because they lacked virtue.</summary>

In ancient times, the Son of Heaven had a thousand officials, and the feudal lords had a hundred officials. Because of these thousand officials, orders were carried out throughout the states of the Middle Kingdom; such a ruler was called a King. Because of these hundred officials, orders were carried out within their own borders; even if a state was not secure, it did not reach the point of collapse, being replaced, or perishing <note>original note: 遂 (sui) is read as 墜 (zhui), meaning to let one's enterprise fall.</note>, and such a ruler was called a Lord. This is the case after the descendants of the Sage Kings have possessed the world and hold the registers of the state, serving as the ancestral house of the world. However, if they are untalented and not centered <note>original note: 不中 (bu zhong) means not centered or upright.</note>, then internally the hundred surnames will suffer, and externally the feudal lords will rebel. Those near them within their borders will not be unified, and those far away, the feudal lords, will not listen. Their orders will not be carried out within their own borders; in extreme cases, the feudal lords will encroach upon them, diminish their territory, and attack them. If things reach this state, even if they have not yet perished, I say they have lost the world. 

When the Sage Kings have passed away and those who hold the registers are weak and unable to secure <note>original note: 罷 (pi) is read as weak and unable to handle affairs; 縣 (xuan) means to secure or fasten.</note> the world, the world has no lord. If among the feudal lords there is one whose virtue is clear and whose prestige has accumulated, the people within the seas will all wish for him to be their lord and teacher. If there is a tyrannical state that is uniquely extravagant and unrestrained, how then can one not punish it <note>original note: 暴國 (bao guo) refers to states like those of Jie and Zhou; 獨侈 (du chi) refers to being unrestrained; 安 (an) is similar to "then".</note>? One must not harm the innocent people, but punish the ruler of the tyrannical state as if punishing a solitary fellow <note>original note: 獨夫 (du fu) refers to a person whom the whole world refuses to help, as if he were a man standing alone.</note>. If one can do this, it can be said that one is able to use the world. Being able to use the world is what is called being a King. 

Tang and Wu did not seize the world; they cultivated their Way, practiced their righteousness, shared the common benefits of the world, and eliminated the common harms of the world, and so the world returned to them <note>original note: This implies the world gave its allegiance of its own accord.</note>. Jie and Zhou did not cast away the world; they turned against the virtues of Yu and Tang, threw the distinctions of ritual and righteousness into chaos, behaved like beasts, accumulated their evils, and exhausted those beneath them.

<summary>This passage defines the distinction between a true King and a mere Lord, arguing that legitimacy is based on virtue and the welfare of the people rather than inherited position alone. It concludes by contrasting the righteous success of Tang and Wu with the self-destructive tyranny of Jie and Zhou.</summary>
<keywords>Xunzi, Correct Argument, Kingly Way, Tang and Wu, Jie and Zhou, Ritual and Righteousness</keywords>

Xunzi, Rectification of Arguments

In ancient times, the Son of Heaven had a thousand officials, and the feudal lords had a hundred officials. Through these thousand officials, decrees were carried out throughout the states of the Central States; this was called being a King. Through these hundred officials, decrees were carried out within their own borders; even if the state was unstable, it did not reach the point of collapse or being destroyed <note>The commentator notes: "Destroyed" here should be read as "fallen," meaning the fall of one's lineage and heritage.</note>; this was called being a Lord. This applies to the descendants of sage kings after they have gained the empire, and to those who hold the imperial records and are the ancestors of the imperial lineage. Yet, if one lacks ability and moral center <note>The commentator notes: "Without moral center" means not upright or correct.</note>, if internally the hundred surnames suffer, and externally the feudal lords rebel, if those nearby within the borders are not united and those far away, the feudal lords, do not listen, if decrees cannot be executed within the borders, and at the extreme, the feudal lords encroach upon, diminish, attack, and invade—if it is like this, even if one has not yet perished, I would say they no longer possess the empire. After the sage kings have passed, if those who hold the records are weak and unable to secure the empire <note>The commentator notes: "Weak" is read as "fatigued," meaning too frail to handle affairs. "Secure" means to bind or tie together.</note>, and the empire is without a ruler, if there is a feudal lord who has brilliant virtue and accumulated prestige such that the people within the seas all desire to have him as their lord and teacher, yet a tyrannical state acts alone in its excess and arrogance, how could he <note>The commentator notes: "How could" is used here in the sense of "then."</note> punish them? One must not harm innocent people, but punish the ruler of a tyrannical state as if punishing a solitary man <note>The commentator notes: "Solitary man" means that everyone in the empire refuses to help him, as if he were just one man.</note>. If this is done, it can be called the ability to employ the empire. The ability to employ the empire is what is called Kingship. Tang and Wu did not seize the empire; they cultivated their Way, practiced their righteousness, shared common benefits with the empire, and eliminated common harms, and so the empire turned to them. Jie and Zhou did not abandon the empire; they acted against the virtues of Yu and Tang, threw the distinctions of ritual and righteousness into chaos, behaved like beasts, accumulated evil, and brought ruin upon their subjects <note>The commentator notes: "Brought ruin" refers to the empire departing of its own accord.</note>.

<summary>This passage defines the distinction between a true King and a failing ruler based on the efficacy of their administration and moral standing, citing the examples of Tang and Wu versus the tyrants Jie and Zhou.</summary>
<keywords>Xunzi, Rectification of Arguments, Kingship, Tang and Wu, Jie and Zhou, Ritual and Righteousness</keywords>

# Correct Discourse <note>original title: "Zheng Lun"</note>

In ancient times, the Son of Heaven <note>the Emperor</note> had a thousand officials and the feudal lords had a hundred officials. When a ruler used these thousand officials to make his commands effective throughout all the Chinese states, he was called a King. When a ruler used these hundred officials to make his commands effective within his own borders, even if the state was not entirely peaceful, it did not reach the point of collapsing or losing its hereditary succession <gloss>original: "falling or being exchanged," interpreted as losing the ancestral line</gloss> <margin>The character for "falling" is read as "to drop," meaning to lose one's professional legacy.</margin>; such a ruler was called a Lord. 

Consider the son of a Sage King. After he inherits the world, he possesses the official records of the land and occupies the position of the head of the Great House of the world. However, if he is without talent and is not upright <margin>Not "middle" means not being middle-and-upright.</margin>, then internally the common people will hate him, and externally the feudal lords will rebel against him. Those near him within his borders will not be unified, and those far away among the feudal lords will not obey. His commands will not even be followed within his own territory. In extreme cases, the feudal lords will encroach upon his land, diminish his territory, and launch military attacks against him. If things reach this state, even if he has not yet perished, I say he no longer "possesses the world."

When a Sage King dies and his successor is weak and unfit for duty <margin>The character for "tired" is pronounced like "pi," meaning weak and incapable of handling affairs. "Suspend" means to keep the world tied or connected to the ruler.</margin>, such that he cannot hold the world together, the world is effectively without a ruler. If among the feudal lords there is one whose virtue is brilliant and whose majesty has accumulated, so that none among the people within the four seas <note>the known world</note> does not wish to have him as their ruler and teacher, yet a violent state remains arrogant and unrestrained <margin>A "violent state" refers to those like the tyrants Jie and Zhou. "Uniquely extravagant" means acting with total license. The word "how" here functions as "then."</margin>, then that leader must be able to punish them. He must not harm the innocent people. Executing the ruler of a violent state is like executing a "lone man" <margin>A "lone man" refers to one whom the whole world has abandoned, leaving him like a single individual without support.</margin>. If he acts in this way, he can be said to be able to "employ the world." One who can employ the world is called a King.

The Kings Tang and Wu did not "seize" the world. They cultivated the Way and practiced righteousness. They shared the same interests as the world and eliminated the common harms of the world, and thus the world turned to them. The tyrants Jie and Zhou did not "lose" the world <margin>This implies the world left them of its own accord.</margin>. They turned against the virtue of Yu and Tang, threw the distinctions of ritual and righteousness into disorder, and behaved like birds and beasts. They accumulated cruelty and perfected their own downfall.

<summary>Xunzi defines true kingship not by hereditary right or title, but by the ability to maintain moral authority and the Mandate of Heaven through ritual and righteousness. He argues that tyrants like Jie and Zhou did not simply lose their empires but were abandoned by the world due to their lack of virtue.</summary>
<keywords>Xunzi, Correct Discourse, Kingship, Tang and Wu, Jie and Zhou, Ritual and Righteousness, Mandate of Heaven, political philosophy</keywords>

Even if the state was not peaceful, it would not reach the point of collapse, removal, or destruction <note>original: "遂亡" - the commentary notes "遂" is read as "墜", meaning to let one's legacy fall/decline</note>; this was called being a ruler. He is the descendant of a sage king. 則不明。是亂之所由作也。故主道利明，不利幽；不利周，故主道明則下安，道幽則下危。故下安則貴上，下危則賤上。故主道莫惡乎難知，莫危乎使下畏己。傳曰：「惡之者眾則危。」書曰：「克明峻德。」詩曰：「明明在下。」故先王明之，豈特玄之耳哉？

世俗之為說者曰：桀紂有天下，湯武篡而奪之。是不然。以桀紂為常有天下子之籍則然，親有天下子之籍則不然。天下謂在桀紂則不然。

①書康誥。②言文王也。③詩大雅大明之篇。④言文王之德明明在下也。⑤常有世相及也，籍位也，親有言身為天子也，天下謂在桀紂則不然，言如謂天下之心歸桀紂則不然也。

When we speak of the original nature of the mind, eternally without thought, we call it eternally unchanged. As the human mind originally does not know the Archetype (the Absolute Reality) the mind does not correspond with the outward universe. Then thought suddenly begins and is called the finite thought.

Confusion from correspondence with the objective. One can be delivered from this confusion by the two lower schools and be kept far from it in the station of full faith of the great school. Confusion arises through feeling corresponding with the objective. One can gradually avoid this by the cultivation of the means of deliverance in the full faith of the great school; by the cultivation to the First station in the pure state of the mind, all the confusion will be gone. (To understand these and the stations below, see Guide to Buddhahood.)

Confusion through knowledge of differences by correspondence with the objective. By means of the second stage of separateness from the world and by means of deliverance in the Seventh station, confusion will be gone.

Confusion through objective forms not corresponding with one another. By means of the Eighth station of freedom from form (or the immoveable) all the confusion will be gone.

### 3. Revealing the Characteristics of the Dependent Origination Mentioned Above
This section concerns the sentences regarding the stained mind.

#### First, the Heading
There are six types of stained minds.

#### Second, the Inquiry
What are the six?
Within each of the six types, there are two parts: first the obstacle, and second the remedy.

#### Third, the Explanation
However, these six stains are matched in reverse order to the six coarse marks <note>from the Awakening of Faith</note>, the first four and the three subtle marks. According to the Commentary on the Awakening of Faith, Volume One:
This first stage corresponds to the third and fourth of those coarse marks, thus there are only six. These names are borrowed to categorize these six types.

#### First: The Mark of Attachment and the Mark of Assigning Names
1. The stained mind associated with attachment. This is distanced through the liberation of the Two Vehicles <gloss>Hearers and Solitary Buddhas</gloss> and in the Stage of Associated Faith. This corresponds to the third and fourth marks among the six coarse marks. It also refers to the growth of the afflictions of views and cravings within the conscious mind. Among the four previous marks, it is the stage of discriminating attachment. Because the coarse mind attaches to external objects and harmonizes with them, it defiles pure conduct and is called a stain. Regarding the liberation of the Two Vehicles, upon reaching the stage of No-More-Learning <gloss>Arhatship</gloss>, the afflictions of views and cultivation are completely abandoned. Regarding the Association of Faith, from the Ten Understandings onward, the root of faith is perfected and there is no falling back, thus it is called the Association of Faith. Therefore, the Treatise on the Stages <note>the Dashabhumika Sutra Shastra</note> says that everything before the first stage <gloss>bhumi</gloss> is collectively called the Stage of Practicing Faith. The Treatise on Non-Attachment by the Bodhisattva Asanga also says the same. This Bodhisattva

<column-break/>

gains the view of the emptiness of the person, so that the afflictions of views and cultivation cannot manifest, which is why it is called distancing. This does not refer to the latent tendencies <note>original: "anuśaya"</note>, as the Bodhisattva retains certain delusions to remain in the world. As the Summary of the Great Vehicle <note>the Mahayana-samgraha</note> says: if one does not cut off the active mind, one is no different from an ordinary person; if one does not retain the seeds of delusion, one is no different from the Two Vehicles. Furthermore, the two intentions for retaining delusion are for oneself and for others. This is explained according to the Final Teaching. If according to the Initial Teaching, it is said that one retains delusion only from the First Stage <gloss>bhumi</gloss> upward, as stated in other treatises. Now, this Bodhisattva does not simply cut off the human attachment of the four dwellings <note>four levels of affliction</note>, but also partially cuts off the dwelling stage of ignorance. Therefore, this treatise later says: those who do not understand the meaning of the single Dharma Realm observe and learn to cut it off from the Stage of Associated Faith. Here, it is only discussed to reveal the coarseness of the ego, so the other aspects are not discussed.

#### Second: The Mark of Continuity
2. The stained mind associated with the uninterrupted. Based on the skillful means of study in the Stage of Associated Faith, one is gradually able to discard it, and upon reaching the Stage of the Pure Mind <gloss>the First Bhumi</gloss>, one is completely distanced from it.
Commentary on the Awakening of Faith, Volume One:
This is the second of the six coarse marks. From here to the sixth, they are again matched in reverse order to the previous five intentions <gloss>five kinds of mind</gloss>. This position is the fifth, where one simply attaches to the continuity of dharmas <note>phenomena</note>, producing them without interruption, which is the meaning of continuity. From the Ten Understandings onward, one uses the skillful means of investigating and reflecting in the meditation on consciousness-only, until the First Stage where one realizes the three types of non-nature and the pervasive True Suchness; then the discrimination of attachment to dharmas cannot manifest.

#### Third: The Mark of Wisdom
3. The stained mind associated with discriminating wisdom. It is gradually distanced based on the Stage of Perfected Precepts <gloss>the Second Bhumi</gloss> until reaching the Stage of Skillful Means in the Markless <gloss>the Seventh Bhumi</gloss>, where it is completely distanced.
This is the first of the six coarse marks and the fourth of the five intentions. Because it can discriminate between the worldly and the world-transcending, and between the stained and the pure, it is called wisdom. This is the subtle delusion of attachment to dharmas. Below the Seventh Stage, there is still a difference between entering and leaving meditative absorption, so there is subtle discrimination regarding objects. However, as it is removed stage by stage, it is said to be gradually distanced. At the Eighth Stage.

<summary>This page analyzes the first three of the six stained minds, explaining how they correspond to the coarse marks of the Awakening of Faith and at which stages of Bodhisattva practice they are eliminated.</summary>
<keywords>stained mind, six coarse marks, attachment, continuity, discriminating wisdom, Bodhisattva stages, bhumi, two vehicles, ignorance</keywords>

Also, this is stated in terms of the door of interdependence between the coarse and the subtle, so it is said to have no before. It also speaks of "suddenness" not in terms of time, but to describe the nature of that suddenness.

○ 3. Clarifying the characteristics of the aforementioned dependent origination: This refers to the passage concerning the "defiled mind."

○ 1. Indication.
The defiled mind has six types.

○ 2. Inquiry.
What are the six?
Within the six, each has two parts: the first is the obstacle, and the latter is the remedy.

○ 3. Explanation.
Regarding these six types of defilement, they are matched in reverse order to the six coarse marks. The first four and the latter three subtle marks are, according to the *Commentary on the Awakening of Faith*, Volume One, identical to this. Furthermore, it corresponds to the "Attachment through Discriminating Grasping" among the four characteristics. Because the coarse mind externally clings and associates with objects, it stains pure conduct; hence it is called "defilement." The "liberation of the Two Vehicles" refers to the ultimate separation from the afflictions of views and cultivation upon reaching the stage of "No-Learning" <note>Arhatship</note>. "Faith-Association" refers to the achievement of the root of faith from the Ten Stages of Understanding <note>original: 十解</note> onward, where there is no longer any falling back. Therefore, the <term>Di Lun</term> <gloss>Treatise on the Ten Stages</gloss> states that all stages prior to the first Bhumi are collectively called the Stage of Faith-Practice. Now, this Bodhisattva does not only sever the "attachments to person" of the four residences, but also partially severs the "residence of ignorance" <note>original: 無明住地</note>. Therefore, the later part of this treatise says that those who do not understand the meaning of the single Dharma-realm learn to sever it through observation from the Ground of Faith-Association. 是故不應取法，不應取非法；以是義故，如來常說：「汝等比丘！知我說法如筏喻者，法尚應捨，何況非法」。

### 無得無說分第七

須菩提！於意云何？如來得阿耨多羅三藐三菩提耶？如來有所說法耶？

須菩提言：如我解佛所說義，無有定法名阿耨多羅三藐三菩提，亦無有定法如來可說；何以故？如來所說法皆不可取、不可說、非法、非非法；所以者何？一切賢聖皆以無為法而有差別。

### 依法出生分第八

須菩提！於意云何？若人滿三千大千世界七寶以用布施，是人所得福德，寧為多不？

須菩提言：甚多，世尊！何以故？是福德即非福德性，是故如來說福德多。

若復有人於此經中，受持乃至四句偈等為他人說，其福勝彼；何以故？須菩提！一切諸佛及諸佛阿耨多羅三藐三菩提法，皆從此經出。須菩提！所謂佛法者，即非佛法。

### 一相無相分第九

Therefore, enlightened disciples ought not to affirm the permanency or reality of qualities or ideas coincident with Law, nor postulate as being of an inviolate nature, qualities or ideas having an existence apart from the concept of Law.

"Thus, we are enabled to appreciate the significance of those words which the Lord Buddha invariably repeated to his followers: 'You disciples must realise that the Law which I enunciated, was presented before your minds in the simile of a raft. If the Law — having fulfilled its function in bearing you to the other shore (Nirvana) — with its coincident qualities and ideas must inevitably be abandoned,' how much more inevitable must be the abandonment of qualities or ideas which have an existence apart from the Law?'"

The Lord Buddha addressed Subhuti, saying: "What think you? Has the Lord Buddha really attained to supreme spiritual wisdom? Or has he a system of doctrine which can be specifically formulated?"

Subhuti replied, saying: "As I understand the meaning of the Lord Buddha's discourse, he has no system of doctrine which can be specifically formulated; nor can the Lord Buddha express, in explicit terms, a form of knowledge which can be described as supreme spiritual wisdom. And why? Because, what the Lord Buddha adumbrated in terms of the Law, is transcendental and inexpressible. Being a purely spiritual concept, it is neither consonant with Law, nor synonymous with anything apart from the Law. Thus is exemplified the manner by which wise disciples and holy Buddhas, regarding intuition as the Law of their minds, severally attained to different planes of spiritual wisdom."

The Lord Buddha addressed Subhuti, saying: "What think you? If a benevolent person bestowed as alms, an abundance of the seven treasures sufficient to fill the universe, would there accrue to that person a considerable merit?"

Subhuti replied, saying: "A very considerable merit, Honoured of the Worlds! And why? Because, what is referred to does not partake of the nature of ordinary merit, and in this sense the Lord Buddha made mention of a 'considerable' merit."

The Lord Buddha rejoined, saying: "If a disciple adhered with implicit faith to a stanza of this Scripture, and diligently explained it to others, the intrinsic merit of that disciple would be relatively greater. And why? Because, Subhuti, the holy Buddhas, and the Law by which they attained to supreme spiritual wisdom, severally owe their inception to the truth of this sacred Scripture. Subhuti, what is ordinarily termed the Buddhic Law, is not really a Law attributive to Buddha."

The Lord Buddha enquired of Subhuti, saying: "What think you? May a Scrotapatti (having entered the stream which bears on to Nirvana) thus moralise within himself, 'I have obtained the fruits commensurate with the merit of a Scrotapatti'?" Subhuti replied, saying: "No! Honoured of the Worlds! And why? Because, Scrotapatti is simply a descriptive term signifying 'having entered the stream.' A disciple who avoids the seductive phenomena of form, sound, odour, taste, touch, and Law, is named a Scrotapatti."

The Lord Buddha enquired of Subhuti, saying: “What think you? May a Scrotapatti (having entered the stream which bears on to Nirvana) thus moralise within himself, ‘I have obtained the fruits commensurate with the merit of a Scrotapatti’?” Subhuti replied, saying: “No! Honoured of the Worlds! And why? Because, Scrotapatti is simply a descriptive term signifying ‘having entered the stream.’ A disciple who avoids the seductive phenomena of form, sound, odour, taste, touch, and Law, is named a Scrotapatti.”

The Lord Buddha again enquired of Subhuti, saying: “What think you? May a Sakridagami (who is subject only to one more reincarnation) thus muse within himself, ‘I have obtained the fruits consonant with the merit of a Sakridagami’?” Subhuti replied, saying: “No! Honoured of the Worlds! And why? Because, Sakridagami is merely a descriptive title denoting ‘only one more reincarnation’; but in reality there is no such condition as ‘only one more reincarnation,’ hence Sakridagami is merely a descriptive title.”

The Lord Buddha once again enquired of Subhuti, saying: “What think you? May an Anagami (having entire immunity from reincarnation) thus reflect within himself, ‘I have obtained the fruits which accord with the merit of an Anagami?’” Subhuti replied, saying: “No! Honoured of the Worlds! And why? Because, Anagami is merely a designation meaning ‘immunity from reincarnation’; but in reality there is no such condition as ‘immunity from reincarnation,’ hence Anagami is merely a convenient designation.”

The Lord Buddha yet again enquired of Subhuti, saying: “What think you? May an Arhat (having attained to absolute quiescence of mind) thus meditate within himself, ‘I have obtained the condition of an Arhat’?” Subhuti replied, saying: “No! Honoured of the Worlds! And why? Because, there is not in reality a condition synonymous with the term Arhat. Honoured of the Worlds! if an Arhat thus meditates within himself, ‘I have obtained the condition of an Arhat,’ there would be obvious recurrence of such arbitrary concepts as an entity, a being, a living being, and a personality. Honoured of the Worlds! When the Lord Buddha declared that in absolute quiescence of mind, perfect observance of the Law, and true spiritual perception, I was pre-eminent amongst the disciples, I did not cogitate thus within myself, ‘I am an Arhat, freed from desire!’ Had I thus cogitated, ‘I have obtained the condition of an Arhat,’ the ‘Honoured of the Worlds’ would not have declared concerning me, ‘Subhuti delights in the austerities practised by the Aranyaka’; but, in reality, Subhuti was perfectly quiescent and oblivious to phenomena; hence the allusion, ‘Subhuti delights in the austerities practised by the Aranyaka.’”

<note>original: 金剛般若波羅蜜經</note>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the four stages of enlightenment and whether a practitioner who has attained them would cling to the concept of having achieved a specific rank or fruit.</meta>

Form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and mental objects <note>referring to the six sense objects or spheres</note>; this is why one is called a <term>Srota-apanna</term> <gloss>Stream-enterer</gloss>.
"What do you think? Does a <term>Sakridagamin</term> <gloss>Once-returner</gloss> have this thought: 'I have attained the fruit of a Once-returner'?"
Subhuti replied, "No, World-Honored One. Why? Because although a <term>Sakridagamin</term> is named a 'Once-returner,' in reality there is no such thing as going or coming. Therefore, he is named a <term>Sakridagamin</term>."
"Subhuti, what do you think? Does an <term>Anagamin</term> <gloss>Non-returner</gloss> have this thought: 'I have attained the fruit of a Non-returner'?"
Subhuti replied, "No, World-Honored One. Why? Because an <term>Anagamin</term> is named a 'Non-returner,' but in reality there is no such thing as not coming. For this reason, he is named an <term>Anagamin</term>."

二者相續相依於智故。生其苦樂覺心起念相應不斷故。

二相續中依於智者明起所依謂依前分別愛境起樂覺受。不愛境起苦受。數數起念相續現前。此明自相續也。又能起惑潤業引持生死。即令他相續故。下文云住持苦樂等也。故云生其乃至不斷故也。

三者執取相者謂於前苦樂等境界。不了虛無深起取。

Since there is an objective world, there arise again six aspects of it according to another classification, viz:—

(a.) Consciousness, which arises from outward objects which the mind distinguishes between one and another—between what it likes and what it dislikes.

(b.) Emotion. This follows consciousness and produces joy and sorrow. These false ideas arise from constant partial enlightenment.

(c.) Attention. This follows emotion, reaching after everything, seizing on joy and sorrow and cleaving to them with the whole mind.

Second: The phase of continuity. This relies on the function of intellectual cognition <term>zhi</term> <gloss>the wisdom that distinguishes</gloss>. It generates the feeling-mind of suffering and pleasure, giving rise to thoughts that are associated and uninterrupted.

Regarding the explanation of this continuity as relying on intellectual cognition: this clarifies that which the continuity depends upon for its arising. Specifically, it relies on the previous discrimination between desirable objects, which gives rise to the perception of pleasure, and undesirable objects, which gives rise to the perception of suffering. These thoughts arise repeatedly, appearing one after another in a continuous stream. This explains the internal continuity of the self. Furthermore, it can give rise to afflictions <term>huo</term> <gloss>klesha or delusions</gloss> which nourish karma and sustain the cycle of birth and death <term>shengsi</term> <gloss>samsara</gloss>. This causes the continuity of the other <note>referring to the chain of future rebirths</note>. As the later text states: it maintains and supports suffering and pleasure. Therefore, the text says it generates feelings up to the point of being uninterrupted.

Third: The phase of grasping. This refers to the aforementioned realms of suffering and pleasure. Because one does not understand that these objects are empty and non-existent, a deep attachment and grasping arises.

<summary>This page explains the second and third phases of the development of the deluded mind, focusing on how intellectual discrimination leads to a continuous cycle of pleasure, pain, and rebirth. It details the transition from simple perception to the deep-seated attachment that binds sentient beings to samsara.</summary>

The second is the aspect of continuity, which depends on knowledge <note>original: 智, referring to the faculty of discernment or discriminatory consciousness</note>. Because of the arising of the perception of suffering and joy, thoughts emerge and continue without interruption.

Regarding the second, the aspect of continuity, the dependence on knowledge means that, based on the aforementioned discrimination, one arises a feeling of joy when encountering desired objects and a feeling of suffering when encountering undesired objects. Thoughts emerge repeatedly and the continuity becomes manifest. This explains the self-continuity. Furthermore, it can give rise to afflictions <term>klesha</term> <gloss>mental defilements</gloss> that nourish actions and draw one into the cycle of birth and death, which also causes the continuity of others. The text below mentions the sustaining of suffering and joy, and so on. Therefore, it is said that it gives rise to these, continuing until there is no interruption.

The third is the aspect of attachment, which means that, regarding the aforementioned objects of suffering and joy, one does not understand their emptiness and deeply gives rise to attachment.

1. A general object, i. e., that the author might induce all beings to liberate themselves from misery and to enjoy blessing, and not that he might gain thereby some worldly advantages, etc.

Question: What were the causes and conditions <note>original: "因緣" <gloss>nidana; primary causes and environmental conditions</gloss></note> for composing this treatise?

The answer contains three parts: the statement of the number, the explanation of their characteristics, and a concluding summary.

Answer: There are eight types of causes and conditions. What are these eight?

Regarding the explanation of characteristics: the first is general, while the remaining seven are specific. The reason for this is that the general condition covers both the primary and secondary objectives, while the specific ones are for the sake of those individuals ready to receive the teaching <note>original: "當機" <gloss>those whose capacity matches the teaching</gloss></note>.

1. The general characteristic of the causes and conditions: namely, to cause all sentient beings to leave behind all suffering and attain ultimate happiness.

Regarding "leaving behind all suffering" in the general characteristic: it means causing sentient beings <note>original: "有情" <gloss>sentient beings; those with consciousness</gloss></note> to leave behind the three types of suffering <note>The suffering of pain, the suffering of change, and the suffering of conditioned existence.</note> and the two types of death <note>Physical death and the "death" of transformative rebirth experienced by advanced practitioners.</note>.

Regarding "attaining ultimate happiness": it means causing them to attain the happiness of Supreme Enlightenment <note>term: "無上菩提" <gloss>Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi</gloss></note> and Great Nirvana <note>term: "大涅槃" <gloss>Mahaparinirvana</gloss></note>.

Regarding "not seeking worldly fame or profit": there are two interpretations. First, it means not wishing to have them seek the benefits or happiness of future lives as humans or heavenly beings <note>original: "人天" <gloss>the higher realms of rebirth within samsara</gloss></note>.

CHAP. VI. The Master said, 'A youth, when at home, should be filial, and, abroad, respectful to his elders. He should be earnest and truthful. He should overflow in love to all, and cultivate the friendship of the good. When he has time and opportunity, after the performance of these things, he should employ them in polite studies.'

CHAP. VII. Tsze-hsia said, 'If a man withdraws his mind from the love of beauty, and applies it as sincerely to the love of the virtuous; if, in serving his parents, he can exert his utmost strength; if, in serving his prince, he can devote his life; if, in his intercourse with his friends, his words are sincere:-- although men say that he has not learned, I will certainly say that he has.'

CHAP. VIII. 1. The Master said, 'If the scholar be not grave, he will not call forth any veneration, and his learning will not be solid.

Regarding the relative weight of the fundamental and the peripheral: in terms of behavior, action is considered more weighty. Therefore, this chapter places action first and culture <note>the study of literature and arts</note> afterward, prioritizing the root over the branches. However, regarding the sequence of knowledge and action, culture is the starting point. This is why the "Four Teachings" chapter lists culture first and action later. By examining these two chapters together, one can see that culture and action must progress in tandem.

***

Master Zi Xia said: "If a person values worthiness so as to replace his desire for physical beauty <note>or "changes his expression/demeanor"</note>; if he can exhaust his strength in serving his parents; if he can devote his very life to serving his prince; and if, in his dealings with friends, his words are trustworthy; even if it is said that he has not yet studied, I would certainly say that he has."

Zi Xia was a disciple of Confucius, surnamed Bu and named Shang, a man of Wei. To "value worthiness" <term>xian xian</term> <gloss>to treat the worthy as worthy</gloss> means to replace the heart that loves beauty with a sincere love for goodness. The Collected Commentaries <note>the *Jizhu* by Zhu Xi</note> ask: how can seeing worthiness change one’s outward appearance? This refers to the sincerity of loving goodness. Master Zhu <note>Zhu Xi</note> remarked that twice it has been said "I have not seen one who loves virtue as he loves beauty." The *Doctrine of the Mean* also considers distancing oneself from beauty as a method. To "devote" <term>zhi</term> <gloss>to hand over or commit</gloss> one's body means to give oneself up entirely, not holding one's life as one’s own. Since this involves the sincerity of replacing the love of beauty, Fan’s explanation is the most excellent.

<summary>This page discusses the relationship between practical action and cultural study, followed by Zi Xia's teaching on the true nature of learning through filial piety, loyalty, and sincerity.</summary>

In terms of the relative importance of the root and the branch, if we speak of action, then action is heavy. Therefore, in this chapter, action comes first, while the subsequent text puts the root before the branch. If we speak in terms of the sequence of knowledge and action, then literature <note>or "the study of texts"</note> comes first. Therefore, the chapter on the four teachings places literature first, followed by action. By examining these two chapters together, it can be seen that literature and action must be pursued in parallel.

○ Zixia said: To appreciate the virtuous as we appreciate beauty, to exert one's full strength in serving one's parents, to be willing to sacrifice one's life in serving one's ruler, and to be sincere in one's words when interacting with friends—even if one says this person has not yet learned, I would certainly call them learned.

Zixia was a disciple of Confucius, surnamed Bu, named Shang, and a man of Wei. To "appreciate the virtuous as we appreciate beauty" means to change one's heart, which prefers physical beauty, to instead prefer virtue with sincerity. The *Collected Commentaries* <note>original: "集註" referring to the *Collected Commentaries on the Analects*</note> ask: How should we interpret this? Seeing the virtuous and changing one’s tendency toward beauty is a matter of turning one's love of beauty toward a love of virtue. Master Zhu <note>Zhu Xi</note> said: The two passages regarding "not having seen one who loves virtue as much as one loves beauty" and the *Doctrine of the Mean* both treat distancing oneself from physical beauty as the way to virtue. "Exert" means to relinquish. "Relinquishing one's life" means not to hold on to one's own body or life. This is the sincerity of changing one's love of beauty. Therefore, Master Fan’s explanation is the superior one.

<margin>Collected Commentaries on the Analects</margin>
<margin>Determining the Punctuation</margin>

<summary>This page discusses the balance between "literature" (study) and "action" in Confucian practice, while providing a commentary on Zixia’s criteria for a learned person.</summary>
<keywords>Zixia, Zhu Xi, virtue, learning, Confucian ethics, root and branch</keywords>

If we speak of the relative importance of the root and the branch, action is heavy and significant, which is why this chapter puts action first, and later sections prioritize the root before the branch. If we speak of the sequence of knowing and acting, literary refinement is the primary stage, which is why the chapter on the four teachings places literary learning before putting it into practice. By examining these two chapters together, it is evident that learning and action cannot be advanced without each other.

○ Zixia said, "If a person replaces their appreciation of beauty with an appreciation of the virtuous, is able to exert all their strength in serving their parents, is able to devote their life in serving their ruler, and is sincere in their speech when interacting with friends, even if they say they have not studied, I will certainly say that they have learned."

Zixia was a disciple of Confucius, surnamed Bu, named Shang, and a man from the state of Wei. To consider the virtuous as virtuous and replace the heart that loves beauty with this; this is to love the good with sincerity. What does the *Collected Commentaries* <note>original: "集註"</note> say? It means to see the virtuous and change one's disposition, lowering one's love of beauty to cultivate a love for the good. Master Zhu <note>original: "朱子"</note> says the two statements in the *Analects* about not yet seeing one who loves virtue as much as one loves beauty, and the *Doctrine of the Mean* <note>original: "中庸"</note> presenting distance as a method to guard against the love of beauty, both show that reaching for virtue is like yielding oneself. "Devoting one's body" means not keeping one's self for oneself. It is the sincerity of replacing the love of beauty. Therefore, Fan's explanation is the most comprehensive.

If we speak of the weight and lightness of the root and the branches, then action is heavy, so this chapter places "action" first and "literature" last, placing the root first and the branch last. If we speak of the sequence of knowledge and action, then literature is the priority, so the chapter on the four teachings places "literature" first and "action" last. By observing these two chapters together, it can be seen that literature and action must be pursued in parallel.

Zixia said: "To value the worthy and replace the lustful <note>original: "賢賢易色"</note>; to exhaust one's strength in serving one's parents; to fully commit one's person in serving one's ruler; and to be trustworthy in one's words when interacting with friends—even if one says he has not learned, I will certainly say that he has learned."

Zixia was a disciple of Confucius, surnamed Bu, personal name Shang, a man of Wey. "To value the worthy and replace the lustful" means to replace the love of beauty with the love of goodness; it is having sincerity. The Collected Commentary says: "Seeing the worthy and changing one's lustful nature is the basis of loving goodness." Zhu Xi says: "The two instances of 'not yet seeing one who loves virtue as much as one loves beauty' in the *Doctrine of the Mean* also take 'replacing' as the method for overcoming the love of beauty, seeing it as yielding—yielding one's person means not to hold anything back for oneself, but to be sincere in replacing the love of beauty." Thus, Fan's interpretation is the superior one.

Regarding the relative importance of the root and the branch: in terms of practice, action is considered heavy <note>primary</note> while words are considered light <note>secondary</note>. Therefore, this chapter places action first and culture <note>the branches of learning</note> second, emphasizing the root before the branch. In terms of the sequence of knowledge and action, culture comes first. For this reason, the "Four Teachings" chapter lists culture first and action later. By observing these two chapters together, one can see that culture and action must progress side by side.

### Zixia said: "One who treats the worthy as worthy and thereby changes his love of sensual beauty; who, in serving his parents, can exert his full strength; who, in serving his prince, can devote his life; and who, in interacting with friends, is trustworthy in his words — even if it is said that such a person has not yet studied, I would certainly call him a man of learning."

Zixia was a disciple of Confucius. His surname was Bu and his given name was Shang; he was a man of the state of Wei. To "treat the worthy as worthy and change sensual beauty" <term>xian xian yi se</term> means to honor the virtue of worthy people and thereby replace the desire for physical beauty. It refers to having a sincere love for the good. The Collected Commentaries <note>referring to the *Lunyu Jizhu* by Zhu Xi</note> state that seeing worthiness changes the expression of the face <note>the "color"</note> to show a love for goodness. Master Zhu said that the Master twice remarked on never seeing anyone who loved virtue as much as they loved sensual beauty. The *Doctrine of the Mean* also considers distancing oneself from beauty as a method for self-cultivation. To "devote" <term>zhi</term> means to give over or entrust. Devoting one's body <note>or life</note> means not holding onto one's self interest. This sincerity in replacing the love of beauty is why Fan’s explanation is considered superior.

<summary>This page discusses the relationship between learning and moral action, specifically interpreting Zixia's teaching that practical virtue in family and social roles defines a learned person more than formal study alone.</summary>

If we speak in terms of the weight given to the root and the branch, then conduct is heavy; therefore, in this chapter, it is placed first, while the subsequent text places the root before the branch. If we speak in terms of the sequence of knowing and acting, then literature is the priority; therefore, in the chapter on the four teachings, literature is placed before conduct. Viewing these two chapters in comparison, it is evident that literature and conduct must advance together.

○ Zixia said: "If a person treats the virtuous as virtuous and alters his lustful heart, if he can exert his utmost strength in serving his parents, if he can dedicate his entire person to serving his ruler, and if he is faithful in his speech when interacting with friends, then even if it is said he has not learned, I will certainly say he has learned."

Zixia was a disciple of Confucius, surnamed Bu, named Shang, and was a man of the state of Wei. To consider the virtuous as virtuous and to alter one's love for beauty means to love goodness with sincerity. The <term>Jizhu</term> <gloss>Collected Commentaries</gloss> asks: "What does this mean?" Seeing the virtuous and changing one's appearance signifies the love of goodness over the love of beauty. Master Zhu <note>Zhu Xi</note> says: "The two instances of 'not yet seeing one who loves virtue as much as he loves beauty' <note>a reference to the Analects 1.7 and 9.17</note>, and the <term>Zhongyong</term> <gloss>Doctrine of the Mean</gloss> also treat distancing oneself as a method for dealing with the love of beauty, show that the sincerity <note>or extreme intensity</note> is similar to 'devoting'. 'Devoting one's person' means one does not hold back one's own body. Altering one's love of beauty is a matter of sincerity; therefore, the explanation by Master Fan is superior."

<margin>Great Compendium of the Collected Commentaries on the Analects</margin>
<margin>Determining the Punctuation</margin>

<summary>This page discusses the prioritization of conduct over literature and presents Zixia's definition of learning through the moral transformation of the self, filial piety, and loyalty.</summary>
<keywords>Zixia, Confucius, learning, conduct, literature, filial piety, loyalty, sincerity, Zhu Xi</keywords>

In terms of the relative importance of the root and the branch, if we speak of action, then action is heavy. Therefore, in this chapter, action comes first, while the subsequent text puts the root before the branch. If we speak in terms of the sequence of knowledge and action, then literature <note>or "the study of texts"</note> comes first. Therefore, the chapter on the four teachings places literature first, followed by action, and then by action again. By examining these two chapters together, it can be seen that literature and action must be pursued in parallel.

○ Zixia said: To appreciate the virtuous as we appreciate beauty, to exert one's full strength in serving one's parents, to be willing to sacrifice one's life in serving one's ruler, and to be sincere in one's words when interacting with friends—even if one says this person has not yet learned, I would certainly call them learned.

Zixia was a disciple of Confucius, surnamed Bu, named Shang, and a man of Wei. To "appreciate the virtuous as we appreciate beauty" means to change one's heart, which prefers physical beauty, to instead prefer virtue with sincerity. The *Collected Commentaries* <note>original: "集註" referring to the *Collected Commentaries on the Analects*</note> ask: How should we interpret this? Seeing the virtuous and changing one’s tendency toward beauty is a matter of turning one's love of beauty toward a love of virtue. Master Zhu <note>Zhu Xi</note> said: The two passages regarding "not having seen one who loves virtue as much as one loves beauty" and the *Doctrine of the Mean* both treat distancing oneself from physical beauty as the way to virtue. "Exert" means to relinquish. "Relinquishing one's life" means not to hold on to one's own body or life. This is the sincerity of changing one's love of beauty. Therefore, Master Fan’s explanation is the superior one.

一言 <gloss>a single word</gloss> may cover one person, and one deed may cover one moment, yet neither represents the whole. Feng of Hou-zhai said: Since he participated in the government and cast the legal code <note>original: "參辟鑄刑書", referring to the legalist reforms of Zi-chan in the state of Zheng</note>, it is true that his shortcomings were many. However, judged by the standards of the Spring and Autumn Annals, his knowledge of the Way of the Gentleman was indeed scarce. The words of the Sage <note>Confucius</note> praise without excessive beauty and criticize without excessive malice. The Collected Commentaries on the matter of "employing the people with righteousness" specifically follow the reality of his actions and cannot conceal them.

Hu said: The three years of mourning was the legacy of love taught by the disciples of Confucius. The cultivation of the fields was the legacy of love taught to our children and brothers. The spirit of Zi-chan is entirely centered on the word righteousness <term>yi</term>. As for the people’s praise of his kindness <term>hui</term> while claiming he did not know how to govern, this originally referred only to the single act of helping people cross the river.

# The Master said: Yan Ping-zhong was skilled at interacting with people. Even after a long time, he maintained respect for them.

Yan Ping-zhong was a high official of the state of Qi named Ying. Master Cheng said: Usually, when people interact for a long time, their respect fades. To be able to maintain respect for a long duration—

<summary>This page evaluates the character and governance of Zi-chan, contrasting his administrative kindness with the Confucian ideal of righteousness, and introduces the praise of Yan Ping-zhong for his lasting respect in social relationships.</summary>
<keywords>Zi-chan, Yan Ping-zhong, Confucius, righteousness, kindness, social etiquette, respect, state of Qi, legal code</keywords>

To say it covers one person or one event, or covers one era, is entirely incorrect. Master Feng of Houzhai says: judging from the account of his revising and casting the penal laws, the things he did not fully address were indeed numerous. Judging from the words of the Spring and Autumn period, the principles of the gentleman were truly few. The sage’s words of praise do not overflow with flattery, and his words of censure do not overflow with malice.
