The Lord Buddha addressed Subhuti, saying: "What think you? If a disciple, having obtained all the treasures of this universe, were to bestow these in the exercise of charity, would such a disciple consequently enjoy a considerable merit?" Subhuti assenting, said: "Honoured of the Worlds! such a disciple would consequently enjoy a very considerable merit."

The Lord Buddha thereupon addressed Subhuti, saying: "If there were any real or permanent quality in merit, the Lord Buddha would not have spoken of such merit as 'considerable.' It is because there is neither a tangible nor material quality in merit, that the Lord Buddha referred to the merit of that disciple as 'considerable.'"

The Lord Buddha addressed Subhuti, saying: "What think you? Can the Lord Buddha be perceived by means of his perfect material body?" Subhuti replied, saying: "Honoured of the Worlds! it is improbable that the Lord Buddha can be perceived by means of his perfect material body. And why? Because, what the Lord Buddha referred to as a 'perfect material body,' is not in reality a 'perfect material body,' it is merely termed a 'perfect material body.'"

<meta>Running header: 金剛經口訣 (Oral Explanation of the Diamond Sutra); page number 七九 (79). Sutra text alternates with Huineng's commentary.</meta>"Subhuti, what do you think? If someone filled the <term>trichiliocosm</term> <gloss>the 'three-thousand great-thousand world system,' a whole Buddhist universe</gloss> with the <term>seven treasures</term> <gloss>gold, silver, lapis, crystal and other precious substances</gloss> and gave them all away in charity, would this person, through this cause, gain much merit?"

"Yes indeed, World-Honored One. Through this cause this person would gain a very great deal of merit."

"Subhuti, if merit had real substance, the <term>Tathagata</term> <gloss>'Thus-Come One,' a title of the Buddha</gloss> would not speak of gaining much merit. It is because merit is without substance that the Tathagata speaks of gaining much merit."

The merit of the seven treasures cannot bring about the fruit of Buddhahood, <term>bodhi</term> <gloss>awakening</gloss>; that is why it is called "without substance." Because it cannot be bounded by any measure or number, it is called "much." But if one is able to pass beyond it, then one no longer speaks of "much."

**Section Twenty: Leaving Behind Form, Leaving Behind Marks** The three bodies <note>the Buddha's three bodies: the Dharma body, the reward body and the transformation body</note> are fully complete, and all the marks are perfectly fulfilled; yet when persons and dharmas are both forgotten, this is "not complete." Therefore it is followed by the section on leaving behind form and leaving behind marks.

"Subhuti, what do you think? Can the Buddha be seen by means of a perfectly complete physical body?"

"No, World-Honored One. The Tathagata

<summary>This page concludes Section Nineteen of the Diamond Sutra, where the Buddha teaches that merit from lavish giving is called "much" precisely because it lacks real substance, with Huineng's comment that such merit cannot produce awakening. It then opens Section Twenty, which asks whether the Buddha can be seen through a perfect physical body.</summary>

<header>金剛經口訣</header>

爾所國土中所有眾生。一一眾生。皆有若干差別心數。心數雖多。總名妄心。識得妄心非心。是名為心。此心即真心。常心。佛心。般若波羅蜜心。清淨菩提涅槃心。

所以者何須菩提過去心不可得現在心不可得未來心不可得。

過去心不可得者。前念妄心。瞥然已過。追尋無有處所。現在心不可得者。真心無相。憑何得見。未來心不可得者。本無可得。習氣已盡。更不復生。了此三心皆不可得。是名為佛。

法界通化分第十九 遍週法界。一化普通。七寶福田。寧如四句。故受之以法界通化分。

佛意恐眾生不見法身。但見三十二相。八十種好。紫磨金耀。以為如來真身。為遣此迷。故問須菩提。佛可以具足色身見不。三十二相即非具足色身。內具三十二淨行。是名具足色身。淨行者。即六波羅蜜是也。於五根中修六

True Regard, serene Regard,
Far-reaching, wise Regard,
Regard of pity, Regard compassionate.
Ever longed for, ever looked for
In radiance ever pure and serene!
Wisdom’s sun, destroying darkness.
Subduer of woes, of storm, of fire,
Illuminator of the world!

Law of pity, thunder quivering.
Compassion wondrous as a great cloud,
Pouring spiritual rain like nectar.
Quenching all the flames of distress!

Voice of the Regarder, wondrous Voice,
Voice of the rolling tide, Brahma-voice,
Voice all world-surpassing,
Ever to be cherished in mind
With never a doubting thought.

World's Cry-Regarder, pure and holy.
In pain, distress, in death or woe,
Potent as a sure reliance.
Perfect in every virtuous merit.
All-beholding with eyes of pity.
Boundless ocean-store of blessings!
Prostrate, let us make obeisance."

"While the Buddha preached this chapter of the All-sided One, the eighty-four thousand living beings in the assembly set their minds on Perfect Enlightenment, with which nothing can compare."

reference_meta.coverage_note: Soothill 1930 is abridged. For this page he renders the verse stanzas 無垢清淨光, 悲體戒雷震, 妙音觀世音, 念念勿生疑…依怙 and 具一切功德, but OMITS the stanza 諍訟經官處…眾怨悉退散 and OMITS Dharaṇīṃdhara's (持地菩薩) speech; only the final sentence of the coda is rendered. Soothill's verse is free, so stanza-to-line matching is approximate. About 75% of the page is covered. One preceding stanza (真觀清淨觀…常願常瞻仰 = 'True Regard… ever looked for') is included as context. Soothill does not mark stanza boundaries exactly where the Chinese does. 'Regardcr' (OCR) is corrected to 'Regarder' per a second scan (archive.org in.ernet.dli.2015.108057). As alternate_reference, Kern's SBE 21 ch. 24 (translated from the SANSKRIT, a different recension) covers the omitted stanza (his v. 23) and Dharaṇīṃdhara's speech. Its verses 21-26 correspond roughly to the page's six stanzas; his vv. 27-33 have no Chinese counterpart and are omitted with a bracketed marker. Kern's footnote numbers are removed and his 'Avalokitejvara/Avalokite^vara' OCR forms are normalised to 'Avalokitesvara'. Kern's name 'Dharaṇiṃdhara' is restored from the scan's diacritic-damaged OCR ('Dhara-windhara').

# 般若波羅蜜多心經

->唐 · 三藏法師玄奘奉詔譯<-

觀自在菩薩行深般若波羅蜜多時，照見五蘊皆空，度一切苦厄。舍利子！色不異空，空不異色；色即是空，空即是色；受想行識亦復如是。舍利子！是諸法空相—不生不滅、不垢不淨、不增不減。是故，空中無色

MISS CHIAO-NO.

K‘ung Hsüeh-li was a descendant of Confucius. He was a man of considerable ability, and an excellent poet. A fellow-student, to whom he was much attached, became magistrate at T‘ien-t‘ai, and sent for K‘ung to join him. Unfortunately, just before K‘ung arrived his friend died, and he found himself without the means of returning home; so he took up his abode in a Buddhist monastery, where he was employed in transcribing for the priests. Several hundred paces to the west of this monastery there was a house belonging to a Mr. Shan, a gentleman who had known better days, but who had spent all his money in a heavy law-suit; and then, as his family was a small one, had gone away to live in the country and left his house vacant. One day there was a heavy fall of snow which kept visitors away from the monastery; and K‘ung, finding it dull, went out. As he was passing by the door of the house above-mentioned, a young man of very elegant appearance came forth, who, the moment he saw K‘ung, ran up to him, and with a bow, entered into conversation, asking him to be pleased to walk in. K‘ung was much taken with the young man, and followed him inside. The rooms were not particularly large, but adorned throughout with embroidered curtains, and from the walls hung scrolls and drawings by celebrated masters. On the table lay a book, the title of which was, “Jottings from Paradise;” and turning over its leaves, K‘ung found therein many strange things.

reference_text: One day the eldest brother, Ch‘êng, who had been carried off by the rebels, returned with his wife; and, after three days’ deliberation, Hsiao and the other two determined that, as he had been so long separated from the family, he had no further claims upon them for house-room, &c. Jen and Yi were secretly delighted at this result, and at once inviting Ch‘êng to stay with them, sent news of his arrival to Yu-yü, who came back directly, and agreed with the others to hand over a share of the property to their elder brother. Hsiao and his clique were much enraged at this purchase of Ch‘êng’s good will, and, hurrying to their brothers’ houses, assailed them with every possible kind of abuse. Ch‘êng, who had long been accustomed to scenes of violence among the rebels, now got into a great passion, and cried out, “When I came home none of you would give me a place to live in. Only these younger ones recognised the ties of blood, and you would punish them for so doing. Do you think to drive me away?” Thereupon he threw a stone at Hsiao and knocked him down; and Jen and Yi rushed out with clubs and gave the three of them a severe thrashing. Ch‘êng did not wait for them to lay a plaint, but set off to the magistrate on the spot, and preferred a charge against his three brothers. The magistrate, as before, sent for Yu-yü to ask his opinion, and Yu-yü had no alternative but to go, entering the yamên with downcast head, his tears flowing in silence all the while. The magistrate inquired of him how the matter stood; to which he replied only by begging His Honour to hear the case; which the magistrate accordingly did, deciding that the whole of the property was to be divided equally among the seven brothers. Thenceforth Jen and Yi became more and more attached to Ch‘êng; and one day, in conversation, they happened to tell him the story of their mother’s funeral. Ch‘êng was exceedingly angry, and declared that such behaviour was that of brute beasts, proposing at the same time that the vault should be opened and that she should be re-buried in the proper place. Jen and Yi went off and told this to Yu-yü, who immediately came and begged Ch‘êng to desist from his scheme; to which, however, he paid no attention, and fixed a day for her interment in the family vault.

Xiao, Ren, and Yi each brought out their staffs and, taking Zhong and Xin along, beat him countless times. Cheng did not wait for them to sue him; he sued them to the magistrate first. The magistrate then sent someone to invite Youyu to testify. Youyu could not help but come. When asked, he bowed his head in shame and remained silent, only shedding tears. The magistrate pressed him for an answer, and he only requested that the official judge the matter. The magistrate then ordered Xiao and the others to each contribute a portion of their land and property to return to Cheng, making the seven shares equal. From this point on, Ren, Yi, and Cheng grew increasingly affectionate and respectful toward one another. During a conversation, the subject of their mother's burial suddenly came up, and they all wept. Cheng stated, "To be this unfilial is to be a beast." He then intended to open the grave and rebury her. Ren and Yi rushed to tell Youyu, who hurried home to remonstrate and stop him. Cheng did not listen and set a date for the act.

I was fortunate that my third younger brother remembered our blood ties, and yet you condemn him? Do you wish to drive me away?" He threw stones at Xiao. Cheng did not wait for them to sue him; he sued them first. The magistrate summoned You-Yu to ask for his counsel. You-Yu, having no other choice, arrived, but he felt only shame. 倒用板子棍子，就站著，不知他拿什麼東西，打了一頓，臉上打破了兩處。我們聽見姨太太這裡有一種藥，上棒瘡的，姑娘尋一丸給我呢。」

寶釵聽了，忙命鶯兒去找了兩丸來與平兒。寶釵道：「既這樣，你去替我問候罷，我就不去了。」平兒向寶釵答應著去了。不在話下。

且說香菱見了眾人之後，吃過晚飯，寶釵等都往買母處去，自己便往瀟湘館中來。此時黛玉已好了大半了，見香菱也進園來住，自是喜歡。香菱因笑道：「我這一進來了，也得空兒，好歹教我做詩，就是我的造化了！」黛玉笑道：「既要學做詩，你就拜我為師。我雖不通，大略也還教的起你。」香菱笑道：「果然這樣，我就拜你為師，你可不許厭煩的。」黛玉道：「什麼難事，也值得去學？不過是起承轉合。當中承轉，是兩副對子：平聲的對仄聲；虛的對實的，實的對虛的。若是果有了奇句，連平仄虛實不對都使的的。」

香菱笑道：「怪道我常弄本舊詩偷兒看一兩首，又有對的極工的，又有不對的；又聽見說，『一三五不論，二四六分明，』看古人的詩上，亦有順的，亦有二四六上錯的：所以天天疑惑。如今聽你一說，原來這些規矩竟是沒事的，只要詞句新奇為上。」黛玉道：「正是這個道理。詞句究竟還是末事，第一是立意要緊。若意趣真了，連詞句不用修飾，自是好的：這叫做『不為辭害意』。」

香菱道：「我只愛陸放翁的『重簾不卷留香久，古硯微凹聚墨多』，說的真切有趣！」黛玉道：「你們因不知詩，所以見了這淺近的就愛。一入了這個格局，再學不出來的。你只聽我說：你若真心要學，我這裡有《王摩詰全集》，你且把他的五言律一百首細心揣摩透熟了，然後再讀一百二十首老杜的七言律，次之再李青蓮的七言絕句讀一二百首。肚子裡先有了這三個人做了底子，然後再陶淵明、應、劉、謝、阮、庾、鮑等人的一看。你又是這樣一個極聰明伶俐的人，不用一年工夫，不愁不是詩翁了！」香菱聽了，笑道：「既這樣，好姑娘，你就這書給我出來，我帶回去，夜裡念幾首也是好的。」黛玉聽說，便命紫鵑將王右丞的五言律拿來，遞與香菱，道：「你只看有紅圈的，都是我選的，有一首念一首。不明白的，問你姑娘；或者遇見我，我講與你就是了。」

香菱拿了詩，回至蘅蕪院中，諸事不管，只向燈下一首一首的讀起來。寶釵連催他數次睡覺，他也不睡。寶釵見他這般苦心，只得隨他去了。

一日，黛玉方梳洗完了，只見香菱吟吟的送了書來，又要換杜律。黛玉笑道：「共記得多少首？」香菱笑道：「凡紅圈選的，我盡讀了。」黛玉道：「可領略了些沒有？」香菱笑道：「我倒領略了些，只不知不是，說給你聽聽。」

He didn't, however, drag him down and strike him with a rattan or cane, but recklessly assaulted him, while he stood before him, with something or other, which he laid hold of, and broke his face open in two places. We understand that Mrs. Hsüeh has in here some medicine or other for applying on wounds, so do try, miss, and find a ball of it and let me have it!"

Hearing this, Pao-ch'ai speedily directed Ying Erh to go and look for some, and, on discovering two balls of it, she brought them over and handed them to P'ing Erh.

"Such being the case," Pao-ch'ai said, "do make, on your return, the usual inquiries for me, and I won't then need to go."

P'ing Erh turned towards Pao-ch'ai, and expressed her readiness to execute her commission, after which she betook herself home, where we will leave her without further notice.

After Hsiang Ling, for we will take up the thread of our narrative with her, completed her visits to the various inmates, she had her evening meal. Then when Pao-ch'ai and every one else went to dowager lady Chia's quarters, she came into the Hsiao Hsiang lodge. By this time Tai-yü had got considerably better. Upon hearing that Hsiang Ling had also moved into the garden, she, needless to say, was filled with delight.

"Now, that I've come in here," Hsiang Ling then smiled and said, "do please teach me, at your leisure, how to write verses. It will be a bit of good luck for me if you do."

"Since you're anxious to learn how to versify," Tai-yü answered with a smile, "you'd better acknowledge me as your tutor; for though I'm not a good hand at poetry, yet I know, after all, enough to be able to teach you."

"Of course you do!" Hsiang Ling laughingly remarked. "I'll readily treat you as my tutor. But you mustn't put yourself to any trouble!"

"Is there anything so difficult about this," Tai-yü pursued, "as to make it necessary to go in for any study? Why, it's purely and simply a matter of openings, elucidations, embellishments and conclusions. The elucidations and embellishments, which come in the centre, should form two antithetical sentences, the even tones must pair with the uneven. Empty words must correspond with full words; and full words with empty words. In the event of any out-of-the-way lines, it won't matter if the even and uneven tones, and the empty and full words do not pair."

"Strange though it may appear," smiled Hsiang Ling, "I often handle books with old poems, and read one or two stanzas, whenever I can steal the time; and some among these I find pair most skilfully, while others don't. I have also heard that the first, third and fifth lines are of no consequence; and that the second, fourth and sixth must be clearly distinguished. But I notice that there are in the poetical works of ancient writers both those which accord with the rules, as well as those whose second, fourth and sixth lines are not in compliance with any rule. Hence it is that my mind has daily been full of doubts. But after the hints you've given me, I really see that all these formulas are of no account, and that the main requirement is originality of diction."

"Yes, that's just the principle that holds good," Tai-yü answered. "But diction is, after all, a last consideration. The first and foremost thing is the choice of proper sentiments; for when the sentiments are correct, there'll even be no need to polish the diction; it's certain to be elegant. This is called versifying without letting the diction affect the sentiments."

"What I admire," Hsiang Ling proceeded with a smile; "are the lines by old Lu Fang;

"The double portière, when not raised, retains the fragrance long.
An old inkslab, with a slight hole, collects plenty of ink.

"Their language is so clear that it's charming."

"You must on no account," Tai-yü observed, "read poetry of the kind. It's because you people don't know what verses mean that you, no sooner read any shallow lines like these, than they take your fancy. But when once you get into this sort of style, it's impossible to get out of it. Mark my words! If you are in earnest about learning, I've got here Wang Mo-chieh's complete collection; so you'd better take his one hundred stanzas, written in the pentameter rule of versification, and carefully study them, until you apprehend them thoroughly. Afterwards, look over the one hundred and twenty stanzas of Lao T'u, in the heptameter rule; and next read a hundred or two hundred of the heptameter four-lined stanzas by Li Ch'ing-lieu. When you have, as a first step, digested these three authors, and made them your foundation, you can take T'ao Yuan-ming, Ying, Liu, Hsieh, Yüan, Yü, Pao and other writers and go through them once. And with those sharp and quick wits of yours, I've no doubt but that you will become a regular poet before a year's time."

"Well, in that case," Hsiang Ling smiled, after listening to her, "bring me the book, my dear miss, so that I may take it along. It will be a good thing if I can manage to read several stanzas at night."

At these words, Tai-yü bade Tzu Chüan fetch Wang Tso-ch'eng's pentameter stanzas. When brought, she handed them to Hsiang Ling. "Only peruse those marked with red circles" she said. "They've all been selected by me. Read each one of them; and should there be any you can't fathom, ask your miss about them. Or when you come across me, I can explain them to you."

Hsiang Ling took the poems and repaired back to the Heng Wu-yüan. And without worrying her mind about anything she approached the lamp and began to con stanza after stanza. Pao-ch'ai pressed her, several consecutive times, to go to bed; but as even rest was far from her thoughts, Pao-ch'ai let her, when she perceived what trouble she was taking over her task, have her own way in the matter.

Tai-yü had one day just finished combing her hair and performing her ablutions, when she espied Hsiang Ling come with smiles playing about her lips, to return her the book and to ask her to let her have T'u's poetical compositions in exchange.

"Of all these, how many stanzas can you recollect?" Tai-yü asked, smiling.

"I've read every one of those marked with a red circle," Hsiang Ling laughingly rejoined.

"Have you caught the ideas of any of them, yes or no?" Tai-yü inquired.

"Yes, I've caught some!" Hsiang Ling smiled. "But whether rightly or not I don't know. Let me tell you."

Hearing this, Baochai immediately ordered Ying'er to find two pills to give to Ping'er. Baochai said, "In that case, please give him my regards; I will not go over myself." Ping'er agreed and left.

As for Xiangling, after she had seen everyone and finished dinner, she went to the Bamboo Lodge while Baochai and the others went to the Dowager’s quarters. By this time, Daiyu was mostly recovered. She was pleased to see that Xiangling had moved into the garden. Xiangling said with a smile, "Now that I'm here and have some free time, if you could only teach me how to write poetry, it would be my great fortune!"

Daiyu laughed. "If you want to learn poetry, you must take me as your teacher. Although I am not an expert, I can probably teach you the basics."

Xiangling laughed. "If that's the case, I'll take you as my teacher. You mustn't get annoyed with me."

Daiyu said, "What's so hard about it that it needs so much effort? It is nothing more than the structure: the opening, the development, the transition, and the conclusion <note>original: "qi cheng zhuan he"</note>. In the middle, the development and transition consist of two pairs of couplets: level tones against oblique tones, empty words against solid words, and solid against empty. If you truly have a brilliant line, you can even ignore the rules of tone and structure."

Xiangling laughed, "No wonder when I used to steal looks at old poetry books, I saw some were perfectly crafted while others were not. I heard people say 'the first, third, and fifth syllables don't matter, but the second, fourth, and sixth must be clear.' Yet in ancient poems, I see some follow this and some don't. I've been puzzled every day. Now that you say it, these rules aren't absolute, as long as the phrasing is novel and fresh."

Daiyu said, "That is exactly the point. Phrasing is secondary; the most important thing is the intent <note>original: "li yi"</note>. If the spirit and interest are genuine, the poem will be good even without ornate language. This is called 'not letting the words harm the meaning.'"

Xiangling said, "I simply love Lu You's lines: 'The heavy curtains are not rolled, keeping the fragrance long; the old ink-stone is slightly concave, gathering much ink.' It's so vivid and interesting!"

Daiyu said, "Because you don't know poetry, you love what is shallow and accessible. If you get stuck in that pattern, you'll never grow out of it. Listen to me: if you truly want to learn, I have the *Complete Works of Wang Wei* <note>original: "Wang Mo-jie"</note> here. You should first carefully study one hundred of his five-character regulated poems until you know them thoroughly. Then read one hundred and twenty of Old Du’s <note>Du Fu</note> seven-character regulated poems, and then one or two hundred of Li Bai’s <note>Li Qinglian</note> seven-character quatrains. With the work of these three as your foundation, you can then look at Tao Yuanming, Ying Yang, Liu Zhen, Xie Lingyun, Ruan Ji, Yu Xin, and Bao Zhao. You are so clever and quick; in less than a year, you will surely be a poet yourself!"

Hearing this, Xiangling laughed. "In that case, good Miss, please lend me the book. I'll take it back and read a few poems tonight."

Daiyu then ordered Zijuan to bring Wang Wei's five-character regulated poems and handed them to Xiangling, saying, "Just look at the ones I’ve marked with red circles; those are my selections. Read them one by one. If you don't understand something, ask your mistress Baochai, or if you see me, I will explain it to you."

Xiangling took the poems and returned to the Garden of All-Pervasive Fragrance. Ignoring everything else, she began to read them one by one under the lamp. Baochai urged her several times to go to sleep, but she refused. Seeing her so dedicated, Baochai let her be.

One day, just as Daiyu finished her morning toilette, Xiangling arrived beaming with the book to exchange it for Du Fu's poems. Daiyu smiled. "How many do you remember?"

Xiangling laughed. "I've read all the ones you marked with red."

Daiyu asked, "Have you gained any insights?"

Xiangling smiled. "I have some insights, but I don't know if they are correct. Let me tell them to you."

<summary>Xiangling begins her dedicated study of poetry under Lin Daiyu's tutelage, learning that meaning and spirit are more important than rigid formal rules.</summary>
<keywords>Xiangling, Lin Daiyu, poetry lessons, Wang Wei, literary theory, study, Bamboo Lodge</keywords>

[They] used boards and sticks on me, and I just stood there. I don't know what they used, but they beat me once, and my face was broken in two places. We heard that the Mistress <note>referring to Aunt Xue</note> has a type of medicine here for treating wounds from beatings. Could you, Miss, find a pill for me?

Baochai heard this and hurriedly ordered Ying'er to find two pills for Ping'er. Baochai said, "Since that is the case, you go and send my greetings on my behalf; I will not go." Ping'er promised Baochai and left. This is left aside for now.

As for Xiangling, after she had seen the others and finished her evening meal, Baochai and the rest went to the mother's place, and she went to the Xiaoxiang Pavilion. By this time, Daiyu was already more than half recovered. Seeing Xiangling had also moved into the Garden to live, she was naturally pleased. Xiangling laughed and said, "Now that I have finally moved in and have some free time, it would be my great fortune if you would teach me how to write poetry." Daiyu laughed and said, "If you want to learn to write poetry, you must take me as your teacher. Although I am not an expert, I can certainly teach you the basics." Xiangling laughed and said, "If that is really so, I will take you as my teacher. You must not get tired of it." Daiyu said, "What is difficult about it? It is nothing more than the <term>qichengzhuanhe</term> <gloss>the four-part structure of a poem: opening, development, transition, and conclusion</gloss>. In the middle, the development and transition are two pairs of couplets: flat tones must be paired with oblique tones; abstract concepts must be paired with concrete ones, and concrete ones with abstract. If you truly have an extraordinary line, it is acceptable even if the flat/oblique tones and the abstract/concrete pairs do not match."

Xiangling laughed and said, "No wonder when I often take an old poetry book and secretly read a few poems, there are some that are perfectly matched and others that are not. I have also heard it said that, 'the first, third, and fifth characters do not matter, while the second, fourth, and sixth must be distinct.' Looking at the poems of the ancients, some follow this, and some have errors in the second, fourth, and sixth characters. That is why I have been puzzled every day. Now that I hear you speak, it turns out that these rules are actually of little consequence; it is only important that the words and phrases are fresh and novel." Daiyu said, "That is precisely the point. The words and phrases are ultimately secondary matters; the most important thing is establishing the intent. If the sentiment and interest are genuine, even if the words and phrases are not polished, it is naturally good. This is what is called 'not letting the words harm the intent'."

Xiangling said, "I only love Lu Fangweng's <note>Lu You, a famous Song dynasty poet</note> lines, 'The heavy curtains are not rolled up, the scent remains for long; the ancient inkstone is slightly worn, the gathered ink is thick,' they are truly vivid and interesting!" Daiyu said, "Because you do not know poetry, you love these shallow and accessible ones. Once you enter this pattern, you will never learn anything else. Listen to me: if you truly want to learn, I have the *Complete Collection of Wang Mojie* <note>Wang Wei, a Tang dynasty poet</note> here. You should first ponder his one hundred five-character regulated verses carefully until you know them thoroughly. Then, read one hundred twenty of Old Du's <note>Du Fu, the Tang dynasty poet</note> seven-character regulated verses. Next, read one or two hundred of Li Qinglian's <note>Li Bai, the Tang dynasty poet</note> seven-character quatrains. Once you have these three people as a foundation in your belly, then take a look at Tao Yuanming, Ying, Liu, Xie, Ruan, Yu, and Bao. Since you are such an extremely clever and sharp person, you won't need a year of effort before you become a true poetess!" Xiangling heard this and laughed, "If that is the case, good Miss, take the book out for me, and I will take it back. It will be good to recite a few poems at night." When Daiyu heard this, she ordered Zijuan to bring Wang Youcheng's <note>Another name for Wang Wei</note> five-character regulated verses and handed them to Xiangling, saying, "Only look at the ones with red circles; they are all selected by me. Read one poem after another. If there is something you don't understand, ask your maid, or if you meet me, I will explain it to you."

Xiangling took the poems and returned to the Hengwu Courtyard. Ignoring all other matters, she sat under the lamp and read them one by one. Although Baochai urged her several times to sleep, she would not. Seeing her such painstaking effort, Baochai had no choice but to let her be.

One day, after Daiyu had just finished washing and combing, she saw Xiangling humming as she delivered the book, wanting to trade it for Du's regulated verses. Daiyu laughed and asked, "How many have you memorized in total?" Xiangling laughed and said, "I have read all the ones marked with red circles." Daiyu said, "Have you grasped some of them?" Xiangling laughed and said, "I have grasped some, but I don't know if I'm right. Let me recite them to you and see."

When Baochai heard this, she at once told Ying'er to find two pills and give them to Ping'er. "In that case," Baochai said, "give him my regards. I won't go myself." Ping'er assented to Baochai and left. Of this no more need be said.

Now Xiangling, after she had greeted everyone and had supper, when Baochai and the others had all gone to Grandmother Jia's, went by herself to the Xiaoxiang Lodge. <note>The Xiaoxiang Lodge, "Bamboo Lodge," is Lin Daiyu's residence in the Grand View Garden.</note> By now Daiyu was mostly recovered, and she was naturally glad to see that Xiangling had moved into the garden too. Xiangling said with a smile, "Now that I've come in here I'll have some spare time. If only you would teach me to write poetry, that would be my great good fortune!" Daiyu laughed. "If you want to learn to write poetry, you must take me as your teacher. I'm no master, but I can teach you the general idea." Xiangling smiled. "If you really will, I'll take you as my teacher, and you mustn't get tired of me." Daiyu said, "What is so hard about it that it's even worth learning? It is nothing but opening, developing, turning and closing. <note>original: "起承轉合"; the four movements of a regulated poem.</note> The developing and turning in the middle are two couplets: level tones answer oblique tones, empty words answer full words, and full words answer empty ones. <note>Classical Chinese prosody divides syllables into level and oblique tones, and words into "full" words (nouns and other content words) and "empty" words (particles and function words); the middle couplets of a regulated poem must be parallel in both.</note> But if you really have a remarkable line, it's quite all right even if level and oblique, empty and full, do not match."

Xiangling smiled. "No wonder! I often take an old book of poems and sneak a look at one or two. Some have couplets matched very exactly, and some don't match at all. I've also heard it said, 'The first, third and fifth syllables don't matter; the second, fourth and sixth must be strict.' Yet in the poems of the ancients, some follow the rule and some go wrong on the second, fourth and sixth. So I've been puzzled day after day. Now that I hear you, it turns out these rules don't really matter; the main thing is just that the words and lines should be fresh and original." Daiyu said, "That's exactly the principle. In the end, wording is a secondary matter; the first essential is the conception. If the meaning and feeling are genuine, then even unpolished words will naturally be good. This is called 'not letting the words harm the meaning.'" <note>A phrase from Mencius, warning against reading a poem so literally that the wording obscures its sense.</note>

Xiangling said, "I just love Lu Fangweng's lines, 'The heavy curtains not rolled up, the incense lingers long; the old inkstone, slightly hollowed, gathers ink in plenty.' They are so true and so delightful!" <note>Lu Fangweng is the Song poet Lu You (1125 to 1210).</note> Daiyu said, "You love something shallow and easy like that because you don't understand poetry. Once you fall into that mold, you'll never learn your way out of it. Just listen to me. If you truly want to learn, I have the Complete Works of Wang Mojie here. First take his hundred five-character regulated poems and study them carefully until you know them through and through. Then read a hundred and twenty of Old Du's seven-character regulated poems, and after that one or two hundred of Li Qinglian's seven-character quatrains. <note>Wang Mojie is Wang Wei, Old Du is Du Fu, and Li Qinglian is Li Bai: the three great poets of the Tang dynasty.</note> Once you have these three poets inside you as a foundation, then take a look at Tao Yuanming, Ying, Liu, Xie, Ruan, Yu, Bao and the rest. <note>Earlier poets of the Han to Six Dynasties period, probably Ying Yang, Liu Zhen, Xie Lingyun, Ruan Ji, Yu Xin and Bao Zhao.</note> And clever and quick as you are, in less than a year you're sure to be a master poet!" Xiangling laughed when she heard this. "In that case, my dear miss, please get the book out for me. I'll take it back with me; even reading a few poems at night would be good." At this Daiyu told Zijuan to bring Wang Youcheng's five-character regulated poems and handed them to Xiangling, saying, "Read only the ones marked with red circles; those are all ones I have chosen. Read each one in turn. If there's anything you don't understand, ask your young mistress, or if you see me, I'll explain it to you."

Xiangling took the poems back to the Hengwu Court, set everything else aside, and began reading them one by one under the lamp. Baochai urged her several times to go to bed, but she would not. Seeing her apply herself so painstakingly, Baochai had no choice but to let her be.

One day Daiyu had just finished washing and doing her hair when she saw Xiangling come in all smiles to return the book and ask to exchange it for Du Fu's regulated verse. Daiyu laughed. "How many have you memorized altogether?" Xiangling smiled. "I've read every one that you marked with a red circle." Daiyu said, "And have you grasped anything from them?" Xiangling smiled. "I have grasped a little, but I don't know whether I'm right or not. Let me tell you about it."

As chief minister Tung Cho was arrogant beyond all reason. When he bowed before the throne he did not declare his name; in going to court he did not hasten. Booted and armed he entered the reception halls. Never had such a thing been seen before. Li Ju impressed upon him constantly to employ men of reputation so that he should gain public esteem. So when they told him Ch‘ai Yung was a man of talent he was summoned. But he would not go. Cho sent a message to him that if he did not come he and his whole clan should be exterminated. Then Ch‘ai gave in and appeared. Cho was very gracious to him and promoted him thrice in a month. He became a Shih-chung and seemed to be on most friendly terms with the tyrant.

Meanwhile the deposed ruler, his mother and the Lady T‘ang were immured in the palace and found their daily supplies gradually diminishing. The deposed Emperor wept incessantly. One day a pair of swallows gliding to and fro moved him to verse.

Spring! and the green of the tender grass,
Flushes with joy as the swallows pass;
The wayfarers pause by the rippling stream,
And their eyes with new born gladness gleam;
With lingering gaze the roofs I see
Of the palace that one time sheltered me.

The messenger, sent by Tung Cho from time to time to the palace for news of the prisoners, got hold of this poem and showed it to his master.

“So he shows his resentment by writing poems, eh! A fair excuse to put them all out of the way,” said Tung.

Li Ju was sent with ten men into the palace to consummate the foul deed. The three were in one of the upper rooms when he arrived. The Emperor shuddered when the maid announced the visitor’s name.

Presently Li entered and offered a cup of poisoned wine to the Emperor. The Emperor asked what this meant.

There is sufficient cause to kill him." <gloss>There is a famous precedent for killing him to teach the world a lesson.</gloss> He then ordered Li Ru to lead eighteen armed guards into the palace to murder the Emperor. The Emperor, the Empress Dowager, and Lady Tang were sitting on the upper floor when a palace maid reported that Li Ru had arrived. The Emperor was terrified. Li Ru presented a cup of poisoned wine to the Emperor. <gloss>It is ironic that this poem, which mentions drinking, would meet its end through this very act of drinking, which is usually a refined affair.</gloss>

<summary>Li Ru pressures the scholar Cai Yong into serving Dong Zhuo, while the imprisoned Young Emperor expresses his despair through poetry, leading Dong Zhuo to order his assassination via poison.</summary>
<keywords>Li Ru, Dong Zhuo, Cai Yong, Young Emperor, Empress Dowager He, Lady Tang, assassination, regicide, poisoned wine</keywords>

Previously, Li Ru advised Dong Zhuo to promote famous scholars to gain public prestige. Most officials followed this path, and thus he recommended the talent of Cai Yong. Zhuo ordered his summons, but Yong initially did not intend to go. Zhuo, enraged, sent a messenger to tell Yong: "If you do not come, I will exterminate your entire clan." Yong was terrified and had no choice but to obey the order and arrive. Zhuo was greatly pleased to see Yong and promoted his rank three times within a single month, appointing him as <term>Shizhong</term> <gloss>Palace Attendant</gloss>. He was treated with great intimacy and favor. <gloss>Just as Yang Xiong relied on Wang Feng, Yong was fated to be consumed like firewood from Mount Kunshan.</gloss>

Meanwhile, the Former Emperor <note>Shao Di, Liu Bian</note>, Empress Dowager He, and Consort Tang were imprisoned in the Everlasting Peace Palace. Their clothing and food supplies gradually dwindled. The Former Emperor’s tears never dried. <gloss>This mirrors what a later king said: "The days and months in this place are unbearable."</gloss> One day, he happened to see a pair of swallows flying in the courtyard and composed a poem. <gloss>In the empty courtyard, birds soar and dance; in the cold, abandoned palace, he is solitary and aged before his time.</gloss> The poem read:

The tender grass is green, condensed in mist,
The pair of swallows fly, fluttering and twisting.
The Luo River flows, a single vein of blue,
People on the path are envied by all. <gloss>The first half of the poem describes the swallows and the view from afar.</gloss>

Deep within the emerald clouds is the hall where I once lived. <gloss>His eyes are fixed on his former palace, but he cannot fly there; he is truly inferior to the swallows who can return to their old nests. How tragic.</gloss>
Who will uphold loyalty and righteousness,
To vent the resentment within my heart? <gloss>The second half is his personal lament. The poetry is fine.</gloss>

Dong Zhuo frequently sent people to spy on them. On this day, they obtained this poem and presented it to him. Zhuo said, "Complaining and writing poetry gives me a justification to kill him." <gloss>To kill him with a stated reason is also a way to instruct the world.</gloss> He then ordered Li Ru to take eighteen warriors into the palace to assassinate the Emperor. The Emperor, the Empress Dowager, and the Consort were upstairs when a palace maid reported that Li Ru had arrived. The Emperor was greatly alarmed. Ru offered the Emperor <term>zhenjiu</term> <gloss>poisoned wine</gloss>. <gloss>Since the poem mentioned wine, this drink is a most elegant response.</gloss>

<summary>Dong Zhuo forces the scholar Cai Yong into service and discovers a poem written by the deposed Emperor Shao Di expressing grief. Using the poem as a pretext for treason, Zhuo sends Li Ru to the palace to execute the imperial family with poisoned wine.</summary>
<keywords>Dong Zhuo, Li Ru, Cai Yong, Shao Di, Empress Dowager He, Consort Tang, assassination, poisoned wine, poetry, Romance of the Three Kingdoms</keywords>

Earlier, Li Ru advised Dong Zhuo to promote famous scholars to gain public support. Dong Zhuo followed this advice in most cases and thus recommended the talented Cai Yong. Zhuo ordered his summons, but Cai Yong did not initially intend to go. Enraged, Zhuo sent a messenger to tell him: "If you do not come, I shall exterminate your entire clan." Fearing for his family, Cai Yong had no choice but to obey the command and arrived. Zhuo was delighted to see him and promoted him three times within a single month, appointing him as a Palace Attendant <note>original: "shizhong"</note>. He was treated with great favor and intimacy. <gloss>One who eternally relies on the powerful, like Yang Xiong following Wang Feng, will ultimately perish like a woodcutter on Mount Kunshan.</gloss>

Meanwhile, the Former Emperor <note>Young Emperor Ling of Han, Liu Bian</note>, Empress Dowager He, and Consort Tang were confined in the Palace of Eternal Peace. Their supplies of clothing and food gradually dwindled, and the Emperor’s tears never dried. <gloss>This mirrors the later King of Shu's lament about the days and months spent in such a place.</gloss> One day, happening to see a pair of swallows flying in the courtyard, the Emperor composed a poem. <gloss>In the empty courtyard, birds fly and dance; in the cold palace of an abandoned temple, his body remains isolated in his waning years.</gloss> The poem read:

The tender grass is green and thick with mist,
Lithely fly the pair of swallows.
A single ribbon of the Luo River flows green,
Upon the paths, the people are envied by me. <gloss>The first half describes the swallows and his distant gaze.</gloss>
Deep within the emerald clouds is the palace that was once my home. <gloss>Gazing toward the old palace, he cannot fly away; he is truly inferior to the pair of swallows that can return to their old nests. How tragic.</gloss>
Who will uphold loyalty and righteousness,
To vent the resentment within my heart? <gloss>The second half expresses his personal desire. The poetry is excellent.</gloss>

Dong Zhuo frequently sent people to spy on them. On that day, they obtained this poem and presented it to him. Zhuo said, "Using a poem of resentment as a pretext, I now have a justification to kill him." <gloss>To have a justification for the killing is a way to instruct the world.</gloss> He then ordered Li Ru to lead eighteen warriors into the palace to assassinate the Emperor. The Emperor was upstairs with the Empress Dowager and the Consort when a palace maid reported that Li Ru had arrived. The Emperor was greatly alarmed. Li Ru offered the Emperor poisoned wine. <gloss>The irony is that his poem invited this; drinking wine is considered the most elegant of matters.</gloss>

<summary>Dong Zhuo forces the scholar Cai Yong into service while the deposed Young Emperor languishes in captivity. After the Emperor writes a poem expressing his sorrow, Dong Zhuo uses it as an excuse to send Li Ru to execute him with poisoned wine.</summary>
<keywords>Dong Zhuo, Li Ru, Cai Yong, Young Emperor, Empress Dowager He, Consort Tang, assassination, poetry, poisoned wine</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>Li Ru advised Dong Zhuo to promote famous scholars to win the support of the people. Following this advice, he recommended the talents of <term>Cai Yong</term> <gloss>a renowned scholar and musician</gloss>. Dong Zhuo ordered him to be summoned, but Cai Yong did not attend. Initially, Dong Zhuo was furious and sent men to tell Cai Yong: "If you do not come, I will exterminate your clan." Fearing for his life, Cai Yong had no choice but to obey the order and arrive. Upon seeing him, Dong Zhuo was delighted and promoted him three times in one month, appointing him as a Palace Attendant. He treated him with great intimacy and favor. <note>original: "Always relying on Wang Feng and Yang Xiong; body ending in firewood, buried in the Kunlun Mountains as a woodcutter."</note>

Meanwhile, the former Emperor <note>the deposed Shao Di</note>, Empress Dowager He, and Consort Tang were trapped in the Yong'an Palace. Their clothing and food supplies grew increasingly scarce. The former Emperor’s tears never dried. <note>original: "As the King said later, the days and months within this place..."</note> One day, he happened to see a pair of swallows flying in the courtyard and recited a poem. <note>original: "Birds flying in the empty courtyard, dancing in the cold palace and ruined temple; the body is isolated, the years pass by themselves."</note> The poem went:

Tender grass turns green in the mist,
A pair of swallows fly back and forth.
On the blue path along the Luo River,
People envy them as they pass.
<note>original: "The first half describes the swallows; looking into the distance."</note>

Deep in the green clouds lies my old palace,
<note>original: "Staring at the old palace, unable to fly, truly not as fortunate as the pair of swallows returning to their old nest. How sorrowful!"</note>
Who will uphold loyalty and righteousness,
To vent the grievances in my heart?
<note>original: "The second half is a self-composed lament. A fine poem."</note>

Dong Zhuo frequently sent men to eavesdrop. That day, they intercepted this poem and presented it to him. Dong Zhuo said, "Writing poems of resentment is a justification for execution." <note>original: "Killing him with justification will also awe the world."</note> He ordered Li Ru to lead eighteen armed soldiers into the palace to execute the former Emperor. The Emperor was with the Empress Dowager and Consort Tang on the upper floor of the palace when palace maids reported that Li Ru had arrived. The Emperor was greatly shocked. Li Ru presented poisoned wine to the Emperor. <note>original: "The implication is that since his poem was so well-composed, this wine is the most elegant gift."</note>

<summary>Dong Zhuo forces scholar Cai Yong into his service and, upon discovering a poem of lament written by the deposed Emperor, sends Li Ru to assassinate him with poisoned wine.</summary>
<keywords>Dong Zhuo, Li Ru, Cai Yong, Emperor Shao, Consort Tang, poisoned wine, execution</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page: Li Ru advised Dong Zhuo to appoint famous scholars to win popular support. Following this, he recommended Cai Yong for his talent, and Dong Zhuo ordered that he be summoned.</meta>

Cai Yong did not comply at first. Dong Zhuo was furious and sent a messenger to tell him, "If you do not come, I will wipe out your clan." Terrified, Cai Yong had no choice but to obey the order and arrive. Dong Zhuo was overjoyed to see him and promoted him three times in a single month, eventually appointing him as a Palace Attendant <note>original: 侍中</note>, treating him with great intimacy and favor. <gloss>He always relied on the patronage of Wang Feng and Yang Xiong; he would end his life as firewood and be buried by the woodcutters of Kunshan.</gloss>

Meanwhile, the Young Emperor <note>original: 少帝</note>, Empress Dowager He, and Consort Tang were trapped in the Yong'an Palace, with clothing and food becoming increasingly scarce. The Young Emperor’s tears never dried. <gloss>As the former king once said, the sun and moon in this place feel endless.</gloss> One day, he happened to see a pair of swallows flying in the courtyard and composed a poem. <gloss>In the empty courtyard, birds dance and fly; in this cold palace and abandoned temple, I am alone, and my years are my own.</gloss>

The poem read:

The tender grass is green, congealed in mist,
The pair of swallows flutter and fly.
The Luo River is a blue stream,
Envied by those upon the road.
<gloss>The first half of the poem describes the swallows and looks into the distance.</gloss>
Deep within the azure clouds lies my former palace,
<gloss>Gazing at the old palace, unable to fly, truly not as fortunate as the pair of swallows returning to their old nest. How tragic.</gloss>
Who will wield loyalty and righteousness,
To vent the grievances in my heart?
<gloss>The second half is an expression of his personal wishes. A fine poem.</gloss>

Dong Zhuo often sent people to eavesdrop. That day, they intercepted this poem and presented it to him. Dong Zhuo said, "He is full of resentment and writes poems. I have a valid reason to kill him." <gloss>Killing him provides a famous justification, setting an example for the world.</gloss>

He then ordered Li Ru to take eighteen armed men into the palace to murder the Emperor. The Emperor and his consorts were on the upper floor when a palace maid reported that Li Ru had arrived. The Emperor was terrified. Li Ru presented the Emperor with a cup of poisoned wine. <gloss>Suggesting that such a poem deserves this wine, which is the most elegant way to end him.</gloss>

<summary>Cai Yong is forced into service by Dong Zhuo, while the imprisoned Young Emperor expresses his despair through a poem, leading Dong Zhuo to plot his execution.</summary>
<keywords>Dong Zhuo, Li Ru, Cai Yong, Young Emperor, Empress Dowager He, Consort Tang, Poisoned Wine</keywords>

66. Example (the root and a fraction both subtracted). Of a flock of geese, ten times the square-root of the number departed for the Mánasa lake, on the approach of a cloud: an eighth part went to a forest of St'halapadminis: three couples were seen engaged in sport, on the water abounding with delicate fibres of the lotus. Tell, dear girl, the whole number of the flock.

Statement: Coeff. 10. Fraction [fraction illegible in OCR]. Given 6.

By the [second] rule (§ 63); unity, less the numerator of the fraction, is [fraction illegible in OCR]; and the coefficient and given number, being both divided by that, become [fraction illegible in OCR] and [fraction illegible in OCR]; and the half coefficient is [fraction illegible in OCR]. With these, proceeding by the [first] rule (§ 62), the number of the flock is found 144.

<meta>This page continues the mathematical problems from Page 61. It presents a classic "word problem" from the Lilavati involving a flock of swans, requiring the solution of a quadratic equation where a portion of the total is expressed as a multiple of the square root of the total.</meta>

<page-num>62</page-num>
<header>Lilavati</header>

# Example—
# Another Example—

> Ten times the square root <note>original: "mūla-daśakaṃ"</note> of a flock of swans flew to Lake Manasa at the arrival of the clouds; one-eighth of the flock flew from the water's edge to a forest of land-lotuses. O girl, three pairs of swans <note>original: "hansa-yuga-trayam," meaning 3 pairs, which is 6 swans</note> were seen sporting in the water beautified by tender lotus stalks. Tell me the total number of the flock. || 3 ||

**Word Order:** O girl! At the arrival of the clouds, ten times the square root of a flock of swans went to Lake Manasa. One-eighth of them flew from the water's edge to a forest of land-lotuses. And three pairs of swans were seen playing with great joy in water adorned with tender lotus stalks. Therefore, tell me the total number of the flock. || 3 ||

**Meaning:** O my dear sixteen-year-old! There was a flock of swans. From it, as the rainy season arrived, ten times the square root of the total went to Lake Manasa, and an eighth part of the total flew from the shore to a forest of land-lotuses. If three pairs (6) of swans were seen playing with great affection in water beautified by soft lotus stalks, then say how many swans were in that group in total? || 3 ||

**Setting-out:** Root-multiplier: 10; eighth part: <gloss>1/8</gloss>; visible quantity: <gloss>6</gloss>. Since the rule states "when increased or decreased by fractions," we divide the visible quantity and the root-multiplier by the remaining fraction <gloss>7/8</gloss>. This results in:
Visible quantity: <gloss>48/7</gloss>
Root-multiplier: <gloss>80/7</gloss>
Half of the multiplier: <gloss>40/7</gloss>
The square of this: <gloss>1600/49</gloss>
Added to [the product of the visible quantity and denominator]: <gloss>1936/49</gloss>
The square root of this: <gloss>44/7</gloss>
Joined with half the multiplier <gloss>40/7</gloss> and then squared, the quantity of swans is produced: 144.

**Detailed Working:** According to the rule mentioned in the second verse above, we subtract the eighth part <gloss>1/8</gloss> from one (1).
Then <gloss>1/1 - 1/8 = 7/8</gloss>.
We divide the visible quantity 6 by this: <gloss>6/1 ÷ 7/8 = 6/1 × 8/7 = 48/7</gloss>. By applying this change, the visible quantity becomes <gloss>48/7</gloss>.
In the same way, we divide the root-multiplier 10 by the remaining 7/8: <gloss>10/1 ÷ 7/8 = 10/1 × 8/7 = 80/7</gloss>. By applying this change, the root-multiplier becomes <gloss>80/7</gloss>.
Now, treating <gloss>48/7</gloss> as the visible quantity and <gloss>80/7</gloss> as the root-multiplier, we perform the operation according to the method described in the previous verse.
That is: half of the root-multiplier is <gloss>40/7</gloss>.
We square this <gloss>40/7</gloss>, which results in <gloss>1600/49</gloss>.

<header>सूर्यसिद्धान्त:</header>

वासुदेव परं ब्रह्म है । इन्हीं की मूर्ति परम पुरुष है, ये अव्यक्त, निर्गुण, शान्त और २५ तत्वों से परे हैं तथा अव्यय हैं, अर्थात् निर्विकार हैं ॥ १२ ॥

->प्रकृत्यन्तर्गतो देवो बहिरन्तश्च सर्वगः ।<-
->सङ्कर्षणोऽपः सृष्टवादौ तासु वीर्यमवासृजत् ॥ १३ ॥<-

शुद्धस्य ब्रह्मणो जगत्कारणत्वासम्भवादाह । प्रकृत्यन्तर्गतो मायोपहितो बहिरन्तश्च सर्वगो जगदुपादानत्वात् । एतानि सर्वाणि विशेषणानि सङ्कर्षणस्य वासुदेवांशस्यापि वासुदेवात्मकाताध्यवसानेन बोध्यानि । वासुदेवांशात्मकः सङ्कर्षणः प्रथमं जलानि निर्माय । तास्वप्सु । वीर्यं शक्तिविशेषम् । अवासृजच्चिक्षेप ॥ १३ ॥

सर्वत्र अनुभव योग्य सङ्कर्षण देव ने इसी प्रकृति के अन्तर्गत प्रविष्ट होकर सर्वप्रथम जल की रचना की । अनन्तर उस जल में बीज स्वरूप अपने तेज को स्थापित किया ॥ १३ ॥

->तदण्डमभवद् हैमं सर्वत्र तमसावृतम् ।<-
->तत्रानिरुद्धः प्रथमं व्यक्तीभूतः सनातनः ॥ १४ ॥<-

ततः किमत आह । तत् तच्छक्तिमिलितं जलं हैमं सौवर्णमण्डं गोलाकारं सर्वत्र बहिरन्तश्च अन्धकारेण आवृतमभवत् । अन्धकारसहिताकाशे सुवर्णाण्डम् अजनीत्यर्थः । तत्र सुवर्णाण्ड आदौ अनिरुद्धः सनातनौ नित्यो वसुदेवांश सङ्कर्षणोऽशरूपत्वात् व्यक्तीभूतोऽभिव्यक्तः । न तु उत्पन्नः । सत्कार्यवादाभ्युपगमात् । यथा तिलेभ्यस्तैलं सदेवाभिव्यक्तं न तु उत्पन्नम् ॥ १४ ॥

वह बीज स्वरूप तेज स्वर्ण अण्ड का रूप धारण कर लिया । वह चारों तरफ से अन्धकार से घिरा हुआ था । वहाँ (अण्ड के भीतर) सर्वप्रथम सनातन भगवान् अनिरुद्ध प्रकट हुये ॥ १४ ॥

->हिरण्यगर्भो भगवानेष छन्दसि पठ्यते ।<-
->आदित्यो ह्यदिभूतत्वात् प्रसृत्या सूर्य उच्यते ॥ १५ ॥<-

अथ अस्याभिधान्तराणि लोकसुज्ञानार्थमाह । एष सङ्कर्षणांशोऽनिरुद्ध भगवान् <term>षाइगुण्यैश्वर्य्य</term> सम्पन्नश्छन्दसि वेदे हिरण्यगर्भः सुवर्णाण्डमध्यरूपगर्भे स्थितत्वात् पठ्यते निरूप्यते । वेदेऽस्य हिरण्यगर्भ इति प्रसिद्धमभिवान्तरमित्यर्थः । हि निश्चयेन आदित्यः प्रथममभिव्यक्तत्वादुच्यते । प्रसृत्या । अस्माज्जगतोऽभिव्यक्ततयामभिनिरुद्धः सूर्य उच्यते ।

->हिरण्यगर्भः समवर्त्तताग्रे भूतस्य जातः पतिरेक आसीत् ।<-

इति श्रुतिः ॥ १५ ॥

यही भगवान् हिरण्य गर्भ हैं जिनका वेदों में उल्लेख है । सर्वप्रथम

12. Vasudeva, the supreme principle of divinity (brahman) whose form is all that is (tat), the supreme Person (purusha), unmanifested, free from qualities, superior to the twenty-five principles, imperishable,

13. Contained within matter (prakrti), divine, pervading everything, without and within, the attractor — he, having in the first place created the waters, deposited in them energy.

14. That became a golden egg, on all sides enveloped in darkness: in it first became manifested the unrestrained, the everlasting one.

15. He in the scripture (chandas) is denominated the golden-wombed (hiranyagarbha), the blessed; as being the first (Adi) existence, he is called Aditya; as being generator, the sun.

reference_meta.licence: public domain (translation published 1860; 1935 reprint reproduces the 1860 text)
reference_meta.style_note: Victorian scholarly crib, close to the Sanskrit, Sanskrit technical terms glossed in parentheses
reference_meta.located: ch. 12 (Bhūgolādhyāya / cosmogony), end of v. 12 (Hindi only) and vv. 13-15 (root verses, commentary, Hindi); Hindi of v. 15 breaks off at page foot
reference_meta.coverage_note: Reference is Burgess's rendering of the root verses 12-15 only; Burgess does not translate Raṅganātha's commentary or the Hindi glosses (the Hindi lines are themselves translations of the root verses, so they map onto the reference). V. 12 appears on the page only as the closing Hindi gloss. Text taken from the 1935 Calcutta University reprint of the 1860 translation (cleaner OCR than the 1860 scan; wording identical, checked against https://archive.org/download/in.ernet.dli.2015.96668/2015.96668.Translation-Of-The-Surya-siddhanta_djvu.txt); diacritics are lost in the OCR (Vasudeva, prakrti, hiranyagarbha). Only hyphen rejoining and whitespace inside parentheses were normalised.
reference_meta.page_content: Hindi rendering of the end of v. 12; root verses 13, 14, 15 each followed by Raṅganātha's Sanskrit commentary and a Hindi translation of the verse; a Ṛgveda quotation (hiraṇyagarbhaḥ samavartatāgre) inside the v. 15 commentary. Root verses plus their Hindi renderings are roughly half the page; the reference covers that half (Raṅganātha's Sanskrit commentary, ~45% of the page, has no reference).

He explains [the verse], because the pure Brahman cannot be the cause of the world. "Dwelling within <term>prakriti</term>" means he is shrouded by <term>maya</term> <gloss>illusion</gloss>; "all-pervading inside and outside" refers to his being the material cause of the world. All these attributes should be understood as belonging to <term>Sankarshana</term>, who is an expansion of <term>Vasudeva</term>, by virtue of his oneness with <term>Vasudeva</term>. <term>Sankarshana</term>, the expansion of <term>Vasudeva</term>, first created the waters and into those waters cast his seed, a specific power. || 13 ||

->That cosmic egg became golden, surrounded everywhere by darkness.<-

->"<term>Hiranyagarbha</term> existed in the beginning; he was the sole lord of all created beings."<-

This is the scriptural text. || 15 ||

->That became a golden egg, surrounded everywhere by darkness; within it, Aniruddha, the eternal, first became manifest.<-

This follows the doctrine of existent effects <note>original: "Satkaryavada"</note>, which holds that the effect already exists within the cause. Just as oil is already present in sesame seeds and is merely expressed, he was manifested, not created.

शङ्कितामभियोक्तरि जाताशङ्कां, रक्षितां शक्तिभिः, भीतां पत्युः,

अहमत्राशक्त इति निश्चयमधिगच्छन् ॥ २७ ॥
इत्यभियोगाश्चतुश्चत्वारिंश प्रकरणम् ॥

इति श्रीवात्स्यायनीयेकामसूत्रटीकायां यशोधररचितायां जयमङ्गलाऽऽख्यायां पारदारिके

तो भवति ॥ १ ॥

मन्त्रमवृणानां दूतयैनां साधयेत् ॥ २ ॥

मन्त्रमवृणानामिति । सांप्रयोगिकं भावमप्रकाशयन्तीं, दूतया साध-
येद् प्रगल्भत्वात् ॥ २ ॥

अप्रतिगृहाभियोगं पुनरपि संसृज्यमानां द्विधाभूतमानसां वि-

A wise man having a regard for his reputation should not think of seducing a woman who is apprehensive, timid, not to be trusted, well guarded, or possessed of a father-in-law, or mother-in-law.

CHAPTER III.

EXAMINATION OF THE STATE OF A WOMAN'S MIND.

When a man is trying to gain over a woman he should examine the state of her mind, and acts as follows.

If she listens to him, but does not manifest to him in any way her own intentions, he should then try to gain her over by means of a go-between.

If she meets him once, and again comes to meet him better dressed than before, or comes to him in some lonely place, he should be certain that she is capable of being enjoyed by the use of a little force. A woman who lets a man make up to her, but does not give herself up, even after a long time, should be considered as a trifler in love, but owing to the fickleness of the human mind, even such a woman can be conquered by always keeping up a close acquaintance with her.

reference_meta.translator: Richard F. Burton & F. F. Arbuthnot
reference_meta.style_note: Victorian paraphrase that merges and reorders sūtras; sense is close but not a sūtra-by-sūtra crib
reference_meta.located: Book V (Pāradārika), ch. 2 closing verse 27 and colophon; ch. 3 (Bhāvaparīkṣā) sūtras 1-3 and the opening of sūtra 4
reference_meta.coverage_note: Reference covers the root text only; the Jayamaṅgalā commentary and the two colophons have no reference. Burton renders freely: verse 27 is folded into the prose paragraph ending ch. II; sūtra 1 = 'When a man is trying ... acts as follows'; sūtra 2 = 'If she listens to him ... go-between'; sūtra 3 (rejects the approach yet meets him again: of two minds, win her gradually) has no clean separate rendering; 'If she meets him once ... better dressed' corresponds to sūtra 4, which the page only begins. The final sentence ('A woman who lets a man make up to her ...') is either Burton's loose rendering of sūtra 3 or the following sūtra; it is kept as the boundary.
reference_meta.page_content: Root text: closing śloka 27 of V.2, the chapter colophon, and V.3 sūtras 1-3 plus the first words of sūtra 4; each followed by Jayamaṅgalā commentary (commentary and colophons are roughly 55-60% of the page; the reference covers the root text, about 40%).

A wise man should not pursue a woman who is suspicious, guarded, afraid, or living under the supervision of her mother-in-law, knowing the risk to himself. 27

This is the second chapter, concerning the causes of acquaintance and the methods of approach, in the fifth section on the wives of others, from the Kamasutra of the venerable Vatsyayana.

"Suspicious": One who has developed doubts about the one approaching her. "Guarded": One protected by various means. "Afraid": One who fears her husband. "Living under a mother-in-law": One under the authority of her mother-in-law. "Should not pursue" means he should not desire her, "knowing the risk to himself," meaning he arrives at the certainty that he is powerless here. 27

This concludes the forty-fourth chapter on approaches.

This concludes the second chapter, concerning the causes of acquaintance and the methods of approach, in the fifth section on the wives of others, from the Jayamangala commentary on the Kamasutra by Yashodhara.

***

Third Chapter

Even when an approach is possible, if the women are courageous, bold, and require examination, they should not be approached if their inner state has not been revealed, and thus there is no special approach to them. Now, the examination of feelings is described:

"When approaching a woman, one should examine her behavior; through that, the feeling is examined." 1

"As if approaching a maiden": One should examine her "behavior," meaning her gestures. Through this, if she is not observed, the feeling is examined. 1

He speaks on how she is to be won over:

"One should win her over through a messenger if she does not reveal her inner state." 2

"Does not reveal": If she does not disclose her amorous feelings, one should win her over through a messenger because of her boldness. 2

"One should recognize a woman who rejects an approach but interacts again, and whose mind is divided; one should win her over gradually." 3

"Rejects an approach": Refusing the approach made by the hero. "Interacts again": Returning to contact with the hero after staying away for some days. "Whose mind is divided": One should recognize this because she must be examined, as she thinks, "What should I do? I do not know." One should win her over gradually, not abandon her suddenly. 3

He speaks of a special case here:

"If she is seen again decorated more than before, after rejecting the approach, one should approach her in the same way, and if she is in a secluded place, one should know she is to be taken by force." 4

## Chapter 3

### The Examination of Feelings <term>Bhavapariksha</term>

Even when seduction is attempted, women who are steady and bold must be tested. Because their true intentions are not easily revealed, one cannot use specialized methods of seduction without first understanding their heart. Therefore, the examination of feelings is now discussed:

A man who is making an approach should observe the behavior of the woman; through her actions, her feelings are tested. <note>verse 1</note>

<margin>Just as one approaches a young maiden, he should observe her tendencies and gestures. By examining these, her internal state is revealed.</margin>

How is she to be won? The author says:

If she does not reveal her secret thoughts, he should win her over through a female messenger. <note>verse 2</note>

<margin>Not revealing her secret means she does not openly show her desire for union. Because she is bold and mature, he should use a messenger to reach her.</margin>

If she rejects the initial approach but continues to associate with him, he should understand that her mind is divided into two. He should win her over gradually. <note>verse 3</note>

<margin>After rejecting the advances made by the hero and staying away for some days, if she then seeks out his company again, he should know she is of two minds. She may be thinking, "I do not know what I should do." He should win her over step by step and not abandon her suddenly.</margin>

The author states a specific detail here:

If she rejects the advance but is seen again even more exquisitely adorned, and in that same state she approaches him...

<summary>This page concludes the chapter on techniques of seduction and begins the chapter on testing a woman's true feelings. It emphasizes observing a woman's behavioral cues and using messengers when she is hesitant or of two minds.</summary>

Regarding this, he mentions a specific detail—
If she is seen again wearing special ornaments after having rejected an approach, one should approach her in that same manner and ...

"Now, Deed!" said the other, "I am constrained to give the enterprising a reward in proportion to their enterprise. The final consequence is your affair. Take it from him yourself." On hearing this, Soft awoke and looked for his bag of gold.

When he found it empty, he thought: "Oh, dear! It was so much trouble to earn the money, and it went in a flash. I have had my work for nothing. I haven't a thing. How can I look my wife in the face, or my friends?" So he made up his mind to return to Growing City. There he earned five hundred gold-pieces in just one single year, and started home again by a different road.

When the sun went down, he came upon the very same banyan tree, and he thought: "Oh, oh, oh! What is fate up to — damn the brute! Here is that same fiendish old banyan tree once more." But he dozed off on a branch, and saw the same two figures.

One of them was saying: "Doer, why did you give this fellow Soft five hundred gold-pieces? Don't you know that he doesn't get a thing beyond food and clothes?"

"Friend Deed," said the other, "I am constrained to give to the enterprising. The final consequence is your affair. So why blame me?"

When poor Soft heard this, he looked for his bag and found it empty. This plunged him into the depths of gloom, and he thought: "Oh, dear! What good is life to me if I lose my money? I will just hang myself from this banyan tree and say goodbye to life."

Having made up his mind, he wove a rope of spear-grass, adjusted it as a noose to his neck, climbed out a branch, fastened it, and was about to let himself drop, when one of the figures appeared in the sky and said: "Do not be so rash, Friend Soft. I am the person who takes your money, who does not allow you one cowrie beyond food and clothes. Now go home. But, that you may not have seen me without result, ask your heart's desire."

विग्रहस्तावत् समुपस्थितश्चेत्कथं देव प्रागेव विग्रहं न विधत्ते ॥ यतः ॥ स किं भृत्यः स किं मन्त्री यद्यादावेव भूपतिं । युद्धयोगं स्वभृत्यागं निर्दिशत्यविचारितं ॥ अपरञ्च ॥ विजेतुं प्रयते चारीन्न युद्धेन कदाचन । अतित्याविजयोग्यादृश्यते युध्यमानयोः ॥ अन्यच्च ॥ साम्ना दानेन भेदेन सामस्तैरथवा पृथक् । साधितुं प्रयते चारीन्न युद्धेन कदाचन ॥ अपरञ्च ॥ सर्वएव जनः शूरोह्यनासादितविग्रहः । अदृष्टपरसामर्थ्यः सदर्पः कोभवेन्न हि ॥ किञ्च ॥ न तथोत्याप्यते यावा प्राणिभिर्दारुणं यथा । अल्पोपायान्नह्यासिद्धिरेतन्नवफलं महत् । किन्तु विग्रहमुपस्थितं विलोक्य अवज्ञीयतां ॥ यतः ॥

संग्राम उपस्थित चक्रवाक বলিতেছে হে মহারাজ পুথ মেতে যুদ্ধ কর্তব্য নয় যেহেতু সে কি দাস আর সে কি মন্ত্রী যে অগ্রেতেই নৃপতিকে বিচার না করিয়া রণের উদ্যম করিতে এবং স্বকীয় স্থান ত্যাগ করিতে পরামর্শ দেয়। অপর বিপক্ষকে জয় করিবার নিমিত্তে সামাদিদ্বারা যত্ন করিবে সংগ্রামদ্বারা কদাচ করিবে না যেহেতু যুধ্যমান দুই জনের মধ্যে কাহার জয় ইহা নিশ্চয় জানা যায় না অপর সাম দান ভেদ ইহার পুত্যকে কিম্বা সমস্ত তে বিপক্ষকে সমাধান করিতে যত্ন করিবে কদাচ যুদ্ধেতে করিবে না। অপর অকৃত যুদ্ধ সকল লোকই বীর কেননা।

As your Highness commands, said the porter: after which he withdrew, taking the Parrot with him. So, said the King, war is now settled. Yet, please your Majesty, said the Chakraváka, war must not be entered upon in a hurry.

41—Is he a prudent minister, or counsellor, who at the very beginning, without due consideration, recommends to his sovereign, preparation for war, or abdication of his country?

Moreover:—

42—He should strive to overcome his enemies, but never by war: because between two combatants, victory is seen to be doubtful.

Moreover:—

43—By gentle means, by gifts, by sowing divisions; by all combined or separately, he should strive to subdue his enemies: but never by battle.

For:—

44—Every man who has never engaged in battle is indeed a hero: and who that has not yet witnessed the strength of the enemy will not be arrogant?

Moreover:—

45—A large stone is not raised with such facility by animal strength as by machinery of timber. Small means, and grand results: such is the great benefit of counsel.

But, seeing war is imminent, let it be prosecuted vigorously. For:—

46—As husbandry will be fruitful from labour bestowed at the proper season; so this political measure, O King! produces fruit after a long time, although not immediately.

If war is imminent, O King, why not prepare for battle beforehand? Because: "He is neither a servant nor a minister who, at the very beginning, advises a King to rush into battle or abandon his own station without due consideration." Moreover: "One should never try to conquer enemies by war. It is not certain which of the two warring sides will be victorious." Furthermore: "One should try to overcome the enemy through <term>sama</term> <gloss>conciliation/peaceful means</gloss>, <term>dana</term> <gloss>gifts/bribery</gloss>, and <term>bheda</term> <gloss>dissension/creating discord</gloss>, either individually or all together; never by war." Moreover: "All people are heroes as long as they have not encountered a fight, have not seen the enemy's strength, and are full of pride." Furthermore: "War is not as easily provoked by living beings as it is terrible; the success of small means is not a small result. However, seeing that war is imminent, it should be treated with disdain." Because:

War is present. The <term>Chakravaka</term> says, "O King, war is not to be done first, because he is no servant and he is no minister who, at the beginning, advises the King to rush into war or to leave his own place without consideration. Furthermore, one should try to conquer the enemy by <term>sama</term> etc. [Conciliation, gifts, and discord], and never by war, because it is not certain who will win between two who are fighting. Furthermore, one should try to resolve the enemy by conciliation, gifts, or discord, separately or altogether, but never by war."

If war has indeed arrived, O King, why did you not prepare for it earlier? For, who is that servant or minister who, without careful consideration, advises a king to prepare for battle and abandon his own post at the very start? Furthermore, one should always endeavor to conquer enemies through means other than war, as the outcome of a struggle between two combatants is never certain. Moreover, one should attempt to subdue the enemy by using diplomacy, bribery, sowing dissension, or all three combined, but never by war alone. Additionally, everyone considers themselves brave when they have not yet encountered the conflict, for who would not be proud when they have not yet seen the power of the enemy? Furthermore, one does not stir up such terrible strife among creatures, as success is rarely achieved through minor means and the fruits of war are never great. Therefore, seeing that war has arrived, let it be disregarded. For:

The <term>Chakravaka</term> <gloss>the ruddy sheldrake, acting as a counselor in this fable</gloss> says, "O King, war is not to be pursued. For what kind of servant or minister is it who advises a king to prepare for battle and abandon his own station without first deliberating? Furthermore, one should endeavor to conquer an opponent by means of conciliation and other strategies, but never by armed conflict, since it is impossible to know for certain which of the two combatants will emerge victorious. Moreover, one should attempt to resolve matters with an enemy by using conciliation, bribery, or sowing dissension, either individually or together, but never by fighting. Besides, every person is a hero as long as they have not yet faced a battle, for who would not be arrogant without having seen the strength of another?"

Since the time for war <note>original: <term>vigraha</term></note> has arrived, why does the King not prepare for battle beforehand? For it is said: What kind of servant or what kind of minister is he who, without any consideration, directs the King toward military engagement and the abandonment of his own position at the very beginning?

Furthermore: One should strive to conquer enemies by any means other than war. Victory is seen to be uncertain when two sides are fighting.

And another thing: One should strive to overcome the enemy through conciliation <note>original: <term>sama</term></note>, gifts <note>original: <term>dana</term></note>, or sowing dissension <note>original: <term>bheda</term></note>, used either separately or all together; but never through war.

Moreover: Every person is a hero as long as they have not encountered a real conflict. Who is not prideful before they have witnessed the strength of the opponent?

Additionally: A great result is not achieved by creatures through harsh means as effectively as it is through mild efforts. Achievement comes from small means. However, seeing that war is at hand, let it be regarded with caution <note>original: <term>avajñīyatām</term> suggests looking down upon or treating it with strategic disregard</note>. For it is said:

When the battle is imminent, the Chakravaka <gloss>ruddy sheldrake or Brahminy duck, serving here as a wise minister</gloss> says: O Great King, war is not the first duty. Furthermore, one should try to defeat the enemy through conciliation and other peaceful means; never by battle. This is because between two combatants, it is not known for certain who will be the victor. Furthermore, one should strive to resolve the enemy through conciliation, gifts, or dissension, either individually or collectively; never through war. <header>सूत्रस्थान-अ० १९. (१४३)</header>

भांति मल निकालकर बिठादे कफ और वायुके व्रणोंके मलको चतुर वैद्य कईवार सूंत सूंत कर निकाले ॥ ३९ ॥ व्रणको नीचेसे दबाकर रोमगतिके अनुसार स्रावित करे (रिसावे) और सब गूढ बंधों (जोडों) को तथा संधियोंको अच्छे प्रकारसे मिलादे ॥ ४० ॥ होठके जोडनेमें यथायोग्य जैसे पहले कह आये हैं वैसे करे तथा जोडोंका जाननेवाला वैद्य हड्डीके जोडनेमें भी अपनी बुद्धिसि विचार कर यथोक्त बंध लगावे ॥ ४१ ॥

उत्तिष्ठनो निपण्णस्य शयनं चापि गच्छतः ॥ गच्छतो विविधाद्यैनैर्नस्य दुष्यति सै व्रणः ॥४२॥ संध्यस्थिकोष्ठप्राप्ताश्च शिरा-स्नायुगतास्तथौ ॥ तथैवगाढगंभीराः सर्वतो विषमस्थिताः ॥ नैते साधयितुं शक्या ऋते वन्धैर्भवंति हि ॥ ४३ ॥

इति सुश्रुतसंहितायां सूत्रस्थानेऽष्टादशोऽध्यायः ॥ १८ ॥

उठते हुए बैठते हुए शयनको प्राप्त होते हुए चलते हुए सवारी करते हुए मनुष्योंका व्रण (यथोक्त बन्ध लगे पीछे) पीडा नहीं देता ॥ ४२ ॥ संधि और हड्डी तथा कोष्ठमें प्राप्त हुए व्रण, शिरा और स्नायुके व्रण, गाढे और गंभीर व्रण तथा जो सब ओरसे विषम हो गये हों ऐसे व्रण यथोक्त बन्धके बिना साधन नहीं किये जासकते ॥ ४३ ॥

इति पण्डितमुरलीधरशर्मभि० सुश्रुतस० भा० टी० सूत्रस्थानेऽष्टादशोऽध्यायः ॥ १८ ॥

### एकोनविंशोऽध्यायः १९.

अथातो व्रणितोपासनीयमध्यायं व्याख्यास्यामः ।

अत्र यहांसे व्रणितोपासनीय (व्रणोंके बरतावकी विधिनामक) अध्यायका व्याख्यान करते हैं ।

व्रणिनः प्रथममेवागारमन्विच्छेत्तच्चागारं प्रशस्तवास्वादिकं कार्यम् ॥ १ ॥ प्रशस्तवास्तुनि गृहे शुचौवातपवर्जिते ॥ निवाते ने च रोगाः स्युः शारीरागन्तुमानसाः ॥ १ ॥ तस्मिञ्छयनमसंबाधं स्वास्तीर्णं मनोज्ञं प्राक्छिरस्कं सशस्त्रं कुर्वीत ॥ ३ ॥ सुखचेष्टाप्रचारः स्यात्स्वास्तीर्णे शयने व्रणी ॥ प्राच्यां दिशि स्थितां देवास्तत्पूर्वाधं नैतं शिरः ॥ ४ ॥

(सूत्र ४२) वधयुक्त व्रण ।

All secreting measures in connection with an ulcer should be continued or stopped according to its condition, whereby the nature and shape of the bandage should be determined as well. An ulcer, due either to the deranged condition of blood or the Pittam, should be dressed and bandaged once a day which may be extended to a number of times in the case of an ulcer brought about by the deranged Kapham and Vayu. The pus or the local morbid matter should be secreted by pressing the base or the bottom of an ulcer and by gently moving the hand along it in a contrary direction (down, upward; and all bandages around joints and Gudasandhis) should be duly tied up.

The rules laid down under the head of adhesioning the parts of a bifurcated ear-lobe would hold good in a case of severed lips as well. The measures amply discussed in the present Chapter should be extended by means of inference, analogy and judgment to apply mutatis mutandis to the bandaging of a fractured or dislocated bone.

An ulcer, properly bandaged, has a greater chance of not being affected by lying down, sitting up, or any other movement of the patient, nor by the joltings of a conveyance he may ride or be carried in. An ulcer affecting a vein or a ligament or the skin (superficial) or the flesh or the bones cannot be healed without bandaging it. An ulcer situated in any of the internal chambers (cavities) of the body, or occurring at any junction of the limbs or organs, etc. or having its seat in a bone and whether of a deep, superficial, malignant, or corrosive character, cannot be brought to a successful termination without the help of a bandage.

Thus ends the eighteenth Chapter of the Sutrasthanam in the Sushruta Samhita which treats of the dressing and bandaging of ulcers.

CHAPTER XIX.

Now we shall discuss the Chapter which treats of the management or nursing of a patient with an ulcer etc. (Vranito-pasaniya-madhyayam).

First of all a suitable chamber should be sought and selected for a patient, suffering from an ulcer. It should be roomy and spacious and situated in a commendable site.

Metrical Text :— Diseases, which are physical, mental or traumatic in their origin, can never attack a person who dwells in a clean and spacious chamber, protected from excessive heat, and strong gusts of wind.

The bed should be spread clean, ample and comfortable, with the head of the beadstead turned towards the east, and provided with some kind of a weapon.

Metrical Texts :— In a spacious and well-spread bed, an ulcer-patient can toss about and move his limbs with the greatest comfort. The reason for the head being turned towards the east is that the patient may easily make obeisance to the (demons and) celestial spirits, who inhabit that quarter of the sky. Thus the patient shall lie in comfortable posture, attended upon by his sweet-talking friends and relations.
