(143)

When the patient is standing, sitting, lying down, or moving about, the wound <note>if bandaged according to the prescribed method</note> will not be afflicted by pain. (42) Wounds involving joints, bones, <term>koṣṭha</term> <gloss>viscera/internal cavities</gloss>, veins, and ligaments, as well as those that are deep-seated or severely irregular, cannot be healed without the application of proper bandages. (43)

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter of the Sūtrasthāna in the Suśruta Saṃhitā. (18)

### Chapter Nineteen

We shall now explain the chapter titled <term>Vraṇitopāsanīyam</term> <gloss>Treatment and Conduct for the Wounded</gloss>.

Here, we begin the exposition of the chapter regarding the conduct for those suffering from wounds.

The physician should first seek out a dwelling for the wounded person, and such a dwelling should be well-constructed and suitable. (1) In a house with a favorable orientation, which is clean, free from exposure to the sun, and protected from drafts, the patient will not be afflicted by physical, external, or mental diseases. (2) In that place, one should prepare a bed that is spacious, well-appointed, pleasant, oriented with the head to the east, and furnished with a protective weapon. (3) On a comfortable bed, the patient can move freely; since the gods reside in the east, the head should be directed toward that quarter for the sake of honoring them. (4)

<note>(Verse 42) This describes the stability provided by correct bandaging during physical activity.</note>

<header>Sūtrasthāna-Ch. 19 (143)</header>

Remove the waste matter thoroughly and then have the patient sit. An adept physician should repeatedly extract the waste matter from the wounds caused by <term>kapha</term> <gloss>phlegm humor</gloss> and <term>vāyu</term> <gloss>wind humor</gloss>. 39. Press the wound from below and cause it to discharge in the direction of the hair growth, and align all deep connections <note>joints or deep tissue layers</note> and junctions properly. 40. In suturing the lips, proceed as previously described; the physician who understands joints should also apply the specified bandages for bone fractures, employing their own intelligence. 41.

Uttiṣṭhano nipaṇṇasya śayanaṃ cāpi gacchataḥ || Gacchato vividhādyairnaiḥ nasya duṣyati sai vraṇaḥ || 42 || Sandhyasthikoṣṭhaprāptāśca śirā-snāyugatāstathau || Tathaivagāḍhagaṃbhīrāḥ sarvato viṣamasthitāḥ || Naite sādhayituṃ śakyā ṛte vandhairbhavanti hi || 43 ||

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter of the Sūtrasthāna in the Suśruta Saṃhitā. 18.

For a person who is rising, sitting, reclining, walking, or riding, the wound (once the proper bandage is applied) does not suffer pain. 42. Wounds located in the joints, bones, or viscera; wounds of the veins and tendons; dense and deep-seated wounds; and those that have become irregular on all sides cannot be treated effectively without the application of appropriate bandages. 43.

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter of the Suśruta Saṃhitā with the Hindi commentary by Pandit Muralidhara Sharma. 18.

### Nineteenth Chapter 19.

Now we shall explain the chapter regarding the care of the wounded <term>Vraṇitopāsanīyam</term> <gloss>rules for the care of the wounded</gloss>.

Here begins the explanation of the <term>Vraṇitopāsanīyam</term> <gloss>chapter on the regimen for the wounded</gloss>.

First, seek a suitable dwelling for the wounded patient; that dwelling should be constructed in an auspicious location. 1. In a house with a favorable site, clean, free from wind and sun, and protected from drafts, there will be no physical, traumatic, or mental diseases. 2. In that place, provide a bed that is uncrowded, well-spread, pleasant, with the head facing east, and accompanied by weapons <note>often for protection or religious warding</note>. 3. The wounded patient will have ease of movement and comfort on a well-spread bed. The gods dwell in the eastern direction, therefore the head should not be placed toward the east. 4.

<note>(Verse 42) connected with the bandage.</note>

<header>Sūtrasthāna-Ch. 19. (143)</header>

The expert physician should repeatedly extract the impurities from the wounds of <term>kapha</term> <gloss>phlegm humor</gloss> and <term>vāyu</term> <gloss>wind/air humor</gloss> in various ways. 39. Pressing the wound from below, he should allow it to drain according to the direction of the pores, and he should properly join all the hidden closures and joints. 40. In joining the lips, he should proceed as previously described; and the physician who understands joints should apply the appropriate bandages for setting bones, after reflecting upon it with his own intelligence. 41.

Uttiṣṭhano nipaṇṇasya śayanaṃ cāpi gacchataḥ ||
Gacchato vividhādyairnaiḥ nasya duṣyati sai vraṇaḥ || 42 ||
Sandhyasthikoṣṭhaprāptāśca śirā-snāyugatāstathau ||
Tathaivagāḍhagaṃbhīrāḥ sarvato viṣamasthitāḥ ||
Naite sādhayituṃ śakyā ṛte vandhairbhavanti hi || 43 ||

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter of the Sūtrasthāna in the Suśruta Saṃhitā. 18.

For a person who is rising, sitting, going to bed, walking, or riding, the wound does not suffer <note>i.e., become aggravated or painful</note> (once the proper bandage is applied). 42. Wounds located in the joints, bones, or viscera; wounds involving the veins and tendons; and wounds that are dense, deep, or uneven on all sides cannot be treated without the proper bandages. 43.

Thus ends the Hindi translation of the eighteenth chapter of the Sūtrasthāna of the Suśruta Saṃhitā, by Pandit Muralidhar Sharma. 18.

### The Nineteenth Chapter 19.

Now we shall explain the chapter on the care of the wounded <term>Vraṇitopāsanīya</term>.

Here we commence the explanation of the chapter on the conduct regarding wounds.

The physician should first look for a dwelling for the wounded person, and that dwelling should be constructed in a place with a favorable environment. 1. In a house with a favorable environment, which is clean and free from wind and sunlight, and sheltered from drafts, there will be no physical, accidental, or mental diseases. 2. He should prepare a spacious, well-spread, and pleasant bed with the head toward the east, provided with weapons <note>traditionally for protection against malevolent spirits</note>. 3. The wounded person will have ease of movement on a well-spread bed. The gods dwell in the eastern direction, therefore one should not have the head oriented toward that direction. 4.

In this manner, having removed the waste material, the expert physician should seat the patient. For wounds caused by <term>kapha</term> <gloss>phlegm or water humor</gloss> and <term>vayu</term> <gloss>wind humor</gloss>, the waste should be squeezed and removed several times. <note>verse 39</note> Pressing the wound from the bottom, the physician should drain the discharge according to the direction of hair growth. All hidden joints and connections must be properly aligned. <note>verse 40</note> In joining the lips, one should follow the methods previously described. A physician knowledgeable in joints should also use their intellect to apply the appropriate bandages for broken bones as prescribed. <note>verse 41</note>

Whether rising, sitting, going to bed, walking, or traveling by various vehicles, the wound of such a person <note>who is properly bandaged</note> does not suffer harm. <note>verse 42</note> Wounds located in the joints, bones, or internal cavities, as well as those in the veins and tendons, deep-seated wounds, and those that are uneven in all directions, cannot be successfully treated without the proper application of bandages. <note>verse 43</note>

Here begins the explanation of the chapter named <term>Vranitopasaniya</term> <gloss>the method of behavior and care for the wounded</gloss>.

First, one should seek a room for the wounded patient. That room should be constructed according to the principles of excellent <term>Vastu</term> <gloss>architectural science</gloss>. <note>verse 1</note> In a house built on favorable ground, which is clean and protected from direct sunlight and strong winds, physical, external, and mental diseases will not occur. <note>verse 2</note> In that room, a bed should be prepared that is spacious, well-covered, pleasant, oriented with the head to the east, and kept with protective weapons nearby. <note>verse 3</note> On a well-spread bed, the wounded patient can move comfortably. The gods reside in the eastern direction, therefore the head is placed toward the east out of respect. <note>verse 4</note>

<note>Glossary note for verse 42: Bandaged.</note>

The wound should be pressed from below, following the direction of the hair growth to drain the fluids, and all deep bindings and joints should be properly aligned. 40.

In the case of joining the lips, one should proceed as previously described. A physician who understands the joints should also use their intellect to apply the appropriate bandages to bone fractures as prescribed. 41.

Whether standing up, sitting down, going to bed, walking, or traveling by various vehicles, a person's wound does not suffer pain if it is properly bandaged. 42.

Wounds located in the joints, bones, or internal cavities, as well as those in the veins and tendons, and those that are deep-seated, severe, or irregularly shaped in every direction, cannot be successfully treated without the use of bandages. 43.

Now we shall explain the chapter titled <term>Vranitopasaniya</term> <gloss>The Nursing and Management of a Wounded Patient</gloss>.

At the beginning, one should seek a room for the wounded person. That room should be constructed on commendable ground. 1.

In a house built on auspicious ground, which is clean and protected from direct sunlight and strong winds, diseases of the body, external injuries, and the mind do not occur. 2.

In that room, one should provide a bed that is spacious, well-covered with soft linens, pleasing to the mind, positioned with the head toward the east, and equipped with defensive weapons nearby. 3.

A wounded person is able to move comfortably on a well-spread bed. The gods reside in the eastern direction; therefore, the head should be placed toward the east out of respect for them. 4.

माषाङ्कुरितान् शुद्धान् मिष्टान् सजडाफलान् ।
घृताढ्य माहिषरसे दधिदाडिमसाधिते ॥
प्रक्षिप्यमावया युक्तो धान्यजीरकनागरैः ।
पीतो भुक्तश्च सरसः कुरुते शुक्रमाक्षयम् ॥ ८ ॥
> इति वृष्यो माहिषरसः ।

आर्द्राणि मत्स्यमांसानि भृष्टाश्च शफरीश्च वा ।
तप्ते सर्पिषि यः खादेत् स गच्छेत् स्त्रीषु न क्षयम् ॥ ९ ॥
> इति वृष्या घृततर्जितमत्स्याः ।

घृतभृष्टान् रसे च्छागे रोहितान् फलसाधिते ।
अनुपीतरसान् सिद्धानपथ्यार्थी प्रयोजयेत् ॥ १० ॥
> इति गर्भाधानकरो योगः ।

कुट्टकं मत्स्यमांसानां हिङ्गुसैन्धवधान्यकैः ।
युक्तं गोधूमचूर्णेन घृते पूपलिकाः पचेत् ॥
माहिषे च रसे मत्स्यान् स्निग्धाऽम्ललवणान् पचेत् ।
रसे चानुगते मत्स्यान् पोथयेत् तत्र चावपेत् ॥
मरिचं जीरकं धान्यमल्पं हिङ्गु नवं घृतम् ।
माषपूपलिकानां तद्भार्थमुपकल्पयेत् ॥
एतौ पूपलिकायोगौ वृष्यौ बलवर्द्धनौ ।
हर्षसौभाग्यदौ पुष्टौ परं शुक्राभिवर्द्धनौ ॥ ११ ॥

The physician should, after the same manner, cause to be prepared boluses and juices of other kinds of clean meat.

The administration of these promotes the supply of semen in one's body. 13

APHRODISIAC MEAT-JUICE OF BUFFELO.

Take a quantity of the seeds of Masha (Phaseolus radiatus).

Drench them in water till sprouts come forth.

These should be carefully separated from other articles that may have been mixed with them;

The seeds, thus separated, should be husked.

With them should be mixed a quantity of the seeds (of the same measure) of Mucuna pruriens.

They should then be thrown into meat-juice made of buffalo-flesh, that has been enriched with ghee and dressed with curds and the juice of pomegranates.

Into it should then be thrown coriander seeds, cumin seeds, and dry ginger, each of proper measure;

By eating and drinking this preparation, one obtains an abundant supply of semen. 14-15

APHRODISIAC FISH AND FLESH.

He who eats fresh fish and flesh, as also Saphari, fried in ghee, obtains an inexhaustible supply of semen. 16

CONCEPTION-INDUCING PREPARATION.

One desirous of progeny should eat 'Rohita' fish fried in ghee and boiled in such meat-juice of goat's flesh as has been dressed with the juice of fruits, and then drink the remnant (that is left in the pot) of the meat-juice itself.

TWO PREPARATIONS OF CAKE HAVING APHRODISIAC VIRTUES.

Take some fish and fowl, and cut them into pieces.

Pound these pieces with assafoedita, 'Saindhava' salt, and corriander seeds.

Add wheat flour.

Make cakes of the product, with the aid of ghee. 18

Take some fish, and cut them into pieces.

Mix with them ghee, the expressed juice of pomegranates and other fruits of the same kind, and salt.

Boil the pieces, thus mixed, in the meat-juice of buffalo flesh.

When the meat-juice enters the fish, the fish should then be pounded. (The bones should all be extracted.)

To the pounded fish should then be added pepper, cumin seeds, corriander seeds, a little assafoedita, and new ghee.

The paste that results should be used as core or kernel of cakes made of the seeds of Phaseolus radiatus. 19-20

These two preparations of cakes possess nutritive virtues. They increase one's strength. They promote cheerfulness and bring good-luck.

Capable of increasing the semen, these prove beneficial in the matter of the birth of progeny. 21

MASHA CAKES OF APHRODISIAC VIRTUES.

Take some seeds of Masha (Phaseolus radiatus), Atmagupta (Mucuna pruriens), wheat-flour, 'Sali' rice, and 'Shastika' rice, and reduce them into a paste.

reference_meta.title: Caraka Saṃhitā, Cikitsāsthāna ch. 2 (Vājīkaraṇa), Sanskrit text
reference_meta.style_note: Victorian-Indian scholarly prose, close in content but recast into step-by-step recipe sentences with added headings and glosses
reference_meta.located: Cikitsāsthāna 2, the quarter on aphrodisiac meat/fish preparations: edition vv. 8-11 (buffalo meat-juice with sprouted māṣa, fried fish, rohita in goat broth, two pūpalikā cake preparations) plus the first line of the next verse (māṣa/ātmaguptā cakes); Kaviratna numbers these 14-21
reference_meta.coverage_note: Reference adds one preceding verse (Kaviratna 13, end of the pork-bolus recipe) as context and ends with the first sentence of the māṣa-cake recipe, which is the last line on the page. Kaviratna restructures each verse into step-by-step imperative sentences and supplies the recipe headings himself (they correspond to the edition's 'iti ...' colophons); his v. 11 has 'fish and fowl' where the Sanskrit has matsya-māṃsa. Page header '1090/1091 CHARAKA-SAMHITA', translator's footnotes and footnote markers dropped; the missing verse number 17 (lost to an OCR'd footnote mark) is omitted rather than supplied; OCR glyph errors corrected to the print (prurietis -> pruriens, drinkfng -> drinking, (^aphari -> Saphari, COPTCEPTION -> CONCEPTION, eorriander -> corriander, £ali -> Sali, stray punctuation). The edition's v. 9 'ārdrāṇi matsyamāṃsāni bhṛṣṭāś ca śapharīś' = Kaviratna 16.
reference_meta.page_content: Printed p. 524. Sanskrit root verses only, with short prose colophons naming each recipe (iti vṛṣyo māhiṣarasaḥ, etc.); no commentary. Reference covers 100% of the page.
